stem:
A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 33 weeks and 2 days gestation attends day assessment with a two-day history of new frontal headache and intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort that has worsened over the last 24 hours. She denies visual disturbance, scotomata, abdominal pain in other regions, vaginal bleeding or reduced fetal movements. Her booking blood pressure at 12 weeks was 108/64 mmHg and all booking bloods (including renal, hepatic and platelet counts) were normal.

Her dating ultrasound was reassuring and there is no personal or family history of hypertensive disease. On three repeated measurements 15 minutes apart today her blood pressure is 152/98 mmHg, 154/96 mmHg and 150/99 mmHg in the seated position with an appropriately sized cuff. A spot urinary protein/creatinine ratio is 18 mg/mmol, below the SOMANZ significant proteinuria threshold of 30 mg/mmol, and she has only trace blood on dipstick.

The midwife notes hyperreflexia without clonus and asks the obstetric registrar whether the patient meets the diagnostic criteria for pre-eclampsia in the absence of significant proteinuria, given the bedside biochemistry shown below.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/98 mmHg (confirmed on three readings), HR 84 bpm, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Hyperreflexia bilaterally without clonus. Mild RUQ tenderness. Uterus soft, fundus appropriate for dates.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 92 x10^9/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, ALT 78 U/L (ULN 35), AST 65 U/L (ULN 35), urate 0.38 mmol/L, urine PCR 18 mg/mmol. CTG normal.

lead_in: Which feature in this presentation independently satisfies the SOMANZ diagnostic criteria for pre-eclampsia in the absence of significant proteinuria?

options.text: Serum urate above the trimester-specific reference range value in isolation alone here
options.rationale: Hyperuricaemia is associated with pre-eclampsia and useful for prognosis but is NOT part of SOMANZ diagnostic criteria. The anti-pattern is conflating risk markers with diagnostic criteria. Hyperuricaemia is correct as a supportive prognostic feature in established PET, not for diagnosis (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Hyperreflexia on clinical examination without any ankle clonus present on today's review
options.rationale: Hyperreflexia is a clinical sign that raises suspicion of CNS involvement but is not a SOMANZ diagnostic criterion; the neurological criteria are eclampsia, persistent severe headache, visual scotomata, or stroke. Hyperreflexia would be correct as a magnesium-toxicity monitor, not as a PET diagnostic criterion (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Platelet count 92 x10^9/L with transaminases above twice the upper limit of normal
options.rationale: SOMANZ defines pre-eclampsia as new hypertension after 20 weeks with at least one maternal end-organ feature or uteroplacental dysfunction. Thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L and transaminases more than twice the ULN are each independently diagnostic criteria (SOMANZ 2014; RANZCOG 2023). SOMANZ thrombocytopenia threshold is <100 x10^9/L; transaminase threshold is >2x ULN.
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: New right upper quadrant pain in clinical isolation without any other PET features
options.rationale: Epigastric/RUQ pain raises suspicion for hepatic capsular stretch but is not a stand-alone SOMANZ diagnostic criterion without biochemical confirmation of hepatic dysfunction. RUQ pain plus transaminitis >2x ULN would be diagnostic; the anti-pattern is using symptoms without confirming biochemistry (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Urine protein/creatinine ratio of 18 mg/mmol on a spot midstream sample today
options.rationale: Significant proteinuria by SOMANZ requires PCR >=30 mg/mmol or 24h urine protein >=300 mg; 18 mg/mmol is below threshold. The anti-pattern is treating sub-threshold proteinuria as diagnostic. PCR >=30 mg/mmol would be diagnostic (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia is a multisystem hypertensive disorder of pregnancy after 20 weeks gestation. The SOMANZ 2014 definition is new-onset hypertension (systolic over 140 or diastolic over 90 on two readings 4 hours apart, or any reading above 160/110) plus one or more of: significant proteinuria (urinary protein-creatinine ratio over 30 mg/mmol), renal insufficiency (creatinine over 90 micromol/L), liver involvement (transaminases over twice ULN, severe RUQ or epigastric pain), neurological complications (eclampsia, altered mental status, severe headache, persistent visual disturbance, hyperreflexia with sustained clonus), haematological involvement (platelets under 100, DIC, haemolysis), or uteroplacental dysfunction (FGR, oligohydramnios, abnormal umbilical artery Doppler, abruption, stillbirth). Severe features mandate admission, antihypertensive control (labetalol, nifedipine, hydralazine), magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and timing of birth balanced against gestation. Definitive cure is delivery of the placenta.
key_points: SOMANZ end-organ criteria: platelets <100 x10^9/L, creatinine >90 micromol/L, ALT/AST >2x ULN, pulmonary oedema, eclampsia/severe headache/visual symptoms/stroke
Uteroplacental dysfunction: fetal growth restriction, abnormal Dopplers, stillbirth
Significant proteinuria: PCR >=30 mg/mmol or 24-hour >=300 mg
Hyperuricaemia is associated but not a diagnostic criterion
explanation.pearls: Pre-eclampsia after 20 weeks no longer requires proteinuria - new hypertension plus any maternal end-organ dysfunction (platelets under 100, creatinine over 90, AST/ALT over 40, neurological features, pulmonary oedema) or uteroplacental dysfunction satisfies SOMANZ criteria (SOMANZ 2014).

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia diagnosis without proteinuria

stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 35 weeks and 2 days gestation presents with three days of progressively worsening right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and increasing fatigue. Her two previous pregnancies were uncomplicated and she has no personal or family history of thrombotic microangiopathy, autoimmune disease or liver disease. Her blood pressure on three readings is 146-150 / 90-94 mmHg, she has 1+ proteinuria with a urine PCR of 42 mg/mmol, and the fetal CTG is reactive with normal growth on a scan one week ago.

She has had no recent gastroenteritis, no bloody diarrhoea and no recent E. coli O157:H7 or shigatoxin-producing organism exposure. Bedside bloods show haemoglobin 96 g/L (anaemia with reticulocytosis), platelets 68 x10^9/L, ALT 285 U/L, AST 312 U/L, total bilirubin 38 micromol/L (predominantly indirect), LDH 850 U/L, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (preserved), INR 1.1, creatinine 84 micromol/L (normal for pregnancy), glucose 5.2 mmol/L, and ammonia within the normal range. A peripheral blood film shows schistocytes, polychromasia and absent platelet clumps. ADAMTS13 activity measured urgently is 65% (well above the 10% threshold for TTP).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Mild scleral icterus, RUQ tenderness. Uterus appropriate for dates, soft.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, platelets 68 x10^9/L, schistocytes on film, LDH 850 U/L, bilirubin 38 micromol/L (mostly indirect), ALT 285 U/L, AST 312 U/L, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, ammonia normal, ADAMTS13 65%.

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this clinical and biochemical picture?

options.text: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets)
options.rationale: HELLP is diagnosed by Haemolysis (anaemia, schistocytes, raised LDH, raised indirect bilirubin), Elevated Liver enzymes (ALT/AST >70 U/L typically) and Low Platelets (<100 x10^9/L), usually with normal coagulation and normal glucose. This patient has all three features with preserved fibrinogen, normal INR, normal glucose and ADAMTS13 >10%, distinguishing it from AFLP, TTP and HUS (RANZCOG 2023; SOMANZ 2014).

options.text: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy with hepatic dysfunction
options.rationale: AFLP typically causes HYPOGLYCAEMIA, COAGULOPATHY (raised INR, low fibrinogen), HYPERAMMONAEMIA, and more pronounced hyperbilirubinaemia. This patient has normal glucose, INR, fibrinogen, and ammonia. AFLP is correct when Swansea criteria are met (RCOG; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with neurological features
options.rationale: TTP is defined by ADAMTS13 activity <10%, severe thrombocytopenia, MAHA, neurological features, and fever; ADAMTS13 of 65% effectively excludes TTP. The anti-pattern is calling any MAHA + thrombocytopenia 'TTP'. TTP is correct only with ADAMTS13 <10% (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.text: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome with complement-mediated injury
options.rationale: HUS is dominated by acute kidney injury with relatively preserved transaminases; this patient has normal creatinine and very high transaminases - opposite pattern. The anti-pattern is conflating HUS and HELLP because both show MAHA + thrombocytopenia. HUS/aHUS is correct with renal-dominant injury (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.text: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with raised bile acids
options.rationale: ICP causes pruritus (often palms/soles) and isolated raised bile acids with modest transaminitis WITHOUT thrombocytopenia or haemolysis. The anti-pattern is reaching for ICP based on transaminitis alone. ICP is correct with bile acids >19 micromol/L and pruritus, without HELLP features (RANZCOG ICP statement).

explanation.summary: Late-pregnancy thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic features spans pre-eclampsia/HELLP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) - each demands different management but shares early presentation. HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) typically appears in the third trimester with epigastric or RUQ pain and pre-eclamptic features; coagulation is initially preserved. AFLP presents with nausea, vomiting, hypoglycaemia, raised ammonia, coagulopathy and renal impairment; the Swansea criteria help diagnose. TTP shows ADAMTS13 activity under 10%, microangiopathy, thrombocytopenia, neurological features and fever, with normal coags - treatment is urgent plasma exchange plus caplacizumab. aHUS is complement-mediated, predominantly renal, and responds to eculizumab. Initial workup in any pregnant woman with thrombocytopenia and microangiopathy: FBC, blood film, LDH, haptoglobin, LFTs, coagulation, fibrinogen, glucose, ammonia, ADAMTS13. Delivery is mandatory for HELLP and AFLP regardless of gestation.
key_points: HELLP: Hb low, platelets <100, AST/ALT >70, LDH >600, INR normal, glucose normal
AFLP: hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, hyperammonaemia, AKI
TTP: ADAMTS13 <10%, severe thrombocytopenia, neuro features
HUS: AKI dominant, often post-diarrhoeal (STEC) or complement-mediated
Mississippi classification grades HELLP severity by platelet count
explanation.pearls: HELLP vs AFLP vs TTP discriminators within hours: HELLP has elevated LFTs with normal coags and glucose; AFLP has hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, hyperammonaemia and creatinine; TTP has ADAMTS13 activity under 10% and prominent neurology. All three demand delivery and tertiary referral (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

subtopic_detail: HELLP vs AFLP vs TTP vs HUS in pregnancy

stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 with booking BMI 27, no diabetes history, no PCOS, no previous GDM has a 75 g OGTT at 27 weeks: fasting 5.3, 1 h 8.4, 2 h 7.1 mmol/L. The midwife asks whether this meets Australian (ADIPS) criteria for gestational diabetes, and if so, what the immediate next step is. The woman has no symptoms and her fetus is growing on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: BMI 28. Uterus appropriate for dates.
data_table.Investigations: Awaiting OGTT result.

lead_in: Which interpretation and next step are correct?

options.text: GDM diagnosed on the fasting >=5.1 mmol/L cut-off; commence dietitian and diabetes educator referral, capillary glucose monitoring 4 times daily, and review at the joint diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic within 1 week
options.rationale: ADIPS 2014 criteria: ANY of fasting >=5.1, 1 h >=10.0, 2 h >=8.5 mmol/L. Her fasting 5.3 meets the threshold; even though the 1 h and 2 h values are below cut-off, GDM is diagnosed. Initial management is multidisciplinary team referral with SMBG (RANZCOG; ADIPS).

options.text: Not GDM; only the fasting result is borderline; repeat OGTT in 4 weeks
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria require only ONE elevated value to diagnose GDM (IADPSG single-value rule); her fasting 5.3 already meets the threshold. The anti-pattern is requiring multiple abnormal values (old WHO/two-step criteria). One-value rule is the Australian standard (ADIPS).

options.text: GDM only if fasting >=5.5 mmol/L; her result is below threshold
options.rationale: The Australian fasting cut-off is 5.1 mmol/L, not 5.5. The anti-pattern is using older/American thresholds in an Australian context. 5.5 mmol/L threshold was used historically but Australia adopted the IADPSG/ADIPS 5.1 in 2014 (ADIPS).

options.text: Type 2 diabetes diagnosed (fasting >=7.0); commence insulin today
options.rationale: Diabetes outside pregnancy uses fasting >=7.0; in pregnancy the GDM cut-off is 5.1. She has GDM, not overt T2DM. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is diagnosed only with fasting >=7.0, HbA1c >=6.5%, or random glucose >=11.1 with symptoms - thresholds for T2DM diagnosis (ADIPS).

options.text: Borderline only; reassure with healthy-eating advice and re-test at 32 weeks
options.rationale: She meets diagnostic criteria; deferral risks fetal complications (macrosomia, stillbirth, neonatal hypoglycaemia). The anti-pattern is reassurance without acting on confirmed diagnostic results. Re-testing is correct only when initial OGTT is in borderline ambiguous range (very rare with the single-value rule) (ADIPS).

explanation.summary: Australia uses ADIPS 2014 (IADPSG-aligned) criteria: 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks for universal screening. Any one value at or above fasting 5.1, 1 h 10.0 or 2 h 8.5 mmol/L makes the diagnosis.
key_points: Universal OGTT at 24-28 weeks
Early OGTT in first or early second trimester if high risk (previous GDM, BMI >=30, age >=40, ethnicity, family hx, PCOS, prior macrosomia)
One abnormal value is enough
Repeat 75 g OGTT 6-12 weeks postpartum
explanation.pearls: Memorise 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 - they are the only three numbers you need for diagnosis in Australia.

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes - ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 30 weeks and 2 days gestation was diagnosed with GDM at 26 weeks (fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 2 h 9.1 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT). She has been on structured dietary modification with a credentialled dietitian and 30 minutes of daily walking for four weeks. Her four-times-daily capillary glucose diary now shows fasting values consistently 5.6-6.2 mmol/L (ADIPS target <5.1 mmol/L) and 2-hour postprandial values 5.8-6.8 mmol/L (target <6.7 mmol/L) after all three meals.

There is no overnight hypoglycaemia, no symptomatic hypoglycaemiabedside testing. Fetal ultrasound at 30 weeks shows estimated fetal weight on the 78th centile with appropriate liquor and normal umbilical and middle cerebral artery Dopplers. Her booking BMI was 31 and she has gained 6 kg in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 82 bpm.
data_table.Examination: BMI 31. Fundal height appropriate.
data_table.Investigations: BSL diary: fasting 5.6-6.2; postprandial within target after all meals. HbA1c 5.6%. Renal function normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence basal-bolus insulin with rapid-acting analogue at meals plus bedtime NPH
options.rationale: Full basal-bolus is reserved for patients with BOTH elevated fasting and postprandial values. This patient has isolated elevated fasting glucose only, so basal alone is sufficient. The anti-pattern is over-treating with multi-injection regimens. Basal-bolus is correct when both fasting and postprandial fail despite stepwise titration (ADIPS 2014; RANZCOG 2023).

options.text: Commence rapid-acting prandial insulin (aspart or lispro) before each meal only, no basal
options.rationale: Prandial insulin would not address the predominant fasting hyperglycaemia and would risk daytime hypoglycaemia. The anti-pattern is mismatching insulin profile to the glucose pattern. Prandial-only insulin is correct for isolated postprandial elevations with normal fasting (ADIPS 2014).

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures only and review fasting glucose again in four weeks
options.rationale: Fasting glucose remains above target despite four weeks of optimised lifestyle; pharmacotherapy is indicated to reduce risk of macrosomia and stillbirth. The anti-pattern is continued lifestyle-only when targets are not met. Continued lifestyle is correct only when targets are achieved (ADIPS 2014).

options.text: Commence empagliflozin 10 mg orally daily as monotherapy in pregnancy
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity concerns and lack of safety data (TGA category D). The anti-pattern is using non-pregnancy diabetes drugs in pregnancy. SGLT2i is never correct in current pregnancy management (TGA; AMH).

options.text: Commence isophane (NPH) insulin at bedtime, titrated to fasting capillary glucose target
options.rationale: For isolated fasting hyperglycaemia in GDM, the ADIPS-recommended first-line pharmacotherapy is bedtime intermediate-acting (isophane/NPH) insulin titrated to achieve fasting glucose <5.1 mmol/L. Metformin is an acceptable alternative or adjunct in suitable patients but insulin is the established first-line agent (ADIPS 2014; RANZCOG 2023).

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes mellitus affects around 15% of Australian pregnancies and is screened with a 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks (or earlier if risk factors). ADIPS diagnostic thresholds are fasting 5.1 or above, 1 hour 10.0 or above, 2 hour 8.5 or above. First-line management is dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy, blood glucose monitoring (fasting plus 1- or 2-hour postprandial), and 30 minutes of moderate exercise daily. Pharmacotherapy is initiated when more than 50% of fasting or postprandial readings exceed targets (fasting under 5.0, 1 hour under 7.4, 2 hour under 6.7) over 1-2 weeks. Insulin is matched to the glucose pattern: isolated fasting hyperglycaemia responds to bedtime isophane; isolated postprandial to prandial rapid-acting analogue; both elevated to basal-bolus regimen. Metformin is an option in women who decline or cannot tolerate insulin, with counselling that it crosses the placenta but has reassuring short-term safety data. Postnatal OGTT at 6 weeks identifies overt diabetes.
key_points: ADIPS targets: fasting <5.1, 1 h <7.4, 2 h <6.7 mmol/L
Isolated fasting hyperglycaemia: bedtime NPH first
Isolated postprandial: prandial rapid-acting analogue
Both: basal-bolus
Metformin: alternative or adjunct; crosses placenta; not for severe hyperglycaemia
SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists: contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Match insulin to glucose pattern in GDM: isolated fasting hyperglycaemia gets bedtime isophane (NPH); isolated postprandial gets prandial rapid-acting (aspart or lispro); both elevated get basal-bolus. Metformin is an option after counselling on placental transfer (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: GDM - insulin titration after lifestyle failure

stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 at 28 weeks with gestational hypertension (persistent BP 144/92 over a fortnight; no proteinuria; bloods normal; normal fetal growth and Dopplers) is asymptomatic. She has well-controlled severe asthma on inhaled budesonide/formoterol with two emergency presentations in the past year requiring oral prednisolone. She has no other medical conditions, no allergies, normal renal and liver function. The consultant is choosing the first-line oral antihypertensive.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 144/90 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Uncomplicated. No oedema. Fundus appropriate for dates.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, ALT 22 U/L, urine PCR <30 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line oral antihypertensive?

options.text: Labetalol 100 mg orally twice daily titrated to target
options.rationale: Labetalol is standard first-line in pregnancy hypertension, but in significant asthma (recent exacerbations on ICS-LABA) beta-blockade risks bronchospasm; SOMANZ and RANZCOG list significant asthma as a relative contraindication. Labetalol is correct in pregnancy hypertension without asthma or other beta-blocker contraindication (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).

options.text: Slow-release nifedipine 20 mg orally twice daily titrated to target
options.rationale: In a woman with significant asthma where labetalol is unsafe, nifedipine (calcium channel blocker) is the preferred first-line alternative; both are SOMANZ-recommended options (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).

options.text: Enalapril 5 mg orally once daily titrated to target
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy due to fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, calvarial hypoplasia, and pulmonary hypoplasia. The classic absolute teratogen anti-pattern. Enalapril is never correct in current pregnancy; pre-conception switch to pregnancy-safe agent is mandatory (SOMANZ; AMH).

options.text: Methyldopa 250 mg orally three times daily titrated to target
options.rationale: Methyldopa is an acceptable second-line agent but is less effective (higher target BP achievement failure) and has higher rates of depression/sedation/postural hypotension. Nifedipine is preferred in this asthma context. Methyldopa is correct as alternative second-line when first-line agents fail (SOMANZ).

options.text: Oral hydralazine 25 mg three times daily titrated to target
options.rationale: Oral hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and unpredictable response; IV hydralazine is used for severe acute hypertension but oral hydralazine is not first-line maintenance. The anti-pattern is using parenteral-only drugs orally. Oral hydralazine is correct only as add-on in resistant pregnancy hypertension with specialist input (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: First-line oral antihypertensives for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy in Australia: labetalol > nifedipine SR > methyldopa. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated. Treatment target BP 110-140 / 80-90 mmHg per SOMANZ.
key_points: Labetalol 100-400 mg BD-TDS (first-line)
Nifedipine SR 20-60 mg BD (second-line)
Methyldopa 250-500 mg TDS-QID (second/third-line)
ACE inhibitors and ARBs: contraindicated
Acute severe BP: IV labetalol or IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine SR
explanation.pearls: Avoid labetalol if the patient has asthma, heart block, or significant bradycardia; switch to nifedipine SR.

subtopic_detail: Hypertension in pregnancy - first-line antihypertensive

stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 woman at 11 weeks and 2 days gestation has a routine booking infection screen which shows Toxoplasma gondii IgM positive and IgG positive with low avidity, a pattern strongly suggesting recent primary infection within the last 12-16 weeks. She has had a new indoor kitten at home since six weeks before conception and recalls cleaning the litter tray on multiple occasions without gloves.

She also recalls eating undercooked lamb skewers at a barbecue 10 weeks ago. She is asymptomatic, has no lymphadenopathy on examination and her partner is well with no symptoms. Toxoplasma PCR on maternal blood is positive.. Her booking ultrasound today shows a viable singleton with normal anatomy for gestation and no calcifications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Well. No lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Toxoplasma IgM positive, IgG positive low avidity, maternal blood PCR positive. Booking ultrasound: viable singleton at 11 weeks, normal anatomy for gestation.

lead_in: Which initial pharmacological strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Spiramycin 1 g TDS, switching to sulphadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid only if amniocentesis confirms fetal infection
options.rationale: Spiramycin is the first-trimester treatment of choice as it concentrates in the placenta and reduces vertical transmission without causing fetal harm. If fetal infection is confirmed (positive amniotic fluid PCR after 18 weeks), therapy switches to sulphadiazine + pyrimethamine + folinic acid to treat established fetal infection (RANZCOG; BMJ Best Practice; RCOG). Spiramycin reduces vertical transmission; sulphadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid is reserved for confirmed fetal infection by amniotic fluid PCR at >=18 weeks.

options.text: Sulphadiazine plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid commenced immediately for all women regardless of fetal status
options.rationale: Pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist and is teratogenic in T1 (neural tube defects, oral clefts); it should be avoided before 14-18 weeks. Treatment of the fetus is reserved for confirmed fetal infection. The anti-pattern is treating mother as if fetus is already infected. Sulphadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid is correct only after confirmed fetal infection on amniotic fluid PCR (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Co-trimoxazole oral monotherapy without folinic acid or any fetal assessment as the definitive treatment
options.rationale: Co-trimoxazole has activity against Toxoplasma but is not standard first-line therapy in pregnancy; spiramycin is preferred to prevent transmission and is the WHO-endorsed agent for prevention. Co-trimoxazole is correct in some non-pregnancy contexts (HIV-positive patients on prophylaxis) (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily as definitive monotherapy without spiramycin, folinic acid or referral
options.rationale: Azithromycin has weak in vitro activity but is not a recommended first-line agent in pregnancy. The anti-pattern is using a familiar antibiotic without recognising it lacks the appropriate spectrum. Azithromycin is correct only as adjunct in some refractory toxoplasmic chorioretinitis regimens (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Termination of pregnancy without treatment given certain severe congenital toxoplasmosis at this gestation
options.rationale: Maternal primary T1 infection carries low vertical transmission risk (~10-15%) although severe consequences if transmitted; treatment with spiramycin substantially reduces transmission. Termination is not default. ToP is correct only after confirmed severe fetal infection (multiple anomalies on US/MRI) with informed maternal choice (RCOG; BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Maternal toxoplasmosis seroconversion during pregnancy carries a transmission risk that rises with gestation (10% in first trimester, 30% in second, 60-70% in third) but disease severity in the fetus is inversely related to timing - earliest infections produce the most severe congenital toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, intellectual disability), while third-trimester infections are usually asymptomatic at birth. Diagnosis is by maternal serology: IgM positive plus IgG positive with low avidity suggests recent infection (within 4 months). Spiramycin 1 g TDS started within 3 weeks of seroconversion reduces vertical transmission by about 50% without crossing the placenta significantly. Amniocentesis after 18 weeks (and at least 4 weeks after maternal seroconversion) with PCR confirms or excludes fetal infection. If confirmed, switch to sulphadiazine plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid (to reduce marrow toxicity) for ongoing treatment until delivery. Serial fetal ultrasound surveillance for hydrocephalus and calcifications.
key_points: Spiramycin: first-line in pregnancy to prevent transmission (does not cross placenta well)
Sulphadiazine + pyrimethamine + folinic acid: for confirmed fetal infection from 14-18 weeks
Folinic acid (leucovorin) protects against pyrimethamine-induced bone marrow toxicity
Diagnose primary infection with low IgG avidity within 16-20 weeks of seroconversion
Vertical transmission risk: T1 ~10-15%, T2 ~30%, T3 ~60% - but severity decreases with gestation
Sources: cat faeces, raw/undercooked meat, unwashed produce, soil
explanation.pearls: Suspected maternal toxoplasmosis: start spiramycin 1 g TDS within 3 weeks of seroconversion to reduce vertical transmission by half; switch to sulphadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid only when amniocentesis (after 18 weeks) confirms fetal infection (RANZCOG; eTG Antibiotic).

subtopic_detail: Toxoplasmosis - first trimester management

stem:
A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 14 weeks and 1 day gestation works as a long-day-care educator caring for children aged 12-24 months and presents to her GP with a fortnight of mild fatigue, low-grade fever, headache, mild cervical lymphadenopathy and arthralgia. She has no rash, no respiratory symptoms and no jaundice. Routine TORCH testing shows CMV IgM positive, CMV IgG positive with low avidity (consistent with infection within the past three months).

Critically, her booking CMV IgG four weeks earlier was negative, providing serological evidence of seroconversion in early pregnancy. A maternal blood CMV PCR is positive at a moderate viral load. She has no prior infectious diseases history, no immunosuppression, and her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a healthy term infant. She asks the maternal-fetal medicine consultant about the difference between primary and non-primary (reactivation or reinfection) maternal CMV infection in pregnancy, the next investigation step including fetal surveillance and timing of any amniocentesis, and the role and evidence base for any antiviral therapy in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 degC, BP 110/72 mmHg, HR 84 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy; otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: CMV IgG positive low avidity, IgM positive, blood PCR positive. Booking CMV IgG (4 weeks prior): negative. LFTs mildly raised (ALT 65). Hb 122 g/L.

lead_in: Which statement most accurately describes the current Australian approach to maternal CMV infection in this case?

options.text: Non-primary CMV infection carries a higher vertical transmission rate than primary infection, so reassurance is appropriate here
options.rationale: Primary maternal CMV has SUBSTANTIALLY HIGHER vertical transmission rate (~30-40%) and higher severity than non-primary (~1-2%). The anti-pattern is misremembering the direction of risk. Non-primary higher-risk reassurance is never correct; the framing should always be 'primary infection = highest risk' (RANZCOG; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.text: Maternal intravenous ganciclovir is the established standard of care to prevent fetal CMV infection in primary seroconversion
options.rationale: IV ganciclovir is teratogenic in animal studies and is not routinely used in pregnancy; valaciclovir trials have shown some benefit. The anti-pattern is using post-natal CMV treatment drug for maternal management. IV ganciclovir is correct for neonatal symptomatic congenital CMV, not maternal pregnancy (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.text: Spiramycin reduces vertical transmission of CMV in the same way that it does for Toxoplasma gondii
options.rationale: Spiramycin has NO role in CMV management; it is specific to toxoplasmosis. The anti-pattern is generalising one intrauterine infection drug to another. Spiramycin is correct only for maternal toxoplasmosis prevention of vertical transmission (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.text: CMV is a rare cause of congenital infection and routine fetal surveillance is unnecessary after maternal seroconversion
options.rationale: Congenital CMV is the MOST COMMON congenital infection in developed countries (~0.5-1% of live births) and the leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss. Serial fetal US plus amniotic PCR after 21 weeks is recommended. Reassurance without surveillance is never correct (RANZCOG).

options.text: Serial fetal ultrasound, amniocentesis for CMV PCR after 21 weeks and 6 weeks post-seroconversion, and high-dose valaciclovir following MFM discussion
options.rationale: This reflects the current RANZCOG/RCOG/BMJ Best Practice approach: confirm primary infection (low avidity, seroconversion), serial fetal ultrasound, amniotic PCR after 21 weeks and at least 6 weeks post-seroconversion to maximise sensitivity, and consider maternal high-dose valaciclovir 8 g/day which a randomised trial showed reduces vertical transmission (RANZCOG; BMJ Best Practice; Shahar-Nissan 2020). Surveillance includes brain biometry and growth; amniocentesis sensitivity rises after 21 weeks and 6 weeks post-seroconversion; high-dose valaciclovir is the only intervention with RCT-supported reduction in vertical transmission.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Congenital CMV is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss. Primary maternal infection transmits in 30-40% of cases; non-primary in 1-2%. Management includes serial fetal ultrasound, amniotic PCR after 21 weeks, and consideration of maternal high-dose valaciclovir.
key_points: Primary infection: 30-40% transmission; non-primary: 1-2%
Diagnose by IgG seroconversion or low IgG avidity + IgM positive
Amniotic PCR: after 21 weeks AND >=6 weeks post seroconversion
Fetal US findings: ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, hyperechogenic bowel, IUGR, hepatosplenomegaly
Valaciclovir 8 g/day may reduce vertical transmission (RCT 2020)
No effective vaccine; childcare hand hygiene is key prevention
explanation.pearls: Maternal CMV is often clinically silent; hearing screening at birth is critical for affected neonates.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: CMV in pregnancy - primary vs non-primary infection

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 24 weeks and 2 days gestation with a background of mild persistent asthma on budesonide-formoterol maintenance (one inhalation twice daily as preventer plus reliever) presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of progressive wheeze, dyspnoea and chest tightness after a viral upper respiratory infection. She is too breathless to speak in full sentences. Her best personal PEFR is 420 L/min; in ED it is measured at 210 L/min (50% of personal best).

SpO2 is 93% on room air. Auscultation reveals widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally and no focal crackles or signs of consolidation. She is afebrile at 37.1 degC, has no calf swelling, no chest pain, the fetus is moving normally and the CTG is reactive with a baseline of 140 bpm. She has stopped her preventer inhaler for the past four days because she was worried about possible effects on the baby and asks whether she should continue inhaled corticosteroids and whether oral prednisolone is safe in pregnancy, given a friend has told her to refuse steroids.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 28 /min, HR 118 bpm, SpO2 93% RA, BP 124/78 mmHg, T 37.1 degC.
data_table.Examination: Speaking in short phrases, accessory muscle use, widespread polyphonic wheeze. CTG reactive.
data_table.Investigations: PEFR 210 L/min (50% of personal best 420). ABG not yet performed. CXR not indicated initially.

lead_in: Which management approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue maintenance inhaled corticosteroid but withhold all systemic corticosteroids in pregnancy due to perceived fetal teratogenic risk
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone is safe in pregnancy and is essential for moderate/severe asthma exacerbation; withholding it risks maternal AND fetal hypoxia, which is FAR more harmful than transient corticosteroid exposure. The anti-pattern is treating pregnancy as steroid-contraindication. Steroid withholding is essentially never correct (Therapeutic Guidelines; National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium if severe, continue ICS, oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg for 5-10 days, plus controlled oxygen
options.rationale: This is the standard exacerbation algorithm. Salbutamol bronchodilation, oxygen to target SpO2 94-98% (95% to maintain fetal oxygenation), maintenance ICS continued, oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg daily for short course are all safe and indicated. Maternal hypoxia harms the fetus far more than these medications (National Asthma Council; Therapeutic Guidelines; RANZCOG). ICS and oral prednisolone are safe in pregnancy and reassurance about safety is part of the management.
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.text: Switch the patient to a leukotriene receptor antagonist (oral montelukast) alone as monotherapy maintenance throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: LTRAs (montelukast) are adjuncts, not first-line, and have NO role in acute exacerbation management. The anti-pattern is using maintenance-only drugs in acute exacerbations. Montelukast is correct as adjunct maintenance in exercise-induced or aspirin-sensitive asthma (National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes given as the immediate first-line therapy in pregnancy
options.rationale: IV magnesium is reserved for severe exacerbations refractory to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy. The anti-pattern is leading with adjunctive therapy before standard care. IV magnesium is correct after 1 hour of maximal nebulised bronchodilator + systemic steroid with inadequate response (National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.text: Discharge home with a short-acting beta-2 agonist alone once PEFR has reached 60% of personal best
options.rationale: PEFR 60% of best with a recent severe exacerbation does not meet safe discharge criteria; she needs systemic corticosteroids, observation, and a written asthma action plan. The anti-pattern is treating PEFR-alone as discharge criterion. Discharge is correct at PEFR >75% best with sustained response 1 hour after last salbutamol (National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Acute asthma in pregnancy is treated identically to non-pregnant patients with the additional priority of avoiding maternal hypoxia. Continue ICS, give salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone for moderate/severe exacerbations, and supplemental oxygen.
key_points: Maintenance ICS: safe and essential in pregnancy
Salbutamol: safe; first-line bronchodilator
Oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg daily for 5-10 days for exacerbation
Target SpO2 94-98% (or >=95% in pregnancy)
IV magnesium for severe refractory cases
Step up therapy if severity criteria escalate; involve obstetric medicine
explanation.pearls: Maternal asthma control is more important than any medication risk; uncontrolled asthma causes IUGR, preterm birth and pre-eclampsia.

sources.label: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

subtopic_detail: Asthma in pregnancy - acute exacerbation

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P0 woman with focal-onset epilepsy attends a joint obstetric-medicine/neurology pre-conception clinic three months before a planned pregnancy. She has been seizure-free for two years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily monotherapy, having previously failed levetiracetam (rash and breakthrough seizures) and carbamazepine (breakthrough seizures with intolerable somnolence) for seizure control. Her previous pregnancy ended in a first-trimester miscarriage while she was on lamotrigine monotherapy two years ago, and she has not used lamotrigine since.

She has no family history of neural tube defects or congenital malformations and her BMI is 23. She is concerned about teratogenicity having read media coverage of valproate, and asks specifically about: relative major congenital malformation rates of the commonly used AEDs, the appropriate periconceptional folate dose for women on AEDs versus the general population, the likely need for therapeutic drug monitoring during pregnancy (particularly for lamotrigine if used), and which medication she should ideally be established on by the time of conception.

She is keen to plan a pregnancy within the next six months and is willing to delay conception if a medication switch is recommended, but wants a clear plan that balances seizure control against teratogenic risk and includes the practical issue of how to monitor any new agent through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Neurologically normal. BMI 23.
data_table.Investigations: Recent EEG and MRI stable. Valproate level within therapeutic range. Renal and hepatic function normal.

lead_in: Which combination of recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue sodium valproate, commence folate 0.5 mg daily, with no need for AED drug levels during pregnancy
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest major congenital malformation rate of all AEDs (~10%) plus 30-40% risk of neurodevelopmental impairment; contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless all alternatives have failed. Folate dose for AED users is 5 mg, not 0.5 mg. Multiple errors. Continuing valproate is correct only after documented failure of all safer alternatives with informed consent (TGA; AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Switch to phenytoin before pregnancy as it carries the lowest teratogenicity profile of all the AEDs available
options.rationale: Phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome (microcephaly, cleft lip/palate, hypoplastic distal phalanges) with major malformation rate ~5-6%, higher than lamotrigine/levetiracetam. The anti-pattern is selecting older AEDs as 'safe'. Phenytoin is correct in some refractory epilepsy without safer alternatives, never as first-line pregnancy choice (Therapeutic Guidelines; AMH).

options.text: Switch (via neurology) from valproate to lamotrigine or levetiracetam pre-conception, folate 5 mg daily, with therapeutic AED level monitoring
options.rationale: Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the lowest major malformation rates (~2-3%, similar to background). Valproate (~10%) is avoided in women of childbearing potential. Folate 5 mg daily is recommended for women on AEDs. Lamotrigine clearance increases substantially in pregnancy, requiring level monitoring and dose adjustment (Therapeutic Guidelines - Neurology; AMH; RANZCOG; NICE). Switch should be 3-6 months pre-conception; lamotrigine levels fall markedly in pregnancy. Continued AED therapy is essential because uncontrolled seizures cause more fetal harm than well-chosen AEDs.

options.text: Continue valproate, add lamotrigine to permit valproate dose reduction, and use folate 0.5 mg daily throughout
options.rationale: Polytherapy increases teratogenic risk in a dose-dependent fashion; valproate remains highly teratogenic at any dose. The goal is monotherapy with the safest agent. The anti-pattern is dose-reduction-instead-of-switch. Polytherapy is correct only in refractory epilepsy on a single safer agent, not adding lamotrigine to valproate (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Stop all antiepileptic medications before conception entirely to eliminate teratogenic risk to the developing fetus completely
options.rationale: Stopping AEDs risks status epilepticus, maternal injury, hypoxia, and fetal loss; uncontrolled seizures cause more fetal harm than well-chosen AEDs. Cessation is appropriate only after 2 or more years seizure-free with neurology confirmation, not reflexively in pregnancy (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Pre-conception epilepsy care: switch from valproate to lamotrigine or levetiracetam (lowest teratogenicity), folate 5 mg daily, plan for AED level monitoring (lamotrigine clearance rises ~2-3 fold), continue therapy because uncontrolled seizures cause more fetal harm than well-chosen AEDs.
key_points: Major malformation rates: lamotrigine ~2.3%, levetiracetam ~2.4%, carbamazepine ~5%, phenytoin ~6%, topiramate ~4-9%, valproate ~10%
Valproate also causes 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment
Folate 5 mg daily for AED users (vs 0.5 mg general population)
Lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy; monitor and dose-adjust
Vitamin K 1 mg IM to neonate at birth (standard)
Breastfeeding is safe on most AEDs (lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, valproate)
explanation.pearls: Switch off valproate at least 3-6 months before conception, not once pregnancy is confirmed - by then the teratogenic window is open.

subtopic_detail: Epilepsy in pregnancy - AED selection and teratogenicity

stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 at 7 weeks is referred for Graves disease. She was diagnosed 6 months ago with tremor, weight loss and palpitations; currently on carbimazole 15 mg daily with normal TFTs and TRAb 5.2 IU/L (positive). She has no goitre and no ophthalmopathy. She is asymptomatic. She and her obstetric medicine team are reviewing her medication plan for the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Clinically euthyroid. No tremor. No goitre. No ophthalmopathy.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.4 mIU/L, free T4 14 pmol/L, free T3 4.2 pmol/L (all within trimester-specific reference). TRAb 5.2 IU/L (positive).

lead_in: Which management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Switch to propylthiouracil (PTU) in trimester 1 then back to carbimazole in trimester 2-3; monthly maternal TFTs; fetal growth/goitre scans; neonatal TFTs and TRAb at birth
options.rationale: Carbimazole/methimazole is associated with aplasia cutis and embryopathy in T1; PTU is preferred in T1 but switched back in T2-T3 due to PTU hepatotoxicity. Positive TRAb requires fetal surveillance for goitre/tachycardia and neonatal monitoring (RANZCOG; ATA; AMH).

options.text: Continue carbimazole at the current dose throughout pregnancy as the fetus is not at risk of aplasia cutis or any other carbimazole embryopathy
options.rationale: Carbimazole in T1 risks teratogenicity (methimazole/carbimazole embryopathy: aplasia cutis, oesophageal/choanal atresia); positive TRAb crosses placenta with fetal goitre/tachycardia/hydrops risk requiring surveillance. PTU is preferred in the first trimester; carbimazole is reintroduced for T2-T3 after the T1 switch (RANZCOG).

options.text: Stop antithyroid drugs entirely as pregnancy is naturally immunosuppressive and Graves disease usually remits spontaneously without medication intervention
options.rationale: Graves may improve in T2-T3 (immune modulation) but T1 has highest activity; abrupt cessation risks thyroid storm and miscarriage. The anti-pattern is assuming pregnancy 'cures' autoimmune disease. Stopping antithyroid drugs is correct only when biochemically euthyroid for >=6 months and TRAb negative (RANZCOG).

options.text: Switch to radioactive iodine ablation now to provide definitive treatment despite the absolute fetal contraindication to radioiodine exposure in utero
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is ABSOLUTELY contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal thyroid ablation, cretinism). The classic teratogen-by-mechanism anti-pattern. RAI is correct only post-partum if breastfeeding ceased and 6-month conception avoidance is acceptable (RANZCOG; AMH).

options.text: Switch to PTU throughout pregnancy without switching back to carbimazole in the second trimester despite the cumulative maternal hepatotoxicity risk
options.rationale: PTU causes severe hepatotoxicity (FDA black box); it should be limited to T1 and switched back to carbimazole in T2-T3. The anti-pattern is assuming one regimen suits all trimesters. PTU throughout is correct only in carbimazole hypersensitivity or thyroid storm (RANZCOG; AMH).

explanation.summary: Graves in pregnancy: PTU in T1 (lower embryopathy risk), then carbimazole/methimazole in T2/T3 (lower hepatotoxicity risk). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated. TRAb positivity confers neonatal thyrotoxicosis risk; neonatal TFTs are mandatory.
key_points: T1: propylthiouracil (PTU)
T2-T3: carbimazole/methimazole (PTU = severe liver injury risk)
Conversion: 1 mg carbimazole ~ 10-20 mg PTU (use 10:1 conventionally)
Target: maternal fT4 at or just above upper limit of trimester-specific range
Radioactive iodine: contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation
TRAb positive: fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis risk - neonatal TFTs day 4-7
explanation.pearls: Methimazole/carbimazole embryopathy includes aplasia cutis and a distinctive choanal/oesophageal atresia phenotype; switch off it before or by 6-10 weeks gestation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum
ATA Guidelines for thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017
