tags: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander maternal health
stem:
A 22-year-old G1P0 Aboriginal woman from a regional NSW community books for antenatal care at 11 weeks. She has no medical conditions, BMI 24, supportive partner, lives with her mother and cousins. She tells the booking midwife she felt unsafe at a previous gynaecology appointment because she did not feel listened to and had to bring her own information; she has missed two prior follow-up appointments at other services for the same reason.

The hospital offers: standard midwifery group practice (MGP); a local Aboriginal Maternal and Infant Health Service (AMIHS) co-led by an Aboriginal Health Worker and continuity midwife linked with the regional ACCHO; obstetrician-led clinic; GP shared care; and telehealth. All five pathways can access morphology USS, OGTT and specialist obstetric review.

data_table.Booking bloods: Hb 122 g/L, blood group O Rh+, rubella immune, syphilis EIA non-reactive, HIV negative, HBsAg negative
data_table.Social: Lives with mother and cousins; supportive partner; previous disengagement from non-culturally-safe services

lead_in: Which model of care is most likely to optimise engagement and outcomes for this woman?

options.text: AMIHS continuity-of-carer model integrating midwife and Aboriginal Health Worker, with ACCHO linkage
options.rationale: Birthing-on-Country and AMIHS-type continuity-of-carer models have evidence for improved engagement, reduced preterm birth and improved cultural safety for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women. Given her history of disengagement from non-culturally-safe services, this is the best option (RANZCOG; AHMAC Birthing on Country).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.text: Standard midwifery group practice with referral to a separate Aboriginal Health Worker as needed
options.rationale: Bolting on an AHW as a separate referral is less effective than an integrated model where AHW and midwife share continuity from start; the anti-pattern is treating cultural safety as 'add-on'. Standard midwifery with AHW referral is correct only when AMIHS is unavailable (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.text: Obstetrician-led care because all Aboriginal pregnancies are inherently high-risk and require specialist supervision
options.rationale: Generalising all Aboriginal pregnancies as high-risk is racist and contradicts evidence; risk should be individually assessed. Obstetrician-led care is correct based on individual clinical risk factors, not ethnicity (RANZCOG; AHMAC).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.text: GP shared care with the regional GP to minimise hospital contact
options.rationale: GP shared care is a valid model but does not provide the integrated cultural and clinical continuity that AMIHS offers. GP shared care is correct in low-risk pregnancies where cultural safety is met by other means (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.text: Telehealth-only antenatal care to reduce her travel burden regardless of her preference
options.rationale: Telehealth is an adjunct, not a substitute for face-to-face culturally safe care; removing in-person AHW/midwife contact reduces engagement. Telehealth is correct as supplement to face-to-face care, not replacement (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

explanation.summary: AMIHS / Birthing on Country / Bubup-Wilam type continuity-of-carer models combining midwife and Aboriginal Health Worker, with ACCHO linkage, have Australian evidence for improved antenatal attendance, reduced preterm birth, increased breastfeeding, and improved cultural safety (NSW Health AMIHS Evaluation; RANZCOG W-WH 22; NACCHO).
key_points: AMIHS = NSW model; analogous services exist in Vic (Koori Maternity), Qld (Birthing in Our Community)
Continuity-of-carer is the active ingredient (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
Aboriginal identity is not itself a risk factor (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
Closing the Gap target 2 measures healthy birthweight (Closing the Gap)
Offer choice; do not force into Aboriginal-specific service if the woman prefers standard care
explanation.pearls: Birthing on Country is a movement returning birthing services to community control; it is not a single model but a principle (NACCHO).

subtopic_detail: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander antenatal care - culturally safe model

subtopic: Indigenous health (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander)
tags: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander maternal health
stem:
A 26-year-old G2P1 Aboriginal woman from a remote NT community presents for booking at 12 weeks. She has a documented history of acute rheumatic fever aged 10 with subsequent moderate mitral regurgitation on echo last year and is on monthly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin (BPG) 1.2 million units secondary prophylaxis through the local clinic. Her last dose was 2 weeks ago.

She has had one previous uncomplicated SVD at term with no cardiac decompensation, breastfed for 12 months, and is currently well with no exertional dyspnoea, no orthopnoea, and NYHA class I. Examination: BP 108/64, HR 82, soft pansystolic murmur at apex unchanged from previous, no peripheral oedema, clear chest. Repeat booking echo shows unchanged moderate MR, mild LA dilation, normal LV function, and pulmonary artery pressure 28 mmHg.

She asks whether she should continue the monthly injections during pregnancy because a friend told her to stop because the penicillin might harm the baby.

data_table.Examination: Soft PSM apex unchanged; no signs of failure; SFH appropriate; fetal heart 156
data_table.Investigations: Echo: moderate MR, mild LA dilation, normal LVEF 60%, PASP 28 mmHg; Hb 120 g/L; ECG sinus
data_table.Medications: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 28 days; pregnancy multivitamin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her secondary prophylaxis during pregnancy?

options.text: Continue 4-weekly IM BPG at the standard dose throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period
options.rationale: Benzathine benzylpenicillin does not cross the placenta in clinically meaningful amounts and is safe and recommended throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding; the dosing interval is unchanged. Multidisciplinary cardiac-obstetric review is required for any rheumatic heart disease in pregnancy (RHDAustralia Guideline; eTG Antibiotic; RANZCOG; NACCHO).

options.text: Switch to oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg BD for the duration of pregnancy to avoid IM injections
options.rationale: Oral prophylaxis has higher failure rates due to adherence and absorption; IM BPG is preferred. Oral PenV is correct only when IM cannot be tolerated and adherence is supervised (RHDAustralia Guideline).

options.text: Cease benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis until after delivery because penicillin readily crosses the placenta
options.rationale: Penicillin is safe across all trimesters; cessation risks ARF recurrence with permanent valve worsening. Cessation is essentially never correct in active RHD secondary prophylaxis (RHDAustralia Guideline; AMH).

options.text: Shorten the BPG interval to every 3 weeks because pregnancy increases drug clearance and lowers troughs
options.rationale: Standard 4-weekly interval is retained for routine prophylaxis; 3-weekly is reserved for documented breakthrough ARF or selected high-risk situations per specialist advice, not pregnancy alone. 3-weekly is correct after documented breakthrough recurrence (RHDAustralia Guideline).

options.text: Convert to azithromycin 1 g monthly as an alternative because penicillin allergy is more common in pregnancy
options.rationale: Macrolides are only used for documented penicillin allergy; pregnancy does not cause allergy. Azithromycin monthly is correct only in confirmed penicillin allergy (RHDAustralia Guideline).

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease remain leading causes of maternal cardiac morbidity in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women in Australia, with incidence rates around 50-100 times non-Indigenous rates. Secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin G (BPG) IM every 4 weeks continues throughout pregnancy and lactation at the standard adult dose (1.2 million units) - penicillin does not harm the fetus, and interruption is a recurring contributor to recurrence and worsening cardiac disease. Multidisciplinary cardiac-obstetric review is recommended for any woman with moderate or severe rheumatic heart disease, ideally pre-conception, then at booking, 28 weeks and 36 weeks, with planning for mode and timing of delivery, anticoagulation if AF or mechanical valve, and intrapartum endocarditis prophylaxis. Echocardiogram should be repeated antenatally to assess progression. Antibiotic prophylaxis for delivery is generally not required unless there is established endocarditis risk per RHDAustralia/Therapeutic Guidelines.
key_points: BPG is Pregnancy Category A and safe in lactation (AMH)
Cessation risks ARF recurrence and progressive valve damage (RHDAustralia)
Moderate/severe RHD requires combined obstetric-cardiac team (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
Echocardiography baseline + each trimester for moderate or severe disease (RHDAustralia)
Anaesthetic and intrapartum planning at 28-32 weeks (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
explanation.pearls: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G 4-weekly IM continues through pregnancy and lactation at the standard dose for any woman with established secondary prophylaxis for ARF/RHD - interruption is a recurring contributor to maternal cardiac morbidity (RHDAustralia Guideline; RANZCOG).

subtopic: Indigenous health (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander)
tags: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander maternal health
stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 Aboriginal woman from a remote community, with known severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (MVA 1.0 cm2, mean gradient 14 mmHg, PASP 56 mmHg on third-trimester echo, NYHA II antenatally) presents to a regional referral centre at 39+2 weeks in spontaneous labour. She has been on monthly BPG, metoprolol 50 mg BD, and prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily, ceased 18 hours ago.

She is 6 cm dilated, contracting 4-in-10, the fetus is cephalic with reassuring CTG, and an epidural has been sited and is providing good analgesia. Over the last 30 minutes she has become increasingly breathless, oxygen saturation has fallen from 98% to 91% on room air, HR has risen from 96 to 132 (sinus tachycardia on ECG with no shortened diastole arrhythmia and no fibrillatory waves), BP is 105/68, JVP is elevated, and she has bibasal crackles.

Chest x-ray shows pulmonary venous congestion with no focal consolidation. Bedside echo confirms unchanged severe MS with no left atrial thrombus and preserved LV function. The cardiac-obstetric-anaesthetic team is gathering at the bedside, blood is cross-matched, and a high-dependency bed is available.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 105/68, HR 132 sinus, RR 28, SpO2 91% RA -> 95% on 4 L NP, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: JVP +4 cm, bibasal crackles, loud P2, mid-diastolic rumble apex; gravid uterus contracting 4-in-10
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachy, no AF; CXR pulmonary congestion; ABG pH 7.40, pO2 78 mmHg on O2, lactate 1.8; troponin negative
data_table.CTG: Baseline 145, variability normal, accels present, no decels
data_table.Medications: Metoprolol 50 mg BD, BPG monthly, enoxaparin 40 mg ceased 18 h ago, epidural sited

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention to stabilise her acutely?

options.text: IV furosemide plus additional IV beta-blocker to lower heart rate and reduce filling pressures
options.rationale: In severe MS the haemodynamic enemy is tachycardia (shortened diastole, raised LA pressure, pulmonary oedema). Lowering rate with beta-blockade and offloading with a loop diuretic is the cornerstone of acute management while planning an assisted second stage to limit Valsalva effort. Emergency caesarean and balloon valvuloplasty are only required if she fails to stabilise (RANZCOG; ESC Pregnancy Cardiovascular Disease Guideline).

options.text: Tocolyse with IV salbutamol to halt labour and proceed to emergency percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty
options.rationale: Beta-agonist tocolysis causes tachycardia and pulmonary oedema in severe MS - contraindicated. Valvuloplasty is considered antenatally in refractory disease, not in established labour at term. Tocolysis is correct in preterm labour without severe MS (RHDAustralia; ESC 2018).

options.text: Proceed to immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia for acute pulmonary oedema
options.rationale: Fetus is reassuring and labour is progressing; GA carries high haemodynamic risk in severe MS. Vaginal birth with assisted second stage under regional anaesthesia is preferred. Emergency CS is correct with fetal distress or maternal cardiovascular collapse (RANZCOG W-WH 22; ESC 2018).

options.text: Give an IV crystalloid bolus of 500 mL Hartmann's to maintain preload before considering further intervention
options.rationale: Fluid bolus in pulmonary congestion from severe MS worsens pulmonary oedema; preload must be preserved but not increased. Fluid bolus is correct only in clear hypovolaemia, never with pulmonary oedema (RHDAustralia; ESC 2018).

options.text: Commence IV amiodarone infusion for presumed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
options.rationale: ECG shows sinus tachycardia, not AF; amiodarone is reserved for arrhythmia and carries fetal thyroid risk. Amiodarone is correct only in confirmed maternal arrhythmia refractory to safer agents (RHDAustralia; AMH).

explanation.summary: Severe MS decompensates with tachycardia and Valsalva. Acute management is rate control with beta-blocker, diuresis, oxygen, and planned assisted second stage to deliver vaginally under regional analgesia (RHDAustralia; RANZCOG W-WH 22; ESC 2018 Pregnancy CVD).
key_points: Diastolic filling time is the critical variable in MS (ESC 2018)
Beta-blocker rate control is first-line acute therapy (RHDAustralia)
Avoid fluid bolus; manage pulmonary congestion with diuresis (ESC 2018)
Assisted second stage (vacuum/forceps) to limit Valsalva (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
GA caesarean carries higher haemodynamic risk than well-conducted epidural (ESC 2018)
Continue endocarditis-prophylaxis consideration per RHDAustralia for high-risk lesions
explanation.pearls: Anaesthetic plan should be written and reviewed by 32 weeks for any severe valvular lesion in pregnancy (RANZCOG W-WH 22).

subtopic_detail: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander intrapartum - rheumatic mitral stenosis decompensation

stem:
A 24-year-old G2P0 woman in regional Victoria presents at 23+1 weeks by dating ultrasound requesting termination of pregnancy. Morphology ultrasound at 21 weeks showed a fetal cardiac anomaly initially read as a ventricular septal defect, but on tertiary review at 23 weeks was confirmed as hypoplastic left heart syndrome with associated coarctation. She has discussed the diagnosis with paediatric cardiology, including the staged Norwood pathway and its long-term survival and morbidity, and feels unable to proceed with the pregnancy.

She has no medical comorbidities, her support network is intact, she has accessed counselling, and her first pregnancy ended in a first-trimester miscarriage. She specifically asks about the legal pathway in Victoria, whether she must travel interstate, and whether an ethics committee or panel needs to approve the procedure before she can be referred to the tertiary service

data_table.Examination: SFH 24 cm; uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Tertiary fetal echo: hypoplastic left heart syndrome with coarctation; karyotype normal; Hb 120 g/L

lead_in: Which statement best describes the lawful pathway for termination of pregnancy in Victoria at this gestation?

options.text: Termination is lawful on request without any additional consultation up to 24 weeks gestation in Victoria
options.rationale: Victorian Act permits TOP on request up to 24 weeks; this is correct on the law, but BEST practice for advanced gestation with fetal anomaly is the two-doctor tertiary pathway (option C). Option A understates the appropriate referral pathway. On-request alone is correct for early gestations without anomaly (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

options.text: Termination is unlawful after 20 weeks in Victoria and the patient must travel interstate to obtain care
options.rationale: Victoria has no 20-week prohibition; TOP is on-request to 24 weeks and lawful after 24 weeks with two doctors. The anti-pattern is misremembering interstate variations. The 20-week limit applies in some other states (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

options.text: Termination is lawful: she is under the 24-week on-request limit and is referred to a tertiary service
options.rationale: Under the Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008, TOP is lawful on request up to 24 weeks; after 24 weeks it requires two medical practitioners. At 23+1 weeks she is within the on-request limit. Standard practice for a confirmed major fetal anomaly at this gestation is referral to a tertiary service, which will offer feticide and induction of labour with multidisciplinary support (RANZCOG; Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

options.text: Termination requires approval by a formal hospital ethics committee at any gestation in Victoria
options.rationale: Victoria does not require ethics committee approval; the framework is the Abortion Law Reform Act 2008 with practitioner-led decision making. Ethics committee approval was the pre-2008 NSW practice (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

options.text: Termination is only lawful where the fetal anomaly is incompatible with life as defined by statute
options.rationale: No statutory list of qualifying anomalies; the test for TOP after 24 weeks is two-doctor reasonable belief considering all relevant circumstances. A statutory-list framework would be correct only in jurisdictions with such legislation (none in Australia) (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

explanation.summary: Victoria: TOP on-request to 24 weeks; after 24 weeks two doctors must reasonably believe it appropriate considering all relevant circumstances (Abortion Law Reform Act 2008). Late TOP for fetal anomaly is provided in tertiary services with feticide and IOL (RANZCOG; The Royal Women's).
key_points: Victoria: on-request to 24+0 (Abortion Law Reform Act 2008)
NSW: on-request to 22+0; after 22 weeks two specialists must agree (Abortion Law Reform Act 2019 NSW)
Qld: on-request to 22+0; after 22 weeks two doctors agree (Termination of Pregnancy Act 2018 Qld)
SA: on-request to 22+6; after 22+6 two doctors agree (Termination of Pregnancy Act 2021 SA)
WA: on-request to 23+0; after 23 weeks Ministerial panel of two specialists (Public Health Amendment Act 2023 WA)
Tasmania: on-request to 16+0; after 16 weeks two doctors agree (Reproductive Health Act 2013 Tas)
explanation.pearls: All states require conscientious objectors to refer to a non-objecting practitioner (RANZCOG TOP).

subtopic_detail: Termination of pregnancy - Australian state-specific gestational limits

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P2 woman presents to ED 10 days after a medical TOP at 8 weeks using mifepristone-misoprostol from her GP. The procedure was reported as successful with passage of products on day 1 and tapering bleeding for 6 days. Over the last 36 hours she has had heavy bleeding soaking 1 large pad per hour, lower abdominal cramping, low-grade fever (37.8 deg C), foul-smelling discharge, and feels lightheaded on standing.

She has no significant past history, takes no medications, blood group O Rh positive, and breastfed her two prior children. On arrival: BP 96/58, HR 116, T 37.9, RR 18, SpO2 99%. Abdomen tender suprapubically with guarding but no peritonism. Speculum: open external os with brisk bleeding and brown malodorous discharge, products visible at the os. Bedside USS: heterogeneous endometrial collection 38 mm with vascularity on colour Doppler and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Bloods: Hb 88 g/L, WCC 16.4 x 10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, lactate 1.6, group-and-hold sent.

data_table.Examination: Tender suprapubic with guarding; open cervical os with brisk bleed, products visible, foul discharge
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, WCC 16.4, CRP 142, beta-hCG 1820 IU/L, lactate 1.6; USS endometrial collection 38 mm vascular
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Outpatient repeat misoprostol 800 microg vaginal plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days, review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Haemodynamic compromise plus sepsis signs plus active bleeding makes outpatient management unsafe with inadequate source control. The anti-pattern is treating a septic patient as outpatient. Outpatient miso + doxy is correct only in stable patients with incomplete TOP and no sepsis (RANZCOG TOP; eTG Antibiotic).

options.text: Resuscitate with IV access, fluids, group-and-hold, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, then proceed to urgent surgical evacuation of retained products
options.rationale: Septic incomplete abortion with haemorrhage requires resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam per eTG), and source control by urgent surgical evacuation. Delaying evacuation prolongs the source of infection and bleeding (RANZCOG TOP; eTG Sepsis; RANZCOG PPH/Gynae emergencies).

options.text: Admit for IV oxytocin infusion with close observation, deferring evacuation pending blood culture results
options.rationale: Oxytocin has limited effect on a non-puerperal uterus; antibiotics should not wait for cultures in sepsis (ANZICS 1-hour rule); source control must not be delayed. Oxytocin-only is correct in atonic PPH at term, not in septic abortion (eTG Sepsis; ANZICS Sepsis).

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV with observation and serial Hb without antibiotic cover until culture results
options.rationale: TXA is adjunctive but does not address source; delaying antibiotics breaches the 1-hour sepsis standard. TXA is correct as adjunct to source control plus antibiotics, not as sole therapy (eTG Sepsis; ANZICS Sepsis).

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 for presumed ongoing intrauterine pregnancy and discharge home to GP
options.rationale: Methotrexate addresses neither retained products nor sepsis, and is contraindicated in active infection. The anti-pattern is using MTX for any pregnancy-related bleeding. MTX is correct only for unruptured ectopic without infection (AMH; eTG).

explanation.summary: Septic incomplete abortion requires concurrent resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and surgical source control by evacuation of retained products. This is a gynaecological emergency (RANZCOG TOP; eTG Sepsis; ANZICS Sepsis).
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour for sepsis (ANZICS Sepsis)
Source control: surgical evacuation of RPOC (RANZCOG TOP)
Antibiotic regimen: amp + gent + metronidazole or pip-taz (eTG Antibiotic)
Anti-D 250 IU if Rh negative and unsensitised (Australian Red Cross)
Major haemorrhage protocol if Hb continues to fall (RANZCOG PPH)
Inform original prescriber and arrange contraception/follow-up
explanation.pearls: Beware Clostridium sordellii / perfringens infection after medical TOP: profound shock without fever, leucocytosis and haemoconcentration (RANZCOG TOP).

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 30 weeks gestation discloses intimate partner violence during a private antenatal visit after the midwife has seen her alone. Her partner has been verbally and physically abusive for 3 years; the frequency and severity have escalated over the past 6 weeks since she told him she was pregnant. Last week he choked her with both hands until she briefly lost consciousness, threatened to kill her if she left, and removed her mobile phone so she could not contact her sister.

He has access to firearms because he is a licensed recreational shooter. She has two children aged 4 and 6 at home, no immediate family support locally, and no current Apprehended Domestic Violence Order. She has not previously disclosed to a clinician. She is asking what to do; she is frightened, oriented, and engaged. There is a social worker on site this afternoon and a state-funded specialist DV service with crisis accommodation available.

data_table.Examination: Tender 4 cm bruise left flank, faint petechiae over neck, no current acute injury; SFH appropriate, FH 144
data_table.Social: Two children at home (4 and 6), no AVO, partner has firearms access, escalating frequency
data_table.Risk factors: Strangulation, threats to kill, controlling behaviour (phone removed), pregnancy, firearms access

lead_in: Which combination of features in this disclosure most strongly indicates EXTREME risk of intimate partner femicide and mandates immediate crisis-response activation?

options.text: Frequency of arguments and verbal abuse over the past 3 years without any physical injury
options.rationale: Frequency and verbal abuse are markers of abuse but are not the specific extreme-risk discriminators; the cluster in option C predicts lethality more strongly. Verbal abuse alone is correct as a marker of IPV but not as an extreme-risk indicator (1800RESPECT; ANROWS).

options.text: A past episode of pushing without injury approximately 18 months ago and now resolved
options.rationale: Historical low-severity violence is concerning but not in the same risk class as recent strangulation + threats + escalation in pregnancy + firearm access. Historical low-severity is correct as background context, not as extreme-risk indicator (ANROWS).

options.text: Recent non-fatal strangulation, threat to kill, escalation in pregnancy, and firearm access
options.rationale: Non-fatal strangulation, an explicit threat to kill, escalation during pregnancy, abuser access to firearms, and coercive control (such as phone removal) are the strongest single predictors of intimate partner femicide. Together they meet criteria for EXTREME risk on the Danger Assessment and DVSAT and mandate immediate crisis-response activation (NSW Health DV Routine Screening; 1800RESPECT; ANROWS; Danger Assessment).

options.text: Disclosure occurring during the antenatal visit itself, without any other contextual features
options.rationale: The act of disclosure is positive engagement, not a risk marker; risk is determined by the content. Disclosure itself signals trust, not danger (ANROWS).

options.text: Absence of any Apprehended Domestic Violence Order despite the long abusive relationship history
options.rationale: Lack of AVO is common and does not by itself stratify extreme risk. Absence of legal protection raises practical concerns but is not predictive of femicide independently of the danger features (1800RESPECT).

explanation.summary: Non-fatal strangulation, explicit threats to kill, escalation in pregnancy, firearm access, and coercive control are the highest-yield extreme-risk features. Pregnancy is itself a peak-risk period. Activate crisis pathway, safety plan, and structured risk assessment (MARAM in Vic, DVSAT in NSW) (ANROWS; 1800RESPECT; MARAM; NSW DVSAT).
key_points: Non-fatal strangulation: ~7x increased risk of subsequent homicide (ANROWS)
Pregnancy is a peak risk period (1800RESPECT)
Firearm access is a major lethality factor (ANROWS)
Coercive control (phone removal, isolation) is a marker of severe pattern (1800RESPECT)
Use a structured framework: MARAM (Vic) or DVSAT (NSW)
Mandatory reporting of child exposure varies by state - check local Act
explanation.pearls: Strangulation may leave minimal external signs - ask specifically and examine for petechiae, voice change, dysphagia (ANROWS).

subtopic_detail: Domestic violence in pregnancy - escalation risk assessment

stem:
A 34-year-old G4P3 woman in NSW discloses ongoing intimate partner violence during her postnatal home visit at day 14. There have been two physical assault episodes in the past 2 weeks, both witnessed by her 5- and 8-year-old children. The youngest child has begun bedwetting and the older child has been refusing school. The newborn is feeding well and gaining weight; there are no injuries on the infant.

She is asking that nothing be reported to child protection because she fears the four children will be removed from her care. She has agreed to a safety plan, accepted a warm referral to a specialist DV service, and confirmed she is safe to remain at her sister's house tonight. The midwife is a mandated reporter under the NSW Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998, and exposure of children to intimate partner violence meets the threshold of Risk of Significant Harm under the NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide.

data_table.Examination: Maternal: healing perineal repair, no acute injury, EPDS 16. Infant: alert, no injuries, weight gaining
data_table.Social: Two children witnessing assault; behavioural change in both; partner unaware of disclosure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding child protection reporting?

options.text: Honour the woman's request not to report because reporting would breach therapeutic trust and engagement
options.rationale: Mandated reporters cannot suspend the legal duty at the patient's request; the threshold ('risk of significant harm') has been reached. The anti-pattern is conflating therapeutic alliance with legal obligation. Therapeutic-trust framing is correct in informing patients about the report, not in declining to make it (NSW MRG; NSW Children and Young Persons Act 1998).
source_refs: NSW Children and Young Persons Act 1998

options.text: Report only the children's behavioural change to the GP and do not lodge any child protection report
options.rationale: Behavioural change in the context of witnessed IPV meets the NSW Risk of Significant Harm threshold and triggers mandated reporting. Reporting-only-to-GP is correct only for concerns below RoSH threshold (NSW MRG).

options.text: Lodge a Risk of Significant Harm report to the NSW Child Protection Helpline and continue the safety plan
options.rationale: Exposure of children to intimate partner violence meets the NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide threshold for Risk of Significant Harm. Reporting does not equal removal; the report triggers a structured response that can include in-home support. The midwife should explain her legal duty, continue the safety plan and warm DV referrals, and document the woman's agreement to ongoing engagement (NSW Children and Young Persons Act 1998; NSW Mandatory Reporter Guide; NSW Health DV Routine Screening).

options.text: Contact NSW Police directly to seek an Apprehended Domestic Violence Order on behalf of the woman
options.rationale: ADVO applications are typically made by police or the protected person; clinicians can encourage and support but the immediate mandated step is child protection reporting because children are involved. Police-direct contact is correct in immediate physical-threat situations (NSW MRG; NSW Police ADVO guidance).

options.text: Wait until the next clinic visit in a fortnight to allow the woman more time to consider
options.rationale: Delaying a RoSH report once threshold is met breaches the mandated reporter duty. Delay is essentially never correct once RoSH threshold is crossed (NSW MRG).

explanation.summary: In NSW, witnessing repeated domestic violence with behavioural change in the children meets the Risk of Significant Harm threshold and mandates a report to the NSW Child Protection Helpline, alongside continued safety planning and specialist DV referral. Transparency with the mother is best practice (NSW MRG; NSW Health DV Routine Screening).
key_points: Risk of Significant Harm threshold triggers mandatory reporting (NSW MRG)
All states have mandatory reporter pathways; thresholds and scope differ (each state Act)
Witnessing IPV counts as exposure to harm (NSW MRG)
Report does not replace DV safety planning - both proceed (NSW Health)
Tell the parent (when safe) that a report is being made
explanation.pearls: Use the NSW MRG decision tree on the spot if uncertain about threshold (NSW MRG).

sources.label: NSW Children and Young Persons Act 1998

stem:
A 26-year-old woman disclosed intimate partner violence 4 weeks ago and you drew up a written safety plan (code words, packed bag at her sister's, 1800RESPECT number). Today she reports her partner has been kind, brought flowers, and agreed to attend couples counselling; she is reconsidering whether she still needs the plan. No acute injuries. The previous incident involved choking, which she had not initially disclosed.

She is calm, oriented, has no children, joint rental, independent income, family interstate. She asks whether the change means the cycle of abuse is over and whether joint counselling would now be safe.

data_table.Examination: No acute injury; old healed bruising right upper arm
data_table.Social: No children; joint rental; independent income; family interstate; partner currently in 'reconciliation' phase per her description

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Validate her experience, explain the reconciliation/honeymoon phase of the cycle, advise against joint couples counselling (which is unsafe in active IPV with prior strangulation), reinforce the safety plan and offer ongoing review
options.rationale: Joint couples counselling is contraindicated in active IPV (especially with non-fatal strangulation, a major homicide risk marker) because it places the victim at risk and reinforces coercive control. Validation, education about the cycle and safety planning are the recommended steps (RACGP; WHO; ANROWS).

options.text: Reassure her that the apology phase usually means violence will not recur and discard the safety plan
options.rationale: The honeymoon phase predictably gives way to renewed tension and incident phases; reassurance and abandoning the plan is unsafe. Reassurance is correct only when the abuser has engaged with intervention and tracked behavioural change is sustained (RACGP; WHO).

options.text: Insist she leave the relationship today as the only safe option
options.rationale: Leaving is the highest-risk time for homicide; her autonomy and timing must be respected with safety planning. Insistence-on-leaving is correct only with consent-based safety planning toward that goal (ANROWS).

options.text: Recommend joint couples counselling because the partner has agreed to attend
options.rationale: Joint counselling is contraindicated in active IPV; it provides the perpetrator a platform and worsens risk. Joint counselling is correct only in non-violent relationship conflict, never in active IPV (WHO; RACGP).

options.text: Discharge her from clinical follow-up because she now feels safe
options.rationale: Ongoing follow-up is recommended through cycles; discharging removes support at the highest-risk time. Discharge is correct only when patient is consistently safe with established external support (RACGP).

explanation.summary: Cycle of abuse (tension, incident, reconciliation) means that the apology/honeymoon phase commonly precedes recurrence. Safety plans should be preserved and updated; couples counselling is contraindicated during active IPV; leaving is itself a high-risk transition requiring planning (1800RESPECT; ANROWS).
key_points: Walker cycle: tension -> incident -> reconciliation -> repeat (1800RESPECT)
Leaving is the highest-risk period (ANROWS)
Couples therapy contraindicated in active IPV (1800RESPECT)
Safety plans: code word, packed bag, important documents, escape route (1800RESPECT)
Document outside hand-held notes; offer 1800RESPECT contact
explanation.pearls: Most women leave 5-7 times before final departure; do not measure success by single-visit resolution (ANROWS).

subtopic_detail: Domestic violence - cycle and safety planning

stem:
A 23-year-old woman presents to ED 5 days (120 hours) after non-consensual unprotected vaginal intercourse with an unknown male at a party. She did not present sooner because of fear of judgement. She is otherwise well, has no medical history, no allergies, takes no regular medications, has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle with last period 11 days ago (so currently around day 11 and within the fertile window), and has previously had her three-dose HPV vaccine and a full primary hepatitis B course as a child.

The local sexual assault medical service is contactable, the on-call gynaecology registrar can insert a copper IUD today, and the assailant's HIV status is unknown.

data_table.Examination: No acute injury; healing 1 cm abrasion left knee; speculum: no acute trauma, no visible discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative; baseline HIV Ag/Ab, HBsAg/HBsAb/anti-HBc, HCV Ab, syphilis EIA, NAATs for chlamydia/gonorrhoea/trichomonas sent
data_table.Cycle: Day 11 of regular 28-day cycle; previous LMP 11 days ago

lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate component of management at this time?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single-dose emergency contraceptive within the 72-hour licensed window
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel EC efficacy is limited to within 96 hours of unprotected intercourse; not first-line beyond that window. LNG-EC is correct within 72-96 hours of exposure, not beyond (Family Planning Australia; eTG).

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single-dose emergency contraceptive within the 120-hour licensed window
options.rationale: Ulipristal extends the window to 120 hours but evidence supports efficacy up to 120 hours, and at exactly 120 hours efficacy is borderline; copper IUD is more reliable. UPA is correct up to 120 hours post-coital when IUD is not desired (Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Copper IUD insertion as emergency contraception, with empirical STI prophylaxis and sexual assault referral
options.rationale: Copper IUD inserted up to 5 days after the earliest predicted ovulation is the most effective emergency contraception (failure rate <1%) and is the only option licensed beyond 120 hours. At day 11 of a 28-day cycle she remains within the fertile window. Empirical STI prophylaxis (ceftriaxone, azithromycin or doxycycline, metronidazole) and warm referral to the sexual assault service complete management (RANZCOG; ASHM Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Guidelines).

options.text: Commence HIV non-occupational post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir-emtricitabine-dolutegravir for a full 28-day course
options.rationale: HIV PEP must be commenced within 72 hours of exposure; at 120 hours the window has closed. PEP is correct only within 72 hours of exposure (ASHM PEP Guidelines).

options.text: Accelerated hepatitis B vaccination course because the patient is presumed unprotected after childhood priming
options.rationale: She has documented completed primary hepatitis B course; check anti-HBs titre rather than re-vaccinate. Re-vaccination is correct only if titre is sub-protective (<10 mIU/mL) and immune memory cannot be relied upon (Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: At 120 hours post-assault, the most effective EC option still available is the copper IUD (up to 5 days). Oral EC efficacy is borderline; HIV PEP is no longer indicated. Empirical STI prophylaxis and sexual assault service referral remain appropriate (Family Planning Australia; Australasian STI Management Guidelines; ASHM; RANZCOG).
key_points: Levonorgestrel EC: up to 96 hours (Family Planning Australia)
Ulipristal EC: up to 120 hours (Family Planning Australia)
Copper IUD EC: up to 5 days after earliest ovulation or 5 days after intercourse (Family Planning Australia)
HIV PEP: must start within 72 hours (ASHM)
Forensic kit: typically <72 h, some samples up to 7 days (RANZCOG)
Sexual assault psychological support remains available regardless of timing
explanation.pearls: Copper IUD is the only EC method that simultaneously provides ongoing contraception (Family Planning Australia).

subtopic_detail: Sexual assault - presentation beyond 72 hours

stem:
A 19-year-old woman presents to ED 18 hours after a night out, with no memory of several hours of the evening, having woken in an unfamiliar bed beside someone she did not know, with disarranged clothing. She is concerned that her drink was spiked. She last urinated on waking 1 hour ago and has had three sips of water since.

She has had no alcohol or illicit drugs to her knowledge other than two drinks she ordered and saw poured. She has no known medical conditions and takes no regular medications. She is alert, oriented, distressed but cooperative. The local sexual assault medical service is contactable and a forensic medical examiner is available within the hour. She has not decided whether to report to police.

The forensic examiner will offer toxicology and asks which sample to collect first given the long window since exposure and the short half-lives of common drug-facilitated sexual assault agents such as GHB and benzodiazepines.

data_table.Examination: No acute injury identified; speculum to be performed by forensic examiner if she consents
data_table.Investigations: Pending forensic samples, baseline STI screen, beta-hCG
data_table.Timing: 18 hours since suspected event; first void available; minimal hydration

lead_in: Which sample provides the highest yield for detection of common drug-facilitated sexual assault agents at this presentation?

options.text: A clotted serum sample taken now for benzodiazepine and GHB quantification analysis
options.rationale: Many DFSA agents (notably GHB) have short serum half-lives (~30-60 min); by 18 hours serum is typically negative even when urine remains positive. Serum is correct for early-window forensic testing (<6 hours), not at 18 hours (RANZCOG sexual assault).

options.text: First-catch urine sample now and a repeat urine sample at the next void
options.rationale: Urine is the highest-yield matrix for drug-facilitated sexual assault toxicology because most agents (GHB, benzodiazepines, ketamine) have short serum half-lives but concentrate in urine and can be detected for 12 to 96 hours depending on the agent. A first-catch sample now plus a repeat at the next void maximises detection (RANZCOG; NSW Health Sexual Assault Services; ANZFSS forensic toxicology guidance).

options.text: Scalp hair sample taken now for later segmental analysis after a 4-week growth window
options.rationale: Hair toxicology has a role but optimal timing is 3-5 weeks after exposure to allow the dosed segment to grow above the scalp. Hair is correct for retrospective single-dose detection, not at 18 hours (RANZCOG sexual assault).

options.text: Gastric aspirate via nasogastric tube to recover any residual ingested drug from the stomach
options.rationale: NG aspirate is not standard in DFSA workup and is invasive without yield. NG aspirate is correct only in known recent acute oral overdose with bowel decontamination intent (RANZCOG sexual assault).

options.text: Oral mucosal swab to recover any drug residues from saliva and the buccal mucosa surface
options.rationale: Oral fluid has a shorter detection window than urine and is not the preferred forensic toxicology matrix for DFSA at 18 hours. Oral fluid is correct for very recent (1-12 hour) exposures in some testing contexts, not at 18 hours (RANZCOG sexual assault).

explanation.summary: Urine is the highest-yield forensic toxicology matrix in suspected drug-facilitated sexual assault within the first 24 hours; collect first void plus serial samples. Hair analysis is reserved for late presentations 3-5 weeks later (RANZCOG sexual assault; Family Planning Australia).
key_points: Urine: best matrix to ~24 h (RANZCOG)
Serum: short window (~12 h for benzo, <6 h for GHB) (RANZCOG)
Hair: collect at 3-5 weeks (RANZCOG)
Always handle via chain of custody (RANZCOG)
Concurrent EC, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP assessment, support
explanation.pearls: Encourage the patient to not pass urine without forensic collection if she presents within 12-24 h of suspected event (RANZCOG sexual assault).

subtopic_detail: Sexual assault - drug-facilitated and toxicology evidence

stem:
A 29-year-old G2P2 woman is reviewed at 5 weeks postpartum at her general practice. She has focal epilepsy controlled on carbamazepine 400 mg BD (level stable, no seizures for 3 years), is exclusively breastfeeding her baby (infant weight tracking the 50th centile, no concerns at the maternal-child health nurse review), and had a normal vaginal birth with no thromboembolic history, no migraine, normotensive, BMI 24, non-smoker, and a normal Hb of 122 g/L.

She has read about long-acting reversible contraception and is aware that carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer. She wishes to space the next pregnancy by at least 3 years and prefers a method that does not require daily adherence or rely on her remembering to attend for 3-monthly injections. She is happy with all options being on the table, including LARCs and combined methods, and asks the GP to recommend the most reliable option that will not be undermined by her antiepileptic.

data_table.Examination: Well, lactating; uterus involuted
data_table.Medications: Carbamazepine 400 mg BD; folic acid 5 mg daily (planned for future pregnancy)
data_table.Pregnancy plans: Spacing at least 3 years; LARC preferred

lead_in: Which contraceptive option is the most appropriate first-line recommendation?

options.text: Etonogestrel 68 mg subdermal implant (Implanon NXT) inserted in the inner upper arm
options.rationale: Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine) significantly reduce etonogestrel via CYP3A4; implant is UKMEC 3. Etonogestrel implant is correct only when not on enzyme-inducing drugs (Family Planning Australia; FSRH UKMEC).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinyloestradiol 30 microg with levonorgestrel) taken daily
options.rationale: Enzyme inducers reduce COCP efficacy and COCP is generally avoided <6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding due to milk supply and VTE concerns. COCP is correct only after 6 weeks postpartum, not breastfeeding-dependent, and not on enzyme inducers (Family Planning Australia; FSRH UKMEC).

options.text: Progestogen-only pill (norethisterone 350 microg) taken at the same time every day
options.rationale: POP efficacy is reduced by enzyme inducers; not recommended. POP is correct in non-enzyme-induced women preferring oral hormonal contraception (Family Planning Australia; FSRH UKMEC).

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine device (Mirena) or copper IUD inserted as a LARC
options.rationale: Intrauterine devices (LNG-IUD and copper IUD) deliver hormone locally or are non-hormonal and have efficacy that is NOT reduced by enzyme inducers; both are UKMEC 1 in women on enzyme-inducing AEDs and compatible with breastfeeding. They provide the long-acting reversible spacing this woman requests (Family Planning Australia; FSRH UKMEC; FSRH Drug Interactions with Hormonal Contraception).

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks as her contraceptive method
options.rationale: DMPA efficacy is not significantly reduced by enzyme inducers (UKMEC 1), so acceptable; however not the single BEST when IUD is suitable and woman wants long-term spacing. DMPA has bone density and weight effects. DMPA is correct when LARC is declined or implant/IUD contraindicated (Family Planning Australia; FSRH UKMEC).

explanation.summary: Enzyme-inducing AEDs reduce efficacy of oestrogen, progestogen-only pill and the etonogestrel implant. IUDs (LNG and copper) and DMPA are not significantly affected. IUD is preferred as long-acting, non-daily, breastfeeding-compatible (Family Planning Australia; FSRH UKMEC; FSRH Drug Interactions).
key_points: Enzyme inducers: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarb, primidone, topiramate >200 mg, rifampicin (FSRH)
Affected: COCP, POP, implant, transdermal patch, ring
Not affected: LNG-IUD, copper IUD, DMPA (FSRH)
If on enzyme inducer and COCP required: 50 microg EE or alternative method (FSRH)
Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, sodium valproate are NOT enzyme inducers
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine levels are themselves reduced by COCP - bidirectional interaction; this is opposite to the carbamazepine direction (FSRH Drug Interactions).

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - breastfeeding + enzyme-inducing AED

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 woman is reviewed 6 weeks postpartum at her general practice. She had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years ago with weight loss from 142 kg to 78 kg (current BMI 28, stable). She is bottle feeding by choice, normotensive, non-smoker, no migraine, no VTE history, and is on regular vitamin and iron supplementation post-bariatric. She is asking the GP for contraception and is happy with all options, including LARCs.

She specifically asks whether she can simply take her sister's combined oral contraceptive pill, because she has heard that any oral hormonal method is reliable. She also asks whether a return of regular cycles is required before she starts a method, given she is not yet menstruating because she is using progesterone-containing analgesia

data_table.Examination: Well, lactation suppressed; surgical scars from RYGB
data_table.Medications: Multivitamin, iron, vitamin B12 IM 3-monthly, calcium + vitamin D

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate consideration when selecting contraception for this woman?

options.text: Oral hormonal contraception is unaffected because Roux-en-Y bypass does not alter small-molecule absorption
options.rationale: Roux-en-Y bypass alters oral hormonal absorption and reduces COCP/POP efficacy; FSRH advises against reliance on oral methods after malabsorptive procedures. Oral methods are correct only after restrictive procedures (sleeve gastrectomy) without malabsorption (FSRH UKMEC; FSRH Overweight/Obesity).

options.text: Long-acting reversible methods are preferred because oral hormonal absorption is reduced post-bypass
options.rationale: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass bypasses the proximal small bowel and reduces absorption of oral hormonal contraceptives, which lowers their reliability. LARCs (LNG-IUD, copper IUD, etonogestrel implant, DMPA) do not depend on enteric absorption and are first-line after bariatric bypass surgery (Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare; UKMEC; RANZCOG).

options.text: Combined hormonal contraception is preferred to ensure cycle regularity post-bariatric surgery in this patient
options.rationale: Oral COCP efficacy is reduced after RYGB; transdermal/vaginal CHC may be considered but post-bariatric weight loss instability and weight rebound make LARC preferred. CHC for cycle control is correct in non-bariatric patients (FSRH Overweight/Obesity).

options.text: Await return of regular menstrual cycles before starting any contraception in this patient
options.rationale: Fertility returns rapidly postpartum (improves dramatically post-bariatric); contraception should be in place to avoid early conception (recommended 12-24 month spacing). Awaiting cycles is correct in non-fertile-period delays only (Family Planning Australia; FSRH Overweight/Obesity).

options.text: Permanent sterilisation should be recommended because pregnancy is unsafe after bariatric surgery
options.rationale: Pregnancy after bariatric is safe with planned spacing and nutritional surveillance; recommending sterilisation is not appropriate without patient-led discussion. Sterilisation is correct only when family is complete and patient-initiated (RANZCOG; FSRH Overweight/Obesity).

explanation.summary: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and other malabsorptive bariatric procedures reduce oral hormonal contraceptive absorption. LARCs (LNG-IUD, copper IUD, implant) and DMPA are the preferred choices because they bypass intestinal absorption. Restrictive procedures alone do not have the same effect (FSRH UKMEC; FSRH Overweight/Obesity; Family Planning Australia).
key_points: Malabsorptive procedures: Roux-en-Y, BPD, duodenal switch (FSRH)
Restrictive only: sleeve gastrectomy, gastric band - oral methods acceptable (FSRH)
LARC bypasses absorption issue (FSRH)
Plan pregnancy 12-24 months post-bariatric (RANZCOG)
Folate, B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D surveillance pre-pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Post-bariatric the patient may be hyperfertile compared to her pre-operative state; do not assume the previous infertility persists (FSRH Overweight/Obesity).

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - post-bariatric surgery

stem:
A 30-year-old G1P1 woman with well-controlled HIV (CD4 720, viral load <50 copies/mL on tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine-bictegravir) is reviewed at 6 weeks postpartum. She is formula feeding per current Australian guidance, an option chosen after counselling once viral suppression was sustained, and the infant has completed post-exposure prophylaxis per ASHM. She is normotensive, BMI 25, non-smoker, no migraine, no VTE history, and no other comorbidity.

She wants reliable contraception for at least 2 years, preferably long-acting and not requiring daily adherence. Her HIV physician confirms she will remain on bictegravir-based therapy and is not on any enzyme-inducing antiretroviral. She specifically asks whether the implant will still work on her HIV regimen and whether she needs efavirenz to be added for the implant to be effective Her infectious-diseases physician has cleared any contraceptive method Her HIV physician noted no enzyme-inducing antiretrovirals on her regimen.

data_table.Examination: Well; uterus involuted
data_table.Medications: Tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine-bictegravir daily; no other medication
data_table.Investigations: CD4 720, HIV viral load <50 copies/mL

lead_in: Which contraceptive option is most appropriate without significant interaction concerns?

options.text: Etonogestrel 68 mg subdermal implant (Implanon NXT) inserted in the inner upper arm
options.rationale: Bictegravir/integrase inhibitor-based regimens (including tenofovir alafenamide-emtricitabine-bictegravir) do not significantly affect hormonal contraceptive efficacy; the etonogestrel implant is suitable. NNRTI-based regimens (efavirenz) and protease inhibitor/ritonavir-boosted regimens can reduce hormonal contraceptive levels (ASHM HIV Management; FSRH Drug Interactions; Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill in the immediate postpartum period because she is not breastfeeding
options.rationale: CHC is contraindicated <6 weeks postpartum due to VTE risk regardless of breastfeeding (UKMEC 4 <3 weeks, UKMEC 3 from 3-6 weeks). Efficacy with bictegravir is preserved but postpartum VTE concern dominates. COCP is correct >6 weeks postpartum without other contraindications (FSRH UKMEC).

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant only if efavirenz is added to her antiretroviral regimen
options.rationale: Efavirenz (NNRTI) is enzyme-inducing and REDUCES etonogestrel efficacy; adding it would worsen interactions. The anti-pattern is conditioning the implant on an interacting drug. Bictegravir as her current regimen preserves implant efficacy (FSRH Drug Interactions; ASHM).

options.text: Avoid all hormonal methods because of HIV-related immune effects on contraceptive efficacy
options.rationale: Well-controlled HIV does not alter hormonal contraceptive efficacy; the relevant issue is specific drug interactions, not HIV. Hormonal avoidance is correct only with documented interacting ARV regimen (FSRH UKMEC; ASHM).

options.text: Permanent surgical sterilisation as the only safe contraceptive option in women with HIV
options.rationale: No contraceptive method is unsafe purely on basis of well-controlled HIV; reproductive autonomy and full method choice apply. Sterilisation is correct only when family complete and patient-initiated, never as 'only safe option' (ASHM HIV Management; UKMEC).

explanation.summary: Modern integrase inhibitor regimens (bictegravir, dolutegravir, raltegravir) do not significantly interact with hormonal contraception; the etonogestrel implant and other LARCs are appropriate. NNRTIs (efavirenz, nevirapine) and ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors reduce contraceptive efficacy. CHC has the usual <6-week postpartum VTE restrictions (ASHM HIV Management; FSRH Drug Interactions; FSRH UKMEC).
key_points: Integrase inhibitors (bictegravir, dolutegravir, raltegravir): no major interaction (FSRH)
NNRTIs (efavirenz, nevirapine): reduce hormonal contraception (FSRH)
Ritonavir-boosted PIs: reduce hormonal contraception (FSRH)
IUDs (LNG and copper) are UKMEC 1 in HIV with no AIDS-defining illness (FSRH UKMEC)
Australian infant feeding guidance: formula feeding currently advised even if maternal U=U (ASHM)
explanation.pearls: Always check the specific ART regimen before assuming interactions; integrase-only era has changed the rules (FSRH Drug Interactions).

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - HIV on ART

subtopic: Indigenous health (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander)
tags: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander maternal health
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 Aboriginal woman from a regional town presents at 11 weeks for booking with her local ACCHO. Her two previous pregnancies were complicated by gestational diabetes managed with diet and metformin, and both babies were macrosomic (birth weights 4.3 kg and 4.5 kg with shoulder dystocia in the second). Between pregnancies she lost touch with primary care and has not had her glucose checked.

Her BMI is 32 and BP is 122/76. There is a strong family history of type 2 diabetes (mother, two siblings). At booking, the GP arranges fasting venous plasma glucose and HbA1c as part of the early antenatal panel recommended by ADIPS and RANZCOG for high-risk women. Results: fasting venous plasma glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.7% (50 mmol/mol), urine ketones negative. She is otherwise well, on folic acid and iodine, and asks whether she has GDM or something different.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no glycosuria today
data_table.Investigations: Fasting plasma glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.7% (50 mmol/mol), urine ketones negative
data_table.Past obstetric: Two prior GDM, macrosomic infants 4.3 and 4.5 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Reassure that values are normal in pregnancy and re-screen with 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks
options.rationale: FPG >=7.0 and HbA1c >=6.5% in early pregnancy meets ADIPS criteria for diabetes in pregnancy (likely pre-existing T2DM), not GDM; treating as normal misses pre-existing disease. Re-screen at 24-28 weeks is correct only for FPG <5.1 with no diabetes-range values (ADIPS Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy 2022).

options.text: Diagnose diabetes in pregnancy, commence lifestyle measures and metformin, refer to multidisciplinary clinic
options.rationale: FPG >=7.0 or HbA1c >=6.5% at any time in pregnancy meets criteria for diabetes in pregnancy (likely pre-existing type 2), not GDM. Management mirrors pre-existing T2DM in pregnancy: lifestyle intervention, metformin, early multidisciplinary diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic review, a detailed fetal anomaly scan, and early ophthalmology and renal screening for undiagnosed end-organ damage (ADIPS; RANZCOG; NACCHO).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes on the FPG threshold of >=5.1 and commence dietary advice only
options.rationale: FPG 5.1-6.0 with no diabetes-range result is GDM; this woman exceeds the diabetes threshold and HbA1c is also in diabetes range. GDM diagnosis is correct only when values are sub-diabetes-threshold (FPG 5.1-6.9 with HbA1c <6.5%) (ADIPS).

options.text: Repeat the fasting plasma glucose in 4 weeks before initiating any pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Delaying intervention by 4 weeks misses critical early-pregnancy organogenesis-period glycaemic control. Delay is correct only for clearly borderline single-test results with no clinical concerns (ADIPS; RANZCOG Diabetes in Pregnancy).

options.text: Commence insulin glargine immediately as monotherapy without any metformin or lifestyle intervention being trialled
options.rationale: First-line pharmacotherapy in pregnancy for overt T2DM is usually metformin with stepwise insulin addition; insulin-only without lifestyle and metformin is not standard. Insulin-first is correct in severe hyperglycaemia (FPG >11) or metformin contraindication (ADIPS; RANZCOG; AMH).

explanation.summary: Early-pregnancy FPG >=7.0 mmol/L OR HbA1c >=6.5% OR random >=11.1 = overt diabetes in pregnancy (typically previously undiagnosed T2DM). Management = treat as pre-existing diabetes with MDT clinic, tight targets, early anomaly screening, retinal and renal baseline. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women have higher T2DM prevalence and benefit from integrated culturally safe care (ADIPS Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy; RANZCOG Diabetes in Pregnancy; RACGP).
key_points: FPG >=5.1, 1h >=10.0, 2h >=8.5 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT = GDM (ADIPS)
FPG >=7.0 or HbA1c >=6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or random >=11.1 = overt diabetes in pregnancy (ADIPS)
Treat overt diabetes in pregnancy as pre-existing T2DM (RANZCOG)
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander-specific early screening recommended at booking (ADIPS; RACGP)
Metformin + insulin if needed; glargine and aspart commonly used (AMH)
explanation.pearls: Macrosomia + prior GDM + family history of T2DM mandates early-booking FPG/HbA1c, not waiting for 24-28 weeks (ADIPS).

subtopic_detail: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander maternal health - hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman in Perth, Western Australia presents at 24+2 weeks gestation by ultrasound requesting termination of pregnancy. She has no medical comorbidities and no fetal anomaly. The pregnancy is unwanted but she had previously been undecided. She is certain of her decision now and asks her GP to refer her. The GP knows the new WA Public Health Amendment (Abortion) Act 2023 was enacted in early 2024 with different rules above and below 23 weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound singleton live IUP 11+0 weeks; blood group O Rh positive

lead_in: Which statement most accurately reflects the legal pathway for her TOP in WA?

options.text: Lawful on request up to 23 weeks with one practitioner; at 24+2 she needs assessment and agreement by two practitioners, at least one being an O&G or in consultation with one
options.rationale: Under the WA Public Health Amendment (Abortion) Act 2023, TOP is lawful on request up to 23 weeks (with one practitioner), and after 23 weeks requires assessment by two medical practitioners with specialist input. Partner consent is not required (WA Department of Health; SHQ WA).

options.text: Unlawful in WA at this gestation under any circumstances; she must travel interstate to access termination of pregnancy at this stage of her current pregnancy
options.rationale: TOP after 23 weeks is lawful in WA with two-practitioner assessment; interstate travel is not required. The anti-pattern is treating all advanced-gestation TOP as illegal. Interstate transfer is correct only when local provider declines (WA Act 2023).

options.text: Partner consent is required before the procedure despite her capacity to consent and the disclosed intimate partner violence in the relationship
options.rationale: No Australian state or territory requires partner consent for TOP. Partner consent is never legally required in Australia (WA Act 2023; equivalent state legislation).

options.text: A mandatory 7-day waiting period applies from first consultation to procedure regardless of clinical urgency or any current safety concerns identified
options.rationale: WA's 2023 Act removed the previous mandatory waiting period and counselling requirement. 7-day waiting is correct only in jurisdictions with such legal requirements (WA Act 2023; SHQ WA).

options.text: Must be performed surgically; medical TOP is not available in WA at any gestation despite the availability of standard misoprostol-based induction regimens
options.rationale: Both medical and surgical TOP are available in WA; choice depends on gestation and clinical factors. Surgical-only is correct only when medical TOP is contraindicated or gestation is too advanced (SHQ WA).

explanation.summary: The WA Public Health Amendment (Abortion) Act 2023 decriminalised TOP and allows on-request access up to 23 weeks with one medical practitioner. After 23 weeks a Ministerial-approved panel of two specialists must agree. Other jurisdictional comparators are in the key points (WA Public Health Amendment Act 2023; RANZCOG TOP).
key_points: WA: on-request to 23 weeks; >23 weeks panel of two specialists (WA Act 2023)
Vic: 24 weeks on-request (Vic Act 2008)
NSW: 22 weeks on-request (NSW Act 2019)
Qld: 22 weeks on-request (Qld Act 2018)
SA: 22+6 on-request (SA Act 2021)
Tas: 16 weeks on-request (Tas Act 2013)
No state requires partner consent
Conscientious objectors must refer (RANZCOG TOP)
explanation.pearls: Cross-jurisdictional travel still occurs for late TOP due to capacity rather than legality (RANZCOG TOP).

subtopic_detail: TOP - state-specific gestational law - WA

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 woman is 34 weeks pregnant and has an active Apprehended Domestic Violence Order in NSW against her former partner, who is the father of the unborn child. The order prohibits him contacting her or approaching within 100 metres of her residence and workplace. She presents to the maternity day-assessment unit for routine review and is anxious because her former partner has been ringing the hospital switchboard asking for her appointment times and 'information about his child'.

She is fully engaged in antenatal care, has a written safety plan, is supported by a hospital social worker, and has a planned hospital birth. She asks specifically whether the ADVO applies inside the hospital, whether her former partner has any right to be told her appointment times because he is the father, and what the hospital can do to ensure he cannot find out when she will be in the building.

data_table.Examination: SFH 34 cm, fetal heart 142, cephalic
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal bloods normal
data_table.Social: Active ADVO; ex-partner attempting information access via switchboard; social worker engaged

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next action with respect to her hospital information access and safety?

options.text: Provide the former partner with appointment times because he has a paternal right to information about the unborn child
options.rationale: No automatic paternal right to maternal health information; the woman is the patient and consent governs disclosure. Disclosure would breach NSW Health privacy and ADVO protective intent. Paternal disclosure is correct only with the patient's explicit consent (NSW Health DV Routine Screening; NSW Health Privacy Manual).

options.text: Flag the medical record as confidential, instruct switchboard and reception not to release any information, and notify security
options.rationale: Hospital information access is a critical component of the safety plan in active intimate partner violence with an ADVO. The medical record should be flagged as confidential, the ADVO documented, switchboard and reception instructed not to release any information, the social worker and hospital security notified, and the safety plan for arrival and discharge confirmed. Paternity does not override the ADVO or confer a right to maternal appointment information (NSW Health DV Routine Screening; NSW Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007).

options.text: Transfer her care to a different hospital to break the trail without involving her in the decision
options.rationale: Transfer without patient agreement breaks continuity, undermines relationship she has built with the team. Transfer is correct only with patient agreement and clear safety benefit (NSW Health DV Routine Screening).

options.text: Tell the partner the ADVO does not apply to the hospital so he may attend appointments
options.rationale: ADVOs apply across all locations as worded by the magistrate; hospital is not exempt. Inviting attendance contradicts the order. Attendance is correct only when the ADVO explicitly permits and the patient consents (NSW Police ADVO guidance; NSW DV Routine Screening).

options.text: Restrict her from public maternity care until the ADVO is formally upgraded by the court
options.rationale: Restricting care is unsafe and inappropriate; the response is to make care safe, not withdraw it. Care restriction is essentially never correct in IPV (NSW Health DV Routine Screening).

explanation.summary: When an active ADVO/DVO is in place, hospital response is to restrict-flag the record, brief switchboard and reception, brief security, coordinate with the social worker, and plan safe arrival and discharge for the birth. There is no automatic paternal right to maternal health information (NSW Health DV Routine Screening; NSW Health Privacy Manual).
key_points: Patient consent governs disclosure of her health information (NSW Health Privacy)
ADVO applies across all locations including hospital (NSW Police)
Restricted record flag is a routine NSW Health mechanism
Coordinate with hospital security and social work for arrival/discharge (NSW Health)
Maintain access to care, not withdraw it
explanation.pearls: Document the ADVO conditions in the safety plan section of the record; review at each contact (NSW Health DV Routine Screening).

subtopic_detail: DV - DVO/AVO interaction with antenatal care planning

stem:
A 49-year-old G3P3 presents with a 9-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding. Cycles have shortened from 28 to 22 days, last 8 to 10 days, and she changes a fully soaked pad every 90 minutes on the worst two days with passage of 5-cent-piece-sized clots. She reports two episodes of intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months. Her BMI is 34, she has type 2 diabetes on metformin, and she has never been on hormonal contraception.

There is no postcoital bleeding, no dyspareunia, and her last cervical screen 18 months ago was HPV negative. She is not sexually active currently and uses no contraception. On examination her abdomen is soft with no palpable mass; speculum shows a healthy cervix and no cervical lesion; bimanual reveals a bulky but mobile uterus, no adnexal mass. Pregnancy test is negative. FBC shows Hb 98 g/L with MCV 74 fL and ferritin 6 microg/L. TSH and coagulation screen are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/84 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, T 36.6 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: BMI 34. Bulky mobile uterus. Cervix healthy. No adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 microg/L, TSH normal, coags normal, HPV negative 18 months ago.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Commence tranexamic acid 1 g tds during menses and review
options.rationale: TXA is first-line medical therapy for HMB without structural cause, but empirical treatment in a woman >45 with IMB and unopposed-oestrogen risk factors without first excluding malignancy is inappropriate. TXA is correct after endometrial sampling excludes hyperplasia/cancer (RANZCOG).

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test with HPV partial genotyping today
options.rationale: She is in routine 5-yearly screening interval with recent negative HPV; bleeding pattern points to endometrial rather than cervical source. Repeat CST is correct with new cervical symptoms or visible cervical lesion (NCSP; RANZCOG).

options.text: Pelvic MRI to characterise the bulky uterus before further management
options.rationale: MRI is second-line imaging used to map fibroids prior to surgery or when TVUS is inconclusive; not first investigation. MRI is correct after TVUS identifies a complex finding requiring better characterisation (RANZCOG).

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound and outpatient endometrial biopsy at this visit
options.rationale: Age over 45 with HMB plus intermenstrual bleeding and obesity/diabetes (unopposed oestrogen risk factors) mandates endometrial assessment to exclude hyperplasia/carcinoma; TVUS plus Pipelle biopsy is the recommended first-line workup (RANZCOG AUB statement; Therapeutic Guidelines Gynaecology).

options.text: Outpatient hysteroscopy without prior endometrial sampling or pelvic imaging
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy is indicated when TVUS shows focal pathology or when blind sampling is non-diagnostic; initial workup is TVUS plus Pipelle. Hysteroscopy-first is correct only when TVUS already shows focal lesion (e.g., polyp) (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

explanation.summary: In HMB, age over 45, intermenstrual bleeding, persistent symptoms despite treatment, or risk factors for unopposed oestrogen exposure (obesity, diabetes, PCOS, tamoxifen, nulliparity, late menopause) require endometrial assessment before empirical medical therapy. TVUS measures endometrial thickness and identifies structural PALM lesions; Pipelle biopsy samples the endometrium for hyperplasia/carcinoma.
key_points: PALM (structural): Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia
COEIN (non-structural): Coagulopathy, Ovulatory, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified
Endometrial sampling indicated in HMB >45, IMB, failed medical Rx, or risk factors
Management ladder if benign: tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, LNG-IUS, COCP, oral progestogen, ablation, hysterectomy
LNG-IUS is first-line long-term medical therapy for HMB without structural cause
explanation.pearls: A bulky uterus on bimanual examination in a perimenopausal woman with IMB is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, regardless of how plausible adenomyosis or fibroids seem.

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding - investigation in a perimenopausal woman

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents with her fifth episode of vulvovaginal candidiasis in the past 12 months. Each episode features intense vulval pruritus, dyspareunia, thick white curd-like discharge, and erythematous vulval skin, and resolves with a single oral fluconazole 150 mg dose. Between episodes she is asymptomatic. She is in a stable monogamous relationship for 5 years, uses copper IUD for contraception, has no history of diabetes, and a recent HbA1c is 5.4% (35 mmol/mol).

She does not use scented soaps, wears cotton underwear, and has not used antibiotics in the last 6 months. She has no immunosuppression. Today on speculum examination there is thick white adherent discharge with vulval erythema and excoriation. Vaginal pH is 4.2. KOH microscopy shows numerous pseudohyphae and budding yeast. A high vaginal swab for fungal culture and speciation is collected and confirms Candida albicans sensitive to fluconazole.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, T 36.5 degC, BMI 24.
data_table.Examination: Thick white discharge, vulval erythema and excoriation.
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 4.2. KOH: pseudohyphae and budding yeast. HVS culture: Candida albicans, fluconazole sensitive. HbA1c 5.4% (35 mmol/mol).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Single dose fluconazole 150 mg orally and reassure this is an isolated acute episode
options.rationale: She has had at least 4 episodes in 12 months, meeting criteria for recurrent VVC; isolated single-dose treatment without induction and suppression has high relapse rate. Single-dose fluconazole is correct for sporadic acute episodes only (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

options.text: Induction fluconazole 150 mg orally days 1, 4, 7, then suppressive fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months
options.rationale: Recurrent VVC (>=4 episodes/year) is managed with an induction regimen of fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses to clear, followed by weekly suppressive fluconazole 150 mg for at least 6 months; this halves recurrence rates (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; CDC STI Treatment 2021).

options.text: Empirical oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for a 7-day course without further investigation
options.rationale: Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, not candidiasis; KOH confirms fungal infection. Metronidazole is correct in BV and trichomoniasis, never in confirmed candidiasis (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

options.text: Refer her for an oral glucose tolerance test before any further antifungal therapy
options.rationale: Diabetes is a risk factor but HbA1c 5.4% effectively excludes it; OGTT not warranted as a precondition for treatment. OGTT is correct only with HbA1c borderline or unexplained recurrent infections persisting after suppression (RACGP Red Book; Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Long-term intravaginal boric acid 600 mg nightly indefinitely as continuous suppressive antifungal therapy regimen
options.rationale: Intravaginal boric acid is reserved for non-albicans species (C. glabrata) or azole-resistant infection; her isolate is fluconazole-sensitive C. albicans. Boric acid is correct after speciation confirms non-albicans Candida (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Recurrent VVC is defined as 4 or more symptomatic episodes per year, confirmed by microscopy or culture. Management combines an induction phase (fluconazole 150 mg orally on days 1, 4 and 7) with suppression (fluconazole 150 mg weekly for at least 6 months). Address modifiable factors: optimise glycaemic control, avoid douching and irritants, and consider non-albicans Candida if treatment-resistant. Liver function should be checked before prolonged azole therapy.
key_points: RVVC: >=4 culture-confirmed episodes per year
Induction: fluconazole 150 mg PO days 1, 4 and 7
Suppression: fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months
Test for non-albicans Candida if resistant (glabrata responds to topical boric acid)
Screen for poorly controlled diabetes and consider HIV in immunocompromised picture
explanation.pearls: Routine OGTT is not needed when HbA1c is well below the diabetes threshold; the diagnostic role of HbA1c here is to exclude diabetes as the driver, not to gatekeep treatment.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis - suppressive therapy

stem:
A 55-year-old G3P3 presents with 18 months of urinary leakage. She leaks small volumes when she coughs, laughs, sneezes, or lifts her grandchildren, has no urgency, no nocturia, and no leakage on the way to the toilet. She empties her bladder 6 times a day, never wakes overnight to void, and does not feel incomplete emptying. There is no haematuria, no dysuria, and no faecal incontinence.

She had three vaginal births with two episiotomies and a forceps delivery for her second child. Her last period was 14 months ago. BMI 31. She smokes 10 cigarettes/day. On examination, abdomen soft, no palpable bladder. On speculum a first-degree anterior wall prolapse is noted. A cough stress test in semi-recumbent and standing positions reproduces leakage of urine from the urethral meatus. Urinalysis is clear and post-void residual on bladder scan is 35 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, BMI 31.
data_table.Examination: First-degree anterior wall prolapse. Positive cough stress test. No pelvic mass.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear. PVR 35 mL. Bladder diary not yet completed.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer for a mid-urethral sling (transobturator tape) surgical procedure now
