options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for women who have failed adequate conservative therapy including supervised pelvic floor training and lifestyle modification; first-line is conservative. Surgery is correct only after >=3 months supervised PFMT with persistent symptoms (RANZCOG; Continence Foundation Australia).

options.text: Commence oral oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily as first-line monotherapy for symptoms
options.rationale: Oxybutynin is antimuscarinic indicated for urgency UI; history is pure stress incontinence so antimuscarinics will not help and may cause cognitive/anticholinergic side effects. Oxybutynin is correct in urgency-predominant UI (AMH).

options.text: Three-day bladder diary, pelvic floor training for 3 months, weight loss and smoking cessation
options.rationale: First-line for stress urinary incontinence is supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months alongside weight loss (5 to 10% reduction halves leakage episodes) and smoking cessation (reduces cough-driven leakage); a bladder diary characterises voiding and is recommended before further intervention (Continence Foundation Australia; RANZCOG).

options.text: Insert a ring pessary for the management of stress urinary incontinence
options.rationale: Continence pessary may be useful for SUI but is second-line conservative after PFMT; first-degree prolapse is not the primary driver here. Pessary is correct as adjunct after failed PFMT or with prolapse contribution (RANZCOG).

options.text: Urodynamic studies as the first step before any conservative therapy is trialled
options.rationale: Urodynamics are not routinely required before conservative management of uncomplicated SUI; indicated when surgery is considered or diagnosis uncertain. Urodynamics is correct before surgical planning (NICE NG123).

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence is classified as stress (leakage on cough/sneeze/exertion), urge (preceded by urgency, part of overactive bladder), mixed, or overflow (chronic retention with leakage, raised PVR). Initial assessment includes history, bladder diary, urinalysis, PVR, and cough stress test. First-line management for stress and mixed UI is conservative: pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) for at least 3 months, weight loss, smoking cessation, and treatment of constipation. Failure of conservative therapy escalates to mid-urethral sling for stress UI or antimuscarinics/beta-3 agonists for urge UI.
key_points: Stress UI: leak with cough/sneeze, no urgency
Urge UI: leak preceded by urgency, often nocturia and frequency
Overflow UI: raised PVR, chronic retention
PFMT first-line for at least 3 months supervised
Antimuscarinics/mirabegron for urge; sling for stress that fails conservative Rx
explanation.pearls: If you cannot reproduce leakage with a cough stress test and the post-void residual is high, you are not dealing with stress incontinence - rethink the diagnosis before recommending a sling.

subtopic_detail: Urinary incontinence - stress vs urge distinction and initial management

stem:
A 68-year-old G4P4 woman presents with 6 months of a vaginal bulge worse at end of day. She also has bothersome stress urinary incontinence on coughing/sneezing and needs to splint to void fully. No faecal incontinence, no dyspareunia. Sexually active with husband, BMI 27, hypertension on perindopril, no other comorbidities. POP-Q: Ba 0, C -2, Bp -3 (stage 2 anterior compartment).

Post-void residual 80 mL. Urodynamic studies confirm urodynamic stress incontinence with no detrusor overactivity and good bladder capacity. She wants the option with the best evidence for both prolapse and urinary symptoms; she is prepared to consider surgery but would also consider a pessary.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 136/82 mmHg, BMI 27.
data_table.Examination: POP-Q: Ba = 0 (anterior wall at hymen on Valsalva), C = -2, Bp = -3. Stage 2 anterior compartment prolapse.
data_table.Investigations: PVR 80 mL. Urinalysis clear.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Trial vaginal ring pessary and supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, with reassessment of urinary symptoms after prolapse reduction
options.rationale: Conservative management (pessary + pelvic floor physiotherapy) is first-line for symptomatic POP including in women with concurrent stress incontinence. Pessary may unmask or improve SUI; reassessment after reduction guides whether surgery for incontinence is needed (RANZCOG; IUGA).

options.text: Anterior colporrhaphy with concomitant retropubic midurethral sling
options.rationale: Mesh midurethral sling implantation has been restricted by TGA in Australia following safety concerns; combined surgery is not first-line. Mesh sling is correct only after conservative failure with formal consent and TGA-compliant device choice (RANZCOG; TGA).

options.text: Sacrocolpopexy with synthetic mesh under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Abdominal mesh sacrocolpopexy is reserved for apical/post-hysterectomy prolapse, not first-line for stage-2 anterior compartment; restricted in Australia. Sacrocolpopexy is correct for refractory apical prolapse after conservative failure (TGA mesh).

options.text: Indwelling urinary catheter to manage the elevated post-void residual long-term
options.rationale: PVR of 80 mL is mildly raised and likely improves with prolapse reduction; long-term catheter risks infection. IDC is correct only with refractory retention not improved by other measures (RANZCOG).

options.text: Topical oestrogen as monotherapy with no other intervention
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen is an adjunct to pessary tolerance but does not treat prolapse or SUI alone. Topical oestrogen is correct as adjunct to pessary use or for atrophic symptoms (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: POP-Q stages prolapse by the most distal point relative to the hymen: stage 0 no prolapse; stage 1 most distal point >1 cm above hymen; stage 2 within 1 cm of hymen; stage 3 >1 cm beyond hymen but not complete eversion; stage 4 complete eversion. Conservative management (pessary, pelvic floor physiotherapy, topical oestrogen if postmenopausal) is first-line for symptomatic prolapse, particularly in women who wish to avoid surgery or have surgical contraindications. Surgical options include native tissue anterior/posterior repair, sacrocolpopexy for apical defect, and colpocleisis in non-sexually-active women with comorbidities.
key_points: POP-Q stage 2 = leading point within 1 cm of hymen (-1 to +1)
Conservative: pessary + PFMT + topical oestrogen if postmenopausal
Pessary types: ring (mild-moderate), Gellhorn (advanced), cube (refractory)
Sacrocolpopexy = gold standard apical repair
Mesh use restricted in Australia following TGA review; native tissue preferred
explanation.pearls: Stage 2 anterior wall prolapse with urinary symptoms often masks occult stress incontinence; reducing the prolapse with a pessary can unmask leakage that the patient did not previously notice.

subtopic_detail: Pelvic organ prolapse - conservative management of symptomatic stage 2 cystocele

stem:
A 32-year-old G0 presents with 14 months of constant pelvic pain rated 5/10 at baseline and 8/10 cyclically. The pain has both cyclical features (worse in the 4 days prior to and during her period) and non-cyclical features (dull background ache present every day for the last 8 months). She reports dyspareunia on deep penetration, dyschezia during menses, and increased urinary frequency without dysuria or haematuria.

She has been trying to conceive for 9 months without success. There is no fever, no postmenopausal bleeding, and no haematuria. Her mother had endometriosis diagnosed at laparoscopy. On bimanual examination there is uterosacral nodularity and a fixed retroverted uterus with cervical excitation. A pelvic ultrasound 2 months ago showed a 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma with ground-glass appearance and normal uterine cavity. STI screen today is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.6 degC, BMI 23.
data_table.Examination: Uterosacral nodularity. Fixed retroverted uterus. Cervical excitation. No palpable adnexal mass on bimanual.
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma. Normal uterine cavity. STI screen pending. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that endometriosis is confirmed on ultrasound and commence the COCP continuously without further investigation
options.rationale: Although picture is consistent with endometriosis, fertility goals, deep endometriosis on examination, and pending STI screen require integrated specialist assessment; COCP suppresses fertility in someone trying to conceive. COCP is correct in endometriosis when not actively conceiving (RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement; ESHRE Endometriosis 2022).

options.text: Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device now and review her symptoms in 6 months
options.rationale: LNG-IUS is effective for endometriosis pain but is contraceptive and inappropriate while actively trying to conceive. LNG-IUS is correct in endometriosis pain management when fertility not desired (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022).

options.text: Start a GnRH agonist with add-back tibolone for 6 months and reassess symptoms
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are second-line for refractory endometriosis; contraceptive and would delay fertility. GnRH agonists are correct in refractory endometriosis after first-line failure when fertility not immediate goal (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022).

options.text: Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without prior imaging or specialist multidisciplinary review at all
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is no longer required to diagnose endometriosis when imaging and clinical features are characteristic; preoperative MRI for deep disease mapping and multidisciplinary planning improves outcomes and protects fertility. Direct laparoscopy is correct only when imaging is inconclusive after MRI mapping (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary endometriosis service, arrange MRI for deep infiltrating disease, and address fertility
options.rationale: Suspected deep infiltrating endometriosis (uterosacral nodularity, dyschezia, fixed retroversion) with an endometrioma and subfertility warrants MRI mapping and multidisciplinary specialist input combining gynaecology, fertility, pelvic pain physiotherapy and psychology; the Australian National Action Plan for Endometriosis recommends this pathway (RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement; National Action Plan for Endometriosis; Pelvic Pain Foundation Australia).

explanation.summary: Chronic pelvic pain workup screens for red flags (postmenopausal bleeding, weight loss, PR bleeding, haematuria, pelvic mass), addresses the bladder, bowel, musculoskeletal, neurological and psychosocial dimensions, and identifies treatable gynaecological pathology (endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID, ovarian cyst). Endometriosis often has clinical and imaging features that are diagnostic without laparoscopy. Deep infiltrating endometriosis (uterosacral, bowel, bladder, ureteric involvement) requires MRI mapping and multidisciplinary surgical planning. Management is biopsychosocial: medical (NSAID, COCP, progestogen, LNG-IUS, GnRH analogues), surgical (excision/ablation, fertility-preserving), pain-focused (CBT, physiotherapy, mindfulness), and fertility-specific (IVF if needed).
key_points: CPP red flags: PMB, weight loss, PR bleeding, haematuria, fever, mass
Endometriosis no longer requires laparoscopy for diagnosis if imaging/clinical features are characteristic
Deep endometriosis suspected: MRI mapping + multidisciplinary review
LNG-IUS, COCP, progestogens are first-line medical Rx (contraceptive)
Fertility goals dictate therapy choice; consider IVF early in deep disease
explanation.pearls: Uterosacral nodularity and a fixed retroverted uterus on bimanual examination are physical signs of deep infiltrating endometriosis - imaging may underestimate disease, so multidisciplinary review precedes any surgical decision.

subtopic_detail: Chronic pelvic pain - red flag identification and biopsychosocial workup

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P1 presents for preconception counselling. Her first child was born 18 months ago at 39 weeks via uncomplicated vaginal birth weighing 3450 g. She takes sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy (last seizure 4 years ago) and is co-managed by neurology. She is otherwise well. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects, no diabetes, no malabsorption, and a BMI of 24.

She is up to date with her cervical screening (HPV negative 8 months ago) and her booking bloods from her last pregnancy showed she was rubella immune and varicella immune. She smokes 5 cigarettes a day, drinks 4 standard drinks twice a week on weekends, and does not use any other supplements. She would like to start trying for a second child in 3 months and asks what she should do to prepare.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 70 bpm, BMI 24.
data_table.Examination: Well, no abnormal findings.
data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG immune (last pregnancy). Varicella IgG immune. Cervical screen HPV negative 8 months ago. HbA1c 5.2% (33 mmol/mol).

lead_in: Which is the most important pre-conception intervention?

options.text: Folic acid 0.5 mg orally daily for 3 months pre-conception and the first trimester only
options.rationale: Standard 0.5 mg is for low-risk women; sodium valproate is major teratogen requiring 5 mg daily. Low-dose folate is correct for women without teratogenic medications, prior NTD, diabetes, malabsorption, or BMI >30 (RANZCOG; NHMRC).

options.text: Iodine 150 microg daily plus vitamin D level testing only without any medication change overall
options.rationale: Iodine 150 microg/day is recommended pre-pregnancy but does not address dominant teratogenic risk from sodium valproate. Iodine alone is correct as standard pre-conception supplement, but inadequate as single intervention here (RANZCOG; NHMRC).

options.text: Reassure her that no change to current AED therapy is needed because she is presently seizure-free
options.rationale: Seizure control does not mitigate teratogenic risk of valproate; the drug itself is the harm irrespective of seizure control. No-change is correct only when alternative AEDs have failed and informed decision is documented (RANZCOG; AMH).

options.text: Administer MMR and varicella booster immunisations now before any pregnancy attempt is made by this patient
options.rationale: She is already immune to rubella and varicella; live vaccines not indicated and contraindicated within 28 days of attempting conception. MMR/varicella is correct only with sub-protective titres and 4-week conception delay (Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Refer to neurology to switch to a safer anti-seizure medication and prescribe folic acid 5 mg daily
options.rationale: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of any anti-seizure medication (10% major congenital malformation rate, neurodevelopmental effects in 30 to 40%); switching to a safer agent (e.g. lamotrigine or levetiracetam) before conception is mandatory and high-dose folate 5 mg is indicated because of the elevated neural tube defect risk (RANZCOG; NHMRC; AMH).

explanation.summary: Pre-conception counselling covers folate (0.5 mg/day low-risk; 5 mg/day high-risk: previous NTD, diabetes, anti-epileptic drugs, malabsorption, family history NTD, obesity BMI >30 in some guidelines), iodine 150 microg/day, rubella and varicella serology with vaccination if non-immune (4 weeks before conception), cervical screening, STI screening, optimisation of chronic disease (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid, epilepsy), medication review for teratogens (valproate, ACE inhibitors, warfarin, retinoids, methotrexate), smoking and alcohol cessation, weight optimisation, mental health, and partner factors.
key_points: Folate low-risk 0.5 mg; high-risk 5 mg from 1 to 3 months pre-conception through 12 weeks
Iodine 150 microg/day pre-conception and throughout pregnancy and lactation
Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) at least 4 weeks before conception attempts
Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic AED; switch pre-conception
Other teratogens: ACEi/ARB, warfarin, isotretinoin, methotrexate, mycophenolate
explanation.pearls: If a woman of reproductive age is taking sodium valproate, the bigger intervention is changing the drug, not adding folate; high-dose folate is mitigation, not protection.

subtopic_detail: Pre-conception counselling - folate dose stratification

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P0 presents after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. The first was a missed miscarriage at 9 weeks managed expectantly, the second was a complete miscarriage at 8 weeks managed at home, and the third was a missed miscarriage at 10+2 managed with misoprostol 4 weeks ago. She conceives easily within 1 to 2 cycles each time and has regular 28-day ovulatory cycles.

She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, or pulmonary embolism, no symptoms of systemic lupus erythematosus (no malar rash, no arthralgia), no autoimmune disease, no fertility treatment, and no live births. She has never smoked, drinks one standard drink per week, has a BMI of 27, and is otherwise well. There is no family history of recurrent miscarriage, balanced translocation, congenital malformation, or genetic disease, and no consanguinity.

A transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, both ovaries normal, and no fibroids; antral follicle count is normal. Karyotype of products of conception from the third miscarriage was 46,XX (euploid). TSH is 1.8 mIU/L and HbA1c is 5.4% (35 mmol/mol). She asks what should be tested before her next pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, BMI 27.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: normal uterine cavity, no fibroids, both ovaries normal. POC karyotype third miscarriage 46,XX (euploid). TSH 1.8 mIU/L. HbA1c 5.4% (35 mmol/mol).

lead_in: Which is the most important next investigation?

options.text: Parental peripheral blood karyotype testing as the very first single investigation in this workup
options.rationale: Parental karyotype is not routinely first-line; reserved for couples with euploid first-trimester loss plus additional features (advanced maternal age, family history) or structural rearrangement on products. Karyotype is correct with structural rearrangement on POC or multiple losses with concerning family history (ESHRE RPL 2023; RANZCOG).

options.text: Inherited thrombophilia screen including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene, protein C, protein S, antithrombin
options.rationale: Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended in recurrent miscarriage outside research because results do not change management. Thrombophilia testing is correct only when there is a separate VTE indication, not for RPL alone (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy with directed biopsies regardless of any prior pelvic ultrasound findings reported recently
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy/SIS is reserved for cases where US is equivocal or suggests cavity abnormality; her TVUS shows a normal cavity. Hysteroscopy is correct when US is suspicious for intrauterine pathology (ESHRE).

options.text: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies repeated on two occasions 12 weeks apart
options.rationale: After 3 consecutive miscarriages (or 2 by RANZCOG criteria), antiphospholipid syndrome screening is the highest yield test that has direct therapeutic implications (aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH in next pregnancy if positive); diagnosis requires laboratory criteria on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart (RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage; ESHRE RPL 2023).

options.text: Peripheral blood natural killer cell assay as the very first single investigation here
options.rationale: NK cell testing is not validated for RPL and is explicitly not recommended by ESHRE and RANZCOG. NK testing is essentially never correct in routine RPL workup (ESHRE RPL 2023).

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined by RANZCOG as 2 or more consecutive miscarriages and by some international bodies as 3 or more. Workup with evidence-based yield includes APS screen (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-GP-I on two occasions 12 weeks apart), thyroid function and TPO antibodies, HbA1c, parental karyotype if products show structural abnormality, and pelvic imaging to exclude uterine anomaly. APS is the only treatable cause with clear therapeutic benefit: low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH improves live birth rates.
key_points: RANZCOG RPL definition: >=2 consecutive miscarriages
APS labs: LA, aCL, anti-beta-2-GP-I, repeated 12 weeks apart
APS treatment: aspirin 100 mg + prophylactic LMWH in pregnancy
Thyroid (TSH, TPO) and HbA1c also worth screening
Inherited thrombophilia and NK cell tests are NOT recommended
explanation.pearls: Half of all recurrent miscarriages remain unexplained even after thorough workup; the most important counselling point is that an unexplained workup still predicts a 60 to 75% chance of subsequent live birth.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent pregnancy loss - antiphospholipid syndrome workup

stem:
A 30-year-old G0 and her 32-year-old male partner present after 13 months of trying to conceive with regular unprotected intercourse 2 to 3 times per week, including timed intercourse around predicted ovulation in the last 4 cycles. She has regular 29-day cycles with predictable ovulatory symptoms (mid-cycle mucus change and mittelschmerz). She has no dysmenorrhoea, no dyspareunia, and was up to date with cervical screening 6 months ago (HPV negative).

BMI 24, non-smoker, no alcohol, no caffeine excess. She takes folic acid 0.5 mg daily and iodine 150 microg daily. Her partner is well, BMI 26, non-smoker, no known fertility issues, no previous children, takes no medications, drinks 6 standard drinks per week, and his work as an electrician does not involve heat exposure. She is concerned and asks what investigations should be done now.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, BMI 24.
data_table.Examination: Normal pelvic examination.
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screen HPV negative 6 months ago. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial set of investigations?

options.text: Semen analysis, day-21 progesterone, TSH and transvaginal ultrasound; reserve HSG for after initial workup
options.rationale: Infertility is defined as 12 months of unprotected intercourse without conception in women under 35 (6 months if 35 or over). First-line investigations are semen analysis (assesses 40 to 50% of contributory causes), confirmation of ovulation (mid-luteal progesterone), thyroid function, and pelvic ultrasound. Tubal patency assessment (HSG or HyCoSy) is performed after initial workup if no abnormality is found (RANZCOG Infertility; NICE CG156).

options.text: Refer immediately for IVF without any further investigation of the couple
options.rationale: IVF is indicated after a defined cause is identified or following empirical workup; jumping to IVF without identifying treatable causes is inappropriate and ignores potential male factor. IVF is correct after workup identifies indications (RANZCOG).

options.text: Continue trying for another 12 months before any investigation of the couple
options.rationale: She is over 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse and meets the definition of infertility; delaying investigation reduces chances of timely treatment. Continued attempts are correct only if duration is below the 12 month (or 6 month if >=35) threshold (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).

options.text: Hysterosalpingogram and diagnostic laparoscopy as the first-line investigations of the couple
options.rationale: Tubal patency assessment is part of workup but follows initial investigations; laparoscopy as first-line is invasive and unjustified. HSG/laparoscopy is correct after initial workup is unrevealing (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).

options.text: AMH for ovarian reserve only and reassure her she can wait given young age
options.rationale: AMH is part of broader workup but does not predict spontaneous conception; reassurance without male factor or tubal workup misses 50% of contributory causes. AMH-only is correct as adjunctive ovarian reserve assessment, never as sole investigation (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

explanation.summary: Infertility is defined as 12 months of unprotected intercourse without conception in women under 35, or 6 months at age 35 or older, or earlier if there is a known cause. Initial workup is parallel investigation of both partners: semen analysis (according to WHO criteria), ovulation assessment (mid-luteal progesterone, cycle history, ultrasound follicle tracking), ovarian reserve markers (AMH, antral follicle count, FSH on day 2 to 5), thyroid, prolactin, and pelvic ultrasound. Tubal patency assessment (HyCoSy or HSG) follows. Laparoscopy is reserved for suspected endometriosis or adhesive disease.
key_points: <35: investigate after 12 months; >=35: investigate after 6 months
Male factor accounts for 40 to 50% - always do semen analysis
Mid-luteal (day 21 in 28-day cycle) progesterone >25 nmol/L = ovulation
Tubal patency: HyCoSy preferred (no radiation) or HSG
AMH for ovarian reserve, not as a predictor of spontaneous conception
explanation.pearls: The most common omission in infertility workup is the semen analysis - both partners must be investigated in parallel from the outset.

subtopic_detail: Infertility workup in a couple under 35

stem:
A 15-year-old presents with her mother because of worsening period pain and bleeding. Menarche was at 12; cycles are regular at 28 days but have become increasingly painful since age 14, now causing her to miss 3 to 5 school days per month. Pain begins 24 hours before bleeding, peaks on day 2, and is associated with nausea, vomiting, and inability to get out of bed.

She soaks through a fully saturated super pad every 90 minutes on days 1 and 2 and reports passing 5-cent-piece-sized clots. She has tried paracetamol 1 g qid and ibuprofen 400 mg tds with only partial relief. Her mother had endometriosis diagnosed at laparoscopy at age 22 and a paternal aunt has known endometriosis. There is no dyspareunia (she is not sexually active), no dyschezia, no haematuria, and no postcoital bleeding.

She is no longer attending netball training and has begun to refuse social outings and sleepovers during her periods, and her mother reports she has been increasingly tearful and withdrawn in the days leading up to bleeding. On abdominal examination there is mild suprapubic tenderness; she declines an internal examination. A pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, T 36.5 degC, BMI 22.
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness. Declines internal examination.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. FBC: Hb 116 g/L, MCV 82 fL, ferritin 18 microg/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Naproxen 500 mg bd (day -1 to 3), continuous COCP and pelvic ultrasound; refer if no improvement
options.rationale: Adolescent dysmenorrhoea with severe functional impact, heavy bleeding, family history of endometriosis, and inadequate response to first-line analgesia warrants empirical scheduled NSAID plus continuous (cycle-suppressing) COCP, transabdominal pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal not appropriate in a non-sexually-active adolescent), and specialist referral if no improvement at 3 months; diagnosis does not require laparoscopy in adolescents (RANZCOG Endometriosis; Pelvic Pain Foundation Australia; ESHRE).

options.text: Reassure her that severe period pain in adolescence is normal and continue her current analgesia regimen long-term
options.rationale: Missing 3-5 school days/month, social withdrawal, and inadequate response to first-line analgesia is NOT normal and reflects high probability of endometriosis or other secondary cause. Reassurance is correct for mild primary dysmenorrhoea responsive to NSAIDs (Pelvic Pain Foundation Australia; RANZCOG).

options.text: Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without trialling any medical management as the first step
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is not first-line in adolescents; empirical medical therapy is trialled first. Laparoscopy is correct after failed 3-6 month trial of medical management or suspected deep disease (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

options.text: Commence a GnRH agonist with hormone add-back therapy as the next immediate step in management
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are reserved for refractory endometriosis after first-line hormonal failure; long-term use in adolescents has bone density concerns. GnRH agonists are correct in refractory disease with bone protection (ESHRE).

options.text: Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system without trialling any prior medical therapy first
options.rationale: LNG-IUS is effective but is second-line after COCP trial in non-sexually-active adolescent; insertion may require GA. LNG-IUS is correct after COCP failure or when COCP contraindicated (Family Planning Australia; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Adolescent endometriosis is under-recognised; diagnostic delay averages 7 to 12 years. School avoidance, heavy menstrual bleeding, severe dysmenorrhoea unresponsive to first-line analgesia, and a family history are red flags. Empirical management combines scheduled NSAID, continuous (suppressive) COCP to eliminate menstruation, transabdominal pelvic ultrasound, and early specialist referral. Transvaginal ultrasound is generally not appropriate in non-sexually-active adolescents. LNG-IUS is a second-line option and may require GA for insertion. GnRH agonists are reserved for refractory disease and require add-back therapy. Laparoscopy is not required to diagnose endometriosis in adolescents when the clinical picture is consistent.
key_points: Diagnostic delay in endometriosis averages 7 to 12 years
Adolescent red flags: school absence, family hx, refractory to first-line
Empirical Rx: scheduled NSAID + continuous COCP; TA ultrasound
TVUS inappropriate in non-sexually-active adolescent
LNG-IUS effective but second-line in adolescents; consider GA for insertion
explanation.pearls: If a 15-year-old is missing school every month for period pain, do not normalise it - empirical treatment plus follow-up is the standard of care, and the family history doubles the prior probability of endometriosis.

subtopic_detail: Adolescent endometriosis - high index of suspicion and empirical management

stem:
A 14-year-old presents to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden severe left iliac fossa pain. The pain began abruptly while she was playing netball, is sharp, constant, radiates to the left flank, and has been associated with vomiting four times in the last 2 hours. She had two previous brief episodes of less severe left-sided pain in the last 6 months, each lasting 30 minutes and resolving spontaneously.

Menarche was at 13; her last menstrual period was 12 days ago and was normal. She has never been sexually active. There is no fever, no urinary symptoms, and no chronic illness. On examination she is in obvious distress, BP 110/68, HR 116, T 37.0, with marked left iliac fossa tenderness and guarding, and a tender palpable mass. Abdomen is otherwise soft.

Beta-hCG is negative. White cell count is 13.4 x 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L. A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound with Doppler shows a 7 cm complex left adnexal mass with peripherally displaced follicles, a hyperechoic whirlpool sign at the suspected pedicle, and absent venous flow with reduced arterial flow within the left ovary. The right ovary is normal. There is no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, T 37.0 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Marked left iliac fossa tenderness with guarding. Tender left adnexal mass palpable.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. WCC 13.4 x 10^9/L. CRP 18 mg/L. TVUS Doppler: 7 cm complex left adnexal mass, peripherally displaced follicles, whirlpool sign, absent venous flow, reduced arterial flow. Right ovary normal. No free fluid.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation and analgesia and repeat the ultrasound in 12 hours
options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a time-critical surgical emergency; every hour of delay increases ovarian necrosis and reduces salvage rate. Observation is correct only with low clinical suspicion and reassuring imaging (RANZCOG; KEMH).

options.text: Pelvic MRI to confirm diagnosis before any surgical decision is made
options.rationale: MRI adds delay without improving on Doppler US findings that are already characteristic; diagnosis is clinical and US-based warranting immediate surgery. MRI is correct only when US is non-diagnostic and clinical suspicion is moderate (RANZCOG).

options.text: Emergency laparoscopy for detorsion and ovarian preservation, with oophoropexy considered intraoperatively
options.rationale: Whirlpool sign, peripherally displaced follicles and absent venous flow on Doppler in an adolescent with characteristic clinical features is ovarian torsion. The standard of care is emergency laparoscopy with detorsion regardless of macroscopic appearance (ovaries that look black often recover function); oophorectomy is reserved for necrotic non-viable tissue or malignancy. Oophoropexy is considered to reduce recurrence (RANZCOG Ovarian Cysts; ESHRE; Royal Women's Hospital Clinical Guidelines).

options.text: Emergency laparoscopy with planned left salpingo-oophorectomy because the ovary appears non-viable on Doppler
options.rationale: Doppler signs do not reliably predict viability; ovaries appearing black often recover function after detorsion. Oophorectomy in adolescent should be reserved for confirmed necrosis or malignancy. Salpingo-oophorectomy is correct only with intra-operative confirmation of non-viability or malignancy (RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital).

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and admit for suspected pelvic inflammatory disease
options.rationale: She has never been sexually active and imaging is diagnostic of torsion; antibiotics do not treat torsion and delay surgery. Antibiotics are correct in confirmed PID, never in torsion (Australian STI Management Guidelines; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency. Clinical features are sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, often with vomiting, intermittent prior episodes, and a palpable adnexal mass. Doppler ultrasound findings of whirlpool sign, peripherally displaced follicles, and absent venous flow with reduced arterial flow support the diagnosis, but normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion (dual ovarian blood supply can preserve arterial flow). Management is emergency laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian preservation; oophorectomy is reserved for confirmed necrosis or malignancy. Oophoropexy is considered to reduce recurrence, particularly when no ovarian mass is found or in cases with redundant ligaments. Outcomes correlate with time to surgery.
key_points: Sudden severe unilateral pain + vomiting + adnexal mass = torsion until excluded
Doppler whirlpool sign, peripheral follicles, absent venous flow = highly suggestive
Normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion (dual blood supply)
Detorsion + ovarian preservation is the standard, even if the ovary looks ischaemic
Oophoropexy reduces recurrence, especially when no mass is present
explanation.pearls: Black does not equal dead - detorsed ischaemic-looking ovaries regularly recover function in adolescents, and the decision to remove an ovary in a 14-year-old should be reserved for clear necrosis or proven malignancy.

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion in an adolescent - urgent surgical management
NCSP - self-collection in under-screened woman with prior LSIL
stem:
A 42-year-old Aboriginal woman attends an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service. Her last cervical screening was 9 years ago on the pre-2017 cytology-based program and was reported as low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL); she was scheduled for a 12-month repeat at the time but did not attend, and has been lost to follow-up since. She declines a clinician-collected speculum today, citing childhood sexual trauma and significant distress with previous examinations.

She has no postcoital bleeding, no intermenstrual bleeding, and no pelvic pain. She is G3P3 (all vaginal), in a monogamous relationship, no immunosuppression, BMI 27. She did not receive HPV vaccination (predates routine cohort). The clinic is accredited to offer self-collection. She wants to participate in screening in a way she can tolerate. There is no visible lesion at external genital examination (which she has agreed to).

The clinician is weighing whether her prior abnormal cytology and long screening gap warrant insisting on clinician-collected sampling or whether self-collected HPV testing is an appropriate program-defined entry point.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no palpable mass. External genital examination unremarkable. Clinician-collected speculum declined today.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer a self-collected vaginal HPV swab today as her cervical screening test, with explicit pathway counselling that any oncogenic HPV result on a self-collected sample will require clinician-collected reflex LBC or direct colposcopy depending on HPV type
options.rationale: Under the NCSP since July 2022, self-collected vaginal HPV swab is available to ALL screen-eligible women aged 25-74 (renewed at 25-30 by HPV-based program), including under-screened women with prior abnormal cytology, as an equivalent-sensitivity option to clinician-collected sampling. Pre-2017 LSIL is not a separate exclusion from self-collection eligibility; the current entry point for an under-screened woman is an HPV test, with risk-stratified follow-up by result. Counselling that a positive HPV result will require a return clinician-collected sample (for reflex LBC) or direct colposcopy (if HPV 16/18) keeps her informed of the next step (NCSP; Cancer Council Australia).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines
Australian Government Department of Health: NCSP

options.text: Refer to gynaecology for examination under anaesthesia and cervical sampling
options.rationale: EUA is reserved for situations where examination is essential and cannot be tolerated; self-collection makes EUA unnecessary for screening. EUA is correct for symptomatic presentations requiring complete examination under sedation (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Decline screening today and rebook for clinician-collected sample at a later visit
options.rationale: Deferral perpetuates under-screening; self-collection answers this exact barrier. Deferral to clinician collection is correct only when clinician sampling is patient's preference (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Send a self-collected urine sample for HPV testing in lieu of vaginal sampling
options.rationale: Urine HPV testing is not part of the Australian NCSP; validated self-collection is vaginal. Urine HPV is not currently approved in Australia (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Send her for direct colposcopy without any HPV test based on the prior LSIL alone, bypassing screening
options.rationale: Pre-2017 LSIL on cytology that was lost to follow-up does not, by itself, mandate immediate colposcopy a decade later in an asymptomatic woman; the current NCSP pathway is an HPV test (clinician- or self-collected), with colposcopy triggered by HPV 16/18 or by non-16/18 with HSIL on reflex LBC (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Self-collection (vaginal flocked swab for HPV) became universally available within the NCSP in July 2022 and is particularly important for under-screened groups. It has equivalent sensitivity to clinician-collected sampling for oncogenic HPV detection (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
key_points: Universal self-collection eligibility since 1 July 2022
Approved sample is a vaginal flocked swab (not urine)
Equivalent sensitivity to clinician-collected HPV testing
Reflex LBC requires clinician-collected sample - patient is recalled if HPV non-16/18 detected on self-collected sample
Patients screened directly by colposcopy if HPV 16/18 is detected on a self-collected sample
explanation.pearls: If a self-collected sample detects non-16/18 oncogenic HPV, the patient must return for a clinician-collected sample for reflex LBC. If HPV 16/18 is detected, the patient is referred directly to colposcopy (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: NCSP - non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with pLSIL reflex cytology
stem:
A 38-year-old G2P2 returns for her cervical screening result: HPV oncogenic non-16/18 detected; reflex liquid-based cytology shows possible HIGH-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (pHSIL). She is asymptomatic; cervix appeared normal at the time of the sample. She is in a monogamous relationship of 12 years, last screened 7 years ago (normal Pap), non-smoker, BMI 24, no immunosuppression. She received Gardasil as a teenager.

She uses the LNG-IUS. She is anxious and asks specifically whether 'non-16/18' means she should just have another screen in 12 months rather than colposcopy.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no palpable mass. Cervix appeared normal at speculum at the time of sample with no visible lesion and no contact bleeding.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to colposcopy now
options.rationale: Under the NCSP, HPV non-16/18 detected with HIGH-grade reflex cytology (pHSIL or HSIL) mandates direct colposcopy, the same as any HPV 16/18 result. The 12-month repeat pathway applies only to HPV non-16/18 with NEGATIVE or pLSIL reflex cytology (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Repeat clinician-collected HPV test in 12 months from today
options.rationale: 12-month repeat is for non-16/18 with NEGATIVE or pLSIL cytology; pHSIL escalates to direct colposcopy. 12-month repeat is correct for non-16/18 + negative/pLSIL only (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Repeat HPV test in 6 months as an interim safety check
options.rationale: No 6-month repeat interval in NCSP for screening results; colposcopy is required. 6-month interval was the old pathway; current NCSP uses 12-month surveillance only (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Return to routine 5-yearly screening as cytology is described as only 'possible'
options.rationale: pHSIL is treated as actionable and triggers colposcopy referral, not routine return. Routine 5-yearly return is correct only with negative HPV (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

options.text: Refer to colposcopy at 6 months if she develops symptoms, otherwise routine screening
options.rationale: Symptom-based delay is unsafe; pHSIL on screening requires prompt colposcopy regardless of symptoms. Symptom-based escalation is essentially never correct in screening-detected pHSIL (NCSP).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with negative/pLSIL/LSIL reflex cytology is intermediate-risk and managed by repeat HPV at 12 months. Most transient infections clear in this interval; persistent infection or progression to HSIL on cytology prompts colposcopy (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
key_points: Intermediate risk pathway: non-16/18 HPV + negative/pLSIL/LSIL LBC -> 12-month repeat HPV
Higher risk: non-16/18 HPV + possible HSIL/HSIL/glandular abnormality -> colposcopy
Highest risk: any HPV 16/18 -> direct colposcopy regardless of LBC
Immunosuppressed patients have a different pathway with closer surveillance
Symptomatic patients always co-tested and referred regardless of result
explanation.pearls: The 12-month repeat is HPV-based, not cytology-based. Many transient HPV infections clear in this interval; only persistent infection requires colposcopy (NCSP National Cancer Screening Register).

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic cervical cancer - postcoital bleeding workup overrides routine screening
stem:
A 35-year-old G1P1 woman attends her GP with a 4-month history of intermittent postcoital bleeding occurring after most episodes of intercourse, with one episode of intermenstrual bleeding lasting 2 days. She has had no abnormal discharge, no dyspareunia and no pelvic pain. Her last cervical screening test was 18 months ago and showed HPV not detected on a clinician-collected sample.

She received Gardasil as a teenager and is otherwise well. She is a current smoker (15 pack-years) and uses the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has one child after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. There is no significant family history. She has been treated empirically by another clinician for presumed chlamydial cervicitis with azithromycin 1 g stat 6 weeks ago, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT both negative; symptoms have persisted unchanged. BMI is 24. She has no fevers, no weight lossymptoms. She is asking for a 'repeat HPV swab to make sure'.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Speculum: cervix has a friable area at 4 o'clock with contact bleeding on swab; no obvious exophytic lesion. Bimanual: uterus normal size, no adnexal mass, no cervical motion tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. Chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT negative 6 weeks ago. HPV screening test 18 months ago: HPV not detected.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the routine NCSP HPV cervical screening test and act on the result
options.rationale: Routine HPV screening is for asymptomatic women; symptomatic patients require co-test PLUS direct referral for colposcopy regardless of HPV result, because negative HPV does not exclude all cervical pathology in a symptomatic patient. Routine HPV alone is correct for asymptomatic women (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Empirical treatment for cervicitis with doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not appropriate when STI testing is negative and symptoms have already failed empirical therapy; persistent postcoital bleeding with friable cervix requires structural assessment. Empirical antibiotics are correct in confirmed/strongly-suspected STI cervicitis (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Reassure patient that symptoms will likely resolve and review in 6 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting in a smoker with 4 months of postcoital bleeding and visibly friable cervix risks missing cervical cancer. Reassurance is correct only after biopsy excludes malignancy (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Perform a co-test (HPV + LBC) and refer for colposcopy regardless of result
options.rationale: Symptomatic cervical bleeding (postcoital, intermenstrual or postmenopausal) is an indication for a co-test PLUS direct referral to colposcopy regardless of HPV or LBC results, because cytology can be falsely negative in invasive cancer and a recent negative HPV does not exclude pathology. A visibly abnormal cervix in a symptomatic patient is colposcopy-urgent (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines; RANZCOG).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Discontinue the combined oral contraceptive pill as likely cause, review 3 months
options.rationale: Breakthrough bleeding on COCP rarely presents with reproducible postcoital bleeding and friable cervix; structural pathology must be excluded first. COCP cessation is correct only after cervical pathology excluded (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Persistent postcoital bleeding, particularly with a visibly abnormal cervix, mandates a co-test PLUS colposcopy regardless of the HPV result, because cervical cancer can present with cytology- and HPV-negative findings. A recent negative HPV screen does not exclude invasive disease in a symptomatic patient (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
key_points: Symptomatic cervical bleeding: co-test AND colposcopy regardless of result
Routine HPV screening assumes the patient is asymptomatic
Smoking is a co-factor for cervical cancer progression
Friable, contact-bleeding cervix warrants direct visualisation
Recent negative HPV does not exclude pathology in a symptomatic patient
explanation.pearls: The biggest pitfall in cervical cancer diagnosis is over-reliance on a recent negative screen in a symptomatic patient. Symptoms override screening (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding - TVUS endometrial thickness >4 mm threshold
stem:
A 64-year-old G3P3 woman attends her GP with two episodes of fresh vaginal bleeding over the past 3 weeks. She experienced natural menopause at age 51 with no further bleeding until now. She has no postcoital bleeding, no discharge and no pelvic pain. Her last cervical screening test was 4 years ago, HPV not detected. She has type 2 diabetes (metformin 1 g BD, last HbA1c 7.4%), essential hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, BMI 34, and a 25-year history of regular menses prior to menopause.

She has never used hormone therapy or tamoxifen. Family history is unremarkable for gynaecological malignancy and Lynch syndrome screening criteria are not met. She does not smoke. She walks 3 km daily and has no urinary or bowel red flags. She has had no recent intercourse and is not on anticoagulation. She is not anaemic on point-of-care testing. She is anxious because her neighbour was recently diagnosed with endometrial cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Speculum: atrophic vaginal mucosa, no cervical lesion, small amount of blood at the os, no friability. Bimanual: uterus normal size, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (115-165). Urinalysis negative. Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrium 8 mm with heterogeneous echotexture; no focal mass identified; both ovaries normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle endometrial biopsy
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness >4 mm on TVUS requires histological assessment; outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle biopsy is the recommended pathway, with the higher diagnostic yield than blind Pipelle alone when the endometrium is thickened or heterogeneous (RANZCOG; eviQ Endometrial cancer).

options.text: Trial topical vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophic vaginitis and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Vaginal atrophy is common cause of PMB but cannot be assumed when endometrium is >4 mm; histological exclusion of endometrial pathology is required first. Topical oestrogen is correct after histology excludes pathology (RANZCOG).

options.text: Reassure as a single episode and review in 3 months if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Any PMB warrants investigation; reassurance without histology is unsafe given endometrial cancer prevalence ~10% in PMB. Reassurance is essentially never correct in PMB without histology (RANZCOG; eviQ).

options.text: Order a serum CA-125 to risk-stratify endometrial pathology before further imaging
options.rationale: CA-125 is used in ovarian cancer risk stratification, not endometrial; histology directly addresses the diagnostic question. CA-125 is correct in suspected ovarian pathology (RANZCOG).

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 6 weeks to assess for any change
options.rationale: Repeat imaging delays diagnosis without altering the indication for histology in PMB with endometrium >4 mm. Repeat US is correct only with inadequate initial imaging (eviQ Endometrial cancer).

explanation.summary: Any episode of postmenopausal bleeding must be investigated. TVUS endometrial thickness of >4 mm in a postmenopausal woman not on HRT, or any focal endometrial abnormality, mandates histological assessment via hysteroscopy and biopsy (RANZCOG; eviQ).
key_points: Any PMB requires investigation - approximately 10% have endometrial cancer
TVUS endometrial thickness threshold for biopsy: >4 mm (postmenopausal, no HRT)
Persistent or recurrent PMB requires biopsy even if endometrium <4 mm
Hysteroscopy + directed biopsy outperforms blind Pipelle when endometrium is thickened/focal
Risk factors: obesity, T2DM, unopposed oestrogen, nulliparity, late menopause, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome
explanation.pearls: If a postmenopausal woman has bleeding but endometrium is <=4 mm with otherwise reassuring TVUS, reassure but warn that recurrent bleeding mandates histology regardless of thickness (RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia - management in postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 58-year-old G2P2 postmenopausal woman is referred to gynaecology after 4 weeks of intermittent vaginal bleeding. TVUS demonstrated an endometrial thickness of 12 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and no focal mass. Outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle biopsies reports endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (also called endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN); no invasive disease seen on the available tissue. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.6%, metformin 1 g BD), hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, BMI 38, and natural menopause at age 53.

She has no family history of Lynch-associated cancers. She has completed her family. She does not wish to continue hormonal therapy long term. She has no thromboembolic history and a normal cardiac assessment on preoperative review. She asks specifically about the risk that this finding already represents cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 140/84 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Bimanual: uterus normal size, mobile, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Pipelle + hysteroscopic directed biopsy: endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (EIN). Hb 122 g/L. TVUS: ET 12 mm heterogeneous, both ovaries normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as definitive surgical management
options.rationale: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (EIN) carries a concurrent endometrial carcinoma rate of approximately 30-40% on final hysterectomy specimens and a substantial future progression risk; in a postmenopausal woman who has completed her family, total hysterectomy with BSO is the recommended definitive treatment (RANZCOG; eviQ Endometrial cancer; RCOG/BSGE Endometrial hyperplasia).

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system with 6-monthly endometrial sampling for surveillance
options.rationale: LNG-IUS with surveillance is reserved for premenopausal patients wishing to retain fertility or unfit for surgery; in postmenopausal woman with completed family, definitive surgery is preferred. LNG-IUS is correct in fertility-sparing context (RCOG/BSGE Endometrial hyperplasia).

options.text: Oral medroxyprogesterone acetate with repeat biopsy in 12 months
options.rationale: Oral progestogens are less effective than LNG-IUS for hyperplasia regression and not first-line in surgical candidate with completed family. Oral MPA is correct only in non-surgical candidates (RCOG/BSGE Endometrial hyperplasia).

options.text: Endometrial ablation to control bleeding and reduce cancer risk
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation is CONTRAINDICATED with hyperplasia + atypia or suspected malignancy because residual buried endometrium can harbour or develop cancer. Ablation is correct for benign HMB without hyperplasia (RANZCOG; RCOG/BSGE Endometrial hyperplasia).

options.text: Watchful waiting with repeat TVUS and endometrial biopsy in 6 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is unsafe for atypical hyperplasia given the high concurrent (~30-40%) and progression risk to invasive cancer. Watchful waiting is correct only in hyperplasia WITHOUT atypia in selected reversible scenarios (eviQ Endometrial cancer).

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (EIN) carries a 30-40% concurrent endometrial cancer rate. Total hysterectomy with BSO is the standard of care in postmenopausal women or those who have completed their family. Fertility-sparing LNG-IUS is reserved for younger patients or those unfit for surgery (RCOG/BSGE).
key_points: Hyperplasia WITHOUT atypia: LNG-IUS first-line, repeat biopsy at 6 months
Hyperplasia WITH atypia (EIN): hysterectomy + BSO if postmenopausal or completed family
Fertility-sparing option in atypia: LNG-IUS with 3-monthly biopsy until regression
Endometrial ablation contraindicated when atypia/malignancy is present or suspected
Risk factors: obesity, T2DM, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome
explanation.pearls: Even with formal hysteroscopy plus Pipelle, 30-40% of atypical hyperplasia cases harbour an undetected concurrent endometrial cancer at hysterectomy (eviQ Endometrial cancer).

subtopic_detail: Ovarian cancer recognition - vague abdominal symptoms + CA-125
stem:
A 62-year-old G2P2 postmenopausal woman attends her GP with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal bloating, early satiety, mild lower abdominal discomfort, increased urinary frequency without dysuria, and unintentional 4 kg weight loss. She initially thought she had developed IBS. There is no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit beyond mild constipation, and no postmenopausal bleeding. She has no significant past medical history, no family history of ovarian, breast or bowel cancer, and is not known to carry BRCA1/2.

She does not smoke and drinks alcohol minimally. She has had no abdominal surgery. Her last cervical screening test was 2 years ago, HPV not detected. She has not used hormone therapy. Examination reveals mild abdominal distension and a vaguely palpable left adnexal fullness. There is no overt ascites but a low-volume effect cannot be excluded clinically. She is afebrile, with stable observations. The GP has already started her on a fibre supplement which has not relieved symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 80 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen mildly distended. Vague left lower-quadrant fullness, no peritonism. Bimanual: left adnexal mass approximately 7 cm, partly fixed; uterus normal size.
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal. Urea, creatinine, LFTs within normal limits. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Colonoscopy as the initial investigation for presumed bowel pathology and constipation
options.rationale: Colorectal cancer is on the differential, but palpable adnexal mass in postmenopausal woman shifts priority to gynaecological assessment. Colonoscopy is correct after gynaecological workup excludes ovarian pathology or in dominant bowel symptoms (RANZCOG; Cancer Australia ovarian cancer).

options.text: Serum HE4 alone as a more specific tumour marker than CA-125
options.rationale: HE4 is not established Australian first-line marker; CA-125 is incorporated in RMI and Australian pathway. HE4 is correct in ROMA-based international pathways (Cancer Australia ovarian cancer).

options.text: Trial of antispasmodic and follow up if symptoms persist beyond 6 weeks
options.rationale: Antispasmodics in postmenopausal woman with palpable adnexal mass risks delaying ovarian cancer diagnosis; symptoms beyond 4 weeks warrant urgent investigation. Antispasmodic trial is correct only without red flags (Cancer Australia ovarian cancer).

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast as first-line imaging investigation
options.rationale: CT has a role in staging once malignancy is suspected, but pelvic US is recommended first-line imaging to characterise the lesion. CT is correct after US suggests malignancy (Cancer Australia ovarian cancer).

options.text: Pelvic transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound with serum CA-125 for RMI/IOTA risk stratification
options.rationale: Persistent abdominal bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency or pelvic pain in a postmenopausal woman, particularly with a palpable adnexal mass, requires urgent gynaecological workup. The Australian pathway is pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal + transabdominal) plus serum CA-125; together these enable Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) or IOTA-based triage to a gynaecological oncology MDT (RANZCOG; Cancer Australia ovarian cancer).

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer typically presents with vague abdominal symptoms (bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency, abdominal/pelvic pain) lasting more than a few weeks; in postmenopausal women these symptoms must trigger TVUS plus CA-125. The combination feeds RMI/IOTA scoring and triages referral to a gynaecological oncology MDT (Cancer Australia; RANZCOG).
key_points: Symptoms: persistent bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency/frequency, pelvic/abdominal pain
First-line investigation: TVUS + transabdominal US + serum CA-125
Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) = U x M x CA-125, with US features, menopausal status
IOTA simple rules / ADNEX model for ultrasound-based malignancy risk
All suspicious adnexal masses in postmenopausal women -> gynae oncology MDT
explanation.pearls: Ovarian cancer is often labelled the 'silent killer' but a careful history elicits 3-6 months of persistent symptoms in most patients; the key skill is taking these complaints seriously in postmenopausal women (Cancer Australia ovarian cancer).

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion - emergency recognition and detorsion
stem:
A 24-year-old G0 woman presents to ED at 02:00 with sudden-onset severe right iliac fossa pain that woke her from sleep 4 hours ago, associated with nausea and two episodes of vomiting. The pain is colicky, radiates to the right groin and posterior thigh, and is currently 9/10 in intensity despite paracetamol 1 g PO taken 90 minutes ago. She had a recent pelvic ultrasound 2 weeks ago for cyclical pelvic discomfort showing a 6 cm right ovarian dermoid (mature cystic teratoma); she was awaiting an outpatient gynaecology appointment.

Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago, regular 28-day cycles, and she has no intermenstrual bleeding or discharge. She is sexually active in a long-term relationship, uses condoms, and beta-hCG taken on arrival is negative. On examination she is in obvious distress, splinted on the right, with cool peripheries from pain.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 112 bpm, RR 22, T 37.1 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen: marked right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, no peritonism. Bowel sounds present. Bimanual: very tender right adnexal mass, palpable approximately 7 cm, with severe pain on cervical motion. Uterus normal size, anteverted.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative. WCC 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 12 mg/L. Urinalysis negative. Bedside TVUS: enlarged right ovary 9 cm with peripheral follicles and a 6 cm complex mass; minimal Doppler flow within the ovarian parenchyma compared with the left.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for serial observation, IV analgesia and a formal radiology TVUS at 08:00
options.rationale: Delaying definitive assessment risks complete vascular compromise and ovarian loss; torsion is time-critical. Observation is correct only with low clinical suspicion and reassuring imaging (RANZCOG; RCH CPG: Ovarian torsion).

options.text: Emergency CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast before any surgical decision
options.rationale: US is the imaging of choice; CT adds delay and radiation without changing surgical management when US already shows enlarged ovary with reduced Doppler flow. CT is correct when US is non-diagnostic (RANZCOG).

options.text: Right salpingo-oophorectomy via laparotomy because the ovary is likely non-viable
options.rationale: Even ovaries appearing dusky/black at surgery should be detorted and reassessed; oophorectomy as initial action sacrifices fertility unnecessarily. Salpingo-oophorectomy is correct only with confirmed necrosis/malignancy after detorsion (RANZCOG; RCH CPG: Ovarian torsion).

options.text: Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian-preserving cystectomy under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles and reduced Doppler flow on TVUS, and a known ovarian mass strongly suggest ovarian torsion; emergency laparoscopy with detorsion and conservative cystectomy preserves ovarian function. Doppler flow is unreliable for excluding torsion and clinical suspicion should drive surgery (RANZCOG; RCH CPG: Ovarian torsion).

options.text: IV opioid analgesia and discharge with outpatient gynaecology follow-up next week
options.rationale: Discharging a patient with suspected torsion is unsafe; emergency surgery is standard. Discharge is essentially never correct in suspected torsion (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a time-critical surgical emergency. Suspicion is clinical and ultrasound supports the diagnosis (enlarged ovary, peripheral follicles, reduced/absent Doppler flow), but preserved Doppler does not exclude torsion. Management is emergency laparoscopy, detorsion and conservative cystectomy where possible to preserve fertility (RANZCOG; RCH CPG).
key_points: Risk factors: ovarian cyst >5 cm, dermoid, pregnancy, ovulation induction
Hallmarks: sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, nausea/vomiting
TVUS: enlarged ovary, peripheral follicles, abnormal Doppler (but preserved flow doesn't exclude)
Treat with emergency laparoscopy + detorsion + cystectomy
Sacrifice ovary only if necrotic and not recoverable after detorsion period
explanation.pearls: Doppler is sensitive but not specific - up to 60% of confirmed torsions have preserved Doppler flow at the time of imaging. Clinical suspicion takes precedence (RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: Lichen sclerosus - ultrapotent topical steroid + cancer surveillance
stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman attends a vulval clinic with a 12-month history of progressive vulval pruritus, soreness, and dyspareunia limiting intercourse with her long-term partner. She has noticed white, paper-thin skin around the labia minora and perineum, with occasional fissuring and contact bleeding when itching at night and during attempts at intercourse. Multiple courses of clotrimazole pessaries and over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% over the past 6 months have not helped.

She has had no postmenopausal bleeding from the cervix and her last cervical screening test 12 months ago was HPV not detected. On examination there is well-demarcated 'figure-of-eight' white atrophic change involving the labia minora, clitoral hood and perianal skin, with partial resorption of the labia minora, narrowing of the introitus, and early posterior fourchette adhesion. There is one persistent indurated nodule 8 mm in diameter on the right labium majus that has been present for 6 weeks and has not responded to topical hydrocortisone.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic, paper-thin white change in classic figure-of-eight distribution. Loss of labia minora architecture. Discrete 8 mm indurated nodule on right labium majus, firm, non-tender. No inguinal lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening 12 months ago: HPV not detected.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Punch biopsy the indurated nodule and start clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment nightly
options.rationale: The clinical picture is classic for lichen sclerosus; treatment is ultrapotent topical steroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) typically nightly for 4 weeks, alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance. The 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC means any persistent indurated, ulcerated or pigmented lesion must be biopsied promptly (RANZCOG; BAD lichen sclerosus guideline).

options.text: Trial topical oestrogen cream for presumed atrophic vaginitis and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Findings (figure-of-eight white atrophic change, architectural loss) are classic for lichen sclerosus, not generalised atrophic vaginitis; oestrogen would not address diagnosis or suspicious nodule. Topical oestrogen is correct for atrophic vaginitis with non-suspicious findings (RANZCOG).

options.text: Commence clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment nightly and review again in 12 weeks
options.rationale: Ultrapotent topical steroids are mainstay for lichen sclerosus, but the new indurated nodule must be biopsied first because lichen sclerosus carries 4-5% lifetime vulval SCC risk. Steroid-without-biopsy is correct only when no suspicious areas are present (RANZCOG; BAD lichen sclerosus guideline).

options.text: Refer for wide local excision of the entire affected vulval area
options.rationale: Vulvectomy/wide excision is not standard treatment for lichen sclerosus; medical control with ultrapotent steroids is first-line and surgery is reserved for biopsy-proven malignancy. Wide excision is correct after biopsy confirms invasive disease (BAD lichen sclerosus guideline).

options.text: Refer to dermatology for systemic methotrexate as steroid-sparing therapy now
options.rationale: Systemic immunosuppression is reserved for refractory disease unresponsive to ultrapotent topical steroids; immediate priority is biopsy of suspicious nodule. Methotrexate is correct after biopsy and after steroid failure (BAD lichen sclerosus guideline).

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is treated with ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) in a tapering regimen with maintenance. Vulval SCC develops in 4-5% lifetime, so any persistent indurated, ulcerated, pigmented or non-responding lesion must be biopsied. Lifelong surveillance is required (RANZCOG; BAD).
key_points: Classic appearance: figure-of-eight white atrophic vulval skin with architectural loss
First-line: clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment - induction then taper to maintenance
Lifetime vulval SCC risk: approximately 4-5%
Biopsy any persistent indurated, ulcerated, pigmented, or steroid-unresponsive lesion
Lifelong surveillance review at least annually
explanation.pearls: Patient self-application is a key skill; demonstrate with a mirror, advise a fingertip-unit per application, and emphasise that maintenance therapy reduces both symptoms and the risk of malignant progression (BAD lichen sclerosus guideline).

subtopic_detail: Bartholin abscess - Word catheter as primary care management
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman presents to her GP with a 3-day history of progressively painful right-sided labial swelling. The swelling is now egg-sized, tense, exquisitely tender and is interfering with sitting and walking. She has had a low-grade fever of 37.8 degC at home but has not had rigors. She is in a monogamous relationship of 5 years and her most recent STI screen 4 months ago was negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV.

She had a similar but smaller episode on the same side 2 years ago that resolved with incision and drainage in ED but recurred 3 months later as a painless cyst that has since fluctuated in size.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 37.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Tense, fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the right posterior introitus (5 o'clock position), overlying erythema, exquisitely tender. No inguinal lymphadenopathy. No vulval ulceration. Speculum deferred due to pain.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management of this Bartholin abscess?

options.text: Simple incision and drainage with packing, no catheter or marsupialisation
options.rationale: Simple I&D without Word catheter or marsupialisation has high recurrence (up to 40%); the duct often re-closes once cavity collapses, particularly with prior recurrence. Simple I&D is correct as initial drainage when Word catheter unavailable (RANZCOG; KEMH Bartholin abscess).

options.text: Outpatient oral antibiotics alone (e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BD) without drainage
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without drainage rarely resolves a tense fluctuant abscess; drainage is the primary intervention. Antibiotic-only is correct in early cellulitic phase without abscess collection (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Incision and drainage with Word catheter insertion retained in situ 4-6 weeks
options.rationale: Word catheter placement after incision and drainage is the recommended primary-care option for an acute Bartholin abscess: it maintains an epithelialised tract while the cavity heals, with a recurrence rate substantially lower than simple I&D. The catheter is removed after 4-6 weeks (RANZCOG; KEMH Bartholin abscess).

options.text: Excision of the Bartholin gland under general anaesthetic as definitive management
options.rationale: Excision is reserved for recurrent abscesses unresponsive to drainage or for suspected Bartholin gland carcinoma (women >40 with solid mass); higher morbidity. Excision is correct after Word catheter/marsupialisation failure or with malignancy concern (RANZCOG).

options.text: Sitz baths and oral analgesia, with re-review in 1 week if not improving
options.rationale: Conservative measures are insufficient for tense fluctuant abscess; while sitz baths help small early lesions, definitive drainage is required. Sitz baths are correct adjunct, not primary intervention (KEMH Bartholin abscess).

explanation.summary: An acute Bartholin abscess is best managed with incision and drainage plus Word catheter placement to maintain an epithelialised tract for 4-6 weeks. Marsupialisation is an effective alternative, particularly for recurrence. Simple I&D alone has a recurrence rate up to 40%. Antibiotics are reserved for systemic features, cellulitis, immunosuppression or pregnancy (RANZCOG; KEMH).
key_points: First-line: I&D + Word catheter, retained 4-6 weeks
Alternative: marsupialisation (suturing cyst wall to skin) - durable but requires more skill
Simple I&D alone -> high recurrence rate
Antibiotics indicated for cellulitis, sepsis, immunosuppression, pregnancy
Excision considered for refractory recurrence or suspected Bartholin gland carcinoma (esp. age >40 with solid mass)
explanation.pearls: In women over 40 with a persistent solid Bartholin mass rather than cystic abscess, biopsy/excision is essential to exclude Bartholin gland carcinoma (RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: Test of cure after LLETZ for HSIL
stem:
A 34-year-old G0 woman had a LLETZ procedure 11 months ago for biopsy-proven HSIL (CIN3) detected after a screening HPV test reported HPV 16 with possible HSIL on reflex cytology. The LLETZ histology confirmed CIN3 with clear excision margins (ectocervical, endocervical and deep margins all clear of dysplasia, no glandular involvement, no microinvasion). Post-LLETZ recovery was uncomplicated with no secondary haemorrhage and no cervical stenosis on subsequent review.

She is asymptomatic, with no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding and no discharge. She is in a monogamous relationship of 2 years and is using the etonogestrel implant for contraception. She is a non-smoker, BMI 24, has no immunosuppression, takes no regular medications and has no family history of cervical or other gynaecological malignancy. She received Gardasil as a teenager and completed her course. She attends her GP today asking what surveillance she now needs and when she can return to routine 5-yearly NCSP screening.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft. Cervix at speculum: smooth, no obvious lesion, no contact bleeding.

lead_in: Which surveillance pathway should she follow under the Australian NCSP?

options.text: Annual HPV cervical screening for 5 years, then return to routine 5-yearly screening
options.rationale: Annual HPV testing is not the NCSP test-of-cure pathway; structured ToC uses co-test at 12 months then yearly until two consecutive negatives. Annual HPV-only is correct in some immunocompromised surveillance, not post-LLETZ (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Single co-test at 24 months and return to routine 5-yearly screening if negative
options.rationale: Single co-test is not adequate; two consecutive negative co-tests at 12 and 24 months are required before returning to routine screening. Single co-test is essentially never sufficient (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Return to routine 5-yearly NCSP screening now because excision margins were clear
options.rationale: Clear excision margins reduce but do not eliminate the risk of recurrent HSIL; structured surveillance is required because residual HPV is strongest predictor. Routine 5-yearly is correct only after two negative ToC co-tests (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: 6-monthly colposcopy for 2 years regardless of cytology or HPV result
options.rationale: Routine 6-monthly colposcopy is not the NCSP pathway after successfully treated CIN3 with clear margins; cytological/HPV co-test surveillance is sufficient. 6-monthly colposcopy is correct only with positive ToC results or persistent disease (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Co-test at 12 and 24 months; both negative returns to 5-yearly screening
options.rationale: After treatment of HSIL (CIN2/3), the NCSP test-of-cure protocol is a co-test (HPV + LBC on the same sample) at 12 and 24 months post-treatment. If both are HPV not detected and LBC negative, the patient returns to routine 5-yearly HPV screening. Any positive result triggers colposcopy referral (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines; NCSP National Cancer Screening Register).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: After treatment of CIN2/3 (HSIL), the NCSP test-of-cure pathway is a co-test (HPV + LBC) at 12 and 24 months.
