Two consecutive negative co-tests return the patient to routine 5-yearly screening. Any positive result triggers colposcopy referral. Persistent HPV positivity is the strongest predictor of recurrent disease (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).
key_points: Test of cure after HSIL treatment: co-test at 12 and 24 months
Two consecutive negative co-tests -> return to routine 5-yearly NCSP screening
Any positive at test of cure -> colposcopy referral
Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) treatment requires longer surveillance
Immunosuppressed patients have a more intensive surveillance protocol
explanation.pearls: Persistent HPV is the strongest single predictor of recurrent CIN2/3 after LLETZ - more important than margin status alone (Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines).

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia NCSP Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Tamoxifen-related endometrial bleeding - investigate symptoms, do not screen asymptomatic
stem:
A 64-year-old G2P2 woman has been taking tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 4 years as adjuvant endocrine therapy for ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative left breast cancer treated 4 years ago with breast-conserving surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy. She was previously postmenopausal (natural menopause age 52, no bleeding for 12 years prior to commencing tamoxifen) and is now referred to gynaecology after presenting to her GP with two episodes of fresh vaginal bleeding over the past 3 weeks, each lasting 2-3 days and requiring two pads daily.

She has had no postcoital bleeding, no dischargery or bowel symptoms. Her last cervical screening 18 months ago was HPV not detected on a clinician-collected sample. She has hypertension (perindopril 5 mg daily, BP 138/82 on review), a BMI of 31, and well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.9%, metformin 1 g BD). She has no personal or family history of Lynch-associated cancers and meets no Lynch testing criteria. She has never used hormone therapy or unopposed oestrogen pre-tamoxifen.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft. Speculum: atrophic mucosa, small amount of blood at the os, no cervical lesion. Bimanual: uterus normal size, mobile, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (115-165). TVUS performed by GP: endometrium 9 mm, heterogeneous, with several small cystic spaces; no focal mass identified; ovaries normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discontinue tamoxifen and substitute an aromatase inhibitor without further gynaecological investigation
options.rationale: Stopping tamoxifen unilaterally compromises breast cancer outcomes; substitution belongs to breast MDT after gynaecological diagnosis is established. Tamoxifen change does not address immediate need to exclude endometrial pathology. Tamoxifen switch is correct after gynaecological diagnosis established (eviQ Endometrial cancer; eviQ Tamoxifen).

options.text: Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy with directed and Pipelle endometrial biopsy
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen requires structural and histological assessment. Tamoxifen causes subepithelial stromal change and cystic atrophy that thicken the endometrium on TVUS even in benign disease, making the standard >4 mm threshold less reliable; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the recommended investigation in any symptomatic tamoxifen user. Routine TVUS surveillance of asymptomatic tamoxifen users is NOT recommended in Australian guidance (RANZCOG; eviQ Endometrial cancer; eviQ Tamoxifen).

options.text: Repeat TVUS in 3 months to assess for any change in endometrial thickness
options.rationale: Repeat imaging delays diagnosis without changing the indication for histology in symptomatic tamoxifen user; TVUS findings are poorly specific. Repeat TVUS is correct only with technically inadequate initial scan (eviQ Endometrial cancer).

options.text: Reassure as endometrial thickness is acceptable for tamoxifen users; review if bleeding recurs
options.rationale: Standard >4 mm threshold cannot be applied to symptomatic tamoxifen users; any PMB on tamoxifen requires histological exclusion. Reassurance is correct only after histology excludes pathology (eviQ Tamoxifen).

options.text: Commence routine 6-monthly TVUS surveillance and biopsy only if thickness exceeds 8 mm
options.rationale: Asymptomatic surveillance of tamoxifen users with TVUS is NOT recommended in Australian guidance; surveillance does not improve outcomes. Bleeding, not thickness, is the investigation trigger. TVUS surveillance is essentially never correct in asymptomatic tamoxifen users (eviQ Tamoxifen; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen approximately doubles endometrial cancer risk in postmenopausal users. Routine TVUS surveillance is NOT recommended for asymptomatic users because tamoxifen-related stromal change reduces the specificity of endometrial thickness measurements. Any abnormal bleeding requires hysteroscopy with directed biopsy. Treatment decisions about continuing tamoxifen are made by the breast MDT (eviQ Tamoxifen; eviQ Endometrial cancer; RANZCOG).
key_points: Tamoxifen has anti-oestrogenic effects on breast but pro-oestrogenic on endometrium
Approximately 2-fold increase in endometrial cancer risk in postmenopausal users
No asymptomatic TVUS surveillance - it doesn't improve outcomes
Any abnormal bleeding -> hysteroscopy + directed biopsy
TVUS thickness threshold of >4 mm is not reliable in tamoxifen users
Tamoxifen continuation decisions made by breast MDT after gynae diagnosis
explanation.pearls: The 'investigate symptoms, don't screen asymptomatic' principle is paramount for tamoxifen surveillance - it is one of the few oncology contexts where active surveillance is explicitly NOT recommended (eviQ Tamoxifen).

stem:
A 44-year-old G2P2 woman attends her GP with an 8-month history of progressively heavier menstrual bleeding. Cycles are regular at 28 days but bleeding now lasts 9 days with flooding through super tampons hourly on days 2-3 and passage of large clots up to 3 cm in size. She reports increasing tiredness, palpitations on minor exertion, and exertional shortness of breath climbing one flight of stairs.

Her work as a primary school teacher has been disrupted and she has had to change pads during teaching sessions. She is not currently sexually active, has had no postcoital bleeding, no intermenstrual bleeding, and no postcoital spotting. There is no abdominal or pelvic pain. There is no easy bruising, no gum bleeding last cervical screening test was negative for oncogenic HPV 18 months ago.

BMI is 34. She has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily and takes no anticoagulants, no antiplatelets and no over-the-counter NSAIDs. She has had two normal vaginal deliveries with no postpartum haemorrhage. She has not yet had pelvic imaging or endometrial sampling in this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae. Abdomen soft, no palpable mass. Bimanual: uterus bulky, mobile, anteverted, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L (115-165), MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 mcg/L. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: In addition to a transvaginal ultrasound and full blood count with ferritin, which further investigation is most important at this visit?

options.text: FSH and oestradiol to assess for perimenopausal anovulation as cause
options.rationale: Random FSH/oestradiol in a 44-year-old with regular cycles is unhelpful; cycle regularity argues against anovulation. Hormonal testing is correct only with established cycle irregularity (RANZCOG HMB).

options.text: Coagulation screen and von Willebrand panel as the first-line bleeding work-up
options.rationale: Inherited bleeding disorder screen is for HMB since menarche or personal/family bleeding cues; her 8-month history without bleeding red flags does not prioritise this. Coag/vWF panel is correct with bleeding history clues (RANZCOG HMB).

options.text: Endometrial Pipelle biopsy at this visit, with TSH and coagulation screen as adjuncts
options.rationale: RANZCOG and NICE NG88 recommend endometrial sampling in women with HMB who are aged 45 or over OR who have risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; obesity (BMI 34) is a major risk factor and TVUS alone is insufficient to exclude endometrial pathology in this setting (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

options.text: Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy as the sole investigation in place of TVUS today
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy is appropriate where TVUS suggests focal pathology or sampling is unsuccessful, but TVUS remains first-line. Hysteroscopy-first is correct only with TVUS showing focal lesion (NICE NG88).

options.text: Serum CA-125 to screen for occult ovarian malignancy in this patient
options.rationale: CA-125 is non-specific in premenopausal women and has no role in HMB workup. CA-125 is correct in suspected ovarian pathology (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Workup of HMB follows PALM-COEIN. TVUS plus FBC/ferritin are universal. Endometrial sampling is indicated at age >=45, persistent intermenstrual bleeding, failed medical therapy, or risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, anovulation, tamoxifen, Lynch). TSH and coagulation screen are adjuncts based on history.
key_points: PALM (structural): Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia
COEIN (non-structural): Coagulopathy, Ovulatory, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified
FBC + ferritin in all; TSH if cycle change or clinical features; coags if bleeding history since menarche
Biopsy if age >=45 OR risk factor for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch, unopposed oestrogen)
TVUS first-line imaging; saline-infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy for focal lesions
explanation.pearls: Obesity lowers the age threshold for endometrial sampling. Don't anchor on age 45 if other risk factors are present.

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding - structured PALM-COEIN workup

stem:
A 39-year-old G1P1 woman has a 2-year history of heavy regular menstrual bleeding with cycle-related bulk symptoms including urinary frequency, mild lower-abdominal pressure, and occasional nocturia. She passes large clots during menses and floods through super tampons every 1-2 hours on the heaviest days. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 4 cm intramural fibroid (FIGO type 4, not distorting the cavity) and a 3 cm subserosal fibroid; the endometrial cavity is regular and the endometrium is 6 mm.

Endometrial biopsy returns benign proliferative endometrium with no atypia. She has completed her family, is in a monogamous relationship using condoms for contraception, and would prefer to avoid surgery if possible. She does not want to lose her fertility surgically and is open to a long-acting hormonal device. She has tried tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses with only modest improvement and has not tolerated mefenamic acid. BMI 26.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, lower-uterine mass palpable just above pubis. Bimanual: bulky irregular uterus approx 12-week size, mobile.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 101 g/L (115-165), ferritin 14 mcg/L. TVUS as above. Beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line medical therapy?

options.text: GnRH agonist (e.g. goserelin 3.6 mg SC monthly) with add-back oestrogen
options.rationale: GnRH analogues are used short-term (3-6 months) to shrink fibroids pre-surgery or to bridge perimenopause; not first-line ongoing therapy due to vasomotor symptoms and bone loss. GnRH is correct as bridge therapy, not chronic (RANZCOG).

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system (Mirena) insertion now
options.rationale: The LNG-IUS is first-line medical therapy for HMB including fibroid-related HMB where the uterine cavity is not distorted by submucosal fibroids; it reduces blood loss by 70-95% and is acceptable for a woman who has completed her family (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily during menses only
options.rationale: TXA reduces blood loss by 40-50% but does not address bulk symptoms and is less effective than LNG-IUS overall. TXA is correct for acute heavy periods or as adjunct (NICE NG88).

options.text: Mefenamic acid 500 mg orally three times daily during menses only
options.rationale: NSAIDs reduce blood loss by ~25-30% and help dysmenorrhoea; useful adjuncts but not first-line for moderate-severe HMB with anaemia. NSAIDs are correct as adjunctive symptomatic therapy (NICE NG88).

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy under GA
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but should be reserved for failed/declined medical therapy; she has not yet trialled LARC. Hysterectomy is correct after failed conservative options or with patient preference (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: For fibroid-related HMB without significant cavity distortion: LNG-IUS first-line. Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are useful adjuncts. GnRH analogues are short-term pre-surgical or perimenopausal bridging agents. Myomectomy preserves fertility; hysterectomy is definitive when family complete and other options failed.
key_points: LNG-IUS: first-line for HMB without cavity distortion (FIGO types 3-7 generally OK)
Submucosal fibroids (FIGO 0-2) distorting cavity: hysteroscopic myomectomy
GnRH agonist: short-term shrinkage pre-op or perimenopausal bridge
Uterine artery embolisation: alternative when fertility not desired
Myomectomy: preserves fertility; hysterectomy: definitive cure
explanation.pearls: Mirena requires a cavity that the device can sit in. A large submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity contraindicates Mirena and instead triggers hysteroscopic myomectomy.

subtopic_detail: Uterine fibroids - choice of medical therapy

stem:
A 27-year-old nulligravid woman presents with 4 years of cyclical pelvic pain (peaks day 1-2, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia during menses, cyclical back pain). She has tried regular ibuprofen and heat-pack regimen with minimal benefit. She is not planning conception in the next 18-24 months but does want children eventually. She has no migraine with aura, no smoking, no VTE history, BMI 24.

Pelvic USS normal (no endometrioma). Bimanual examination shows tender uterosacral nodularity. She is now keen for the most evidence-based next step that does not commit her to surgery if it can be avoided.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no masses. Bimanual: uterus anteverted, mobile, mildly tender. No palpable nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. No adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic USS: normal-appearing ovaries, no endometrioma, no deep infiltrating lesion visualised.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial continuous combined oral contraceptive pill with NSAID for breakthrough pain, with review at 3-6 months and laparoscopy if refractory or fertility planning advances
options.rationale: RANZCOG and ESHRE endometriosis guidance support empirical hormonal therapy (continuous COCP or progestogen) as first-line in suspected endometriosis without requiring laparoscopic confirmation, especially if fertility is not imminently sought. Laparoscopy is reserved for refractory cases or fertility planning (RANZCOG; ESHRE 2022).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal biopsy before any medical therapy
options.rationale: Empirical hormonal therapy is now preferred first-line over diagnostic laparoscopy for suspected endometriosis. Laparoscopy is correct after failed medical therapy or for surgical planning (ESHRE 2022; RANZCOG).

options.text: Serum CA-125 to support the working diagnosis
options.rationale: CA-125 has poor sensitivity and specificity for endometriosis. CA-125 is correct in suspected ovarian pathology, not endometriosis diagnosis (ESHRE 2022).

options.text: MRI pelvis as the next investigation to confirm the working diagnosis
options.rationale: MRI is reserved for suspected deep infiltrating endometriosis with surgical planning, not primary diagnosis. MRI is correct for deep endometriosis surgical mapping (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

options.text: GnRH agonist with add-back HRT as first-line therapy
options.rationale: GnRH agonists are second/third line after COCP/progestogens due to bone density and menopausal symptoms. GnRH is correct after first-line hormonal failure (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects about 1 in 9 Australian women and is consistently diagnosed late, with average symptom-to-diagnosis interval of 7-12 years. Cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, and subfertility are the core presentation. Examination may show tender nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments or a fixed retroverted uterus, but is often normal. Transvaginal ultrasound detects endometriomas and deep infiltrating disease in expert hands but is normal in superficial peritoneal disease - so a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis. Laparoscopy with histological confirmation is the gold standard but is not required to start empirical therapy. First-line medical management is NSAIDs plus continuous combined oral contraceptive (or POP or LNG-IUS), with 3-6 month review of symptom response. Second-line is GnRH agonist with add-back HRT, or dienogest. Laparoscopic excision is for confirmed disease, treatment-failure, infertility workup, or endometrioma over 3 cm.
key_points: Classic features: cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, dysuria
Empirical hormonal therapy precedes laparoscopy in straightforward presentations
TVUS first-line imaging; MRI for suspected deep disease
Laparoscopy: failed medical therapy, suspected deep disease, infertility, severe symptoms
Refer to gynaecologist if no response in 3-6 months or red flags
explanation.pearls: Endometriosis is a clinical diagnosis - TVUS is normal in superficial peritoneal disease, MRI and CA-125 add nothing to first-line management. Trial continuous COCP plus NSAID and review at 3-6 months; laparoscopy is for treatment failure or fertility concerns (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis - diagnostic pathway

stem:
A 33-year-old nulligravid woman attends her GP with 6 months of secondary amenorrhoea following a 12-month history of progressively irregular cycles. She reports new hot flushes (around 6-8 per day), troublesome night sweats with disturbed sleep, vaginal dryness with deep dyspareunia, low mood, reduced libido and increased fatigue. She is in a stable long-term relationship and is open to future fertility consideration, although they have not actively been trying to conceive.

There is no recent significant weight change, no excessive exercise, no medication changesoms. She has had no chemotherapy, no pelvic radiotherapy and no previous ovarian surgery. She had menarche at age 12 with previously regular 28-day cycles. Family history: her mother had menopause at age 41 and her maternal aunt had menopause in her early forties; one cousin has Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

BMI 23. She is not using contraception currently. Beta-hCG is negative today. Initial bloods 5 weeks ago: FSH 56 IU/L, oestradiol low, prolactin normal, TSH normal, total testosterone normal. Today's repeat FSH and oestradiol have been collected and are pending.

data_table.Examination: BMI 23. No goitre. No visual field defect. Speculum: pale dry vaginal mucosa.
data_table.Investigations: Five weeks ago: FSH 56 IU/L (premenopausal <10), oestradiol low, LH 38, prolactin normal, TSH 1.8, beta-hCG negative. Today: bloods repeated, pending.

lead_in: If today's repeat FSH is similarly elevated (>25 IU/L), which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure and recheck FSH in 6 months as a single elevated FSH is non-diagnostic alone
options.rationale: POI diagnosis requires two FSH >25 IU/L at least 4 weeks apart; her first sample was 5 weeks prior, so confirmatory second now is appropriate. Reassurance with re-check at 6 months is correct only with isolated borderline FSH and no amenorrhoea (Australasian Menopause Society POI).

options.text: Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill solely for menopausal symptom control without further workup needed
options.rationale: COCP can be used in POI but HRT provides more physiological replacement and better bone protection. COCP is correct when contraception desired alongside replacement (BMS).

options.text: Bone density scan and fertility counselling referral, but defer hormonal therapy until age 40 years
options.rationale: Delaying oestrogen replacement until 40 risks cardiovascular, bone, and neurocognitive harm; replacement should commence at diagnosis. Defer HRT is essentially never correct in confirmed POI (ESHRE).

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for an adrenal failure work-up before initiating any hormonal therapy in her
options.rationale: Adrenal autoimmune screen (21-hydroxylase antibodies) is part of POI workup but does not need to precede HRT commencement. Adrenal screen is correct concurrently, not before HRT (ESHRE).

options.text: Systemic HRT, fertility counselling, screen for adrenal/thyroid antibodies and karyotype, plus baseline bone densitometry
options.rationale: POI confirmed by FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart with amenorrhoea >=4 months in a woman <40 mandates HRT until at least the average age of natural menopause to protect bone and cardiovascular health; concurrent work-up includes karyotype, fragile X premutation, adrenal antibodies, thyroid antibodies, and a fertility discussion (ESHRE 2016; Jean Hailes).

explanation.summary: POI: amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea >=4 months + FSH >25 IU/L on 2 readings 4+ weeks apart, in a woman aged under 40. Work-up: karyotype, fragile X premutation, adrenal (21-OH) and thyroid antibodies, baseline DXA. Treat with HRT until at least the average age of natural menopause (~51) for bone, CV and neurocognitive protection. Spontaneous pregnancy possible in ~5-10%; HRT is not a contraceptive.
key_points: Diagnosis: amenorrhoea >=4 months + 2 x FSH >25 IU/L, 4+ weeks apart, age <40
Causes: idiopathic, genetic (Turner, fragile X), autoimmune, iatrogenic (chemo/radiotherapy/surgery)
HRT (or COCP) until ~age 51
Discuss contraception separately - HRT not contraceptive
Refer for fertility counselling early
explanation.pearls: POI is not just early menopause - women may still ovulate intermittently and conceive; HRT does not prevent pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Premature ovarian insufficiency - diagnosis and HRT

stem: A 21-year-old sexually active woman presents with 4 days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, mucopurulent vaginal discharge, fever 38.4 C, HR 110, BP 100/64. Examination: bilateral lower-quadrant tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, mucopurulent endocervical discharge, AND a 6 cm tender right adnexal mass with bedside USS demonstrating a multilocular cystic mass with internal debris consistent with tubo-ovarian abscess. She is unable to tolerate oral intake due to nausea and vomiting. Urine beta-hCG negative. WCC 18, CRP 180. NAAT swabs sent. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 37.1 degC.
data_table.Examination: Abdomen: bilateral lower abdominal tenderness. Bimanual: cervical motion tenderness, mucopurulent endocervical discharge, no palpable adnexal mass.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit and commence IV ceftriaxone, doxycycline (or azithromycin if intolerant) and metronidazole, with surgical or interventional drainage if no improvement at 48-72 hours
options.rationale: Severe PID with tubo-ovarian abscess, systemic features (fever, tachycardia, vomiting) requires hospital admission and IV combination therapy. Drainage is added if there is no response in 48-72 hours or the abscess is large (RANZCOG PID; eTG).

options.text: Outpatient ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus oral doxycycline plus oral metronidazole for 14 days despite the imaging-confirmed tubo-ovarian abscess here
options.rationale: Outpatient regimen is for mild-moderate PID without abscess or systemic features; her TOA, fever, tachycardia, vomiting require IV in hospital. Outpatient is correct in mild PID (RANZCOG PID; eTG).

options.text: Single-dose IM ceftriaxone and discharge home with safety-net advice despite the imaging-confirmed tubo-ovarian abscess on the recent pelvic scan
options.rationale: Single-dose monotherapy is inadequate for any PID, let alone severe with TOA. Single-dose IM is essentially never sufficient in PID (eTG).

options.text: Proceed immediately to laparoscopy and salpingectomy as the primary intervention before any trial of intravenous antibiotic therapy for the abscess
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, ruptured TOA, or failure of antibiotic therapy at 48-72 hours. Surgery is correct after antibiotic failure or rupture (RANZCOG).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin monotherapy for 14 days despite the polymicrobial pelvic infection with anaerobic and gonococcal coverage gaps in this regimen
options.rationale: Amoxicillin is not first-line PID therapy and does not cover gonorrhoea, anaerobes, or atypicals. Amoxicillin is correct in confirmed susceptible Listeria or strep infections, not PID (eTG).

explanation.summary: Empirical outpatient PID regimen per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days. Take partner notification, STI screen, and HIV/hepatitis screening at presentation.
key_points: Ceftriaxone covers gonorrhoea
Doxycycline covers chlamydia and M. genitalium (test/retest if treatment failure)
Metronidazole covers anaerobes
Admit and treat IV if pregnant, severe, TOA, sepsis, or failed oral therapy
Partner notification and contact tracing essential
explanation.pearls: PID is a clinical diagnosis - don't wait for swab results before starting antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: PID - Therapeutic Guidelines regimen

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P2 woman attends her 6-week postnatal check with her local GP. She had an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth of a healthy term infant 6 weeks ago and is exclusively breastfeeding on demand, day and night, with no formula supplementation and no expressed-milk bottle feeds. The baby is feeding 8-12 times in 24 hours and weight gain is on track.

She has not yet had a return of menses. She wishes to space pregnancies for at least 2 years and would prefer the most reliable method that is compatible with breastfeeding. She has no history of VTE, no thrombophilia25. She does not smoke. She has not used the lactational amenorrhoea method as her sole strategy and is concerned about pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Well. BP 118/74. BMI 25. Soft well-involuted uterus, no lochia, perineum healed. Lactating breasts, no mastitis.
data_table.Investigations: None required today; routine 6-week postnatal review.

lead_in: Regarding contraception, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The combined oral contraceptive pill is the first-line choice as BP has normalised and gestational hypertension has resolved
options.rationale: CHC is UKMEC 4 <6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding, UKMEC 2 from 6 weeks to 6 months. CHC is correct >6 months postpartum or not breastfeeding (FSRH UKMEC).

options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) is acceptable as a sole contraceptive method indefinitely while she remains amenorrhoeic
options.rationale: LAM requires all three: amenorrhoea, exclusive/near-exclusive breastfeeding, AND <6 months postpartum; reliability falls thereafter. LAM is correct when all three criteria met (FSRH UKMEC).

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system or copper IUD can be inserted today, and etonogestrel implant or progestogen-only pill are also suitable
options.rationale: Intrauterine contraception (LNG-IUS or Cu-IUD) can be safely inserted from 4-6 weeks postpartum (UKMEC 1-2); progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA) are also suitable in breastfeeding women from any time postpartum (FSRH UKMEC; Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Etonogestrel implant should be delayed until 6 months postpartum because of an adverse effect on milk supply
options.rationale: Etonogestrel implant does not adversely affect milk supply and can be inserted at any time postpartum. Implant delay is essentially never required (FSRH; WHO MEC).

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is contraindicated during breastfeeding and should not be used at all here
options.rationale: DMPA is UKMEC 1 from 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding (UKMEC 2 before). DMPA is correct from 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (FSRH UKMEC).

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception in breastfeeding women: progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUS) are all safe at 6 weeks. Cu-IUD or LNG-IUS can be inserted from 4-6 weeks postpartum (or immediately postpartum within 48 h of birth). CHC is avoided <6 weeks (UKMEC 4) and category 2 between 6 weeks and 6 months while breastfeeding. LAM is ~98% effective only when ALL three criteria are met: <6 months, amenorrhoea, exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding.
key_points: POP can start day 21 postpartum without need to wait
IUD/IUS: insert immediately postpartum (within 48 h) or from 4-6 weeks
CHC: avoid <6 weeks if breastfeeding; from 6 weeks UKMEC 2; from 6 months UKMEC 1
DMPA: UKMEC 2 before 6 weeks if breastfeeding, then UKMEC 1
LAM strict criteria: amenorrhoea + exclusive BF + <6 months postpartum
explanation.pearls: Day 21 postpartum is the earliest fertility could return in non-breastfeeding women - that's why POP and CHC have day 21 as the earliest start if other criteria allow.

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception in a breastfeeding woman

stem:
A 38-year-old woman has her routine 5-yearly cervical screening test through her general practice. She is not pregnant, has had two previous CSTs at ages 28 and 33 which were both negative for oncogenic HPV, and has had no abnormal vaginal bleeding, no postcoital bleedingpelvic pain. She is in a stable monogamous relationship of 11 years and uses the LNG-IUS 52 mg (Mirena, inserted 4 years ago for both contraception and HMB control) and is currently amenorrhoeic.

She has had a total of 4 lifetime sexual partners and has never had a sexually transmitted infection identified. She received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine series at age 14 through the school-based program. Her practitioner-collected sample returns: oncogenic HPV detected (non-16/18 type); reflex liquid-based cytology performed automatically by the laboratory shows no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is immunocompetent and has no history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cervical excisional treatment. She does not smoke.

data_table.Examination: Routine speculum normal at time of collection.
data_table.Investigations: HPV test: oncogenic non-16/18 detected. Reflex LBC: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy.

lead_in: Under the Australian National Cervical Screening Program, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Direct referral for colposcopy with cervical biopsy now
options.rationale: Direct colposcopy is for HPV 16/18 regardless of cytology, or any oncogenic HPV with pHSIL/HSIL, or persistent HPV at 24 months. Direct colposcopy is correct in those higher-risk pathways (NCSP 2022).

options.text: Repeat HPV testing in 12 months (intermediate-risk pathway)
options.rationale: Oncogenic non-16/18 HPV with reflex LBC negative or low-grade abnormality places the patient in the intermediate-risk group; repeat HPV at 12 months. If still HPV-positive then refer to colposcopy; if negative, return to 5-yearly screening (NCSP 2022).

options.text: Return to routine 5-yearly cervical screening immediately
options.rationale: 5-yearly screening resumes only after HPV becomes negative; any oncogenic HPV detection triggers 12-month repeat or colposcopy. Routine 5-yearly is correct only with negative HPV (NCSP 2022).

options.text: Repeat HPV test for partial genotype in 6 months
options.rationale: 6-month repeat is not NCSP-recommended; intermediate-risk repeat is at 12 months. 6-month repeat was the old pathway, now obsolete (NCSP 2022).

options.text: Refer for excisional treatment (LLETZ) without further investigation
options.rationale: Treatment is based on histological diagnosis from colposcopy/biopsy, not on HPV status with negative cytology. LLETZ is correct after histology confirms high-grade dysplasia (NCSP 2022).

explanation.summary: Under the NCSP: HPV 16/18 detected -> direct colposcopy regardless of LBC. Oncogenic HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade reflex LBC -> repeat HPV in 12 months (intermediate risk). Oncogenic HPV non-16/18 with possible high-grade or worse on LBC -> colposcopy. Persistent oncogenic HPV at 24 months -> colposcopy.
key_points: HPV 16/18 (any LBC): direct colposcopy
Other oncogenic HPV + negative/low-grade LBC: repeat HPV at 12 months
Other oncogenic HPV + possible high-grade or worse LBC: colposcopy
If 12-month repeat HPV negative -> return to 5-yearly screening
Self-collected vaginal swab is now universally available since July 2022
explanation.pearls: Reflex LBC is performed automatically by the lab if oncogenic HPV is detected; the practitioner does not need to order it separately.

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening - oncogenic non-16/18 HPV management

stem:
A 62-year-old G3P3 woman presents to her general practice with a 6-week history of intermittent painless vaginal bleeding. She has been menopausal since age 51 (last menstrual period at 51) and has had no episodes of bleeding in the intervening 11 years until now. The current bleeding is light to moderate, requires a pad most days, and has been ongoing intermittently for the last 6 weeks.

There is no associated abdominal or pelvic pain, no urinary symptoms, no bowel change and no weight loss. She has never been on menopausal hormone therapy, has never used tamoxifen, and has no family history of endometrial, ovarian, breast or bowel cancer (specifically no features of Lynch syndrome on family history). Her BMI is 33, she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 g twice daily (HbA1c 6.6%), and her hypertension is well controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily.

She has had three previous spontaneous vaginal births, none complicated, and no postpartum haemorrhage. Her last cervical screening test was negative for oncogenic HPV 18 months ago. She is on no anticoagulants and no antiplatelets. A transvaginal ultrasound is being arranged today.

data_table.Examination: BMI 33. Speculum: small amount of dark blood at cervix, no visible cervical lesion. Bimanual: uterus mobile, normal size, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, platelets 240. UEC and LFTs normal. Beta-hCG not indicated. Cervical screening negative 18 months ago.

lead_in: Regarding TVUS endometrial thickness in this clinical setting, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: If TVUS endometrial thickness is <=2 mm then endometrial sampling is mandatory regardless of other factors
options.rationale: Endometrial thickness <=4 mm has very low cancer risk and TVUS alone may be sufficient initial triage; sampling not mandatory below this cut-off. Mandatory sampling at <=2 mm is over-treatment (RANZCOG).

options.text: A TVUS endometrial thickness of 3 mm essentially excludes endometrial cancer and no further investigation is needed even if recurrent bleeding
options.rationale: Although thin endometrium has high NPV, recurrent or persistent PMB requires sampling regardless of TVUS thickness. Reassurance without sampling is correct only for single PMB episode with thin endometrium and resolution (RCOG).

options.text: Tamoxifen use makes TVUS thickness measurement unreliable due to subepithelial cysts; saline sonohysterography or hysteroscopy is preferred
options.rationale: True but not directly relevant - she is not on tamoxifen. This option is a red herring (RANZCOG).

options.text: She should proceed directly to hysteroscopy without prior TVUS, given her constellation of risk factors
options.rationale: TVUS is appropriate first-line imaging; hysteroscopy is for thickened endometrium >=4 mm, recurrent PMB, or non-diagnostic Pipelle. Direct hysteroscopy is correct after TVUS shows thickened or focal endometrium (RCOG; RANZCOG).

options.text: Endometrial thickness >=4 mm on TVUS warrants endometrial sampling (Pipelle), with hysteroscopy if focal lesions or non-diagnostic sampling
options.rationale: The widely used 4 mm cut-off has a sensitivity of ~95% for endometrial carcinoma in postmenopausal bleeding; endometrial sampling is indicated above this threshold, with hysteroscopy +/- directed biopsy if focal pathology is suspected or Pipelle is non-diagnostic (RCOG Green-top 67; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: TVUS endometrial thickness <=4 mm has a high negative predictive value (~99%) for endometrial cancer in PMB; sampling not mandatory if bleeding is a single episode. Thickness >=4 mm triggers Pipelle biopsy +/- hysteroscopy. Recurrent PMB warrants sampling regardless of TVUS. Risk factors: obesity, T2DM, nulliparity, late menopause, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome.
key_points: TVUS endometrial thickness >=4 mm -> Pipelle biopsy
Recurrent PMB -> sample regardless of TVUS thickness
Hysteroscopy if focal lesion, non-diagnostic Pipelle, or thickened endometrium
Risk factors: obesity, DM, PCOS, nulliparity, tamoxifen, Lynch, unopposed oestrogen
Approximately 10% of PMB has endometrial cancer
explanation.pearls: Any PMB warrants investigation. A thin endometrium does not equal a benign outcome if bleeding recurs.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding - TVUS endometrial thickness threshold

stem:
A 53-year-old G2P2 woman presents to her GP with 18 months of disabling vasomotor symptoms: 8-12 hot flushes per day with drenching night sweats requiring change of nightwear most nights, fragmented sleep with average 4-5 hours, persistently low mood (PHQ-9 score 11), and reduced libido. She has tried fan, cooling clothing, regular exercise, alcohol avoidance and trigger-diary approaches with limited benefit.

Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago and she is therefore postmenopausal by clinical criteria. She has an intact uterus and has had no episodes of postmenopausal bleeding. Her BMI is 31, BP 132/84 mmHg, fasting lipids in target range and HbA1c 5.5%. She had a single provoked DVT after a long-haul flight 8 years ago and was anticoagulated for 3 months; no thrombophilia was identified and she has had no subsequent VTE.

She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no ischaemic heart disease, and no migraine with aura. She does not smoke. Cervical screening and mammography are up to date and normal. She does not want a monthly bleed and would prefer a no-bleed regimen if possible.

data_table.Examination: BMI 31. BP 132/84. Breast examination normal. Pelvic examination unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Fasting lipids: total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.1. HbA1c 5.5%. TSH 1.6 mIU/L. Mammogram normal 10 months ago.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate MHT regimen for her?

options.text: Oral oestradiol 1 mg daily plus cyclical medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg for 12 days each month
options.rationale: Cyclical progestogen produces monthly bleed and is preferred in perimenopausal women still cycling; this woman is >12 months postmenopausal preferring no-bleed. Cyclical regimen is correct in perimenopausal HRT (BMS; Jean Hailes).

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily plus continuous medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg orally
options.rationale: Oral oestrogen increases VTE risk ~2-fold; transdermal at standard doses does not. Oral CEE is correct only in women without VTE risk factors (BMS; Jean Hailes).

options.text: Tibolone 2.5 mg orally once daily as monotherapy for menopausal symptom control alone
options.rationale: Tibolone is reasonable for vasomotor and libido symptoms but increases stroke risk (especially age >60) and is not first-line in women with elevated stroke risk. Tibolone is correct in younger women without stroke risk factors (BMS).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 mcg/24 h twice weekly plus levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD (Mirena)
options.rationale: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and does not increase VTE risk at standard doses, making it the preferred route in women with prior VTE, obesity or other VTE risk factors. The LNG-IUS provides effective endometrial protection in a no-bleed manner. Together this provides combined MHT for a woman with an intact uterus (BMS 2024; Jean Hailes).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 mcg/24 h applied twice weekly alone, with no progestogen at all
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; progestogen mandatory. Oestrogen-alone is correct only after hysterectomy (BMS; Jean Hailes).

explanation.summary: MHT principles: oestrogen alone if hysterectomy; combined (oestrogen + progestogen) if uterus intact. Cyclical progestogen for perimenopausal women still having periods; continuous combined for women >=12 months postmenopausal who want no bleed. Transdermal oestrogen preferred when VTE risk is elevated (prior VTE, obesity, age) - no first-pass hepatic effect. LNG-IUS is an effective progestogen for endometrial protection.
key_points: Uterus intact -> add progestogen (mandatory)
Hysterectomy -> oestrogen alone
Cyclical progestogen if still cycling; continuous if >12 months amenorrhoea
Transdermal oestrogen: no increased VTE risk; preferred if VTE risk factors
Absolute contraindications: current/recent breast cancer, oestrogen-dependent malignancy, undiagnosed PV bleeding, active VTE/PE, active liver disease, untreated endometrial hyperplasia
explanation.pearls: If a woman has a uterus and you forget the progestogen, you cause endometrial cancer. LNG-IUS plus transdermal oestrogen is an elegant solution in many women.

subtopic_detail: MHT - regimen selection and route

stem:
A 67-year-old woman presents to her GP with 18 months of progressive vaginal dryness, deep dyspareunia and urinary urgency without incontinence. She has had three episodes of culture-confirmed E. coli urinary tract infection in the past 12 months, each requiring antibiotics, with no upper-tract involvement. She had a left-sided early-stage T1N0 oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer treated with breast-conserving lumpectomy, sentinel node biopsy, adjuvant radiotherapy and 5 years of adjuvant tamoxifen completed 12 months ago.

She did not receive an aromatase inhibitor. She is currently in remission with no evidence of disease on her most recent annual surveillance mammogram and clinical breast examination 4 months ago. She is not on systemic MHT. She has tried over-the-counter water-based vaginal lubricants for intercourse and a non-hormonal hyaluronic acid-based vaginal moisturiser (Replens) used three times weekly consistently for 4 months with only modest symptomatic benefit. She is sexually active with her long-term partner and her quality of life and intimate relationship are significantly affected.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: pale thin atrophic vaginal mucosa, friable, loss of rugae. No discharge, no lesions. Bimanual: normal-sized uterus, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Urine MCS today: no growth. Last surveillance mammogram and clinical breast examination 4 months ago: no evidence of disease.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Avoid all oestrogen-containing therapies indefinitely and continue non-hormonal vaginal moisturisers and lubricants only
options.rationale: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen has minimal systemic absorption; recent observational data suggest no increased recurrence in non-AI users. Strict avoidance is correct only on aromatase inhibitor therapy or with patient/oncology preference (BMS; Jean Hailes).
source_refs: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.text: Commence systemic oestradiol patch 50 mcg/24 h plus an LNG-IUS for endometrial protection
options.rationale: Systemic MHT is generally avoided in breast cancer survivors; local low-dose vaginal oestrogen is more appropriate and effective for GSM. Systemic MHT is correct only in selected refractory vasomotor symptoms with oncology consent (BMS; Jean Hailes).

options.text: Trial low-dose vaginal oestriol cream after discussion with breast oncologist, continuing non-hormonal moisturisers
options.rationale: Local vaginal oestrogen in a breast cancer survivor not on aromatase inhibitors is appropriate after shared decision-making with the oncology team; severe GSM significantly affects quality of life and the systemic absorption is minimal. Current evidence does not show increased recurrence risk for most survivors. She is on no current endocrine therapy (completed tamoxifen 12 months ago) (BMS 2024; Jean Hailes; NAMS 2020).
source_refs: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.text: Refer for fractional CO2 vaginal laser treatment as first-line alternative in this patient
options.rationale: Vaginal laser therapy lacks high-quality efficacy/safety evidence; TGA and international societies caution against use outside trials. Laser is correct only in clinical trial settings (TGA; NAMS).
source_refs: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.text: Commence ospemifene orally as the first-line therapy for her dyspareunia in this setting
options.rationale: Ospemifene is contraindicated in current/recent breast cancer due to oestrogen agonist effects on breast tissue. Ospemifene is correct in postmenopausal dyspareunia without breast cancer history (FDA labelling).

explanation.summary: GSM (vaginal atrophy + urinary symptoms) responds well to low-dose vaginal oestrogen with minimal systemic absorption. In breast cancer survivors, local vaginal oestrogen is increasingly used after shared decision-making with the oncologist, especially in those not on aromatase inhibitors and with significant symptom burden. Non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants are first-line; vaginal oestrogen is added when symptoms persist.
key_points: First-line: non-hormonal moisturisers (Replens) + lubricants
Second-line: low-dose vaginal oestriol cream or oestradiol pessary
Local vaginal oestrogen: minimal systemic absorption
In breast cancer survivors: shared decision with oncology; tamoxifen users generally acceptable; AI users more contentious
GSM also reduces recurrent UTIs in postmenopausal women
explanation.pearls: Recurrent UTIs in a postmenopausal woman are often a manifestation of GSM and respond to vaginal oestrogen better than to recurrent antibiotic courses.

sources.label: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

subtopic_detail: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause - local oestrogen

stem:
A 64-year-old G2P2 postmenopausal woman has a 6-year established diagnosis of vulval lichen sclerosus, biopsy-confirmed at the time of diagnosis. She has been managed with topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment using a structured regimen (nightly for 4 weeks, then alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance long-term) and has been reasonably symptom-controlled until recently, with annual review by her gynaecologist.

Over the past 4 months she has noticed a persistent fissured area on the right labium majus that has not healed despite optimisation of her steroid technique (correct application, adequate quantity confirmed at recent review). Symptoms include localised pruritus that has worsened, occasional spotting when wiping after micturition, and increasing discomfort with intercourse despite use of personal lubricant. She has no postcoital bleeding aside from the localised spotting described.

She is on no immunosuppressive medications and is otherwise well, with controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily. There is no history of previous vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, no previous vulval surgery, and her last cervical screening 18 months ago was negative for oncogenic HPV.

data_table.Examination: Vulva: classic white atrophic 'cigarette paper' skin extending in a figure-of-eight around vulva and perianal area, loss of labia minora architecture. New finding: 1.2 cm hyperkeratotic, fissured, indurated plaque on right labium majus that has not healed.
data_table.Investigations: None done today; review appointment for chronic LS surveillance.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase topical clobetasol propionate to nightly application for a further 8 weeks and review symptoms
options.rationale: Unhealed, indurated, or hyperkeratotic lesion in longstanding lichen sclerosus must NOT be assumed steroid-responsive; biopsy required to exclude differentiated VIN/SCC. Steroid increase is correct only after biopsy excludes neoplasia (BSSVD).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.text: Add topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment as a second-line steroid-sparing agent for symptomatic control of disease
options.rationale: Topical tacrolimus is recognised second-line steroid-sparing agent, but priority here is biopsy of the suspicious lesion before changing therapy. Tacrolimus is correct after biopsy excludes neoplasia (BSSVD).

options.text: Reassure that surveillance is not required after 5 years of stable disease and discharge to self-management with PRN steroid only
options.rationale: Lichen sclerosus carries 4-5% lifetime vulval SCC risk; long-term surveillance with prompt biopsy of suspicious lesions is recommended. Reassurance is essentially never correct in lichen sclerosus (BAD).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.text: Refer for wide local excision of the suspicious vulval lesion without prior histology being obtained
options.rationale: Diagnostic biopsy precedes any wide excision; excisional treatment depends on histology. Wide excision is correct after histological confirmation of malignancy (BSSVD; RCOG).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.text: Refer urgently to gynaecology/vulval clinic for punch biopsy of the persistent fissured lesion, continuing topical clobetasol and at least annual surveillance
options.rationale: Persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque, induration, or non-healing lesion in established lichen sclerosus requires prompt biopsy to exclude differentiated VIN (the precursor most associated with LS-related vulval SCC, typically HPV-negative) and invasive SCC. Long-term annual surveillance is recommended due to ~4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC. Topical potent steroid (clobetasol) remains the cornerstone of medical management (BSSVD 2018; RCOG; Cancer Council).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with a 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma (via differentiated VIN, typically HPV-negative). Management: potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol 0.05% ointment) induction then maintenance, plus long-term clinician surveillance. Any persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque, induration or non-healing lesion warrants prompt biopsy. Self-management alone is inappropriate due to malignancy risk.
key_points: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment is the gold-standard topical therapy
Structured induction then maintenance (typically twice weekly long-term)
Lifetime vulval SCC risk ~4-5% via differentiated VIN (HPV-negative pathway)
Biopsy: persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque, induration, non-healing lesion
At least annual clinician review long-term, more frequent if uncontrolled or atypical features
Tacrolimus second-line; surgery reserved for adhesions/scarring or malignancy
explanation.pearls: Differentiated VIN looks innocuous and is easy to miss - any unhealed area in LS deserves a biopsy regardless of how unremarkable it appears.

sources.label: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

subtopic_detail: Lichen sclerosus - surveillance and malignancy risk

stem:
A 27-year-old G1P0 at 40+3 in spontaneous labour has had an epidural sited two hours ago with a top-up given 25 minutes ago for a left-sided breakthrough. Her booking BMI was 24, she is a non-smoker, has no medical comorbidities, and the GBS swab at 36 weeks was negative. The last vaginal examination 40 minutes ago showed 8 cm dilatation, +0 station, direct OA, intact caput, no moulding.

Membranes ruptured spontaneously 6 hours ago with clear liquor. Oxytocin augmentation was started 90 minutes ago for slow progress between 6 and 8 cm and is currently at 12 mU/min with contractions 4 in 10, lasting 70 seconds, palpating moderate. The CTG over the last 30 minutes shows a baseline of 145 bpm, reduced variability of 3 to 5 bpm, no accelerations, and recurrent late decelerations occurring with more than 50% of contractions for the last 25 minutes.

There has been no prolonged deceleration. The mother is comfortable and the partogram shows progress consistent with primary dysfunctional labour. The obstetric registrar is at the bedside and theatre is available.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: 8 cm, +0, direct OA, clear liquor. Uterus soft between contractions. Palpates 4 in 10 moderate.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 145 bpm, variability 3-5 bpm, no accelerations, recurrent late decelerations >50% of contractions x 25 min. No tachysystole on tocodynamometer.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.text: Stop oxytocin, reposition to left lateral, give 500 mL IV crystalloid, perform fetal scalp lactate within 15 minutes
options.rationale: This CTG is FIGO pathological (recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability) but without a sustained bradycardia, so intrauterine resuscitation plus fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate is the appropriate next step before escalating to category 1 caesarean (RANZCOG IFSM 2019; FIGO 2015).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019
FIGO consensus guidelines on intrapartum fetal monitoring 2015

options.text: Continue oxytocin and observe for a further 30 minutes to determine if the pattern resolves spontaneously
options.rationale: Recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability for 25 minutes is pathological; continuing oxytocin worsens fetal acidosis. Observation is correct only with normal/suspicious traces (RANZCOG IFSM 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

options.text: Proceed immediately to a category 1 caesarean section with a 30-minute decision-to-delivery interval
options.rationale: Category 1 CS is for acute decompensation (bradycardia, abruption, cord prolapse); pathological trace without acute decompensation warrants fetal scalp sampling first. Category 1 CS is correct with acute compromise (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

options.text: Administer terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously for acute tocolysis and continue oxytocin at the current rate
options.rationale: Terbutaline tocolysis is indicated for tachysystole-related compromise; no tachysystole here. Terbutaline is correct in tachysystole-driven decelerations (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

options.text: Perform an artificial rupture of membranes and apply a fetal scalp electrode without further intrauterine resuscitation
options.rationale: Membranes already ruptured and FSE without addressing the pathological pattern is insufficient. FSE alone is correct only with maternal-fetal CTG confusion needing direct trace (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

explanation.summary: A FIGO pathological CTG without acute decompensation is managed with intrauterine resuscitation (stop oxytocin, left lateral, IV fluid, exclude hypotension, exclude tachysystole, consider tocolysis) and fetal scalp lactate sampling. Lactate >=4.8 mmol/L mandates delivery; 4.2-4.7 repeat in 30 minutes; <4.2 reassuring.
key_points: FIGO pathological = >=2 abnormal features OR sinusoidal OR prolonged bradycardia >5 min
Reduced variability + recurrent late decelerations = pathological
Intrauterine resuscitation mnemonic: SPOILT (Stop oxytocin, Position, Oxygen [no longer routinely recommended], IV fluid, Lower BP causes, Tocolysis)
Fetal scalp lactate cut-offs: <4.2 normal, 4.2-4.7 borderline, >=4.8 abnormal
Category 1 CS target decision-to-delivery 30 minutes
explanation.pearls: Reduced variability is the most predictive single feature of fetal acidosis. Recurrent late decelerations with a flat trace is the pattern that should provoke action even without bradycardia.

sources.label: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019
FIGO consensus guidelines on intrapartum fetal monitoring 2015

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum CTG - recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 at 39+1 in spontaneous labour at 6 cm has an epidural in situ that was sited 90 minutes ago and has provided good analgesia until the last hour, when she began to feel a sharp left-sided sensation with contractions. Her booking BMI was 27, she has no cardiac, respiratory or neurological comorbidities, no allergies, no anaphylaxis history, and her booking bloods including FBC and group and screen were unremarkable.

Five minutes ago the anaesthetic registrar gave a top-up of 10 mL of 0.1% ropivacaine with 2 microg/mL fentanyl for breakthrough pain. Her BP has now dropped from 122/74 to 84/46 mmHg with a maternal HR of 102. She feels light-headed but is conscious and is not nauseated, has no perioral numbness, no tinnitus and no metallic taste. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 80 bpm that has now been ongoing for 4 minutes after previously reassuring features (baseline 140, variability 10-15, accelerations present).

There has been no vaginal bleeding, the uterus is soft between contractions (no hypertonus), the liquor was clear at ARM 30 minutes earlier, and there is no concern for cord prolapse on bedside vaginal examination. The anaesthetic registrar is at the bedside and IV access is patent through a 16G cannula.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/46 mmHg, HR 102 bpm (maternal), T 36.7 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Awake, light-headed. Uterus soft between contractions. No PV bleeding. Cord not palpable.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: prolonged deceleration to 80 bpm for 4 minutes following epidural top-up.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Ephedrine 6 mg IV bolus, repeat at 1-2 minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: Ephedrine is acceptable but contemporary obstetric anaesthesia favours phenylephrine because ephedrine crosses placenta and increases fetal acidaemia. Ephedrine is correct only when phenylephrine unavailable or maternal bradycardia (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

options.text: Metaraminol 0.5 mg IV bolus, repeat at 1-2 minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: Metaraminol is a reasonable alpha-agonist alternative commonly used in Australia, but phenylephrine has the strongest evidence base. Metaraminol is correct as second-line alpha-agonist (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

options.text: Phenylephrine 100 microg IV bolus, repeat at 1-2 minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: Phenylephrine 50-100 microg IV bolus is the first-line vasopressor for neuraxial-induced maternal hypotension because it preserves uterine blood flow and reduces fetal acidaemia compared with ephedrine; combined with left uterine displacement and a fluid bolus this typically resolves the prolonged deceleration (ANZCA; SOAP consensus 2018).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia
SOAP Consensus Statement on hypotension management 2018

options.text: Adrenaline 10 microg IV bolus and prepare for category 1 caesarean
options.rationale: Adrenaline boluses are reserved for cardiac arrest or anaphylaxis; this is treatable neuraxial hypotension. Adrenaline is correct in cardiac arrest or anaphylaxis only (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

options.text: Atropine 600 microg IV bolus to correct the maternal heart rate
options.rationale: Maternal HR is 102; atropine treats bradycardia not hypotension and would not correct uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Atropine is correct in bradycardia-driven hypotension only (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

explanation.summary: Prolonged deceleration following an epidural top-up is most commonly due to maternal hypotension reducing uteroplacental perfusion. Manage with full left lateral position, IV crystalloid bolus 250-500 mL, and phenylephrine 50-100 microg IV bolus (first-line). If the deceleration does not resolve within 9 minutes, prepare for category 1 caesarean.
key_points: Phenylephrine first-line for neuraxial hypotension in obstetrics
Ephedrine causes more fetal acidaemia (crosses placenta, beta-agonist on fetal heart)
Metaraminol is an acceptable Australian alternative
Always exclude cord prolapse, abruption and uterine rupture as causes of prolonged deceleration
9-minute rule: prolonged deceleration not recovering requires immediate delivery decision
explanation.pearls: Treat the maternal BP first; the fetal heart rate almost always follows. If you are reaching for atropine for the baby, you have the wrong drug.

sources.label: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia
SOAP Consensus Statement on hypotension management 2018

subtopic_detail: Prolonged deceleration after epidural top-up - vasopressor choice

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 40+1 in spontaneous labour, admitted 6 hours ago at 5 cm, is re-examined and is now 6 cm at +0 station in direct OP position with mild caput and no moulding. Membranes ruptured spontaneously 4 hours ago with clear liquor. Contractions: palpate 3 in 10 lasting 40 seconds, mild intensity. CTG normal. Hb 124. Her mother is reminding the registrar that her own labour had to be 'started with the drip' and asks them to do the same.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: 6 cm, +0, direct OP, mild caput, no moulding. Contractions 3 in 10, 40 s, mild.
data_table.Investigations: CTG normal. GBS negative. Hb 124 g/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence IV oxytocin infusion starting at 1-2 mU/min, titrated every 30 minutes to achieve 4-5 contractions per 10 minutes
options.rationale: Membranes are already ruptured and there is inadequate contraction frequency/strength causing slow progress in the active first stage. Oxytocin augmentation at 1-2 mU/min titrated every 30 minutes is the correct Australian protocol; faster titration risks hyperstimulation (RANZCOG; eTG).

options.text: Perform ARM and reassess in 4 hours before considering oxytocin
options.rationale: Membranes already spontaneously ruptured; ARM not applicable. ARM is correct in intact membranes with poor progress (RANZCOG).

options.text: Proceed to category 2 caesarean section for failure to progress
options.rationale: Failure to progress requires demonstration after adequate uterine activity (after oxytocin); proceeding to caesarean before oxytocin is premature. Cat 2 CS is correct after oxytocin trial fails (RANZCOG).

options.text: Commence IV oxytocin infusion starting at 6 mU/min with no titration interval shorter than 60 minutes
options.rationale: Starting at 6 mU/min risks hyperstimulation and fetal compromise; standard starts at 1-2 mU/min titrated every 30 minutes. High-dose start is correct only with maximum-dose review and continuous fetal monitoring in selected protocols (RANZCOG).

options.text: Site an epidural and re-examine her in 6 hours without commencing any augmentation now
options.rationale: Pain relief is reasonable but does not address slow progress with inadequate contractions; delay risks fetal compromise. Epidural without augmentation is correct when contractions are adequate (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Primary dysfunctional labour in a nullipara at 6 cm with inadequate contractions and intact membranes is managed with oxytocin augmentation (after ARM if membranes intact). Start at 1-2 mU/min and double every 30 minutes to a usual maximum of 32 mU/min, titrated to 4-5 contractions per 10 minutes. Diagnose labour dystocia only after at least 4 hours of adequate contractions with no progress, then proceed to CS.
key_points: Active phase: >=6 cm with regular contractions (Zhang/ACOG)
Adequate progress nullipara: ~0.5-1 cm/h after 6 cm
Oxytocin start 1-2 mU/min, double every 30 min, max ~32 mU/min
Target: 4-5 contractions per 10 min, 45-60 s, moderate-strong
Diagnose dystocia after >=4 h adequate contractions without progress
explanation.pearls: Direct OP at 6 cm is a common cause of slow progress; many will rotate spontaneously with adequate contractions plus mobility/epidural.

sources.label: KEMH Clinical Guideline: Augmentation of labour
Royal Women's Hospital - Oxytocin in labour

subtopic_detail: Failure to progress in active first stage - oxytocin augmentation

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 at 38+2 in spontaneous labour at 10 cm dilatation has just had a spontaneous rupture of membranes with a large gush of clear liquor. The midwife performing a vaginal examination immediately feels a pulsating loop of cord in the vagina at +0 station. The fetal head is at -2 station and direct OA, with 3/5 of the head still palpable abdominally.

The CTG was previously reassuring (baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present, no decelerations) but now shows a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm starting within the last minute. The mother is comfortable on her right side with an epidural in situ; her observations are BP 122/78, HR 88, T 36.9, SpO2 99%. She is otherwise well, has no obstetric or medical comorbidities, and her 36-week growth scan was unremarkable.

The emergency buzzer has been pulled and the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams are en route. She has had no previous abdominal surgery, no caesarean section, and is otherwise low risk for surgical complications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: 10 cm, -2 station, direct OA, pulsating cord at +0 in vagina. Liquor clear. Bladder catheterised.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm, starting within the last minute.

lead_in: Which immediate set of actions is most appropriate?

options.text: Reduce the cord back into the uterus through the cervix and proceed to instrumental vaginal delivery in the room
options.rationale: Cord replacement is no longer recommended due to cord trauma and vasospasm; manual elevation of presenting part is preferred. Cord replacement is essentially obsolete (RANZCOG; RCOG Green-top).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical cord prolapse

options.text: Continue oxytocin augmentation, reposition the mother to left lateral and reassess CTG again in 5 minutes
options.rationale: Oxytocin must be STOPPED immediately to reduce contractions compressing cord; 5-minute observation is unsafe with prolonged deceleration. Continued oxytocin is essentially never correct in cord prolapse (RANZCOG).

options.text: Administer terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously and proceed immediately to assisted vaginal birth using a ventouse now
options.rationale: Tocolysis with terbutaline may be considered for hyperstimulation or transfer delay, but ventouse at -2 station is contraindicated (station must be >=+2). Tocolysis + ventouse combination is never correct (RANZCOG).

options.text: Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord, knee-chest or exaggerated Sims, fill bladder 500 mL if delay, category 1 caesarean
options.rationale: At -2 station vaginal delivery is not imminent. Manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord (or bladder filling with 500-700 mL warmed saline if transfer delay) plus knee-chest/Sims position plus category 1 CS within 30 minutes is the standard pathway (RANZCOG; RCOG Green-top 50).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical cord prolapse

options.text: Wait for the next contraction at full dilatation and perform a fundal pressure delivery to expedite vaginal birth
options.rationale: Fundal pressure contraindicated; head is at -2 station with vaginal delivery not feasible. Category 1 CS required. Pushing-fundal pressure is essentially never correct in cord prolapse (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with a non-imminent vaginal delivery requires manual elevation of the presenting part (or bladder filling with 500-700 mL warmed saline for transfer delay), knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position, stop oxytocin, consider tocolysis if hyperstimulation, and category 1 caesarean section with a 30-minute decision-to-delivery interval.
key_points: Diagnosis: pulsating cord palpated below the presenting part
Manual elevation preferred over cord replacement
Bladder filling 500-700 mL saline if transfer delay
Stop oxytocin; consider terbutaline 250 microg SC if hyperstimulation
Category 1 CS, decision-to-delivery target 30 min (RANZCOG/NICE)
Instrumental vaginal birth only if fully dilated AND station >=+2 AND operator confident
explanation.pearls: Keep the examiner's hand in the vagina elevating the presenting part during transfer; do not handle the cord more than necessary because handling causes vasospasm.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical cord prolapse

subtopic_detail: Cord prolapse - immediate management at full dilatation

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 40+0 with an epidural is in active second stage. She has been pushing for 110 minutes without descent of the presenting part beyond +1 station. The fetal head is at +1, direct OA, with no caput or moulding palpable, and 0/5 of the head is palpable abdominally on Crichton assessment. The maternal pelvis was clinically adequate on assessment by both registrar and consultant.

The CTG shows a baseline of 145 with variability 5-10 bpm, no accelerations and variable decelerations with most contractions but no late or prolonged decelerations and no sinusoidal pattern. Membranes are ruptured with clear liquor of normal volume. Contractions are 4 in 10 with oxytocin running at 16 mU/min. The mother is exhausted, asking for help to deliver, and has had a thorough antenatal discussion of birth options including operative delivery.

The bladder is empty after recent catheter in/out. Adequate epidural top-up has been given and the block is dense to ice. The neonatal team has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 37.0 degC.
data_table.Examination: +1 station, direct OA, 0/5 head palpable abdominally, no caput, no moulding. Bladder empty. Epidural adequate.
data_table.Investigations: CTG suspicious (variable decelerations, reduced variability), not pathological.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate instrument and approach for this delivery?

options.text: Kielland's rotational forceps for a deep transverse arrest under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Position is direct OA, not transverse arrest; Kielland's restricted to experienced operators for rotational deliveries. Kielland's is correct in deep transverse arrest by experienced operators (RANZCOG; RCOG GTG).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted Vaginal Birth

options.text: Low-cavity non-rotational outlet forceps (Neville-Barnes or Simpson) under regional anaesthesia
options.rationale: Direct OA at +1 station with maternal exhaustion and adequate epidural is suitable for low-cavity non-rotational forceps. Forceps have a lower failure rate than ventouse in maternal exhaustion and a suspicious (but not pathological) CTG (RANZCOG; RCOG GTG 26).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted Vaginal Birth

options.text: Sequential ventouse then forceps if the initial vacuum extraction attempt fails to descend
options.rationale: Sequential instrument use significantly increases neonatal morbidity (ICH, subgaleal); generally avoided. Sequential is correct only when head on perineum and primary instrument fails (RCOG).

options.text: Kiwi OmniCup soft ventouse with traction synchronous with maternal contractions only and pulls
options.rationale: Ventouse has higher failure rate than forceps in maternal exhaustion and suspicious CTG, plus higher cephalohaematoma/subgaleal rates. Ventouse is correct in early descent and adequate maternal effort (RANZCOG).

options.text: Proceed directly to a category 2 caesarean section now without attempted instrumental delivery
options.rationale: At +1 station with 0/5 palpable abdominally and direct OA, trial of instrumental is appropriate. Category 2 CS is correct after failed instrumental or with malposition not amenable to instruments (RANZCOG; NICE).

explanation.summary: For mid-cavity or low-cavity OA position with maternal exhaustion and a suspicious (not pathological) CTG, non-rotational forceps have a higher success rate than ventouse and a lower neonatal cephalohaematoma rate, but a higher rate of maternal perineal trauma. Sequential instrument use is associated with higher neonatal morbidity and should be avoided. Document fetal station, position, caput/moulding, bladder, epidural, and consent prior to commencing.
key_points: Pre-instrumental checklist: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, head <=1/5 palpable abdominally, defined station, defined position, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, consent
Forceps: higher success rate, more maternal trauma
Ventouse: higher failure rate, more cephalohaematoma/subgaleal haemorrhage
Sequential use significantly increases neonatal morbidity
Failed instrumental: stop after 3 contractions with no descent or after 20 minutes total
explanation.pearls: Choose the instrument most likely to succeed first. If you would normally choose ventouse but conditions are marginal (exhaustion, suspicious CTG, OP), forceps usually has the better outcome.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted Vaginal Birth

subtopic_detail: Instrumental birth - forceps vs ventouse selection

stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 39+4 having a trial of labour after caesarean (one previous LSCS for breech) is in active labour at 7 cm with epidural. The CTG develops a sudden prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm, not recovering after 4 minutes despite stopping oxytocin, left lateral, 500 mL crystalloid and exclusion of hypotension. Fresh PV bleeding develops, scar tenderness, and the previously palpable head becomes ballotable abdominally (suspected uterine rupture). The registrar calls a category 1 caesarean section.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Scar tender, fresh PV bleeding, head ballotable abdominally.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: prolonged deceleration 60 bpm, not recovering at 4 minutes.

lead_in: Which combination most accurately describes the standards for category 1 caesarean and the immediate priorities?

options.text: Decision-to-delivery interval target 30 minutes; concurrent MTP activation, theatre transfer, anaesthetic preparation; do not delay for re-examination
options.rationale: The Australian/NICE standard for category 1 caesarean is delivery as soon as possible, with a 30-minute auditable threshold; bypassing further bedside investigation is appropriate when uterine rupture is suspected, and parallel resuscitation and MTP activation are essential (RANZCOG; RCOG).

options.text: Decision-to-delivery 15 minutes; defer MTP activation until intraoperative blood loss is confirmed
options.rationale: 15 minutes is idealised target rarely achieved; audited standard is 30 minutes. MTP should be activated proactively given suspected rupture. 15-minute target is correct only in immediate intra-theatre rupture (RANZCOG).

options.text: Decision-to-delivery 60 minutes; obtain confirmatory bedside ultrasound before transfer to theatre
options.rationale: 60 minutes is threshold for category 2 CS; rupture is category 1 emergency. 60 minutes is correct for category 2 (RANZCOG).

options.text: Decision-to-delivery 75 minutes if epidural is already sited and theatre is in-house
options.rationale: Epidural availability does not change category-1 timing; target is 30 minutes. 75 minutes is essentially never appropriate in suspected rupture (RANZCOG).

options.text: Decision-to-delivery 45 minutes; abandon TOLAC pathway only after delivery is achieved
options.rationale: TOLAC is abandoned the moment rupture is suspected, not after delivery; target is 30 minutes. 45 minutes is appropriate only in category 2 status (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Categorisation of urgency for caesarean section (RANZCOG/NICE): Cat 1 - immediate threat (target 30 min decision-to-delivery); Cat 2 - maternal or fetal compromise, not immediately life-threatening (target 60-75 min); Cat 3 - early delivery needed but no compromise; Cat 4 - delivery timed to suit woman or staff.
key_points: Cat 1: 30 minutes (audit standard)
Cat 2: 60-75 minutes (audit standard)
30 minutes is an audit standard, not a strict outcome threshold
Common Cat 1 indications: cord prolapse, abruption, uterine rupture, scalp pH <7.20, prolonged bradycardia
explanation.pearls: Document time of decision, time of arrival in theatre, time of knife-to-skin, and time of delivery for every Cat 1 CS for departmental audit.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Categorisation of urgency for caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Decision-to-delivery interval for category 1 caesarean

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth at 40+2 of a 4.0 kg neonate after a 9-hour first stage and a 45-minute second stage with oxytocin augmentation for slow progress in the first stage. Active management of the third stage with IM oxytocin 10 units has been given and the placenta is delivered intact 8 minutes after the baby.

There is now ongoing brisk PV bleeding estimated at 1200 mL over 10 minutes with a soft, boggy uterus that is poorly contracted at the umbilicus. The bladder has been catheterised and is empty. Bimanual compression has been commenced. IV oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's at 250 mL/h is already running through a 16G cannula. Her observations are BP 96/58, HR 118, T 36.7.

She has a history of asthma (mild, intermittent, no recent exacerbations) but no hypertensive disorder of pregnancy and no other medical comorbidities. Blood has been sent for FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen and group and crossmatch.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, T 36.7 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and boggy, fundus at umbilicus. Bladder empty. No genital tract trauma visible. Placenta delivered intact.
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL. FBC/coags/fibrinogen/X-match sent. Asthma history (mild, intermittent).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next pharmacological step in addition to ongoing IV oxytocin infusion?

options.text: PR misoprostol 800 microg with antiemetic precaution and continue the IV oxytocin infusion at current rate
