Sequential instruments: significantly higher neonatal morbidity - avoid
Trial of instrumental in theatre when high failure risk (BMI >30, EFW >4 kg, OP/OT, mid-cavity, prolonged second stage)
Category 1 CS decision-to-delivery interval target 30 minutes
explanation.pearls: If forceps fails, the next stop is theatre, not the ventouse. The trolley is on standby for a reason.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Operative Vaginal Birth guideline

subtopic_detail: Operative vaginal delivery - prerequisites and failed forceps disposition

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 37+5 is in spontaneous labour. Twin 1 is cephalic and growth-appropriate on the 45th centile, twin 2 has been transverse throughout the third trimester on serial scans with the back inferior and is 200 g smaller than twin 1 (35th centile, within the 20% inter-twin discordance threshold and with no growth discordance suggestive of selective FGR).

There is no previous caesarean, no uterine surgery and no medical comorbidities. Both fetuses have reassuring CTGs on dual monitoring. The cervix is 6 cm, station of the leading twin is -1, membranes are intact for the leading twin and ARM has not been performed, and an experienced obstetric consultant with extensive twin delivery experience is available throughout the labour.

The anaesthetist is in the unit and an epidural has been sited and is providing good analgesia. She has expressed a clear preference for a vaginal birth if safe. After 4 hours she is fully dilated, twin 1 head is at +3, and she pushes for 25 minutes to deliver a 2900 g cephalic infant with normal Apgars. On bedside rescan by the consultant immediately after delivery of twin 1, twin 2 remains transverse with the back inferior.

The CTG of twin 2 is reassuring at this point, membranes of twin 2 are intact, and the consultant is at the bedside in the delivery suite with a theatre and a paediatric team on standby.

data_table.Antenatal: DCDA twins, twin 1 cephalic, twin 2 transverse back-inferior. EFW concordance within 20%.
data_table.After twin 1 delivery: Twin 2 remains transverse, back inferior, reassuring CTG, intact membranes.
data_table.Operator: Experienced consultant at bedside, theatre available, paediatrics on standby.
data_table.Maternal: Epidural in situ, good analgesia, haemodynamically stable.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for delivery of twin 2?

options.text: Internal podalic version followed by breech extraction of twin 2
options.rationale: With twin 2 transverse after delivery of twin 1 and an experienced operator available, internal podalic version (operator inserts a hand through the cervix, identifies a fetal foot, brings it down through the introitus) followed by breech extraction is the preferred approach in Australia and is supported by the Twin Birth Study (Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013). External cephalic version is an alternative but has lower success after delivery of the first twin and risks fetal distress and abruption. Combined vaginal-CS delivery has worse outcomes than planned CS. The reassuring CTG provides a window for intervention, and internal podalic version with breech extraction is the most reliable mode in experienced hands. CS should be reserved for failed manoeuvres or non-reassuring CTG (RANZCOG Management of Twin Pregnancy 2022; RCOG Green-top 51 Twin and Triplet Pregnancy).
source_refs: Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013 (Twin Birth Study)
RCOG Green-top 51 Twin and Triplet Pregnancy

options.text: External cephalic version under ultrasound, then expect spontaneous cephalic delivery
options.rationale: ECV has lower success rate than internal podalic version (~60% vs >90%); any delay risks cord prolapse, abruption, or cervical closure. ECV is correct in earlier antenatal management (RANZCOG).

options.text: Category 2 caesarean section for delivery of twin 2 now
options.rationale: Combined vaginal-CS delivery is associated with worse outcomes for both mother and twin 2 versus internal podalic version; reserve CS for failed manoeuvres. CS is correct after failed manoeuvres (RANZCOG).
source_refs: Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013 (Twin Birth Study)

options.text: Await spontaneous descent of twin 2 for up to 60 minutes before any intervention
options.rationale: Twin 2 transverse will not descend spontaneously; inter-twin interval should be as short as practical (commonly within 30 minutes). Waiting 60 minutes is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).

options.text: Perform ARM of twin 2 membranes immediately to allow descent
options.rationale: ARM with transverse lie is contraindicated due to high cord prolapse risk; version must occur first. ARM-first in transverse lie is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Twin delivery: twin 1 cephalic and twin 2 cephalic = planned vaginal birth. Twin 1 cephalic, twin 2 non-cephalic = vaginal birth is appropriate where an experienced operator is available; CS only if both non-cephalic or if specific contraindications. After delivery of twin 1 with non-cephalic twin 2: internal podalic version + breech extraction (preferred) or ECV if back-superior. ARM of twin 2 only after presenting part engaged. Inter-twin interval should be minimised.
key_points: Twin Birth Study (Barrett NEJM 2013): planned vaginal birth equivalent to planned CS for selected DCDA/MCDA at 32+0 to 38+6 with twin 1 cephalic
Twin 2 non-cephalic: internal podalic version + breech extraction is preferred
ECV alternative for transverse twin 2 with back superior
Monoamniotic twins always CS (cord entanglement risk)
Inter-twin interval typically <30 min to minimise cervical closure and abruption risk
Combined vaginal-CS delivery worse than planned CS for both
explanation.pearls: Twin 1 cephalic + experienced operator = trial of vaginal birth even if twin 2 is breech or transverse. The non-cephalic second twin is not by itself a CS indication.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Twin Pregnancy guideline
Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013 (Twin Birth Study)
RCOG Green-top 51 Twin and Triplet Pregnancy
NICE NG137 Twin and triplet pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Twin delivery - mode of birth with second twin non-cephalic

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P2 woman, three weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding her well term infant, presents to her GP with a 24-hour history of a tender, hot, wedge-shaped erythematous area in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. She feels feverish and shivery, has been continuing frequent feeds and effective expression after feeds, and the area has continued to enlarge over the last 12 hours.

There is no fluctuance, no skin breakdown and no axillary adenopathy. She is otherwise well. Her recorded drug allergy is to phenoxymethylpenicillin during childhood, when she developed an urticarial rash and lip swelling within 1 hour of a dose; she has never tolerated a penicillin or cephalosporin since. She has no other allergies, has not had antibiotics in the past 12 months, has no recent hospital contact and is not from a community with known high MRSA prevalence. She wishes to continue breastfeeding throughout treatment and her infant has no medical conditions and was born at term with no neonatal complications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 degC, HR 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Wedge-shaped erythema upper outer left breast, hot and tender, no fluctuance, no skin breakdown, no axillary lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear. Bedside ultrasound not yet performed.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin would be first-line but is contraindicated with immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin. Flucloxacillin is correct in non-allergic women (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Cephalosporins are avoided when penicillin reaction was immediate (Type 1) hypersensitivity with angioedema due to unpredictable cross-reactivity. Cefalexin is correct in non-immediate penicillin allergy (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Clindamycin 450 mg orally three times daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Clindamycin is the eTG-recommended alternative for lactational mastitis in patients with immediate penicillin hypersensitivity; it covers S. aureus including most CA-MRSA, is compatible with breastfeeding per LactMed and concentrates well in breast tissue (Therapeutic Guidelines; LactMed).

options.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate contains penicillin and is contraindicated in immediate hypersensitivity. Augmentin is correct in non-allergic women with suspected polymicrobial infection (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: TMP-SMX is reserved for confirmed MRSA and avoided in mothers of infants <1 month due to theoretical kernicterus risk. TMP-SMX is correct in MRSA mastitis in older infants (Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis with systemic features warrants oral antibiotics for 5-7 days plus effective milk removal. First-line is flucloxacillin; with immediate penicillin hypersensitivity the eTG alternative is clindamycin, which is breastfeeding-compatible (LactMed).
key_points: Most common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus
Continue breastfeeding/expressing - drainage is therapeutic
Immediate (Type 1) penicillin allergy excludes cephalosporins as well
Clindamycin covers most CA-MRSA and concentrates in breast tissue
TMP-SMX avoided in mothers feeding infants <1 month (kernicterus risk)
explanation.pearls: If the mother fails to improve at 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, image with ultrasound for abscess before broadening cover.

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis - antibiotic choice in penicillin allergy

stem: A 27-year-old primipara, 6 weeks postpartum, exclusively breastfeeding her thriving term infant, attends with a 14-hour history of a discrete tender lump in the lower inner right breast. Overlying skin has faint pink mottling but no defined erythema. T 36.8, no rigors, no flu-like symptoms, infant feeding effectively. Recent change: baby has slept a longer 5-hour stretch the past two nights. No fluctuance, no axillary adenopathy. She has read online that 'aggressive deep massage' and 'pump-and-dump' are recommended.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 degC, HR 78 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16.
data_table.Examination: Tender 3 cm lump lower inner right breast, faint overlying pink mottling, no defined erythema, no fluctuance, no axillary adenopathy.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue feeding from both breasts on demand, apply cold packs between feeds, ibuprofen for pain, and review in 24 hours; avoid deep massage and pump-and-dump
options.rationale: The Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine 2022 protocol describes this as ductal narrowing/inflammatory mastitis spectrum, not bacterial mastitis. Management is on-demand feeding, cold packs, NSAIDs, and AVOIDANCE of deep massage and pumping (both can worsen inflammation/oedema). Antibiotics are reserved for bacterial mastitis (RANZCOG; ABM 2022).

options.text: Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg qid for 7 days now
options.rationale: No fever, systemic symptoms, or defined erythema. Antibiotics are not indicated for inflammatory mastitis/ductal narrowing and may worsen dysbiosis. Flucloxacillin is correct in bacterial mastitis with fever/erythema (ABM 2022).

options.text: Aggressive deep breast massage every 2 hours with hot compresses for 48 hours
options.rationale: Aggressive massage worsens tissue oedema and risks abscess - the major anti-pattern that ABM 2022 specifically warns against. Aggressive massage is essentially never correct (ABM 2022).

options.text: Cease feeding from the affected breast and pump-and-dump for 48 hours
options.rationale: Cessation worsens engorgement and inflammatory cycle; on-demand feeding remains essential. Pump-and-dump is correct only with documented contraindications (ABM 2022).

options.text: Urgent breast ultrasound and surgical referral for incision and drainage
options.rationale: No fluctuance, abscess features, or failure of conservative management; surgical referral premature. Surgical referral is correct after failed conservative management or abscess (ABM 2022).

explanation.summary: The lactation inflammation spectrum runs from ductal narrowing/blocked duct (focal lump, no systemic features) through inflammatory mastitis (erythema, pain) to bacterial mastitis (systemic features) to abscess. Current evidence-based care de-emphasises deep massage and heat; the cornerstones are physiological feeding, lymphatic drainage and cold for symptom control.
key_points: Blocked duct: focal lump, no fever, no defined erythema
Inflammatory mastitis: erythema and pain, no systemic features
Bacterial mastitis: above plus fever/tachycardia, or non-resolution
Abscess: fluctuant collection on USS
Cold preferred over heat per ABM 2022 protocol
explanation.pearls: A long overnight feed gap is the classic precipitant of a blocked duct in an established 6-week breastfeeding dyad.

subtopic_detail: Blocked duct vs inflammatory mastitis vs bacterial mastitis discrimination

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P3 woman, 4 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding, was diagnosed with right-breast bacterial mastitis 5 days ago and commenced flucloxacillin 500 mg orally four times daily with continued feeding and expression. Her fevers settled within 48 hours but the erythematous area has now developed a discrete, fluctuant tender lump over the past 24 hours despite ongoing antibiotics and effective drainage.

She is afebrile today, haemodynamically stable, and the skin overlying the lump is intact, non-necrotic and not under tension. Bedside ultrasound performed by the GP demonstrates a well-defined, unilocular hypoechoic collection measuring 38 mm x 24 mm at 1.5 cm depth, with no overlying skin necrosis. She has no recurrent abscess history, no immunosuppression breastfeeding. She is comfortable being managed in primary care if the lesion is amenable to office-based drainage and the local Breast Centre offers ultrasound-guided procedures on a same-day basis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 degC, HR 84 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg.
data_table.Examination: Right breast, 4 cm fluctuant tender mass, overlying skin intact and non-necrotic, no axillary adenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside USS: unilocular 38 x 24 mm hypoechoic collection, 1.5 cm depth, no skin necrosis. Hb 124 g/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 48 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current oral flucloxacillin and review in 5 days without drainage
options.rationale: Drained collection requires drainage to resolve; antibiotics alone are inadequate and risk chronicity/fistula. Antibiotics-alone is correct only in early cellulitic phase without collection (ABM).

options.text: Refer for ultrasound-guided needle aspiration with culture; continue antibiotics, reaspirate if needed
options.rationale: For a lactational abscess under approximately 5 cm with intact non-necrotic skin, ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (often serial) with cultured aspirate and continued antibiotics is first-line; it preserves duct architecture, allows ongoing breastfeeding and avoids a surgical wound that complicates feeding (ABM; BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Refer for theatre incision and drainage with packing under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgical I&D is reserved for very large abscesses, multiloculated, or thinned/necrotic skin; leaves wound that may interfere with feeding. I&D is correct for large/complex abscesses (ABM).

options.text: Stop breastfeeding from the affected breast and continue antibiotics only
options.rationale: Cessation worsens milk stasis and slows resolution; current guidance is to continue feeding or express. Cessation is essentially never correct in mastitis/abscess (ABM).

options.text: Switch to oral clindamycin 450 mg three times daily and observe without drainage
options.rationale: Antibiotic broadening without drainage is inadequate; established collection needs source control. Clindamycin alone is correct only without abscess collection (ABM).

explanation.summary: Lactational breast abscesses require source control. Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration with cultured aspirate is first-line for abscesses up to around 5 cm with intact skin and is repeated as needed; surgical drainage is reserved for larger, multiloculated, or skin-compromised collections.
key_points: Continue breastfeeding throughout treatment
USS-guided aspiration preserves duct anatomy
Send aspirate for culture to guide ongoing antibiotics
Surgical I&D for large, multiloculated, or skin-necrosed abscesses
Antibiotics alone are inadequate once a collection has formed
explanation.pearls: An apparently improving mastitis that develops a new fluctuant area at day 5 is an abscess until ultrasound proves otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Lactational breast abscess - drainage strategy

stem:
A 28-year-old primiparous woman attends with her 3-week-old term infant for a same-day appointment because she is convinced her milk supply has dropped. The baby is now feeding for 60-80 minutes per feed, 10-12 times in 24 hours, and is unsettled between feeds. She produces only 30 mL when she expresses after a feed and feels her breasts are softer than they were at 10 days.

The infant had a birthweight of 3.4 kg, was discharged at 3.15 kg on day 4 (regained birthweight by day 12), and today weighs 3.55 kg on the practice scales. The infant is alert, has 6-8 heavy wet nappies and 3-4 mustard-yellow stools per day, has no jaundice, and feeds with audible swallowing during feeds. She has been advised by family to start formula top-ups.

She is not on any medications, has no breast surgery history, has normal-appearing breasts that grew through pregnancy, and breastfed her older nieces' children briefly without difficulty.

data_table.Infant assessment: Birthweight 3.4 kg; day 4 discharge 3.15 kg; today 3.55 kg (mean gain ~30 g/day from nadir).
data_table.Feeding: 10-12 feeds/24h, audible swallowing, 6-8 heavy wet nappies, 3-4 mustard stools/day.
data_table.Maternal: Soft breasts, no surgery, infant alert.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence formula top-ups of 60 mL after each breastfeed to meet caloric requirements
options.rationale: Supplementation without indication suppresses prolactin-driven supply and undermines breastfeeding; growth and output are normal. Formula top-ups are correct with documented poor growth/output (ABA; RANZCOG).

options.text: Reassure: growth, nappy output and feeding behaviour indicate adequate transfer; review in 1 week
options.rationale: Soft breasts after the early hyperlactation phase, low expressed volumes (a poor proxy for transfer), and cluster-feeding behaviour are normal at 3 weeks. Adequate weight gain (>20-30 g/day after nadir), regaining birthweight by 2 weeks, and 6+ heavy wet nappies confirm adequate intake; perceived low supply without objective markers is the most common cause of unnecessary supplementation (ABA; RCH; ABM).

options.text: Commence domperidone 10 mg three times daily as a pharmacological galactagogue
options.rationale: Galactagogues are considered only after structured assessment confirms inadequate supply, identifies reversible cause, and addresses technique. Domperidone is correct after structured supply assessment failure (ABM).

options.text: Arrange measured pre-feed and post-feed test-weighs over 24 hours at home
options.rationale: Test-weighing is anxiety-provoking, prone to error, and rarely changes management with reassuring growth/output. Test-weighing is correct only in specific research/clinical questions about transfer (ABA; ABM).

options.text: Refer for maternal pituitary MRI to exclude Sheehan syndrome as the cause
options.rationale: No clinical suspicion for Sheehan (no severe PPH, no other pituitary dysfunction); imaging not indicated. Pituitary MRI is correct in suspected Sheehan or other pituitary disease (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Perceived low supply is far more common than true low supply. Assess transfer using objective markers (weight gain >20-30 g/day after nadir, regaining birthweight by 2 weeks, 6+ heavy wet nappies, mustard stools, audible swallowing) before introducing supplementation or galactagogues.
key_points: Expressed volume is a poor proxy for milk transfer
Cluster feeding and softer breasts are normal after 2-3 weeks
Confirm adequate output with weight + nappies + stools before intervening
Premature top-ups suppress supply (negative feedback)
Galactagogues are second-line after a structured assessment
explanation.pearls: Counsel that breasts feeling 'less full' often reflects normal calibration of supply to demand, not failing supply.

subtopic_detail: Low milk supply - first step in assessment

stem:
A 30-year-old primiparous woman attends the GP at 3 weeks postpartum with her term infant. She has persistent bilateral cracked, bleeding nipples that have not improved despite three lactation consultant reviews focused on positioning and attachment; the latch has been optimised across multiple holds and she has tried nipple shields without lasting benefit. Feeds last 50-70 minutes and the infant frequently breaks suction with a clicking sound.

Infant weight gain has fallen below the expected trajectory: birthweight 3.5 kg, discharge weight 3.25 kg, today's weight 3.4 kg at 3 weeks (mean gain ~10 g/day from nadir, below the 20-30 g/day threshold). On examination by an experienced lactation consultant, the infant has a thin anterior tongue frenulum that restricts tongue elevation to less than midline when crying, a heart-shaped tongue tip when the tongue is lifted, and a Hazelbaker tongue-function score that meets criteria for ankyloglossia with impaired function. The infant has no other oral, craniofacial or neurological abnormalities and is otherwise well.

data_table.Infant assessment: Birthweight 3.5 kg, nadir 3.25 kg, today 3.4 kg at day 21 (~10 g/day from nadir, below threshold).
data_table.Feeding: 50-70 min feeds, audible clicking, nipple trauma persists.
data_table.Examination: Restricted tongue elevation, heart-shaped tongue tip, Hazelbaker confirms functionally significant anterior tongue tie.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an experienced clinician for assessment and frenotomy of the anterior tongue tie
options.rationale: When ankyloglossia is associated with functionally significant feeding problems persisting despite optimised positioning and attachment (nipple trauma + impaired transfer + objective tongue-function deficit), frenotomy by an experienced clinician is appropriate and improves both maternal pain and infant transfer in RCT-level evidence (RANZCOG; RCH; ABM Protocol 11).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.text: Continue positioning and attachment optimisation for another 4 weeks before considering frenotomy
options.rationale: Positioning already optimised with three lactation consultant reviews and infant growth faltering; further delay risks supply failure and breastfeeding cessation. Continued positioning is correct only with adequate transfer and growth (RCH; RANZCOG).

options.text: Commence formula top-ups and discontinue breastfeeding given the persistent nipple trauma
options.rationale: Mother wishes to continue and reversible structural cause identified; cessation not first-line when treatable lesion present. Formula transition is correct only after failed intervention or maternal preference (RCH; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.text: Refer for posterior tongue tie and upper-lip tie release out of hours regardless of findings
options.rationale: RANZCOG and RCH caution against indiscriminate posterior tongue tie or upper-lip tie release; evidence is weak and over-diagnosis documented. Posterior/lip-tie release is correct only with rigorous criteria and specialist assessment (RCH).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.text: Prescribe long-term nipple shields and review at the 6-week postnatal check
options.rationale: Shields already failed and do not address underlying restriction; reliance can worsen transfer. Nipple shields are correct as short-term adjunct, not long-term solution (RCH).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

explanation.summary: Frenotomy for ankyloglossia is indicated only when feeding is functionally impaired AND optimised positioning/attachment has not resolved the issue AND examination confirms restricted tongue function. RANZCOG and RCH caution against routine posterior tongue or lip tie release.
key_points: Frenotomy indicated only when function is impaired
Optimise positioning and attachment with IBCLC support first
RCT evidence supports anterior tongue-tie frenotomy when functionally significant
Posterior tongue tie and lip tie release evidence base is weak
Refer to an experienced clinician (paediatrician, ENT, paediatric dentist with training)
explanation.pearls: If the latch has been optimised across multiple reviews and the mother still has nipple trauma, look in the baby's mouth - not at the mother's technique.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

subtopic_detail: Tongue tie - indications for frenotomy referral

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P2 woman, 5 days post-vaginal birth of a healthy term infant, presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of pleuritic right-sided chest pain, mild dyspnoea on exertion and a swollen tender right calf. Bedside observations and ECG are detailed below. CTPA confirms a segmental right lower lobe pulmonary embolus and Doppler ultrasound shows acute right popliteal-femoral DVT.

She has no haemodynamic instability, no right heart strain and no hypoxia at rest. She is exclusively breastfeeding her term, well infant and is highly motivated to continue. She has no other medical conditions, takes no medications, has no allergies, no history of bleeding disorder and her postnatal Hb is 118 g/L with normal platelets, INR and APTT.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, T 37.0 degC.
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: segmental RLL PE. Doppler: right popliteal-femoral DVT. Hb 118 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, APTT 32 s, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m2.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant regimen?

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin transitioning to warfarin with bridging until INR therapeutic; continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Both LMWH (negligible oral bioavailability in the infant) and warfarin (high protein binding, undetectable in milk) are compatible with breastfeeding and are the RANZCOG-recommended options for postpartum VTE; DOACs are NOT recommended in lactation due to insufficient safety data (RANZCOG VTE; LactMed).
source_refs: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

options.text: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, continuing breastfeeding
options.rationale: DOACs not recommended in lactation; manufacturer data and LactMed advise against use. Apixaban is correct only outside breastfeeding (LactMed; AMH).

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, continuing breastfeeding
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban excreted into milk in animal studies; not recommended in lactation. Rivaroxaban is correct only outside breastfeeding (LactMed; AMH).

options.text: Unfractionated heparin infusion only with discontinuation of breastfeeding for the treatment period
options.rationale: UFH is also compatible with breastfeeding but not preferred over LMWH for routine VTE outside renal failure or imminent procedure. UFH is correct in severe renal impairment or procedural bridging (AMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily and graduated compression stockings as primary treatment for VTE
options.rationale: Aspirin not adequate for acute PE or DVT; therapeutic anticoagulation required. Aspirin is correct for extended secondary prevention only after initial therapeutic period (RANZCOG; eTG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE in a breastfeeding woman is treated with LMWH (preferred for ease and predictability) or warfarin; both are compatible with breastfeeding. DOACs are NOT recommended in lactation due to inadequate infant safety data.
key_points: LMWH: negligible oral bioavailability in infant - safe in lactation
Warfarin: high protein binding, undetectable in milk - safe in lactation
DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): avoid in lactation
Acute PE/DVT requires therapeutic, not prophylactic, anticoagulation
Duration usually at least 3 months for provoked postpartum VTE
explanation.pearls: Tell the patient explicitly that LMWH and warfarin do not require pump-and-dump - common misconception that interrupts breastfeeding unnecessarily.

sources.label: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice in breastfeeding mother

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P2 woman is reviewed in the GP-IBCLC combined clinic at 5 weeks postpartum with confirmed insufficient milk supply contributing to faltering infant growth despite four weeks of structured input. Positioning and attachment have been optimised, frequency of feeds increased, post-feed expression added, and a structural cause has been excluded (no tongue tie, no breast surgery, normal thyroid). Infant weight gain remains below 20 g/day with documented inadequate transfer on test-weighs over 24 hours.

The mother wishes to use a galactagogue as adjunctive therapy to maintain breastfeeding while continuing the non-pharmacological measures. She has no personal cardiac history, but on review of her medications she takes citalopram 20 mg daily for anxiety. Her resting baseline ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with QTc 460 ms (Bazett) and normal electrolytes including K+ 4.4 mmol/L and Mg2+ 0.85 mmol/L. She has no family history of sudden cardiac death and no syncope. The IBCLC asks specifically whether domperidone is appropriate in her situation.

data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm 78 bpm, QTc 460 ms (Bazett), no AV block.
data_table.Electrolytes: K+ 4.4 mmol/L, Mg2+ 0.85 mmol/L, Ca2+ corrected 2.35 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Citalopram 20 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding domperidone?

options.text: Commence domperidone 10 mg three times daily for 7 days as a galactagogue
options.rationale: TGA and ABM safety guidance contraindicate domperidone with concurrent QT-prolonging medication and QTc >=450 ms; citalopram is QT-prolonging. Domperidone is correct only with normal QTc and no QT drugs (TGA).

options.text: Avoid domperidone; review citalopram with her psychiatrist and intensify non-pharmacological measures
options.rationale: Domperidone is contraindicated when QTc is prolonged or when a patient is on concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (including citalopram); the safe step is to avoid it, address the modifiable risk (review citalopram) and continue evidence-based milk-removal optimisation (TGA; ABM).

options.text: Increase domperidone dose to 20 mg four times daily to maximise the milk yield
options.rationale: TGA limits dosing to no more than 10 mg three times daily; cardiac risk dose-dependent. Plus active contraindications here. Higher dose is essentially never correct (TGA).

options.text: Substitute metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily as a long-term galactagogue
options.rationale: Metoclopramide has weaker galactagogue evidence and significant risks of extrapyramidal effects and depression with prolonged use. Metoclopramide is correct in short-term postpartum nausea, not long-term galactagogue (TGA).

options.text: Commence fenugreek 600 mg three times daily as a herbal galactagogue without other changes
options.rationale: Fenugreek has limited inconsistent evidence and is not a substitute for addressing milk removal or QT-drug review. Fenugreek is correct only as adjunctive lay-supported intervention, not medical recommendation (ABM).

explanation.summary: Galactagogues are pharmacological agents used to augment milk supply when comprehensive non-pharmacological measures (positioning and attachment optimisation, frequent expressing, skin-to-skin contact, addressing maternal stress and fatigue) have failed. Domperidone (10 mg three times daily for 7-14 days) is the most evidenced agent in Australia, working as a peripheral dopamine antagonist that raises prolactin. Safety concerns centre on dose-dependent QTc prolongation and sudden cardiac death; the TGA contraindicates concurrent QT-prolonging drugs, baseline QTc 450 ms or more, significant electrolyte disturbance, and known cardiac conduction disease. ECG and electrolyte check before starting are standard practice. Metoclopramide is an alternative but carries tardive dyskinesia risk and is generally avoided. Fenugreek and other herbal galactagogues lack evidence and have no place as first-line therapy. Address any modifiable factors first: most low supply is from inadequate effective milk removal, not from intrinsic deficiency.
key_points: TGA dose ceiling: 10 mg TDS
Baseline ECG indicated before starting domperidone
Avoid with concurrent QT-prolonging drugs
Avoid with QTc >=450 ms or electrolyte derangement
Galactagogues are adjuncts, not replacements, for milk removal
explanation.pearls: Domperidone prolongs QTc dose-dependently and is contraindicated with concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (citalopram, escitalopram, ondansetron, clarithromycin, methadone, fluconazole) or baseline QTc 450 ms or more - check ECG before starting (TGA Safety Advisory).

subtopic_detail: Domperidone as galactagogue - safety considerations

stem: A 71-year-old G4P4 postmenopausal woman attends a urogynaecology outpatient clinic with 18 months of progressive vaginal pressure that is now associated with a visible bulge at the introitus when she stands at the end of the day, occasional difficulty completing defaecation that improves when she splints the posterior vaginal wall, and intermittent urinary hesitancy. Speculum and POP-Q examination on maximal Valsalva in the supine position record the following measurements: Aa -1, Ba +1, C +3, GH 5 cm, PB 3 cm, TVL 9 cm, Ap -2, Bp -2, D +1. The most dependent point of prolapse is therefore the cervix at +3 cm beyond the hymen.

data_table.POP-Q (supine, Valsalva): Aa -1, Ba +1, C +3, GH 5, PB 3, TVL 9, Ap -2, Bp -2, D +1.
data_table.Examination: Cervix descends 3 cm beyond hymen; anterior and posterior walls supported at hymen or above; PVR 30 mL.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate description of this prolapse?

options.text: POP-Q stage 2 anterior compartment prolapse (cystocele)
options.rationale: Most dependent point is C (cervix) at +3, not Ba; anterior wall at Ba +1 is stage 2 in isolation but dominant defect is apical. Stage 2 cystocele is correct with anterior dominant + apex above hymen (IUGA).

options.text: POP-Q stage 3 apical (uterine) prolapse
options.rationale: POP-Q staging uses the most dependent point: C at +3 (>1 cm beyond hymen but TVL is 9 cm so not complete eversion) is stage 3, with the apex (uterus) being the dominant compartment. Stage 4 would require complete eversion (most distal point at +/- TVL - 2 cm) (IUGA/ICS).

options.text: POP-Q stage 4 complete vaginal vault eversion
options.rationale: Stage 4 requires most distal point at TVL -2 cm or beyond (essentially complete eversion); cervix at +3 with TVL 9 cm does not meet criterion. Stage 4 is correct in complete vaginal eversion (IUGA).

options.text: POP-Q stage 3 posterior compartment prolapse (rectocele)
options.rationale: Bp is -2, well above hymen; posterior compartment is not the dominant defect. Stage 3 posterior is correct with Bp beyond hymen (IUGA).

options.text: POP-Q stage 1 mixed compartment prolapse
options.rationale: Stage 1 requires most distal point >1 cm ABOVE hymen; cervix at +3 well beyond that threshold. Stage 1 is correct with all points >1 cm above hymen (IUGA).

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is staged using the standardised POP-Q (Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification) system, which measures defined points along the anterior vaginal wall, posterior wall, and apex relative to the hymenal ring. Stage 0 means no descent; stage 1 means the leading edge sits more than 1 cm above the hymen; stage 2 within 1 cm of the hymen (above or below); stage 3 more than 1 cm beyond the hymen but not full eversion (which is stage 4). The dominant compartment - anterior (cystocele), posterior (rectocele), or apical (uterine or vault) - is named by the most dependent point at maximum Valsalva. Apical defects often coexist with anterior descent, so apical support (sacrohysteropexy, sacrocolpopexy or sacrospinous fixation) is integral to anterior repair. Conservative options (pessary, pelvic floor physiotherapy) are first-line; surgery is reserved for symptomatic patients after conservative trial.
key_points: Six points: Aa, Ba (anterior); Ap, Bp (posterior); C (cervix/cuff), D (posterior fornix if uterus present)
TVL, GH and PB are static landmarks
Most distal point sets the stage
Stage 4 requires near-complete eversion (TVL - 2 cm)
Vault prolapse = apical descent in a post-hysterectomy patient
explanation.pearls: POP-Q stages are anchored to the hymen: stage 1 leading edge over 1 cm above hymen, stage 2 within 1 cm, stage 3 over 1 cm beyond but not complete eversion, stage 4 essentially complete vault eversion. The most dependent point names the dominant compartment.

subtopic_detail: POP-Q staging and compartment identification

stem:
A 64-year-old G3P3 postmenopausal woman attends urogynaecology with 12 months of progressive vaginal vault prolapse 9 years after a total abdominal hysterectomy for benign menorrhagia. She has previously trialled a ring pessary for 6 months with recurrent expulsion despite refit, and supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy for 4 months with no symptomatic benefit. POP-Q examination shows vaginal vault descent to +4 with anterior wall to +2 and posterior wall to 0; TVL is 8 cm.

She is sexually active and wishes to preserve coital function; she has no obesity-related surgical risk (BMI 24), no significant cardiopulmonary disease, no diabetes and is otherwise healthy.

data_table.History: TAH 9 years ago. Pessary failed (recurrent expulsion). PFMT 4 months no benefit. Sexually active, BMI 24, no comorbidities.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate surgical procedure?

options.text: Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy with type 1 polypropylene mesh fixed to the anterior sacral ligament
options.rationale: Sacrocolpopexy (open or laparoscopic) using type 1 macroporous polypropylene mesh is the gold-standard procedure for symptomatic vault prolapse where coital function is to be preserved; it has the lowest recurrence rate and best preserves vaginal length; abdominal (non-vaginal) mesh placement is not subject to the TGA's transvaginal mesh restriction (RANZCOG; NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Transvaginal mesh kit repair of the vaginal vault using a synthetic mesh device
options.rationale: Transvaginal mesh kits withdrawn by TGA in Australia in 2017 due to harm signals; not available. TV mesh is essentially never correct in current Australian practice (TGA mesh statement).

options.text: Sacrospinous ligament fixation of the vaginal vault through a vaginal surgical approach
options.rationale: Sacrospinous fixation is reasonable native-tissue alternative for poor abdominal surgical candidates but higher recurrence than sacrocolpopexy. SSLF is correct in patients unsuitable for abdominal surgery (RANZCOG).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Le Fort colpocleisis with obliteration of the vagina for definitive vault support
options.rationale: Colpocleisis is obliterative procedure for older, frail, non-sexually-active women who accept loss of coital function; she remains sexually active. Colpocleisis is correct in elderly non-sexually-active women (RANZCOG).

options.text: Repeat pessary trial with a Gellhorn pessary plus indefinite topical oestrogen therapy
options.rationale: Already failed conservative with recurrent pessary expulsion and ineffective PFMT; another pessary unlikely to succeed. Pessary is correct as initial trial or in patients declining surgery (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Sacrocolpopexy (open or laparoscopic) with type 1 polypropylene mesh is the durability gold-standard for symptomatic vault prolapse where sexual function is to be preserved. Sacrospinous fixation is the principal native-tissue alternative. Colpocleisis is reserved for frail, non-sexually-active patients. Transvaginal mesh kits are not available in Australia since 2017.
key_points: TGA withdrew transvaginal mesh kits in 2017; sacrocolpopexy mesh is placed abdominally and remains available
Sacrocolpopexy preserves vaginal length and axis better than vaginal approaches
Sacrospinous fixation: native tissue, vaginal route, higher recurrence
Colpocleisis: obliterative, only for non-sexually-active
Conservative measures should be trialled first unless not feasible
explanation.pearls: The Australian Senate Inquiry into transvaginal mesh shaped the current TGA stance and is why the abdominal vs vaginal mesh distinction is essential to know.

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Vault prolapse after hysterectomy - surgical choice

stem:
A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 24) presents to her GP with 9 months of urinary urgency, urge incontinence approximately twice daily and nocturia 3 times. She has had a structured trial of bladder training and supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy for 12 weeks under a continence nurse, with caffeine and evening fluid restriction implemented, and reports modest but inadequate improvement.

There is no stress component on her bladder diary, no haematuria, and PVR is 30 mL. Urinalysis is clear; recent FBC, UEC, glucose and Ca2+ are normal. She has well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg, no untreated narrow-angle glaucoma, no severe constipation and her resting heart rate is 72 bpm with BP 134/82 mmHg. She does not have severe uncontrolled hypertension. She is concerned about adding medications that might worsen her memory. Her geriatrician and GP agree to add pharmacotherapy to her ongoing conservative measures.

data_table.Bladder diary: Urgency, urge UI x2/day, nocturia x3, no stress component. PVR 30 mL.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate pharmacological agent?

options.text: Oxybutynin immediate-release 5 mg orally twice a day
options.rationale: Oxybutynin (especially IR) has highest CNS penetration; associated with cognitive decline in older adults. Listed as potentially inappropriate. Oxybutynin is correct only in younger patients without cognitive concern (Beers Criteria; STOPP).

options.text: Mirabegron 25 mg orally daily, titrating to 50 mg if needed
options.rationale: Mirabegron is a beta-3 adrenergic agonist with no anticholinergic burden, making it preferred in older patients with cognitive impairment when conservative measures are inadequate, provided severe uncontrolled hypertension is excluded (NICE NG123; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Solifenacin 5 mg orally daily as a long-acting antimuscarinic
options.rationale: Solifenacin is more bladder-selective with lower CNS penetration than oxybutynin but still anticholinergic burden best avoided in cognitive impairment. Solifenacin is correct in moderate OAB without cognitive concern (Beers).

options.text: Duloxetine 40 mg orally twice daily for the urinary symptoms
options.rationale: Duloxetine is used for stress UI; diary shows no stress component. Duloxetine is correct in stress-predominant or mixed UI (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Desmopressin 0.1 mg orally at night for the urge incontinence
options.rationale: Desmopressin restricted in older patients due to hyponatraemia risk; not first-line for OAB. Desmopressin is correct in younger patients with nocturnal polyuria and no hyponatraemia risk (Continence Foundation; AMH).

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder in older Australians is initially managed with bladder retraining, scheduled voiding, fluid optimisation (cap caffeine and alcohol, avoid excessive evening fluids) and pelvic floor physiotherapy - typically delivered over 6-12 weeks before pharmacotherapy. Antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, solifenacin, darifenacin, tolterodine) carry a cumulative anticholinergic burden linked to cognitive decline, falls, constipation, dry mouth and acute urinary retention; oxybutynin IR has the worst CNS penetration. Mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) achieves comparable continence outcomes without anticholinergic effects but is contraindicated in uncontrolled severe hypertension - check BP at baseline and at 4 weeks. Always measure a post-void residual before any pharmacotherapy in older patients to exclude chronic retention masquerading as urge incontinence. Onabotulinum toxin A intradetrusor injection is the next step for refractory disease.
key_points: First-line: bladder training, PFMT, caffeine reduction, weight loss
Mirabegron: beta-3 agonist, no anticholinergic burden, check BP
Antimuscarinics rank by CNS burden: oxybutynin (worst) > tolterodine > solifenacin/darifenacin (lowest)
Desmopressin restricted in >65 (hyponatraemia)
Duloxetine is for stress UI, not urge UI
explanation.pearls: Anticholinergic burden compounds across medications in older adults - oxybutynin IR alone increases dementia risk after 3+ years of use; mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) is anticholinergic-free and the preferred second-line agent if uncontrolled HTN is excluded (eTG Urological; AMH).

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Urge incontinence pharmacological choice in older woman

stem:
A 52-year-old G3P3 woman attends with 12 months of urinary leakage. On a 3-day bladder diary she records: 8 leakage episodes total - 6 preceded by sudden urgency (mostly on the way to the toilet or hearing running water), and 2 small-volume leaks on coughing or sneezing. Daytime void frequency is 9, nocturia 2, urgency score on Patient Perception of Bladder Condition is severe, and quality-of-life impact is dominated by the urge episodes (she has stopped attending her grandson's school events because of fear of leakage with running to a toilet).

PVR is 40 mL, urinalysis is negative, and a cough stress test reproduces a small leak with full bladder. BMI 31, no smoking, no relevant medications. She declines surgery at this stage and has not yet had any structured conservative therapy or pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Bladder diary: 8 leakage episodes; 6 urge, 2 stress. Frequency 9, nocturia 2.
data_table.Tests: PVR 40 mL, urinalysis negative, cough stress test +ve (small leak).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management approach?

options.text: PFMT, bladder training, weight loss and caffeine reduction; review at 3 months
options.rationale: NICE and Continence Foundation Australia advise structured conservative therapy as initial management for mixed UI, with treatment then directed at the predominant symptom (urge here). PFMT helps both components, bladder training targets urge, and weight loss helps both; structured trial for at least 3 months before escalation (NICE NG123; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Refer immediately for a tension-free vaginal tape mid-urethral sling procedure
options.rationale: Surgery not first-line for mixed UI; stress-incontinence surgery may worsen pre-existing urge symptoms. Plus she declines surgery. Surgery is correct after failed conservative + pharmacological management (RANZCOG; NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Commence an antimuscarinic plus duloxetine combination from the outset of management
options.rationale: Combined pharmacotherapy from outset not recommended; conservative first-line with single-agent for predominant component. Combined therapy is correct after single-agent failure (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Refer for invasive urodynamic studies before offering any conservative management
options.rationale: Urodynamics not required before conservative management of uncomplicated mixed UI; reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or pre-surgical planning. Urodynamics is correct pre-surgery (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Insert a continence pessary and commence indefinite topical oestrogen therapy
options.rationale: Continence pessaries useful mainly for stress UI driven by hypermobility; topical oestrogen for urogenital atrophy; neither addresses mixed UI primarily. Pessary is correct in stress UI with hypermobility (Continence Foundation; NICE NG123).

explanation.summary: Mixed UI is managed with a structured conservative bundle first (PFMT at least 3 months, bladder training, weight loss if BMI >30, caffeine and fluid optimisation, smoking cessation). When pharmacotherapy is needed, target the predominant symptom; urodynamics are reserved for selected indications.
key_points: Bladder diary identifies the predominant component
PFMT >=3 months helps both stress and urge
Weight loss of 5-10% halves leakage episodes
Pharmacotherapy targets predominant symptom (antimuscarinic/mirabegron for urge; duloxetine for stress)
Urodynamics not routine before conservative management
explanation.pearls: Treating the predominant component first often unmasks or relieves the secondary component without separate intervention.

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Mixed urinary incontinence - prioritising treatment by predominant symptom

stem:
A 72-year-old G3P3 postmenopausal woman with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.4%, on metformin + dapagliflozin) presents with 6 months of small-volume continuous urinary leakage, daytime urinary frequency 12, nocturia 4 with leakage on rising, and a sensation of incomplete emptying. She has no urgency that precedes the leakage. Her GP has been treating her empirically as urge incontinence with oxybutynin for 8 weeks with worsening of her leakage.

On examination she has a palpable bladder to the umbilicus, mildly impaired ankle reflexes with reduced light touch and pinprick over both feet bilaterally, and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Speculum reveals a stage 2 cystocele to the hymen with no other prolapse. Urinalysis: protein 1+, no nitrites, no leucocytes. Bedside bladder scan post-void shows a PVR of 720 mL. Bloods: Hb 118 g/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 36 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 68), K+ 5.3 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.4%. Renal tract ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Palpable bladder to umbilicus, peripheral neuropathy, stage 2 cystocele.
data_table.Investigations: PVR 720 mL on bladder scan. Creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 36, K+ 5.3 mmol/L. Renal USS: bilateral hydronephrosis. Urinalysis: protein 1+, no infection.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease oxybutynin, insert indwelling catheter and refer urgently to urology
options.rationale: PVR 720 mL with new bilateral hydronephrosis and rising creatinine indicates high-pressure chronic retention with obstructive AKI - bladder decompression with an indwelling catheter and urgent urology review is the immediate priority; antimuscarinics worsen retention and must be stopped (NICE NG112; Continence Foundation Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NICE NG112 Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (decompression principles applicable)

options.text: Add mirabegron 50 mg daily to the oxybutynin and review again in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Adding pharmacotherapy for assumed OAB ignores high-volume retention with renal compromise; risks worsening retention and renal injury. Mirabegron is correct in confirmed OAB without retention (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Refer for urgent mid-urethral sling surgery for presumed stress urinary incontinence now
options.rationale: She has OVERFLOW incontinence from chronic retention, not stress; sling will precipitate complete retention and worsen renal injury. Sling is correct in confirmed stress UI without retention (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Commence frusemide 40 mg daily to manage her presumed nocturnal polyuria
options.rationale: Frusemide increases urine production into already obstructed bladder; worsens retention and AKI. Frusemide is correct in fluid overload only, never in obstructive uropathy (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange outpatient urodynamics in 6 weeks and continue current therapy unchanged
options.rationale: Outpatient delay unsafe with post-obstructive AKI with bilateral hydronephrosis; immediate decompression required. Outpatient delay is essentially never correct in obstructive AKI (NICE; Continence Foundation).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

explanation.summary: Continuous small-volume leakage with high PVR, palpable bladder, and rising creatinine with hydronephrosis is overflow incontinence from high-pressure chronic retention with post-obstructive AKI. Immediate bladder decompression with an indwelling catheter and urgent urology review is mandatory. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and hyperkalaemia.
key_points: Overflow UI: continuous leakage, high PVR, no urgency, often diabetic or neurogenic
High-pressure retention with hydronephrosis + rising creatinine = obstructive AKI
Decompress immediately with IDC
Stop all antimuscarinics
Watch for post-obstructive diuresis (replace half losses cautiously)
explanation.pearls: Any patient on antimuscarinics whose leakage gets worse should have a PVR scan before any further dose change - the most common missed cause of overflow incontinence is iatrogenic.

sources.label: NICE NG112 Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (decompression principles applicable)
NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Overflow incontinence with chronic urinary retention

stem:
A 55-year-old G3P3 woman is referred to urogynaecology after 12 months of stress urinary incontinence symptoms refractory to a documented 6-month programme of supervised pelvic floor muscle training and weight loss (lost 7 kg, BMI now 28). Her bladder diary shows leakage with cough/sneeze/exertion only, no urgency or urge episodes, no voiding difficulty. PVR is 20 mL and a positive cough stress test reproduces leakage in clinic.

There is no haematuria and no recurrent UTI; POP-Q examination shows Ba -1 (no prolapse beyond the hymen). She has been counselled about a mid-urethral sling and an autologous fascial sling and is keen to proceed surgically. She has not had urodynamic studies. The clinical fellow asks whether urodynamics should be performed before sling surgery. She has not had any previous incontinence surgery, no pelvic radiotherapy and no relevant neurological disease.

data_table.Diary: Pure stress symptoms; no urgency or urge.
data_table.Tests: PVR 20 mL, positive cough stress test, no prolapse beyond hymen.
data_table.Trials: 6 months PFMT + 7 kg weight loss without resolution.

lead_in: Which approach to urodynamics is most consistent with current guidance?

options.text: Routine urodynamic studies in every woman before any incontinence surgery
options.rationale: NICE NG123 advises against routine urodynamics before primary mid-urethral sling for clinically clear uncomplicated stress UI. Routine urodynamics-for-all is essentially never correct (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Urodynamics not required before primary sling here; reserve for mixed or complex
options.rationale: Her presentation is uncomplicated pure stress UI with normal PVR, no voiding symptoms, no prior surgery and no prolapse beyond the hymen; NICE NG123 and the Continence Foundation Australia consensus indicate urodynamics in this scenario do not change management (NICE; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Urodynamic studies only after a failed primary mid-urethral sling procedure
options.rationale: Failed primary procedure is one indication but not the only one; urodynamics may be appropriate before surgery in complicated cases. Failed-primary indication is correct but not exclusive (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Urodynamic studies required only when the post-void residual exceeds 100 mL
options.rationale: PVR is one input; symptom pattern, prior surgery, neurological history, and prolapse all guide decision. PVR-alone trigger is correct only as one of multiple criteria (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Urodynamics is mandatory whenever any pharmacotherapy is being considered
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy for urge UI does not require urodynamics; conservative measures and empirical trial first-line. Urodynamics for any pharmacotherapy is essentially never correct (NICE; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

explanation.summary: Urodynamic studies are NOT required before a primary procedure for clinically straightforward stress urinary incontinence. They are indicated when: symptoms are mixed or urge-predominant, voiding dysfunction is suspected (high PVR, hesitancy), there is previous incontinence/pelvic surgery, concurrent prolapse repair is planned (occult SUI assessment), or there is neurogenic disease.
key_points: Pure, uncomplicated SUI -> no urodynamics needed before primary sling
Mixed UI with discordant findings -> urodynamics often helpful
Prior incontinence surgery -> urodynamics before redo
Neurogenic bladder -> urodynamics needed
Suspected occult SUI before prolapse surgery -> urodynamics
explanation.pearls: The single biggest indication people forget is concurrent prolapse repair, where reducing the prolapse can unmask stress incontinence.

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Indications for urodynamic studies

stem:
A 48-year-old G3P3 woman attends the gynaecology outpatient clinic 4 weeks after a total laparoscopic hysterectomy for symptomatic fibroids. The procedure was complicated by adhesions at the vesicouterine peritoneum requiring sharp dissection from the bladder; the surgeon documented bladder integrity at the end of the case using bladder filling without leak observed. For the past 8 days she has had continuous painless watery leakage into her underwear regardless of position or activity, with no urge, no stress trigger, and unchanged daytime voids of normal volume.

There is no fever, no flank pain. Urinalysis is negative for blood, nitrites and leucocytes. Speculum examination reveals clear fluid pooling in the vaginal vault but no visible defect on direct inspection. The vault is well healed; there is no apparent vault dehiscence. She is on no medications other than recent post-operative paracetamol and is otherwise well.

data_table.History: Continuous painless watery leakage 8 days after TLH complicated by bladder dissection.
data_table.Examination: Clear fluid in vault, no visible defect, vault intact.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear, no infection, no haematuria.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Three-swab dye test: instil dilute methylene blue into the bladder and inspect vaginal swabs
options.rationale: The three-swab (tampon) test with intravesical dye distinguishes vesicovaginal from ureterovaginal and urethrovaginal fistulae and can identify a fistula site too small to see at speculum; it is a simple bedside test and is the standard first-line investigation alongside, or before, formal cystoscopy (RANZCOG; FIGO Fistula manual).
source_refs: FIGO Global Competency-Based Fistula Surgery Training Manual

options.text: Empirical oral antibiotics for 7 days then outpatient review of the leakage pattern
options.rationale: Urinalysis clear and clinical picture not UTI; antibiotics will not address fistula. Antibiotics are correct in UTI, not fistula (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Urodynamic studies as first-line to characterise the pattern of continuous leakage
options.rationale: Urodynamics characterise bladder/sphincter function and not used to diagnose fistula. Urodynamics is correct in functional incontinence workup (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: MRI pelvis with rectal contrast to define the suspected genitourinary tract fistula
options.rationale: MRI may help anatomical mapping for surgical planning of complex fistulae but not first step; dye testing plus cystoscopy is standard. MRI is correct in complex fistula surgical planning (RANZCOG).

options.text: Outpatient pelvic floor physiotherapy with re-review in 3 months without imaging
options.rationale: Continuous painless leakage after pelvic surgery with bladder dissection is fistula until proven otherwise; physiotherapy delays diagnosis. PT is correct in functional UI without fistula features (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Continuous painless urinary leakage after pelvic surgery is a vesicovaginal or ureterovaginal fistula until proven otherwise. The three-swab dye test (intravesical methylene blue plus tampons in upper, middle and lower vagina) localises the leak and distinguishes urethral, vesical and ureteric sources; cystoscopy and CT-IVU or CTU then characterise the defect for repair planning.
key_points: Continuous painless leakage post-pelvic surgery -> fistula until proven otherwise
Three-swab dye test: upper swab stained suggests ureterovaginal; mid/upper bladder; lower urethrovaginal
If dye test negative for vesical source, suspect ureterovaginal: oral phenazopyridine or IV indigo carmine plus CT-IVU
Cystoscopy maps the bladder defect for repair planning
Obstetric fistula remains the leading global cause; in high-income settings most fistulae are iatrogenic post-hysterectomy
explanation.pearls: If the upper vaginal tampon stains blue and the middle does not, suspect a ureterovaginal fistula and proceed to ureteric imaging.

sources.label: FIGO Global Competency-Based Fistula Surgery Training Manual
NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Vesicovaginal fistula - diagnostic approach

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with HIV (CD4 540, viral load undetectable on ART) is referred to a vulval clinic with 9 months of mild vulval pruritus. Examination shows two well-demarcated, slightly raised, pigmented and acetowhite plaques on the right labium minus measuring 8 mm and 12 mm, with no ulceration, induration or vascular atypia. There is no clitoral hood resorption, no labial fusion and no porcelain-white skin.

Vulvoscopy-directed punch biopsy from each lesion shows high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (vulvar HSIL, also called usual-type VIN) with full-thickness dysplasia, koilocytotic change and p16 block-positive immunohistochemistry consistent with HPV-driven disease; there is no invasion, no microinvasion and no features of differentiated VIN (no basal atypia on a background of lichen sclerosus). She has had previous CIN 2 treated by LLETZ 5 years ago and is up to date with HPV-based cervical screening.

She is sexually active with one partner, both fully HPV-vaccinated, no immunosuppressive medications other than ART, no other comorbidities and is keen to preserve vulval anatomy if possible.

data_table.Lesions: Two pigmented/acetowhite plaques right labium minus (8 mm and 12 mm), no induration.
data_table.Histology: Vulvar HSIL (uVIN), p16 block-positive (HPV-driven), no invasion.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical imiquimod 5% three times weekly for up to 16 weeks
options.rationale: For non-invasive, HPV-driven vulvar HSIL (uVIN) in unifocal or limited multifocal lesions where anatomy preservation matters, topical imiquimod is RANZCOG/BSSVD-recommended first-line, with documented clinical clearance in ~50-80% and a re-biopsy threshold for any persistent lesion to exclude occult invasion (RANZCOG; BSSVD).

options.text: Watchful waiting with annual vulvoscopy and no active treatment
options.rationale: HSIL/uVIN carries ~5-10% progression risk to invasive SCC if untreated; active management required. Watchful waiting is essentially never correct in HSIL/uVIN (RANZCOG; BSSVD).

options.text: Radical vulvectomy with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy for vulval HSIL
options.rationale: Radical vulvectomy + lymphadenectomy reserved for invasive vulvar carcinoma, not preinvasive HSIL. Radical surgery is correct for invasive disease only (RANZCOG).

options.text: Topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment to lesions for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Potent topical steroids are for inflammatory dermatoses (lichen sclerosus, lichen planus), not HSIL/uVIN; do not treat preinvasive dysplasia. Topical steroid is correct in inflammatory vulval dermatoses (BSSVD).

options.text: Topical 5-fluorouracil cream applied daily indefinitely as primary therapy
options.rationale: 5-FU largely supplanted by imiquimod due to high rates of vulval chemical burn and lower tolerability; indefinite application not recommended. 5-FU is correct in specific resistant cases under specialist care (BSSVD).

explanation.summary: Vulvar HSIL (uVIN) is HPV-driven and managed with one of: imiquimod (anatomy-sparing first line for selected lesions), wide local excision, or laser ablation. Differentiated VIN (dVIN), associated with lichen sclerosus and HPV-independent, has higher cancer risk and is managed with surgical excision (not imiquimod). Any non-responding or atypical area requires re-biopsy.
key_points: Vulvar HSIL = uVIN, HPV-driven, p16-positive, multifocal more common, lower per-lesion cancer risk
Differentiated VIN = dVIN, HPV-independent, p16-negative, on background of LS, HIGHER cancer risk, surgical excision
Imiquimod: anatomy-sparing for uVIN; ~50-80% clearance
Wide local excision: definitive histology, suitable for unifocal or suspicious lesions
Long-term surveillance after any treatment because of recurrence and dysplasia elsewhere
explanation.pearls: A non-healing or hyperkeratotic vulval lesion in a woman with long-standing lichen sclerosus should make you think dVIN/SCC, not uVIN - excise, do not topical-treat.

subtopic_detail: VIN - management of HSIL (uVIN) vs differentiated VIN

stem:
A 28-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively painful right vulval swelling, now interfering with walking. T 37.1, no rigors, no STI symptoms. Examination: 4 cm fluctuant tender mass at the right posterolateral introitus (5 o'clock) consistent with a Bartholin abscess; intact non-necrotic skin, no cellulitis spreading beyond. This is her THIRD Bartholin abscess at the same site in the last 12 months.

The two previous episodes were treated with simple incision and drainage with packing, and both recurred within 3 months. She is otherwise well, on no medications, and wants definitive treatment that minimises further recurrence.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1 degC, HR 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg.
data_table.Examination: 4 cm fluctuant tender mass right posterolateral introitus at 5 o'clock, intact non-necrotic skin, no cellulitis.
data_table.History: No prior Bartholin episodes, no STI symptoms.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Simple incision and drainage with packing under local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Simple I&D + packing has high recurrence rates (this is third recurrence); definitive procedure now needed. Simple I&D is correct for first acute presentation (RANZCOG; eTG).

options.text: Marsupialisation under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: After recurrent Bartholin abscesses at the same site despite Word catheter or I&D, marsupialisation provides definitive long-term drainage with lower recurrence than I&D and is preferred over excision (which is reserved for failed marsupialisation or suspicion of malignancy) (RANZCOG; eTG).

options.text: Word catheter insertion under local anaesthetic for 4-6 weeks
options.rationale: Word catheter is acceptable first-line for primary or single recurrence; with three recurrences at same site, more definitive marsupialisation indicated. Word catheter is correct for first/second presentation (RANZCOG).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days without drainage
options.rationale: Abscess requires drainage; antibiotics alone do not resolve. Antibiotics reserved for surrounding cellulitis or sepsis. Antibiotics are correct as adjunct to drainage (eTG; RANZCOG).

options.text: Excision of the Bartholin gland as primary management
options.rationale: Excision reserved for failed marsupialisation or suspected malignancy (usually women >40); higher morbidity. Excision is correct after failed marsupialisation (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Primary Bartholin abscess is managed with a fistulising drainage procedure - Word catheter insertion is the office/ED first-line; marsupialisation is the operating theatre equivalent. Simple I&D recurs frequently and gland excision is reserved for recurrent failure. Antibiotics are adjunctive only if cellulitis, systemic features, immunosuppression or pregnancy.
key_points: Word catheter: local anaesthetic, low morbidity, in situ 4-6 weeks
Marsupialisation: equivalent recurrence, requires GA
Simple I&D: highest recurrence
Antibiotics adjunctive only with cellulitis, systemic features or immunosuppression
In women aged 40+ with a Bartholin mass, consider biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: A new Bartholin mass in a postmenopausal woman is carcinoma until biopsy proves otherwise - very different from the under-40 abscess pathway.

subtopic_detail: Bartholin abscess - drainage technique
Epilepsy - preconception folate dose
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with focal epilepsy attends her GP for preconception counselling. She has been seizure-free for 4 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily as monotherapy, prescribed by her neurologist who has been unable to wean her without seizure recurrence. She is in a stable relationship, drinks no alcohol, BMI 24, no other medications. There is no personal or family history of neural tube defects.

She wishes to conceive within the next 6 months and has not yet started any vitamins. She has read online that 'folic acid 5 mg' is recommended in epilepsy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, weight 68 kg, BMI 24 kg/m2.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no neurocutaneous markers, no goitre.
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 200 mg BD. No other medications. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preconception advice?

options.text: Continue valproate, start folic acid 5 mg daily and aim to conceive in 6 months
options.rationale: Continuing valproate is wrong because it is highly teratogenic (NTD, cardiac, craniofacial, cognitive impairment) and is contraindicated in women of reproductive age unless a TGA Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place AND no alternative controls seizures; folate alone does not mitigate the teratogenic risk. Would be acceptable only when every alternative antiepileptic has failed and PPP criteria are fully met, never as routine preconception advice (RANZCOG; TGA valproate PPP; AMH).

options.text: Refer to neurology for transition to a less teratogenic antiepileptic (e.g. lamotrigine or levetiracetam) and start folic acid 5 mg daily, deferring conception until stable on the new agent
options.rationale: Valproate must be avoided in pregnancy where possible. Neurology should switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam, conception is deferred until seizure-free on the new agent, and folic acid 5 mg daily is started preconception until 12 weeks (RANZCOG; AMH; TGA valproate PPP).

options.text: Stop valproate today without neurology input and start folic acid 400 mcg daily
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation is wrong because antiepileptic withdrawal risks status epilepticus, which carries higher maternal and fetal mortality than the drug itself; the anti-pattern is patient-driven cessation without neurology cover. Would be correct only inside a supervised neurology switch with overlap onto a safer agent, not as standalone advice (RANZCOG; AMH).

options.text: Continue valproate and add lamotrigine to allow pregnancy on combination therapy
options.rationale: Adding lamotrigine on top of valproate is wrong because polytherapy multiplies teratogenic risk rather than reducing it, and valproate must be removed entirely whenever possible. Would be correct only as a transient bridge during a planned cross-titration off valproate under neurology, not as a maintenance plan for pregnancy (RANZCOG; AMH).

options.text: Continue valproate and start folic acid 400 mcg daily, the standard dose for low-risk women
options.rationale: Folic acid 400 mcg is wrong because women on antiepileptics require the high-dose 5 mg regimen preconception until 12 weeks, and even adequate folate does not neutralise valproate teratogenicity. Would be correct as the dose for a low-risk woman not on antiepileptics; here both the dose and the drug choice need to change (RANZCOG; AMH).

explanation.summary: All women on any antiepileptic drug should receive folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally and through the first trimester, irrespective of the specific agent. The dose change should be made before conception because neural tube closure occurs by 28 days post-conception (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
key_points: High-dose folate (5 mg) is also recommended for diabetes, previous NTD-affected pregnancy, BMI >30 kg/m2 and some haemoglobinopathies
Lamotrigine is one of the safer antiepileptics in pregnancy but does not exempt the patient from the 5 mg recommendation
Start folate at least 1 month (ideally 3 months) preconception and continue until 12 weeks gestation
Do not stop antiepileptic therapy in a stable patient without specialist input
explanation.pearls: If a woman taking any antiepileptic asks about pregnancy, the answer to folate is almost always 5 mg, not 400 micrograms.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy counselling and routine antenatal assessment
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology - epilepsy and pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Asthma - continuation of inhaled corticosteroid
stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 at 9 weeks gestation has had asthma since childhood, well-controlled on budesonide 200 mcg bd plus salbutamol PRN. Over the past month she has needed reliever 4-5 times per week with two episodes of nocturnal cough. Spirometry today: FEV1 78% predicted (baseline 95% pre-pregnancy). No infective symptoms, no exposure changes. She tells you a friend advised her to stop the budesonide because 'steroids cross the placenta'. She is up to date with influenza vaccination and folic acid.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 99% on air.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no wheeze, peak flow at her usual personal best.
data_table.Medications: Budesonide 200 micrograms BD inhaled, salbutamol 100 micrograms PRN.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her asthma now?

options.text: Continue current budesonide 200 mcg bd and reassess in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Continuing the same ICS dose is wrong because deteriorating control (reliever more than twice weekly, nocturnal symptoms, falling FEV1) defines uncontrolled asthma, which is more dangerous in pregnancy than dose escalation; the anti-pattern is therapeutic inertia in the second trimester. Would be correct only if control were stable and symptoms minimal, which is not the case here (RANZCOG; TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Step up inhaled corticosteroid (e.g. budesonide-formoterol combination) per the Australian Asthma Handbook and continue throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the pregnancy than inhaled corticosteroids. The Australian Asthma Handbook recommends standard step-up of inhaled therapy in pregnancy, including ICS-LABA combinations. Stopping ICS is the anti-pattern to avoid (RANZCOG; TSANZ).

options.text: Stop budesonide and use salbutamol alone for the duration of pregnancy
options.rationale: Stopping ICS is wrong because pregnancy is the exact setting where the Australian Asthma Handbook insists ICS be continued; cessation is associated with exacerbations, pre-eclampsia, prematurity and low birth weight. Would never be correct as a planned change in pregnancy (TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Switch to oral prednisolone 10 mg daily for the duration of pregnancy
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone as maintenance is wrong because oral corticosteroids are reserved for exacerbations, not chronic baseline therapy, due to maternal glycaemic, hypertensive and bone effects; the step-up ladder goes through inhaled ICS-LABA first. Would be correct only if she had severe steroid-dependent asthma already on optimised inhaled therapy (TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Switch to montelukast 10 mg daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Montelukast monotherapy is wrong because leukotriene receptor antagonists are an add-on, not a substitute for ICS, in the GINA/TSANZ pathway. Would be correct as a continuation if she was already on montelukast preconception with good control, not as a first-line switch (TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Asthma affects about 12% of pregnant Australian women and tends to worsen in around a third, improve in a third and stay stable in a third. The dominant clinical risk is preventer non-adherence driven by misplaced concern about fetal harm. All inhaled corticosteroids are pregnancy category A or B3 and continued at the pre-pregnancy dose minimum; budesonide has the largest safety dataset and is preferred when starting therapy de novo. Stepped-up therapy follows the Australian Asthma Handbook: low-dose ICS, then ICS-LABA combination (budesonide-formoterol or fluticasone-salmeterol), then specialist input for biologics or oral steroids. Salbutamol PRN is safe in pregnancy.
