Acute exacerbations are managed exactly as in non-pregnant adults: oxygen to keep SpO2 over 94%, back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium, systemic prednisolone 37.5-50 mg, IV magnesium sulfate, and continuous fetal monitoring once viable.
key_points: Uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the fetus than asthma medication
Budesonide has the most extensive pregnancy safety data among ICS
Use a written asthma action plan and review every 4-6 weeks in pregnancy
Influenza vaccine is recommended for all pregnant women with asthma
explanation.pearls: Budesonide is the inhaled corticosteroid with the most pregnancy safety data; uncontrolled maternal asthma trebles the risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and SGA, far outweighing any theoretical risk of preventer therapy (National Asthma Council Australia).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - asthma in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Acute severe asthma in pregnancy - escalation
stem:
A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks gestation presents to the obstetric assessment unit with two days of worsening cough, breathlessness and wheeze on a background of moderate persistent asthma. She had a viral upper respiratory infection last week and her partner had similar symptoms. She is on budesonide/formoterol 200/6 micrograms twice daily and reports using salbutamol every 30 minutes overnight without sustained relief.

She has had two previous emergency department presentations with asthma in the last 18 months but no ICU admissions and no history of intubation. She has no fevers, no chest painal movements; she received corticosteroid coverage for lung maturity two days ago at booking with respiratory. On arrival 30 minutes ago she was given continuous nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 500 micrograms, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and high flow oxygen titrated to SpO2 95%, with minimal subjective improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 32, HR 132 bpm, BP 134/86 mmHg, T 37.4 degC, SpO2 94% on 8 L/min mask, peak flow 38% of personal best.
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, audible wheeze, accessory muscle use, unable to complete full sentences. SFH 28 cm, CTG normal baseline 140 with variability and accelerations.
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 8 L: pH 7.36, PaCO2 36 mmHg, PaO2 78 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L. CXR (with shielding): hyperinflated, no consolidation.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step in management?

options.text: Oral leukotriene receptor antagonist loading dose of montelukast 20 mg
options.rationale: Oral montelukast loading is wrong because LTRAs have no acute bronchodilator effect and onset is hours to days; they are chronic add-on agents, not rescue therapy. Would be correct only as part of chronic step-up after discharge, not in acute severe asthma (National Asthma Council Australia).

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline loading dose then maintenance infusion
options.rationale: IV aminophylline is wrong because of its narrow therapeutic window, arrhythmogenic risk and lack of mortality benefit over magnesium; current Australian practice reserves it for refractory cases after IV magnesium has failed. Would be correct only when IV magnesium has been given and the patient is still deteriorating in ICU, not as the next step (Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - acute severe asthma

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 500 micrograms intramuscular every 5 minutes
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is wrong because it is anaphylaxis therapy, and in pregnancy uteroplacental vasoconstriction is a specific concern; the anti-pattern is reaching for adrenaline when the diagnosis is severe asthma not anaphylaxis. Would be correct only if anaphylaxis were the actual mechanism (ASCIA; National Asthma Council Australia).

options.text: Emergency caesarean delivery to improve maternal oxygenation now
options.rationale: Emergency caesarean is wrong because delivery is not a treatment for maternal asthma and the fetus is currently reassured; surgery and intubation would worsen bronchospasm. Would be correct only if maternal arrest were imminent or peri-mortem caesarean criteria were met, not at this stage (RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital).

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes once now
options.rationale: Severe acute asthma not responding to back-to-back bronchodilators and IV corticosteroid warrants IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes; this is recommended in Australian asthma-in-pregnancy guidance and a normalising PaCO2 with rising lactate signals impending respiratory failure (Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory; National Asthma Council Australia).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - acute severe asthma

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma in pregnancy is one of the most common medical emergencies in obstetric practice and carries higher maternal and fetal mortality than non-pregnant asthma if undertreated. Pharmacological management is identical to non-pregnant adults: continuous high-flow oxygen titrated to SpO2 above 94%, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms every 20 minutes, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if oral not tolerated), then IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes if no response. Salbutamol IV, aminophylline, and intubation follow if needed. Pregnancy-specific points include early continuous fetal monitoring once viable, left lateral position to reduce aortocaval compression, and a low threshold for tertiary transfer. A normal or rising PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic indicates fatigue and impending respiratory failure - not improvement - and is an indication for urgent intensivist involvement. Document and continue preventer therapy during admission; discharge planning includes inhaler technique review and written action plan.
key_points: A normalising PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic is a red flag for tiring, not improvement
Position left lateral from 20 weeks to relieve aortocaval compression
Continuous CTG once viable; involve obstetrics and ICU early
Document discussion about steroids for fetal lung maturation if preterm delivery considered
explanation.pearls: Acute severe asthma in pregnancy is treated identically to non-pregnant adults: oxygen for SpO2 above 94%, back-to-back salbutamol with ipratropium, early systemic prednisolone or hydrocortisone, then IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes if not improving. A 'normal' PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic signals fatigue, not improvement (National Asthma Council).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - acute severe asthma

subtopic_detail: Hypothyroidism - thyroxine dose escalation on confirming pregnancy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism after thyroidectomy for benign multinodular goitre two years ago presents at 6 weeks of a confirmed singleton pregnancy. She has been stable on levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily for 18 months with TSH consistently between 1.2 and 1.8 mIU/L. Her last TSH four months ago was 1.4 mIU/L. She conceived spontaneously after stopping the combined oral contraceptive eight weeks ago and reports nausea but no vomiting.

She has no other medical problems and is on no other regular medications. She has commenced folic acid 500 micrograms daily and iodine 150 micrograms daily as advised by her GP. She has not yet had pregnancy bloods drawn and asks whether she should change her thyroxine dose now or wait for the booking blood results, which she will have done in the next few days. She has not had any change in body weight, energy, cold tolerance or constipation. There is no family history of thyroid autoimmunity.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, weight 64 kg.
data_table.Examination: Well, no goitre (thyroidectomy scar healed), no proximal weakness, reflexes normal.
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods not yet returned. Last TSH 4 months ago 1.4 mIU/L (free T4 within range).
data_table.Medications: Levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, folic acid 500 micrograms, iodine 150 micrograms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adjustment to her levothyroxine?

options.text: Maintain 100 micrograms daily and recheck TSH in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Maintaining 100 mcg is wrong because thyroid hormone requirements rise 25-50% in the first trimester driven by hCG-stimulated TBG; delay risks maternal hypothyroidism with neurodevelopmental impact on the fetus, and the Endocrine Society recommends an empirical bump on confirmation of pregnancy. Would be correct only if pre-pregnancy TSH was already optimised at the lower end and a recheck-only strategy was agreed, which is not standard (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.text: Stop iodine supplementation because she is taking levothyroxine
options.rationale: Stopping iodine is wrong because NHMRC recommends 150 mcg iodine for all Australian pregnant and lactating women regardless of thyroxine status; iodine supports placental and fetal thyroid synthesis, while levothyroxine replaces maternal hormone. Would never be correct in an Australian antenatal context (NHMRC).
source_refs: NHMRC: Iodine supplementation in pregnancy and lactation

options.text: Double the dose to 200 micrograms daily and recheck in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Doubling to 200 mcg is wrong because the evidence-based empirical increment is 20-30% (typically two extra tablets per week); doubling risks iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis with atrial fibrillation and growth restriction. Would be correct only in newly diagnosed overt hypothyroidism with very high TSH at booking, not for stable preconception disease (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.text: Switch to liothyronine 20 micrograms three times daily here
options.rationale: Switching to liothyronine is wrong because T3 crosses the placenta poorly and the fetus depends on maternal T4 for cerebral development; combination or T3-only therapy is explicitly discouraged in pregnancy. Would be correct only in extremely rare specialist scenarios, never in routine antenatal care (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).

options.text: Increase to approximately 125 micrograms daily and recheck TSH in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance recommends a 20-30% empirical dose increase on confirmation of pregnancy in known hypothyroid women, typically achieved by taking two extra tablets per week or rounding up to the next strength, with TSH rechecked 4 weeks later (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Women with treated hypothyroidism should empirically increase their levothyroxine by about 20-30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, before booking bloods are back, because thyroid binding globulin rises rapidly under oestrogen stimulation. Target TSH is <2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
key_points: Practical method: take two extra tablets per week or move up to next available strength
Recheck TSH 4 weeks after dose change and every trimester
Maintain iodine 150 micrograms daily across all pregnant women
Avoid liothyronine in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Empirical dose-up first, bloods later. Waiting for the lab risks first-trimester hypothyroxinaemia.

sources.label: NHMRC: Iodine supplementation in pregnancy and lactation
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Graves disease - antithyroid choice by trimester
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman with Graves disease diagnosed 18 months ago is reviewed at her booking visit at 7 weeks gestation. Initial treatment was with propylthiouracil and propranolol, but she was switched to carbimazole 10 mg daily six months ago after biochemical control was achieved and has remained euthyroid since. Her TSH is 2.1 mIU/L and free T4 is within range on bloods drawn yesterday.

She has no eye signs and no goitre on examination today. TSH receptor antibody titre four months ago was mildly elevated at 2.5 IU/L (cut-off 1.75 IU/L).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/64 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, weight 68 kg.
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no exophthalmos, no tremor, no proximal weakness.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, free T4 within range, TRAb 2.5 IU/L 4 months ago (mildly raised).
data_table.Medications: Carbimazole 10 mg daily, folic acid 500 micrograms, pregnancy multivitamin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her antithyroid medication for this stage of pregnancy?

options.text: Continue carbimazole 10 mg daily throughout the pregnancy and recheck thyroid function tests every trimester
options.rationale: Continuing carbimazole in the first trimester is wrong because it is associated with embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia, omphalocoele) during organogenesis; the standard carve-out is PTU until 16 weeks then switch back. Would be correct only after the first trimester is complete, not from 6 weeks (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.text: Refer for definitive radioactive iodine ablation this week and commence levothyroxine replacement therapy immediately afterwards
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine ablation is wrong because it is an absolute contraindication in pregnancy due to fetal thyroid ablation and teratogenic radiation exposure. Would be correct only postpartum after cessation of breastfeeding with appropriate isolation precautions (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Stop all antithyroid medication now and monitor maternal TSH and free T4 every two weeks until delivery
options.rationale: Stopping all antithyroid drug is wrong because biochemically active Graves disease with raised TRAb risks maternal thyroid storm, fetal goitre and fetal tachycardia; the anti-pattern is treating pregnancy itself as remission. Would be correct only if she were in true biochemical remission with negative TRAb and stable off therapy preconception (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.text: Switch to propylthiouracil now and review at the start of the second trimester for return to carbimazole
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance is to use propylthiouracil during the first trimester to avoid carbimazole embryopathy, then switch back to carbimazole from around 16 weeks to reduce ongoing risk of PTU hepatotoxicity (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.text: Add propranolol 40 mg three times daily to her current carbimazole and continue both throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Adding propranolol while continuing carbimazole is wrong because beta blockade addresses adrenergic symptoms (which she does not have) without removing the teratogenic exposure during organogenesis. Would be appropriate as a short-term adjunct in symptomatic thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm, not as a strategy to neutralise carbimazole risk (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: First-trimester carbimazole exposure causes a recognisable embryopathy. Australian practice is to use propylthiouracil through organogenesis (typically up to about 16 weeks) and then switch back to carbimazole because of cumulative PTU hepatotoxicity. TRAb should be measured in the third trimester to predict neonatal thyroid disease (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
key_points: Carbimazole embryopathy: aplasia cutis, choanal/oesophageal atresia, omphalocele
PTU rare but serious hepatotoxicity - hence switch back at ~16 weeks
Target free T4 at the upper limit of the trimester-specific reference range
Check TRAb in the third trimester; high titres warn of fetal/neonatal Graves
explanation.pearls: First trimester = PTU. Second trimester onward = carbimazole. Always raise TRAb in the third trimester.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: SLE - anti-Ro/La and neonatal lupus risk
stem:
A 30-year-old G2P0 woman with SLE diagnosed seven years ago is reviewed in a combined obstetric medicine clinic at 11 weeks gestation. She has been in clinical remission for two years on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and low dose prednisolone 5 mg daily. Her one previous pregnancy ended in a first-trimester miscarriage at 9 weeks with no known cause identified at the time.

Her most recent rheumatology bloods three months ago confirmed normal complement, negative dsDNA, and positive anti-Ro at 120 U/mL (positive >10) and positive anti-La at 70 U/mL. She has no past history of lupus nephritis, no thromboembolism and her antiphospholipid antibody screen has been repeatedly negative on three occasions over the last two years. She has commenced folic acid 5 mg daily and aspirin 100 mg daily for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis at 11 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 mmHg, HR 70 bpm, weight 62 kg.
data_table.Examination: No active joint synovitis, no rash, no oral ulcers.
data_table.Investigations: Anti-Ro 120 U/mL positive, anti-La 70 U/mL positive, dsDNA negative, C3/C4 normal, APL screen repeatedly negative, urine PCR 3 mg/mmol.
data_table.Medications: Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, prednisolone 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which surveillance plan is the most appropriate addition for this pregnancy?

options.text: Serial fetal echocardiograms from 16 to 28 weeks for congenital heart block
options.rationale: Anti-Ro and anti-La cross the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus, of which congenital complete heart block is the most serious feature. Australian and EULAR guidance is to perform serial fetal echocardiography (typically weekly to fortnightly) between 16 and 26-28 weeks in anti-Ro positive women (RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital Vic; EULAR SLE pregnancy guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: SLE in pregnancy
EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE

options.text: Stop hydroxychloroquine at the start of the second trimester now
options.rationale: Stopping hydroxychloroquine is wrong because HCQ is the one drug we deliberately keep going through pregnancy in SLE: it reduces flares, reduces recurrence of congenital heart block in subsequent pregnancies, and may reduce pre-eclampsia. Would be correct only if she developed retinopathy or another HCQ-specific adverse effect, not because of the pregnancy itself (EULAR SLE pregnancy guidelines; RANZCOG).
source_refs: EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE
RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy

options.text: Empirical IVIG infusions from 16 weeks to prevent congenital heart block
options.rationale: Empirical IVIG is wrong because trials have failed to show that IVIG prevents first-occurrence congenital heart block; the established strategy is fetal echo surveillance with prompt intervention if first-degree block emerges. Would be considered only as research therapy or in selected high-risk recurrence cases at specialist discretion, not as routine primary prevention (EULAR).
source_refs: EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE

options.text: Stop aspirin because anti-Ro positive SLE increases bleeding risk
options.rationale: Stopping aspirin is wrong because SLE carries a high pre-eclampsia risk and SOMANZ recommends low-dose aspirin from before 16 weeks for this exact indication; anti-Ro status does not change bleeding risk meaningfully. Would be correct only with active bleeding or genuine aspirin allergy (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy

options.text: Routine empirical low molecular weight heparin from 12 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Empirical LMWH is wrong because thromboprophylaxis is reserved for antiphospholipid syndrome, prior VTE or otherwise high VTE risk; SLE alone with negative APL antibodies does not meet RCOG thromboprophylaxis criteria. Would be correct in coexisting APS, not in isolated SLE (RCOG; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies cross the placenta and may cause neonatal lupus syndromes, with congenital heart block as the most feared. Serial fetal echocardiography between 16 and 28 weeks is the surveillance standard. Hydroxychloroquine should be continued throughout pregnancy (RANZCOG; EULAR).
key_points: Risk of congenital heart block ~2% in anti-Ro positive first pregnancies, ~15-20% recurrence
Hydroxychloroquine reduces recurrence of neonatal lupus and SLE flares
Aspirin 100-150 mg daily from before 16 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in SLE
Plan delivery and neonatology input if any conduction abnormality detected
explanation.pearls: Anti-Ro changes the fetal cardiology pathway, not the rheumatology drug list. Keep the hydroxychloroquine.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: SLE in pregnancy
EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE

subtopic_detail: HIV - mode of delivery decision by viral load
stem:
A 30-year-old G1P0 woman with HIV diagnosed three years ago attends her 36 week obstetric review. She has been on combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir disoproxil, emtricitabine and dolutegravir) since diagnosis and has been virologically suppressed throughout this pregnancy. Her viral load four weeks ago was undetectable (<20 copies/mL) and her CD4 count was 620 cells/microlitre. She has no opportunistic infections, no co-infections (HBV and HCV negative) and no other comorbidities.

Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with a normally grown cephalic fetus on the 50th centile and reassuring serial umbilical artery Dopplers. She wishes to plan a vaginal birth and asks the obstetric registrar what the recommendation is regarding mode of delivery given her status and her preference. She has no obstetric contraindications to vaginal birth and there are no concerns on CTG today. She has not yet ruptured membranes and is not in labour. The infectious diseases physician has been co-managing her care.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 114/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: SFH 36 cm, cephalic, FHR 140, longitudinal lie.
data_table.Investigations: HIV viral load <20 copies/mL at 36 weeks, CD4 620 cells/microlitre, HBV/HCV negative, syphilis negative.
data_table.Medications: Tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine/dolutegravir once daily, pregnancy multivitamin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at 38 weeks regardless of viral load
options.rationale: Routine elective caesarean is wrong because the ASHM/BHIVA threshold for offering caesarean is viral load at or above 50 copies/mL (or unknown) near term; with sustained suppression, vaginal birth has equivalent transmission risk and lower maternal morbidity. Would be correct only with detectable or undocumented viral load close to delivery (ASHM; BHIVA).

options.text: Plan a vaginal birth at term with continuation of antiretroviral therapy
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance is that elective caesarean is not required if the viral load is suppressed (<50 copies/mL) near term; vaginal birth has similar or lower morbidity with comparable vertical transmission risk on suppressive ART (ASHM; RANZCOG; BHIVA pregnancy guidelines).

options.text: Stop antiretroviral therapy two weeks before planned vaginal birth
options.rationale: Stopping ART is wrong because viral rebound after cessation is rapid and would directly increase vertical transmission risk in late pregnancy and labour; the anti-pattern is treating ART as optional once viral load is suppressed. Would never be correct in pregnancy (ASHM).

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks plus intravenous zidovudine
options.rationale: Elective caesarean plus IV zidovudine is wrong because intrapartum IV zidovudine is reserved for viral load at or above 400 copies/mL or unknown status; layering caesarean plus IV zidovudine on a virologically suppressed woman adds morbidity without benefit. Would be correct only if her viral load were not suppressed (BHIVA).

options.text: Induction of labour at 37 weeks to minimise duration of ruptured membranes
options.rationale: Induction at 37 weeks is wrong because there is no evidence early induction reduces vertical transmission in suppressed women; obstetric indications drive timing of birth, and iatrogenic prematurity carries neonatal morbidity. Would be correct only for standard obstetric reasons, not as HIV-specific intervention (ASHM; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: In women with sustained HIV viral suppression (<50 copies/mL) at 36 weeks on combination ART, vaginal birth is recommended unless an obstetric reason exists for caesarean. Vertical transmission rates with suppressed viraemia are well under 1% and equivalent across delivery modes (ASHM; BHIVA).
key_points: Check viral load at 36 weeks to plan mode of delivery
Detectable VL >=50 copies/mL near term: elective caesarean at 38-39 weeks
VL >=400 copies/mL or unknown: intrapartum IV zidovudine plus elective caesarean
Continue ART through labour; avoid invasive fetal monitoring (FSE) and prolonged ROM
explanation.pearls: Suppressed viral load is the key determinant. Vaginal birth is not contraindicated by HIV status alone.

subtopic_detail: HIV - infant prophylaxis and feeding choice in Australia
stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 woman with HIV diagnosed prior to pregnancy is reviewed postnatally on the maternity ward six hours after a normal vaginal birth at 39+2 weeks of a 3.2 kg infant. She has been on combination antiretroviral therapy throughout pregnancy and her most recent HIV viral load at 36 weeks was <20 copies/mL. The infant is well and feeding cues are emerging.

She is hepatitis B surface antigen negative and hepatitis C negative. She has no other comorbidities and her partner is HIV negative and on PrEP. She lives in a major Australian city, has stable housing, a refrigerator, reliable formula supply and supportive family. She asks the midwife about safe feeding choices and what medication, if any, the baby needs. The neonatologist is also reviewing the infant and confirms the baby is well, term and not requiring resuscitation. The infectious diseases physician has been involved throughout pregnancy and is available to discuss the neonatal plan.

data_table.Vital signs (mother): BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.8 degC, well.
data_table.Vital signs (neonate): HR 138 bpm, RR 40, T 36.8 degC, SpO2 98% on air, weight 3.2 kg.
data_table.Investigations: Maternal HIV VL <20 copies/mL at 36 weeks. HBsAg negative. HCV antibody negative.

lead_in: Which combination of advice and prophylaxis is most appropriate for this infant in an Australian setting?

options.text: Formula feeding plus oral triple antiretroviral therapy to the infant for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Triple infant ART is wrong because high-risk neonatal regimens (zidovudine plus lamivudine plus nevirapine or raltegravir) are reserved for infants of mothers with detectable VL near term, late diagnosis or seroconversion in pregnancy; this infant is low risk. Would be correct only if maternal viral load were not suppressed at delivery (BHIVA).

options.text: Exclusive breastfeeding for six months plus oral zidovudine for the infant
options.rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding is wrong because Australian ASHM guidance recommends formula feeding in high resource settings: residual transmission risk is not zero even on ART, and formula is safe and accessible. Would be the WHO recommendation in resource-limited settings where replacement feeding is not AFASS, not in Australia (ASHM; WHO).

options.text: Exclusive formula feeding plus oral zidovudine monotherapy for 2-4 weeks
options.rationale: In high resource settings such as Australia, exclusive formula feeding is recommended because formula is safe, accessible and eliminates postnatal transmission risk; an infant born to a virologically suppressed mother receives 2-4 weeks of oral zidovudine as low-risk infant prophylaxis (ASHM; RANZCOG; BHIVA).

options.text: Mixed feeding (breast and formula) plus zidovudine to the infant for 2 weeks
options.rationale: Mixed feeding is wrong because it is the highest-risk feeding pattern: HIV exposure from breast milk combined with mucosal disruption from formula. Would never be correct for HIV-exposed infants (WHO; ASHM).

options.text: Exclusive formula feeding alone with no antiretroviral prophylaxis required
options.rationale: No infant prophylaxis is wrong because all HIV-exposed infants receive at least short-course zidovudine even with suppressed maternal VL to cover residual transmission risk. Would be correct only if HIV status had been completely excluded antenatally, not after confirmed maternal HIV (ASHM; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Australian practice for infants born to HIV-positive mothers includes exclusive formula feeding plus a short course of infant zidovudine when the mother is virologically suppressed at term. The combination drives vertical transmission rates to well under 1% (ASHM; RANZCOG).
key_points: Formula provides nutritional equivalence in a high resource setting
Low risk infant prophylaxis: zidovudine 2-4 weeks
High risk: triple ART (e.g. zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine) for 6 weeks plus specialist input
Test infant with HIV NAT at birth, 6 weeks and 12 weeks; HIV antibody at 18 months
explanation.pearls: Formula + a short zidovudine course is the default. Breastfeeding is not recommended in Australia even with suppression.

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B - infant immunoprophylaxis and maternal tenofovir
stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman who emigrated to Australia from a high HBV prevalence country is reviewed at 26 weeks gestation in the obstetric medicine clinic. She was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B 8 years ago during routine antenatal screening in her first pregnancy. She is HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, anti-HBe negative, and her HBV DNA at 24 weeks is 2.3 x 10^8 IU/mL.

Her ALT is 28 U/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L, INR 1.0 and her FibroScan was 5.6 kPa six months ago, consistent with minimal hepatic fibrosis. She has no co-infection with HIV, HCV or HDV on booking serology and no clinical features of chronic liver disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, SFH 26 cm.
data_table.Investigations: HBsAg+, HBeAg+, anti-HBe-, HBV DNA 2.3 x 10^8 IU/mL, ALT 28 U/L, platelets 220, INR 1.0, FibroScan 5.6 kPa (low fibrosis).
data_table.Medications: None.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate maternal intervention to reduce vertical transmission in this pregnancy?

options.text: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin to the mother at 28 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Maternal HBIG is wrong because passive immunoglobulin given to the mother does not reduce viral load and HBIG has no role in maternal antenatal prevention; HBIG belongs to the infant within 12 hours of birth. Would be correct only for non-immune individuals after high-risk exposure, not as antenatal prophylaxis (Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Entecavir 0.5 mg daily from 28 weeks until 4-12 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Entecavir is wrong because Australian guidance prefers tenofovir disoproxil in pregnancy due to a much larger safety dataset; entecavir is Pregnancy Category B3 with limited human data. Would be correct only in tenofovir intolerance or resistance, not first-line (ASHM; GESA).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Chronic hepatitis B recommendations

options.text: Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily from 28 weeks until 4-12 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance recommends maternal tenofovir disoproxil from approximately 28 weeks gestation for women with HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL (or HBeAg positive with high VL) because this substantially reduces the residual vertical transmission risk that remains despite infant immunoprophylaxis (ASHM; Gastroenterological Society of Australia; AASLD/EASL).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Chronic hepatitis B recommendations
EASL Clinical Practice Guideline: Hepatitis B

options.text: Routine elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce transmission risk
options.rationale: Elective caesarean is wrong because mode of delivery does not change HBV transmission when infant HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine are given; the anti-pattern is using caesarean as a viral barrier the way it works for HIV. Would be appropriate only for standard obstetric indications (ASHM; RANZCOG).

options.text: Advise no breastfeeding because of high maternal HBV DNA levels here
options.rationale: Advising against breastfeeding is wrong because HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine makes breastfeeding safe even with high maternal DNA; the Australian Immunisation Handbook explicitly endorses breastfeeding in HBV-positive women. Would be correct only with cracked nipples and uncovered infant (Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASHM).

explanation.summary: Women with HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL should commence tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily from about 28 weeks to reduce residual vertical transmission. The infant additionally receives HBIG and the hepatitis B vaccine birth dose within 12 hours of birth, with completion of the vaccine schedule (ASHM; GESA; Australian Immunisation Handbook).
key_points: Treatment threshold for antiviral in pregnancy: HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/mL or > 5.3 log10
Tenofovir disoproxil is preferred over entecavir in pregnancy
Infant receives HBIG + first vaccine dose within 12 hours of birth in Australia
Breastfeeding is safe once infant has received immunoprophylaxis
explanation.pearls: High HBV DNA in pregnancy means tenofovir for the mother and HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine for the baby.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Chronic hepatitis B recommendations
EASL Clinical Practice Guideline: Hepatitis B

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis C - antenatal counselling and breastfeeding
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman with chronic hepatitis C diagnosed two years ago presents at her booking visit at 10 weeks gestation. She acquired HCV through past injecting drug use and has been abstinent for three years with current support from an addiction medicine service. Her HCV RNA is 5.2 x 10^5 IU/mL with genotype 1a and ALT 32 U/L. She has no co-infection with HIV or HBV.

Her liver synthetic function is preserved with INR 1.0, albumin 38 g/L, platelets 220 x10^9/L and a FibroScan of 5.1 kPa nine months ago indicating minimal fibrosis. She has not commenced direct-acting antiviral therapy. She has no other medical issues, takes folic acid 500 micrograms daily and has no allergies. She is in stable accommodation with her supportive partner who is HCV antibody negative. She asks the obstetric team about treatment in pregnancy, vertical transmission risk and whether she will be able to breastfeed her baby.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no chronic liver disease stigmata.
data_table.Investigations: HCV RNA 5.2 x 10^5 IU/mL, genotype 1a, ALT 32 U/L, albumin 38 g/L, INR 1.0, platelets 220, FibroScan 5.1 kPa.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate advice to give now?

options.text: Defer direct-acting antiviral therapy and plan breastfeeding once nipples intact
options.rationale: Direct-acting antivirals are not yet routinely recommended in pregnancy in Australia outside trial settings; treatment is deferred to postpartum. Breastfeeding is encouraged in HCV-positive women unless nipples are cracked or bleeding (ASHM; GESA; Australian Breastfeeding Association).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Hepatitis C consensus statement

options.text: Start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir at 12 weeks and continue for 12 weeks total
options.rationale: Starting DAA at 12 weeks is wrong because sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is not yet recommended outside research protocols in Australian pregnancy due to limited pharmacokinetic and safety data; deferring to postpartum is standard. Would be correct only within a registered trial, not as routine care (ASHM; GESA).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Hepatitis C consensus statement

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce vertical transmission
options.rationale: Elective caesarean is wrong because HCV vertical transmission is not reduced by caesarean delivery; intrapartum factors (prolonged ROM, fetal scalp electrodes) matter more than mode of birth. Would be appropriate only for standard obstetric indications (ASHM; RANZCOG).

options.text: Advise no breastfeeding because of detectable HCV RNA in her serum
options.rationale: Advising against breastfeeding is wrong because HCV is not transmitted through intact lactation; ASHM and ABA explicitly recommend breastfeeding with the carve-out to pause feeding from a side with cracked or bleeding nipples. Would be correct only with active nipple trauma on the involved side (ASHM; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Test the newborn with HCV antibody within 48 hours of delivery here
options.rationale: Neonatal anti-HCV at 48 hours is wrong because passively acquired maternal antibody persists in the infant for up to 18 months, making early antibody testing uninformative; HCV PCR at 2 and 6 months or antibody after 18 months is the recommended schedule. Would be correct only for documenting transient maternal antibody, not for diagnosing infant infection (ASHM).

explanation.summary: Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C are deferred until after pregnancy in current Australian practice. Vertical transmission is approximately 5-6% and is not reduced by elective caesarean; breastfeeding is safe except when nipples are cracked or bleeding (ASHM; GESA).
key_points: Treat HCV postpartum, ideally before any subsequent pregnancy
No role for routine elective caesarean section for HCV alone
Infant follow-up: HCV PCR at 2 and 6 months or antibody from 18 months
Higher transmission with HIV co-infection - test for both at booking
explanation.pearls: HCV currently waits. The biggest risk factor for vertical transmission you can act on antenatally is HIV co-infection.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Hepatitis C consensus statement

subtopic_detail: ITP - platelet threshold for neuraxial anaesthesia
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 woman with ITP diagnosed three years ago presents to obstetric day assessment at 36 weeks gestation. Her ITP has previously responded to oral prednisolone but she has been off all therapy for the past 12 months with platelet counts between 90 and 110 x10^9/L. Today her routine bloods show a platelet count of 72 x10^9/L, down from 95 x10^9/L two weeks ago.

She has no bleeding, no petechiae and no bruising, and the rest of her FBC and a peripheral blood film show isolated thrombocytopenia consistent with her known ITP. She has no signs of pre-eclampsia, no other medical problems and no allergies. She is on iron supplementation only and her booking HIV, HBV and HCV serology was negative. She is keen to have an epidural in labour. The obstetric anaesthetist and obstetric haematologist are reviewing her at 36 weeks and discussing a plan to optimise her platelets prior to expected delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No petechiae or bruising. SFH 36 cm, cephalic.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 72 x10^9/L (95 two weeks ago), Hb 116 g/L, WCC 7.0, INR 1.0, blood film: isolated thrombocytopenia consistent with ITP.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan with respect to neuraxial anaesthesia and delivery?

options.text: No treatment required because platelets above 50 x10^9/L allow epidural use
options.rationale: Doing nothing is wrong because >50 x10^9/L is the threshold for vaginal birth without instrumentation, not for neuraxial anaesthesia, which requires >70-80 x10^9/L per ASH 2019 and Australian practice. Would be correct only if she planned vaginal birth without epidural and no operative interventions (ASH 2019; KEMH).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone aiming for platelets above 80 x10^9/L by labour
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance aims for platelets above 80 x10^9/L for neuraxial anaesthesia and above 50 x10^9/L for vaginal delivery in ITP; first-line therapy is oral prednisolone, escalating to IVIG if response is inadequate or delivery is imminent (RANZCOG; ASH ITP guideline; KEMH).

options.text: Plan immediate platelet transfusion to bring the count above 100 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Pre-emptive platelet transfusion is wrong because platelet survival is short in ITP due to antibody-mediated destruction, so transfusion does not provide durable counts; it is reserved for active bleeding or imminent surgery. Would be correct only at the time of caesarean or with bleeding, not as antenatal optimisation (ASH 2019).

options.text: Start eltrombopag 50 mg orally daily and continue throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Eltrombopag is wrong because TPO receptor agonists are second/third-line in ITP and have limited pregnancy safety data; first-line in pregnancy is prednisolone with IVIG as second-line. Would be correct only in refractory ITP after corticosteroids and IVIG have failed (Therapeutic Guidelines; ASH 2019).

options.text: Splenectomy after delivery is no longer indicated for chronic ITP
options.rationale: Discussing splenectomy is wrong because the question asks about delivery-time platelet optimisation and splenectomy does not address the current pregnancy; it is also factually misleading - splenectomy remains an option for selected refractory chronic ITP. Would be a postpartum discussion only after standard therapies fail (ASH 2019).

explanation.summary: In ITP in late pregnancy the team should target platelets above 50 x10^9/L for vaginal birth, above 70-80 x10^9/L for epidural and above 80 x10^9/L for caesarean section. Oral prednisolone is first line with IVIG used for steroid failure or rapid response need (RANZCOG; ASH 2019; KEMH).
key_points: First line: oral prednisolone 20-30 mg daily aiming for response in 1-2 weeks
Second line: IVIG 1 g/kg for faster onset close to delivery
Avoid scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling, vacuum and difficult forceps in neonates at risk of thrombocytopenia
Check neonatal platelet count - mother's count does not predict baby's
explanation.pearls: Memorise 50/80: 50 for vaginal birth, 80 for epidural/caesarean. Prednisolone first, IVIG if you are running out of time.

subtopic_detail: IBD - medication safety in pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 woman with Crohn disease presents for preconception counselling. She has been in clinical and biochemical remission for 18 months on azathioprine 150 mg daily and adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks. Three years ago, before stable remission, she had a flare during which she received a 6-month course of methotrexate that was subsequently stopped. She is now planning pregnancy in the next three months.

She has no other medical problems and no allergies. Her gastroenterologist is part of the discussion and her preconception bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP and faecal calprotectin <50 micrograms/g) are reassuring. She has commenced folic acid 5 mg daily. She asks specifically which of her current and past medications might need to change before conception. Her vaccinations including MMR, varicella and pertussis are up to date and her partner is well with no relevant medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, weight 60 kg.
data_table.Examination: No active perianal disease. Soft abdomen. No mucocutaneous EIM.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs normal, CRP 2 mg/L, faecal calprotectin <50 micrograms/g.
data_table.Medications: Azathioprine 150 mg daily, adalimumab 40 mg SC fortnightly, folic acid 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate medication advice for preconception?

options.text: Stop azathioprine preconception and switch to oral budesonide as her sole maintenance therapy for the pregnancy
options.rationale: Stopping azathioprine and switching to budesonide is wrong because thiopurines maintain remission whereas budesonide is induction therapy with limited long-term maintenance efficacy; flares in pregnancy harm the fetus more than the drug. Would be correct only if she were intolerant of azathioprine and seeking short-term flare control, not as preconception maintenance (GESA; ECCO).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.text: Continue azathioprine and adalimumab; ensure methotrexate has been stopped for at least 3-6 months
options.rationale: Thiopurines and most anti-TNF agents are continued through pregnancy because flare risk outweighs medication risk and both are considered low risk; methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped for 3-6 months preconception in both partners (GESA; ECCO IBD pregnancy consensus; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.text: Stop adalimumab at conception and avoid all biologic therapy for the duration of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Stopping adalimumab at conception is wrong because anti-TNF agents are continued at least through to 24-30 weeks (often to delivery, depending on the specific biologic) because flare risk outweighs theoretical immunogenicity; the anti-pattern is reflexive drug holidays. Would be correct only if she were in deep remission with biomarker confirmation and accepted flare risk, and even then most guidelines do not endorse cessation (GESA; ECCO).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.text: Restart methotrexate 15 mg weekly if any biochemical evidence of flare during this pregnancy emerges
options.rationale: Restarting methotrexate is wrong because methotrexate is teratogenic (folate antagonism, NTDs, craniofacial anomalies) and is contraindicated through pregnancy and the 3-6 month preconception window for both partners. Would never be correct during conception attempts or pregnancy (Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Switch azathioprine to mycophenolate mofetil preconception for stronger maintenance immunosuppression during pregnancy
options.rationale: Switching to mycophenolate is wrong because MMF is teratogenic (EMFO syndrome - cleft lip/palate, microtia, cardiac, oesophageal) and explicitly contraindicated in pregnancy; pregnancy prevention is required during MMF use. Would be correct only outside pregnancy planning, never as preconception maintenance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Most IBD medications including 5-ASAs, thiopurines and anti-TNF biologics are continued in pregnancy because relapse worsens maternal and fetal outcomes more than the drug. Methotrexate and mycophenolate are absolutely contraindicated and must be stopped well in advance of conception (GESA; ECCO).
key_points: Azathioprine: continue; check TPMT once; routine monitoring of bloods
Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab): continue; consider holding final dose if active disease is well controlled to limit transplacental transfer late in pregnancy
Avoid live vaccines in the infant for 6 months after intrauterine biologic exposure (e.g. rotavirus, BCG)
Methotrexate teratogenicity: aim 3-6 months washout in both partners
explanation.pearls: The general rule: most IBD drugs continue. The exceptions are methotrexate and mycophenolate, both teratogenic.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes - preconception HbA1c target
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 11 attends preconception clinic with her partner. She uses multiple daily injections (insulin glargine 18 units nocte and insulin aspart with meals) with continuous glucose monitoring. Her most recent HbA1c is 8.4% (68 mmol/mol), down from 9.2% (77 mmol/mol) six months ago. She has background diabetic retinopathy on screening last year but no proliferative changes, urine ACR 1.8 mg/mmol, normal renal function and no neuropathy.

She has no other medical problems, no allergies and is not on any other regular medication. She is taking a standard prenatal multivitamin but no separate folic acid supplement. She has been smoke free for two years and drinks no alcohol. She tells you she would like to start trying to conceive in the next six months and asks whether her current glucose control and supplementation are adequate. Her partner is well.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, BMI 26 kg/m2.
data_table.Examination: No peripheral neuropathy, monofilament intact, fundoscopy: background retinopathy.
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.4% (68 mmol/mol), urine ACR 1.8 mg/mmol, eGFR >90, TSH normal.
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine 18 units nocte, insulin aspart with meals, standard prenatal multivitamin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her preconception care?

options.text: Switch from insulin to metformin 1 g twice daily before conception and continue throughout the pregnancy
options.rationale: Substituting metformin for insulin is wrong because metformin does not provide adequate glycaemic control in type 1 diabetes and does not address the absolute insulin deficiency; pre-existing T1DM requires intensive insulin therapy. Would be appropriate only as an adjunct in type 2 diabetes or PCOS, not as substitution in T1DM (ADIPS).

options.text: Reassure that the current HbA1c of 8.4% is acceptable for proceeding immediately to conception attempts
options.rationale: Reassuring about HbA1c 8.4% is wrong because this level corresponds to substantially elevated rates of major congenital anomaly, miscarriage and stillbirth; ADIPS targets <6.5% (or <7.0% if hypoglycaemia limits) before conception attempts. Would be correct only if no further optimisation were achievable and she had been counselled on residual risk, which is not the case here (ADIPS).

options.text: Intensify glucose management aiming for HbA1c below 6.5% and start folic acid 5 mg daily
options.rationale: ADIPS, RANZCOG and the Australian Diabetes Society recommend HbA1c below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) preconception when achievable without significant hypoglycaemia, plus folic acid 5 mg daily for at least 1-3 months before conception in pre-existing diabetes (ADIPS; RANZCOG; Australian Diabetes Society pre-existing diabetes guideline).
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes management in pregnancy

options.text: Advise indefinitely against pregnancy because of background diabetic retinopathy and the current HbA1c level
options.rationale: Advising against pregnancy is wrong because background retinopathy is not a contraindication; pregnancy is permitted with optimised glycaemia and antenatal ophthalmology surveillance every trimester. Would be correct only for severe untreated proliferative retinopathy or advanced cardiac/renal complications (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

options.text: Start a SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin preconception to reduce HbA1c rapidly before conception attempts
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors are wrong because they precipitate euglycaemic DKA in T1DM, are contraindicated in pregnancy and have no role in preconception glycaemic intensification. Would never be correct in T1DM preconception planning (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Preconception care in pre-existing type 1 diabetes targets HbA1c below 6.5% where safely achievable, folic acid 5 mg daily, retinal and renal review, and review of all non-insulin medications. Achieving these targets substantially reduces congenital anomaly and miscarriage rates (ADIPS; RANZCOG).
key_points: Target HbA1c <6.5% (or <7.0% if hypoglycaemia limits)
Folic acid 5 mg daily for diabetes is one of the standard 5 mg indications
Stop teratogenic agents preconception: ACE-i/ARB, statin, SGLT2i
Retinal screening before pregnancy and at least once per trimester
explanation.pearls: T1DM preconception target HbA1c is <6.5% and folate is 5 mg, not 400 micrograms.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes management in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum glucose targets in pre-existing diabetes
stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with type 1 diabetes for 15 years is admitted in spontaneous labour at 38+3 weeks. She has been on insulin pump therapy throughout pregnancy with an HbA1c at 36 weeks of 5.9% (41 mmol/mol). Growth has tracked along the 80th centile with an estimated fetal weight 3.7 kg one week ago. There is no polyhydramnios. She has no diabetic complications other than background retinopathy and no pre-eclampsia.

She is currently 4 cm dilated, contracting regularly and requesting an epidural. On admission her capillary blood glucose is 8.2 mmol/L and she has trace ketones on urine dip. The midwifery team is asking the obstetric registrar about the appropriate glucose target during labour and the optimal way to manage her insulin from now on. She has no allergies and no other regular medications. The neonatal team has been notified to attend delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm/fully effaced, station -2, contractions 3:10, CTG normotypical baseline 140.
data_table.Investigations: CBG 8.2 mmol/L, urine ketones trace, U&E normal, recent HbA1c 5.9%.
data_table.Medications: Insulin pump (basal aspart). Folic acid 5 mg until 12 weeks (stopped), iodine.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum glucose management?

options.text: Continue subcutaneous insulin pump unchanged with 4-hourly capillary glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Continuing the pump with 4-hourly checks is wrong because intrapartum T1DM needs hourly capillary glucose to stay in the narrow 4-7 mmol/L band; pumps may continue only with strict hourly monitoring and a written failure protocol. Would be correct only with hourly testing and explicit pump-continuation protocol, not 4-hourly (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

options.text: Switch to variable-rate IV insulin infusion targeting CBG 4-7 mmol/L
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance is to target intrapartum capillary glucose 4-7 mmol/L, monitored hourly, using a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion with dextrose where needed; this reduces neonatal hypoglycaemia (ADIPS; RANZCOG; NICE Diabetes in Pregnancy).

options.text: Stop all insulin in labour and recommence after delivery of the placenta
options.rationale: Stopping all insulin is wrong because basal insulin withdrawal in T1DM precipitates DKA within hours; the anti-pattern is treating T1DM like T2DM where insulin can be paused. Would never be correct in T1DM intrapartum (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Aim for capillary glucose 8-10 mmol/L to reduce maternal hypoglycaemia risk
options.rationale: Higher targets are wrong because intrapartum maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinism and neonatal hypoglycaemia after cord clamp; 4-7 mmol/L is the established target. Would be correct only as a transient ceiling during hypoglycaemia recovery, not as a deliberate target (ADIPS).

options.text: Give a single dose of long-acting insulin glargine 20 units now
options.rationale: Single long-acting glargine bolus is wrong because long-acting analogues are not titratable and cannot match the rapid changes in insulin requirement during labour and immediately postpartum; variable rate IV insulin is preferred. Would be correct only as an outpatient regimen, not in active labour (ADIPS).

explanation.summary: Intrapartum care of T1DM uses a variable rate IV insulin infusion with hourly capillary glucose monitoring, targeting 4-7 mmol/L to reduce neonatal hypoglycaemia. After delivery of the placenta insulin requirements fall sharply and infusion rates must be halved or stopped to avoid maternal hypoglycaemia (ADIPS; RANZCOG).
key_points: Target intrapartum CBG 4-7 mmol/L
Hourly CBG, ketone check if CBG >12 or symptoms
Halve infusion or revert to subcut basal/bolus after placenta delivered
Neonatal CBG checks per local pathway (e.g. before second feed, then 3-4 hourly)
explanation.pearls: 4 to 7 in labour, halve the insulin after the placenta.

subtopic_detail: Mechanical mitral valve - anticoagulation by trimester
stem:
A 34-year-old G1P0 woman with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement for rheumatic heart disease attends preconception clinic with her cardiologist and an obstetric physician. Her rheumatic disease was acquired in childhood before she immigrated to Australia at age 12; surveillance now demonstrates only the prosthetic valve as a residual lesion. She has been on warfarin 4 mg daily with stable INR 2.5-3.5 since her surgery five years ago, monitored at a community anticoagulation clinic, with no thrombotic or bleeding events.

She is currently in sinus rhythm, NYHA functional class I with no exertional symptoms during stair climbing, and her most recent transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal mechanical valve function with no regurgitation, no left atrial enlargementft ventricular ejection fraction of 60%.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm regular.
data_table.Examination: Mechanical S2, no murmurs, no signs of failure, NYHA I.
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.8, LVEF 60%, normal valve function on TTE.
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 4 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate to plan from conception through to delivery?

options.text: Use therapeutic-dose enoxaparin with anti-Xa monitoring for the entire pregnancy from positive test until 36 weeks then switch to unfractionated heparin
options.rationale: LMWH throughout is wrong because mechanical mitral valve thrombosis rates are higher on LMWH-only regimens than on warfarin-containing strategies despite anti-Xa monitoring; ESC reserves this approach for women who decline warfarin after structured counselling. Would be correct only as a patient-preference option after counselling, not as default (ESC 2018).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.text: Continue warfarin at the same dose from conception through to elective induction at term to minimise mechanical valve thrombosis risk throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Warfarin throughout is wrong because it carries warfarin embryopathy risk between 6 and 12 weeks (nasal hypoplasia, chondrodysplasia punctata) and fetal intracranial haemorrhage at delivery; pure-warfarin strategy is acceptable only when daily warfarin dose is low (<5 mg) with explicit counselling. Would be correct only when warfarin dose is <5 mg/day and the woman accepts fetal risk after counselling, not as default for high-dose warfarin requirements (ESC 2018).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.text: Switch to therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from positive pregnancy test, return to warfarin from 13-36 weeks, switch back to LMWH from 36 weeks to delivery
options.rationale: ESC and RANZCOG guidance recommend dose-adjusted LMWH (with anti-Xa monitoring) in the first trimester to avoid warfarin embryopathy when the daily warfarin dose is moderate to high, warfarin in the second and early third trimester for stable INR and lowest thrombotic risk on the valve, then LMWH again from 36 weeks to allow safe neuraxial anaesthesia and delivery (ESC 2018 Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy; RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - anticoagulation in pregnancy

options.text: Switch to rivaroxaban 20 mg orally daily preconception and continue this direct oral anticoagulant throughout the entire pregnancy and puerperium
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is wrong because DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy and ineffective at preventing mechanical valve thrombosis (RE-ALIGN trial showed harm with dabigatran). Would never be correct in mechanical valves, pregnant or not (ESC 2018; AMH).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.text: Stop all anticoagulation in the first trimester to avoid warfarin embryopathy and reintroduce therapeutic LMWH at 14 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Stopping anticoagulation in the first trimester is wrong because mechanical mitral valves have very high thrombotic risk and require uninterrupted anticoagulation; periods without anticoagulant cause valve thrombosis and maternal death. Would never be correct (ESC 2018).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation in mechanical heart valves in pregnancy balances maternal valve thrombosis (best minimised with warfarin) and fetal embryopathy/bleeding (worse with warfarin). A common sequenced strategy is LMWH in the first trimester (especially if warfarin dose >5 mg), warfarin in mid-pregnancy, and LMWH again from 36 weeks for safe peridelivery management (ESC 2018; RANZCOG).
key_points: Daily warfarin dose <5 mg: lower embryopathy risk so warfarin throughout is more acceptable
Therapeutic LMWH requires anti-Xa monitoring (peak 4 hours post dose)
Plan delivery on LMWH; convert to IV unfractionated heparin 36 hours before and stop 4-6 hours before neuraxial
Restart anticoagulation 6-12 hours after vaginal birth or 12-24 hours after caesarean if no bleeding
explanation.pearls: Mechanical valves are anticoagulation jigsaws: never stop entirely, plan the trimester swaps in advance.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - anticoagulation in pregnancy
ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Postnatal VTE prophylaxis - risk-based dosing
stem:
A 36-year-old G3P2 woman delivers a healthy 3.6 kg infant by emergency caesarean section at 39+1 weeks for failure to progress in the first stage of labour. Her BMI on booking was 33 kg/m2 and her current weight is 92 kg with proportionate gestational weight gain. She is otherwise well with no personal or family history of thrombosis, no known thrombophilia and no immobilising disease.

The caesarean was technically straightforward with estimated blood loss 600 mL, no transfusion required and no postpartum haemorrhage. She is now on the postnatal ward six hours after delivery, observations stable, mobilising with assistance, no signs of bleeding, lochia normal and the wound dressing dry.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, dressing dry, lochia normal, calves soft and non-tender, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L (booking 122), platelets 240 x10^9/L, U&E normal, INR 1.0.
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol PRN, ibuprofen PRN. No anticoagulant yet.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate VTE prophylaxis plan for this patient?

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily orally for 7 days post-discharge
options.rationale: Apixaban is wrong because DOACs are not recommended for postpartum thromboprophylaxis in Australia, partly due to limited lactation data and partly because LMWH has stronger evidence; the anti-pattern is extrapolating non-pregnant orthopaedic practice. Would be correct only outside the postpartum/breastfeeding context (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Mechanical thromboprophylaxis with TED stockings alone for duration of admission
options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is wrong because emergency caesarean plus multiple risk factors crosses the threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis; stockings are an adjunct, not a substitute. Would be correct only when LMWH is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) (RCOG Green-top 37a).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 90 mg twice daily for 6 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Therapeutic-dose LMWH is wrong because therapeutic dosing is for confirmed VTE or very-high-risk prophylaxis (recent VTE, APS with prior thrombosis); the bleeding risk is unjustified for prophylactic indications. Would be correct only if she had had a recent VTE or thrombotic APS (RCOG Green-top 37a).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for at least 10 days postoperatively
options.rationale: Emergency caesarean plus age >=35 plus BMI >=30 plus parity >=3 each adds points on Australian and RCOG postnatal VTE risk scoring; this combination indicates pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 10 days postpartum. Enoxaparin 40 mg daily is appropriate at her weight (RCOG Green-top 37a; RANZCOG; KEMH).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium
RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium
KEMH: VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for 6 weeks postpartum as VTE prophylaxis
options.rationale: Aspirin is wrong because aspirin lacks evidence for postnatal VTE prevention in this risk profile and is not recommended by RCOG Green-top 37a; LMWH is the agent of choice. Would be correct only as pre-eclampsia prophylaxis, not VTE (RCOG Green-top 37a).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk assessment uses cumulative risk factors. Emergency caesarean alone earns prophylaxis for at least 10 days; combined with BMI >=30, age >=35 and parity >=3 the indication is robust. Standard agent is prophylactic-dose LMWH starting 6-12 hours after delivery if no bleeding (RCOG; RANZCOG; KEMH).
key_points: Score in late pregnancy and again postnatally; rescore if status changes
Standard prophylactic enoxaparin dose 40 mg daily for weight 50-90 kg; weight-band adjust outside this range
Continue 10 days postpartum at minimum; 6 weeks if previous VTE, persistent risk factors or thrombophilia
LMWH compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Emergency caesarean plus any second risk factor almost always equals 10 days of enoxaparin.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium
KEMH: VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

subtopic_detail: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy - UDCA and delivery timing
stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 35+2 weeks presents with two weeks of progressive generalised itching that is worst on the palms and soles and worse at night. She has no rash, no jaundice and no right upper quadrant pain. She has no significant past medical history and her booking bloods including viral screen were normal. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated.

Her LFTs today show ALT 110 U/L (ULN 35), AST 88 U/L (ULN 35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L, GGT 60 U/L, ALP 280 U/L, and total fasting bile acids 56 micromol/L. Her INR is 1.0 and platelets are 220 x10^9/L. She has no signs of pre-eclampsia, urine PCR is 4 mg/mmol and her CTG is reassuring. Liver ultrasound shows no gallstones, normal hepatic parenchyma and patent portal vessels. She has had no other liver insults and is on no regular medications other than a pregnancy multivitamin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Excoriations on palms, soles, abdomen. No jaundice. SFH 35 cm. CTG normotypical.
data_table.Investigations: ALT 110 U/L, AST 88 U/L, GGT 60 U/L, ALP 280 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, fasting bile acids 56 micromol/L, INR 1.0, platelets 220, urine PCR 4 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combined plan for medication and timing of delivery?

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily and plan delivery at 37-38 weeks
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves maternal symptoms and is the recommended pharmacological treatment for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. For moderate disease (bile acids 40-99 micromol/L) Australian and RCOG guidance recommends planning delivery at 37-38+6 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk (RANZCOG; RCOG Green-top 43 ICP 2022; Royal Women's Hospital Vic).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Obstetric cholestasis

options.text: Topical emollients only and plan delivery at term 39-40 weeks
options.rationale: Emollients alone with 39-40 week delivery is wrong because emollients are purely symptomatic and do not address the underlying cholestasis; the stillbirth curve at bile acids 56 micromol/L rises substantially after 38 weeks, making term expectancy unsafe. Would be correct only for mild ICP (bile acids <40 micromol/L) where 39-40 week delivery is acceptable (RCOG ICP 2022).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.text: Cholestyramine 4 g three times daily and plan immediate delivery now
options.rationale: Cholestyramine plus immediate delivery is wrong because cholestyramine has fallen out of first-line use due to fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (including vitamin K) and immediate delivery at 35+2 is reserved for severe disease at bile acids >=100 micromol/L. Would be correct only at severe-disease thresholds, not at 56 micromol/L (RCOG ICP 2022; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 12 mg daily for 7 days as definitive symptomatic therapy
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is wrong because corticosteroids are not effective primary treatment for ICP; UDCA is the established pharmacological agent. Would be correct only for antenatal lung maturation if early preterm delivery were planned, not as ICP therapy (RCOG ICP 2022).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.text: Antihistamine therapy with chlorphenamine and expectant management to 40 weeks
options.rationale: Antihistamines plus 40-week expectancy is wrong because chlorphenamine only modestly improves itch and does not change bile acid kinetics or stillbirth risk; delivery to 40 weeks at this bile acid level exceeds the safety window. Would be correct only for benign pruritus of pregnancy without raised bile acids (RCOG ICP 2022).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is suggested by pruritus without rash, deranged transaminases and a raised total bile acid; bile acid level guides delivery timing. UDCA improves maternal pruritus and is standard of care. Delivery at 37-38+6 weeks is appropriate for bile acids 40-99 micromol/L; consider earlier delivery for >=100 micromol/L (RANZCOG; RCOG ICP 2022).
key_points: Stillbirth risk relates predominantly to peak bile acid concentration
UDCA 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses, typically 500 mg BD
Bile acids 40-99 micromol/L: deliver 37-38+6 weeks; >=100 micromol/L: consider 35-36 weeks
ICP usually resolves within days of delivery; consider recurrence in future pregnancies
explanation.pearls: UDCA helps the itch and bile acid level drives the calendar.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Obstetric cholestasis
RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy versus HELLP
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 36+4 weeks presents to the maternity assessment unit with 36 hours of nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant pain. She is increasingly fatigued and her partner reports she has been progressively confused for the last few hours, with intermittent disorientation to time and place. There is no headache, no visual disturbance, no vaginal bleeding and she reports no reduced fetal movements but feels generally unwell.

On arrival her BP is 138/88 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 98% on air and she appears jaundiced with mild asterixis. Her abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant without rebound; CTG shows a normotypical baseline of 145 bpm with reduced variability. Her bedside capillary glucose is 2.6 mmol/L. Urgent bloods reveal an ALT of 540 U/L, AST 520 U/L, bilirubin 78 micromol/L, INR 1.9, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 95 x10^9/L, ammonia 92 micromol/L, urate 0.46 mmol/L and creatinine 138 micromol/L. Lactate is 4.2 mmol/L and the blood film shows no schistocytes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/88 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, T 36.9 degC, SpO2 98%, CBG 2.6 mmol/L.
data_table.Examination: Jaundice, mild asterixis, RUQ tenderness, GCS 14, no peripheral oedema, CTG reduced variability.
data_table.Investigations: ALT 540 U/L, AST 520 U/L, bilirubin 78 micromol/L, INR 1.9, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L, platelets 95 x10^9/L, ammonia 92 micromol/L, urate 0.46 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, urine PCR 28 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours acute fatty liver of pregnancy over HELLP syndrome?

options.text: Mild hypertension with a urine PCR above 30 mg/mmol
options.rationale: Hypertension and proteinuria is wrong because it is more characteristic of HELLP (which sits on the pre-eclampsia spectrum) than AFLP, where blood pressure is often only modestly elevated and proteinuria less prominent. Would point to HELLP/pre-eclampsia rather than AFLP (RANZCOG).

options.text: Right upper quadrant pain with raised transaminases above 500 U/L
options.rationale: RUQ pain with transaminases >500 is wrong because both AFLP and HELLP can present with this picture; it is shared rather than discriminating. Would be neutral, not diagnostic, between the two (Swansea criteria).
source_refs: Swansea criteria (Knight et al.) for acute fatty liver of pregnancy

options.text: Platelet count below 100 x10^9/L on this presentation
options.rationale: Platelets <100 is wrong because it is part of HELLP criteria and can occur in AFLP from synthetic failure too; in AFLP the platelet drop is usually modest relative to the coagulopathy. Would be a HELLP criterion not a discriminator (RANZCOG).

options.text: Maternal hypoglycaemia with raised ammonia and coagulopathy out of proportion to platelet drop
options.rationale: Hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia and a coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, raised INR) that is disproportionate to the relatively modest thrombocytopenia are highly suggestive of acute fatty liver of pregnancy, reflecting hepatic synthetic failure rather than microangiopathic haemolysis (Swansea criteria; RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital Vic).
source_refs: Swansea criteria (Knight et al.) for acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

options.text: Serum urate above the upper limit of normal in the third trimester
options.rationale: Hyperuricaemia is wrong because raised urate is a classic pre-eclampsia/HELLP marker (placental ischaemia, reduced renal clearance) and is not specific to AFLP. Would point to HELLP/pre-eclampsia (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a hepatic synthetic failure syndrome of the third trimester. Distinguishing features versus HELLP include hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and a coagulopathy that exceeds what platelet count alone would explain. Definitive treatment for both is prompt delivery with maternal stabilisation (Swansea criteria; RANZCOG).
key_points: Swansea criteria: vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia/polyuria, encephalopathy, bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, urate, leucocytosis, ascites/bright liver, transaminitis, ammonia, AKI, coagulopathy, microvesicular steatosis (>=6 of 14)
Maternal stabilisation focuses on glucose, coagulopathy reversal and timely delivery
Consider LCHAD deficiency screening in the infant after maternal AFLP
Multidisciplinary management with hepatology and intensive care
explanation.pearls: Hypoglycaemia and hyperammonaemia in a third-trimester woman = think AFLP, not HELLP.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Swansea criteria (Knight et al.) for acute fatty liver of pregnancy

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 with a confirmed MCDA twin pregnancy at 19+5 weeks attends fortnightly surveillance. The 16-week scan was unremarkable. Today's ultrasound: twin 1 (donor) EFW 22nd centile, DVP 1.6 cm, bladder not seen on three sweeps over 30 minutes; twin 2 (recipient) EFW 56th centile, DVP 9.2 cm, distended bladder, normal MCA-PSV. Umbilical artery Dopplers normal both twins, no fetal hydrops, cervix 38 mm.

She has no contractions, no bleeding, no symptoms of pre-eclampsia. The tertiary fetal medicine unit is 2 hours away and offers fetoscopic laser ablation daily. She wants the option that maximises the chance of two healthy survivors.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus appropriate for 24 weeks size
data_table.Investigations: Twin 1: EFW 22nd centile, DVP 1.6 cm, bladder not seen. Twin 2: EFW 56th centile, DVP 9.2 cm, bladder distended, MCA-PSV normal. UA Dopplers normal both twins. Cervix 38 mm closed.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent referral to a tertiary fetal medicine unit for fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
options.rationale: She has stage I/II TTTS (Quintero stage II given absent donor bladder, with oligohydramnios <2 cm vs polyhydramnios >8 cm; normal Dopplers excluding stage III; no hydrops). Fetoscopic laser ablation between 16-26 weeks gives the best dual-survival outcome and is recommended over amnioreduction (RANZCOG twins; ISUOG).

options.text: Reassure and continue routine fortnightly surveillance for 2 more weeks
options.rationale: Reassurance and fortnightly surveillance is wrong because untreated Quintero stage II TTTS has high perinatal mortality; the anti-pattern is waiting for progression. Would be correct only for Stage I with stable Dopplers under close specialist review, not Stage II (RANZCOG).

options.text: Amnioreduction of the recipient sac in the local maternity unit
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is wrong because the Eurofetus and subsequent trials showed fetoscopic laser ablation gives superior dual-survival and lower neurological morbidity than amnioreduction in stage II-IV TTTS at 16-26 weeks. Would be acceptable only if laser is unavailable, the woman declines transfer, or gestation is outside the laser window (RANZCOG; ISUOG).

options.text: Admit for antenatal corticosteroids and plan delivery this week
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids and delivery at 19+5 is wrong because 19+5 weeks is pre-viable; delivery would result in dual neonatal loss. Would be correct only at periviable gestations after 24 weeks with stage III-IV TTTS refractory to laser (RANZCOG).
