options.text: Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin by cord occlusion now
options.rationale: Cord occlusion of the donor is wrong because selective reduction by cord occlusion is reserved for Stage IV-V or when laser has failed/is not feasible (e.g. severe hydrops in one twin, anterior placenta with poor access); at Stage II laser is first line. Would be correct only as salvage therapy when laser is unsuitable (RANZCOG; ISUOG).

explanation.summary: TTTS complicates around 10 to 15 percent of MCDA pregnancies and is diagnosed by discordant amniotic fluid (DVP under 2 and over 8 cm) before 20 weeks. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is first-line.
key_points: Fortnightly TVS and US from 16 weeks for MCDA (RANZCOG)
Quintero staging: I fluid only; II absent bladder donor; III abnormal Dopplers; IV hydrops; V demise
Laser ablation reduces perinatal death and neurological injury vs amnioreduction
explanation.pearls: DVP, not AFI, is the standard discordance measure in twins.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy
NICE NG137: Twin and triplet pregnancy

subtopic_detail: TTTS - screening and recognition

stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 with an MCDA twin pregnancy is reviewed at 26 weeks. Booking, anatomy scan, and TTTS surveillance to date have been unremarkable. Today the smaller twin has an EFW on the 4th centile with a 28 percent inter-twin weight discordance. The larger twin tracks the 48th centile. Amniotic fluid is normal in both sacs. Umbilical artery Doppler of the smaller twin shows intermittently absent end-diastolic flow that alternates with normal forward flow within a single tracing; the larger twin's UA Doppler is normal. Both ductus venosus a-waves are positive. The cardiotocograph of both twins is reactive. The woman is well with a closed cervix of 34 mm.

data_table.Investigations: Smaller twin EFW 4th centile, discordance 28%, UA Doppler intermittent AEDF (Type III). Larger twin EFW 48th centile, UA Doppler normal. DV a-waves positive both. CTG reactive both. Cervix 34 mm.

lead_in: Which classification and surveillance plan best fits this pattern?

options.text: Type I sIUGR; fortnightly growth scans, aim for planned delivery at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Type I labelling is wrong because Gratacos Type I has persistently positive UA end-diastolic flow with a favourable prognosis; intermittent absent end-diastolic flow defines Type III. Would be correct only if UA Dopplers remained continuously positive (Gratacos sIUGR classification).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Type II sIUGR; weekly Doppler and CTG surveillance, plan delivery at 32 weeks
options.rationale: Type II labelling is wrong because Type II shows persistently absent or reversed UA flow with progressive deterioration and earlier delivery (often 28-30 weeks); the intermittent pattern here is Type III. Would be correct only if AEDF or REDF were persistent across studies (Gratacos sIUGR classification).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Type III sIUGR; twice-weekly Doppler with corticosteroid cover and delivery at 32 to 34 weeks
options.rationale: Intermittent AEDF in the smaller MCDA twin defines Type III, which carries unpredictable risk of sudden co-twin demise from large anastomoses; close surveillance and planned preterm delivery are recommended.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Discordant growth without sIUGR; reassure the woman and re-scan in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Reassuring as benign discordance is wrong because EFW below the 10th centile in either twin combined with greater than 25% discordance meets the consensus definition of sIUGR; the anti-pattern is treating this as physiological variation. Would be correct only if both twins were AGA with milder discordance, not here (ISUOG).

options.text: Stage I twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome; refer urgently for fetoscopic laser ablation now
options.rationale: TTTS labelling is wrong because TTTS requires discordant fluid (DVP <2 cm in one and >8 cm in the other); fluid is normal in both sacs, so the pathology is sIUGR not TTTS. Would be correct only if oligohydramnios-polyhydramnios were present (RANZCOG; ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

explanation.summary: sIUGR in MCDA twins is classified by UA Doppler: Type I positive EDF, Type II persistent AEDF or REDF, Type III intermittent AEDF. Type III carries a particular risk of unexpected single-twin demise.
key_points: Definition: EFW under 10th centile in one twin or inter-twin discordance over 25% (ISUOG)
MCDA Type III: large arterio-arterial anastomoses cause unpredictable shunt reversal
Plan delivery 32 to 34 weeks with corticosteroids per RANZCOG
explanation.pearls: Co-twin demise risk and neurological injury risk rise sharply in MCDA Type III sIUGR.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Selective IUGR in monochorionic twins

stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 RhD-negative woman with a DCDA twin pregnancy (two viable embryos at 7+1) re-presents at 13+0 with a single episode of pink spotting yesterday, now resolved. She is haemodynamically stable. Ultrasound today: twin A viable, CRL appropriate for 13+0; twin B sac collapsed, embryo CRL 7+5 with no cardiac activity (demised). Antibody screen at booking and today: negative. She has not previously received anti-D in this pregnancy. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, closed cervical os, scant brown discharge
data_table.Investigations: TVS: twin A viable, twin B demised (CRL 7+5, no FH). Blood group O Rh-positive.

lead_in: Which combination of management is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure regarding minimal increased risk to the surviving twin from the early loss; administer anti-D 625 IU IM as the bleeding episode is at 13+0; continue routine DCDA twin surveillance
options.rationale: Early vanishing twin (before 14 weeks) confers minimal increased risk to the surviving co-twin. As she is now 13+0 with a sensitising event, anti-D 625 IU IM is required (NBA gives 625 IU from 13 weeks). DCDA surveillance continues 4-weekly from 24 weeks (NBA; RANZCOG).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti-D Ig guidelines

options.text: Administer anti-D 250 IU IM as the dose for sensitising events before 20 weeks
options.rationale: Anti-D 250 IU is wrong because the NBA dose increases to 625 IU IM from 13+0 weeks for sensitising events; 250 IU is the pre-12-week dose. Would be correct only before 13 weeks, not at exactly 13+0 (National Blood Authority Anti-D guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti-D Ig guidelines

options.text: Withhold anti-D until 28 weeks routine prophylaxis as the antibody screen is negative
options.rationale: Withholding anti-D until 28 weeks is wrong because sensitising events require anti-D within 72 hours regardless of negative antibody screen or upcoming routine prophylaxis; waiting risks sensitisation. Would be correct only for a non-sensitising event with no bleeding (National Blood Authority).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti-D Ig guidelines

options.text: Surgical evacuation of the demised gestational sac to prevent later miscarriage of the surviving twin
options.rationale: Surgical evacuation is wrong because vanishing twins resorb naturally and instrumentation risks loss of the surviving twin from membrane disruption or infection. Would be correct only if there were septic retained products threatening the surviving pregnancy, which is not described (RANZCOG).

options.text: Admit for serial coagulation studies given the increased maternal risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation
options.rationale: Serial coagulation studies for DIC is wrong because maternal DIC risk applies to single-twin demise after viability (typically >=20 weeks) with prolonged in-utero retention; first-trimester vanishing twin does not generate the necessary thromboplastin load. Would be correct only for second/third-trimester co-twin demise (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis prevents alloimmunisation that would cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in subsequent pregnancies. The Australian National Blood Authority dose schedule is 250 IU before 12 weeks for sensitising events (miscarriage, ectopic, CVS, termination), then 625 IU IM from 13 weeks onward for any sensitising event (vanishing twin, antepartum bleed, ECV, abdominal trauma, amniocentesis). Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks. After birth, a Kleihauer-Betke quantifies feto-maternal haemorrhage and any volume above 4 mL warrants additional anti-D 125 IU per 1 mL FMH. Vanishing twin in a DCDA pregnancy has a generally good prognosis for the survivor; in monochorionic pregnancies, single intrauterine death triggers urgent referral for assessment of the co-twin given shared circulation and risk of co-twin death or neurological injury.
key_points: DCDA vanishing twin in T1: routine antenatal care, no specific intervention
MC vanishing twin: risk of neurological injury or co-twin demise via shared anastomoses
Anti-D only if Rh-negative per NBA guidance
explanation.pearls: In any RhD-negative woman, single first-trimester sensitising events under 12 weeks (chorionic villus sampling, ectopic, termination, vanishing twin) require 250 IU anti-D; from 13 weeks onward, the dose is 625 IU IM (NBA Anti-D Guidelines).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for genetic conditions

subtopic_detail: Vanishing twin

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P0 with a confirmed MCMA twin pregnancy is reviewed at 31+4. Booking confirmed a single placental mass, no inter-twin membrane on serial scans, and entangled cords on colour Doppler. Growth has tracked the 35th to 45th centiles concordantly, Dopplers are normal, and there is no evidence of TTTS. She has been an inpatient since 26 weeks for daily CTG monitoring.

Both twins are presently non-cephalic on today's presentation scan. The cervix is closed at 32 mm on TVS. She received a complete course of antenatal corticosteroids at 26 weeks and an additional rescue course was given two weeks ago. She has received daily inpatient CTG surveillance without abnormal traces, no episodes of bleeding or rupture of membranes, and a recent maternal infection screen is unremarkable. The neonatal unit on site routinely supports infants from 28 weeks. She is keen to proceed with planned delivery once the team agrees timing.

data_table.Examination: Inpatient, comfortable, daily CTG reactive for both twins
data_table.Investigations: Concordant growth, normal Dopplers, no TTTS, both non-cephalic, cervix 32 mm

lead_in: Which delivery plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Planned caesarean between 32+0 and 34+0 weeks after corticosteroids
options.rationale: MCMA twins are recommended to deliver by planned caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 weeks due to risk of cord entanglement and intrauterine death rising sharply after 32 weeks (RANZCOG, KEMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Planned caesarean at 36+0 to 36+6 after steroids
options.rationale: 36+0 to 36+6 is wrong because that is the MCDA window; in MCMA, cord entanglement risk rises after 32 weeks and waiting to 36 is unsafe. Would be correct for MCDA, not MCMA (RANZCOG; KEMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Planned vaginal birth at 32+0 to 34+0 with continuous CTG
options.rationale: Vaginal birth with CTG is wrong because cord entanglement in a shared sac makes labour intrinsically high-risk regardless of presentation; the anti-pattern is treating MCMA like MCDA. Would never be correct in MCMA, even with cephalic-cephalic presentation (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Continue inpatient monitoring and aim for vaginal birth at 37+0
options.rationale: Aiming for 37+0 vaginally is wrong because it stacks the worst of both errors: extending well past the MCMA safety window plus exposing twins to labour-related entanglement risk. Would never be correct in MCMA (RANZCOG; KEMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Immediate caesarean today at 31+4 regardless of stability
options.rationale: Immediate caesarean at 31+4 is wrong because without a deterioration trigger (abnormal CTG, sIUGR progression, TTTS), birth at 31+4 imposes prematurity morbidity that the 32-34 week window is designed to avoid. Would be correct only with evidence of fetal compromise or maternal indication (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

explanation.summary: MCMA twins share a single amniotic sac with high cord entanglement risk. Inpatient surveillance from around 26 weeks and planned caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 after corticosteroids is the Australian standard.
key_points: MCMA delivery: planned caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 (RANZCOG, KEMH)
Inpatient daily CTG often offered from 26 to 28 weeks
Cord entanglement risk underlies the early delivery decision
explanation.pearls: MCMA is rare (around 1 percent of MC twins) but high-risk; centralise care.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Mode and timing of delivery - MCMA twins

stem:
A 25-year-old G1P0 at 28+3 presents to the birth suite with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes for the past 2 hours. She has had no bleeding, no rupture of membranes, and no fever. Her booking and pregnancy have been uncomplicated. She has well-controlled chronic hypertension on labetalol 200 mg BD with booking BP averaging 130/82 and today 134/86. She has known mild aortic stenosis (peak gradient 22 mmHg, asymptomatic) and is followed by cardiology.

Examination shows a soft tender uterus with palpable tightenings, cephalic presentation, and the cervix is 2 cm dilated and 50 percent effaced on speculum. Fetal heart is reassuring. Fetal fibronectin is not available at this hour. The plan is to give corticosteroids and MgSO4 for neuroprotection and transfer to a tertiary unit.

data_table.Examination: Uterus contracting q4min, cephalic, cervix 2 cm 50% effaced, membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Fetal heart reassuring, MSU pending, FBC and UEC normal
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg BD

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate tocolytic to commence while corticosteroids and transfer are organised?

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release with continuous maternal BP monitoring and a held dose if systolic falls below 90 mmHg
options.rationale: Nifedipine (off-label) is the RANZCOG first-line tocolytic in Australia. Concurrent labetalol and mild aortic stenosis are cautions rather than absolute contraindications: nifedipine is given with close maternal BP monitoring and withheld if systolic <90 mmHg, with cardiology input. There is no PBS-listed parenteral alternative routinely available in Australia (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

options.text: Intravenous atosiban infusion as oxytocin-receptor antagonist tocolysis, with continuous maternal monitoring and titration to contraction frequency
options.rationale: Atosiban is an oxytocin-receptor antagonist used in some European jurisdictions but is NOT routinely available in Australia (not PBS-listed and not stocked by Australian maternity services). It cannot be selected as the practical first-line tocolytic here. Nifedipine is the Australian first-line per RANZCOG (RANZCOG: Tocolysis).

options.text: Oral indomethacin 50 mg loading dose then 25 mg six-hourly for up to 48 hours with fetal ductal monitoring on echocardiography
options.rationale: Indomethacin is an acceptable alternative under 32 weeks but carries fetal renal and ductal risks with prolonged use, and is reserved for cases where nifedipine is contraindicated. Nifedipine, with careful BP monitoring, remains the first-line choice (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion used primarily as tocolysis with continuous maternal monitoring of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is ineffective as a tocolytic and is instead reserved for fetal neuroprotection at <30 weeks. Would be correct only as neuroprotection (the question separately requires this), not tocolysis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for preventing preterm birth

options.text: Intravenous salbutamol infusion as beta-2 agonist tocolysis with continuous maternal cardiac monitoring and held dose if maternal HR exceeds 120 bpm
options.rationale: Beta-agonists are no longer recommended in Australia for tocolysis (maternal tachycardia, pulmonary oedema, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia) and are particularly hazardous in maternal cardiac disease. Would never be first-line in current Australian guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

explanation.summary: Tocolysis aims to delay birth for 48 hours to allow corticosteroid effect and in-utero transfer. In Australia, nifedipine (off-label) is the first-line tocolytic per RANZCOG, including in women on antihypertensives, provided maternal BP is monitored closely and dosing held for hypotension. Indomethacin is an alternative under 32 weeks. Atosiban (oxytocin-receptor antagonist) is used in some overseas settings but is not routinely available in Australia.
key_points: First-line tocolytic in Australia: nifedipine (RANZCOG, eTG; off-label)
Indomethacin: alternative under ~32 weeks; ductal constriction and oligohydramnios above 32 weeks
Atosiban: NOT routinely available in Australia (not PBS-listed)
Beta-agonists no longer used; magnesium sulfate is for neuroprotection, not tocolysis
explanation.pearls: In Australia, when antihypertensives are co-prescribed, nifedipine is still first-line for tocolysis - the management is dose vigilance and BP monitoring, not a switch to atosiban (which is not stocked here). Tocolysis is only justified when corticosteroids or transfer will meaningfully change neonatal outcome.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for preventing preterm birth

subtopic_detail: Preterm labour - tocolysis choice

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 at 33+1 presents with painful tightenings every 6 minutes for 4 hours. She had a previous preterm birth at 31 weeks. She has no rupture of membranes or bleeding. Examination shows a cephalic presentation, cervix 1 cm dilated and 30 percent effaced; CTG is reactive. She has no maternal medical comorbidities and is on no regular medication.

Her registrar suggests indomethacin tocolysis to allow corticosteroid effect, citing its rapid onset. She has no antepartum haemorrhage and no fever. Maternal observations are normal, urine dipstick is clear and the fetal heart on continuous CTG is reactive with normal variability. Booking scans were unremarkable and a recent fetal anatomy review at 31 weeks was normal. The local maternity unit has nifedipine, indomethacin and magnesium sulfate available. The team is balancing tocolytic options to allow corticosteroids to take effect, and the registrar has specifically asked about indomethacin given its rapid onset.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 1 cm/30%, cephalic, FH reassuring
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: Which is the strongest reason to avoid indomethacin in this patient?

options.text: Risk of fetal ductus arteriosus constriction and oligohydramnios at this advanced gestation
options.rationale: Indomethacin is generally avoided from around 32 weeks because of dose-dependent fetal ductal constriction and oligohydramnios; nifedipine is preferred at 33+1 per RANZCOG.

options.text: Substantially increased risk of maternal pulmonary oedema compared with other tocolytics
options.rationale: Pulmonary oedema is wrong because that adverse profile belongs to beta-agonists (and prolonged combination tocolysis), not indomethacin; the question targets indomethacin-specific harm at 33+1. Would point to salbutamol concerns instead (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

options.text: Indomethacin causes significant maternal hypotension via systemic vasodilation in pregnancy
options.rationale: Maternal hypotension is wrong because vasodilator hypotension is a calcium channel blocker (nifedipine) effect, not an indomethacin effect; indomethacin acts on prostaglandin synthesis. Would describe nifedipine, not indomethacin (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics).

options.text: Indomethacin is absolutely contraindicated whenever there is any prior preterm birth
options.rationale: Prior preterm birth as absolute contraindication is wrong because prior preterm birth is the indication for treatment, not a contraindication; gestational age and renal/GI status are the relevant flags. Would never be a valid contraindication (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics).

options.text: Indomethacin significantly reduces lung-maturation efficacy of antenatal corticosteroids in pregnancy
options.rationale: Reduced steroid efficacy is wrong because there is no evidence indomethacin attenuates betamethasone lung maturation effect; the late-gestation concern is fetal ductus and oligohydramnios. Would not be a recognised concern (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics).

explanation.summary: Indomethacin (a non-selective COX inhibitor) is a reasonable tocolytic before about 32 weeks where prostaglandin-driven ductal patency is less mature and the latency benefit may outweigh harms. Past 32 weeks the fetal ductus becomes increasingly sensitive to prostaglandin inhibition: constriction can produce right-heart strain and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, and reduced fetal renal blood flow drives oligohydramnios within days. RANZCOG and KEMH guidance therefore use nifedipine (off-label) as the third-trimester tocolytic of choice in Australia. Atosiban (oxytocin-receptor antagonist) is used in some European jurisdictions but is not routinely available in Australia. Tocolysis at any gestation is for buying 48 hours to complete antenatal steroids, in-utero transfer, or both - not for prolonging pregnancy indefinitely.
key_points: Indomethacin upper limit ~32 weeks (RANZCOG, eTG)
Nifedipine is the Australian first-line tocolytic 32+ weeks
Fetal renal and ductal effects are dose- and duration-dependent
explanation.pearls: After 32+0 weeks, indomethacin closes the fetal ductus arteriosus within 24-48 hours of starting and shrinks amniotic fluid through reduced fetal urine output; nifedipine is the preferred tocolytic in the third trimester (RANZCOG; KEMH).

subtopic_detail: Indomethacin tocolysis - gestational limit

stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 at 31+5 presents with threatened preterm labour. She had a complete course of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart at 26+0 for an earlier admission with threatened preterm labour that subsequently settled. Today she is contracting every 3 minutes, has a cervix 3 cm dilated and 70 percent effaced on speculum, and a fetal fibronectin from 4 weeks ago was positive. The CTG is reactive. The team plans to start tocolysis, transfer to a tertiary unit, and give magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm/70% effaced, cephalic, contractions q3min
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: Regarding antenatal corticosteroids, which is most appropriate now?

options.text: Give a single rescue dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now
options.rationale: RANZCOG supports a single rescue dose when the initial course was given over 7 days ago, gestation is under 34+0, and birth is anticipated within the next 7 days.

options.text: Give a full repeat course of betamethasone (two doses 24 h apart)
options.rationale: Full repeat course is wrong because Australian guidance favours a single rescue dose rather than a full repeat; multiple repeat courses are associated with reduced birth weight and head circumference. Would be correct only in some international protocols, not RANZCOG (RANZCOG).

options.text: Do not give further corticosteroids as one course is sufficient lifetime exposure
options.rationale: Withholding steroids entirely is wrong because evidence (ACTORDS, MACS analyses) shows a rescue dose provides meaningful neonatal benefit when the prior course was over 7 days ago and birth is now imminent. Would be correct only if the original course were within the past 7 days (RANZCOG).

options.text: Give dexamethasone 6 mg IM as a single rescue dose
options.rationale: Dexamethasone 6 mg single dose is wrong because Australian dexamethasone dose is 12 mg per dose, and the preferred rescue agent is betamethasone 11.4 mg IM; the dose stated is half-strength. Would never match Australian rescue dosing (RANZCOG).

options.text: Withhold steroids until cervix is more than 5 cm dilated
options.rationale: Withholding until >5 cm is wrong because steroid fetal benefit takes hours to develop; the anti-pattern is treating steroid timing as a labour-progress decision rather than an anticipation-of-birth decision. Would never be correct (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis and perinatal death when given to women at risk of preterm birth within 7 days at gestations between 23+0 and 34+6. The Australian standard is betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart (or dexamethasone 12 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart). Maximum benefit is seen 24 hours after the second dose and persists for about 7 days. A single rescue dose is given when the original course was more than 7 days previously, birth is anticipated within the next 7 days, and gestation is still under 34+0. Repeated full courses are not recommended because of evidence of reduced birth weight and head circumference. Late preterm (34+0 to 36+6) steroids reduce respiratory morbidity but increase neonatal hypoglycaemia; offer with shared decision-making in selected high-risk cases. Document time of every dose contemporaneously to inform later rescue decisions.
key_points: Rescue: single dose, not a repeat full course (RANZCOG)
Eligibility: prior course >7 days ago, gestation <34+0, birth likely within 7 days
Multiple repeats associated with lower birthweight
explanation.pearls: A single rescue dose of antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg IM is given when the original course was more than 7 days ago, birth is anticipated within the next 7 days, and gestation is under 34+0 (ACTORDS; RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: Antenatal corticosteroids - rescue dosing

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 at 29+4 with a singleton pregnancy has progressed in spontaneous preterm labour despite nifedipine tocolysis. She is now 7 cm dilated, contracting every 2 minutes, and birth is expected within the next 2 hours. She has had a complete course of betamethasone 36 hours ago. She has no antepartum haemorrhage, no rupture of membranes, and no features of pre-eclampsia.

The CTG is reactive and maternal observations are normal. Her booking BMI was 23, her booking bloods were unremarkable and she has not received magnesium sulfate at any earlier point in this pregnancy. The unit routinely uses MgSO4 for neonatal neuroprotection in line with RANZCOG and Australian Antenatal Magnesium sulfate Neuroprotection guidance. Birth is now genuinely expected within 1 to 2 hours given her rapid cervical progress.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 7 cm, cephalic, contractions q2min
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, UEC normal (creat 60), CTG reactive

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for fetal neuroprotection?

options.text: Commence intravenous MgSO4 loading and maintenance now, aim for at least 4 hours before birth
options.rationale: RANZCOG and SOMANZ recommend antenatal MgSO4 for neuroprotection at gestations under 30 weeks when birth is anticipated within 24 hours; ideally given at least 4 hours pre-birth.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.text: Do not give magnesium sulfate, as it is only indicated in pre-eclampsia for seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Saying MgSO4 is only for pre-eclampsia is wrong because the fetal neuroprotection role is established independently (ACTOMgSO4, Cochrane meta-analysis NNT ~50 to prevent CP at very preterm gestations). Would be correct only if neuroprotection benefit had not been demonstrated, which is now well established (RANZCOG; SOMANZ).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for neuroprotection of the preterm fetus

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of magnesium sulfate now for fetal neuroprotection
options.rationale: Single IM dose is wrong because the regimen for neuroprotection is IV loading (4 g over 20-30 min) then maintenance infusion (1 g/hr); IM dosing does not achieve the required serum levels. Would never be the correct route (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.text: Withhold magnesium sulfate because a complete course of antenatal corticosteroids has been given
options.rationale: Withholding magnesium because steroids were given is wrong because corticosteroids (lung maturation) and magnesium (neuroprotection) act on different pathways and have independent benefit; the anti-pattern is treating them as interchangeable. Would never be correct (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.text: Defer magnesium sulfate now as the gestation has progressed beyond 28 weeks
options.rationale: Deferring at 29+4 is wrong because Australian guidance offers neuroprotection up to <30 weeks (with some centres extending to <32 weeks); 29+4 sits inside the window. Would be correct only at gestations beyond local cutoffs (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

explanation.summary: Antenatal magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is one of the largest preterm-birth interventions to reach Australian practice. RANZCOG recommends magnesium when birth is anticipated within 24 hours at less than 30 weeks gestation, with at least 4 hours of infusion ideally achieved before delivery. The protocol is a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour maintenance, continued until birth or 24 hours, whichever is sooner. Maternal monitoring is hourly: respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes, urine output, BP. Toxicity (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, ECG changes) is reversed with 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV. Magnesium is not given for tocolysis or general neuroprotection beyond 30 weeks; if maternal or fetal compromise demands urgent delivery, magnesium must not delay birth.
key_points: Window: <30 weeks Australian standard; some centres <32 weeks (RANZCOG)
Loading dose 4 g IV over 20 to 30 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion
Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output, magnesium level if prolonged
explanation.pearls: IV magnesium sulfate (4 g loading over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour maintenance) given within 4 hours of preterm birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy by about 30% (number needed to treat about 60); the protective effect is gestation-dependent (RANZCOG; PReCISE).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for neuroprotection of the preterm fetus

stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 at 36+5 presents 3 hours after a gush of clear fluid. She has no contractions, the fetal heart is reassuring, and she is afebrile. Speculum confirms PROM with a pool of clear fluid; the cervix appears favourable. She is GBS positive on a 36-week swab. Her last birth was a spontaneous vaginal birth at term without complication.

data_table.Examination: Pool of clear AF, cervix favourable, no contractions, FH reassuring
data_table.Investigations: GBS positive at 36 weeks, FBC normal, CRP normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Plan induction of labour now with intrapartum benzylpenicillin for GBS
options.rationale: PPROM at or beyond 36+0 with a GBS-positive mother is managed by induction rather than expectant care to limit chorioamnionitis and neonatal early-onset GBS sepsis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management at home for 96 hours with daily review
options.rationale: Outpatient expectant management is wrong because near-term PPROM with GBS positivity carries clear risk of chorioamnionitis and early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis, and outpatient observation prevents timely intrapartum penicillin. Would be correct only if she were GBS-negative and could tolerate close inpatient observation, not at home with GBS positivity (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Tocolysis with nifedipine and a course of corticosteroids
options.rationale: Tocolysis plus steroids is wrong because steroids are not routinely given beyond 35 weeks and tocolysis only prolongs membrane rupture while increasing infection; the anti-pattern is treating 36+5 like a much earlier preterm scenario. Would never be correct at this gestation (RANZCOG).

options.text: Caesarean section now due to PPROM beyond 36 weeks
options.rationale: Caesarean for PPROM at this gestation is wrong because PPROM is not a caesarean indication; vaginal birth after induction is the preferred route in the absence of other contraindications. Would be correct only with obstetric indications for caesarean (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Expectant management as an inpatient until 39+0 weeks
options.rationale: Inpatient expectancy to 39+0 is wrong because prolonging ruptured membranes with GBS positivity drives chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis; the TERMPROM trial and RANZCOG support expediting birth. Would be correct only with reassuring clinical picture and GBS negativity, perhaps to 37 weeks, not 39 (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Term and late-preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) carries a chorioamnionitis risk that climbs with each additional hour of membrane rupture, particularly past 18 hours. From 36+0 weeks the fetal benefit of waiting for spontaneous labour does not outweigh the rising infection risk, so RANZCOG and most Australian units offer immediate induction with oxytocin or balloon. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for early-onset group B streptococcal disease is given to women who are GBS-positive on swab, have GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, a previous GBS-affected infant, intrapartum fever, prolonged rupture beyond 18 hours, or preterm labour with unknown GBS. Benzylpenicillin is first-line; cefazolin for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; vancomycin or clindamycin (with susceptibility) for anaphylactoid allergy. Document time of rupture, antibiotic doses, and maternal observations contemporaneously.
key_points: PPROM 36+0 or more: plan induction rather than expectant care (RANZCOG)
Use benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV q4h intrapartum for GBS positivity
Steroids not routinely indicated 35+0 or more in Australia
explanation.pearls: At 36+0 or later with PROM the latency benefit of expectant management is lost; immediate induction with intrapartum benzylpenicillin (3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours for GBS-positive women) cuts early-onset neonatal sepsis by about half (RANZCOG; RCH CPG).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: PPROM near term - expectant vs delivery

stem: A 30-year-old G3P0 attends preconception clinic having recently had a third painless mid-trimester loss at 19 weeks. The two prior losses were at 18 and 20 weeks; on each occasion she presented with bulging membranes and minimal contractions, and the cervix was widely dilated on speculum. Anatomy scans had been normal, there was no antepartum bleeding, and she has had no infections or instrumentation between pregnancies. She is keen to conceive again and asks how the next pregnancy will be managed.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no abnormalities
data_table.Investigations: Previous losses at 18, 20, 19 weeks; anatomy scans normal; no infection or instrumentation

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for her next pregnancy?

options.text: History-indicated cervical cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks of pregnancy
options.rationale: Three or more prior second-trimester losses or preterm births consistent with cervical insufficiency is the classic indication for history-indicated (elective) cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks per RANZCOG.

options.text: Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly from 16 weeks without cerclage
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone alone is wrong because progesterone is indicated for asymptomatic short cervix on TVS or singleton prior preterm birth, not as a substitute for cerclage in three prior second-trimester losses. Would be correct only as adjunct, not as sole strategy in this history (RANZCOG).

options.text: Serial cervical length scans from 16 weeks with rescue cerclage if shortening
options.rationale: Serial scans with rescue cerclage is wrong because women with three prior mid-trimester losses meet criteria for history-indicated (elective) cerclage; ultrasound-indicated cerclage is the strategy for women with one prior preterm birth where the cervix may not shorten. Would be correct only with one prior preterm birth, not three losses (RANZCOG; RCOG cerclage guideline).

options.text: Pre-conception transabdominal cervical cerclage placement before next pregnancy attempt
options.rationale: Preconception transabdominal cerclage is wrong because TAC is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or anatomical features (very short cervix, extensive trachelectomy) precluding vaginal placement; not first-line. Would be correct after a failed vaginal cerclage in a previous pregnancy (RANZCOG; RCOG).

options.text: Insertion of cervical pessary at 14 to 16 weeks of pregnancy
options.rationale: Cervical pessary is wrong because the evidence is mixed (PECEP positive, ProTWIN/OPPTIMUM neutral) and pessary is not first-line in Australian practice for this history. Would be correct only in research settings or specific resource-limited contexts (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is a clinical diagnosis based on a pattern of painless mid-trimester loss with progressive dilation and bulging membranes, not on any single ultrasound measurement. RANZCOG recommends history-indicated (elective) cervical cerclage at 12-14 weeks for women with three or more such losses; two losses warrant ultrasound-indicated cerclage triggered by cervical shortening below 25 mm before 24 weeks. Transvaginal McDonald cerclage is the default; transabdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal stitches or absent vaginal cervix. Vaginal progesterone is added when cervix shortens despite cerclage. Rescue (physical-exam-indicated) cerclage may be offered up to about 24 weeks if no contractions, no bleeding, and no clinical or biochemical infection.
key_points: History-indicated cerclage: 3+ prior mid-trimester losses / early PTB
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage: 1+ prior PTB and TVS cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks
Rescue cerclage: cervix dilated with intact membranes <24 weeks
explanation.pearls: Three or more painless second-trimester losses meets the RANZCOG criterion for history-indicated cerclage at 12-14 weeks; an elective McDonald stitch in this scenario approximately doubles term delivery rates compared with surveillance alone.

subtopic_detail: Cervical insufficiency - cerclage

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 at 22+0 with a singleton pregnancy attends for a planned TVS cervical length assessment because of one prior spontaneous preterm birth at 32 weeks. She has no symptoms today: no bleeding, no fluid loss, and no contractions. Anatomy scan was normal at 20+1. TVS today shows a cervix of 18 mm with no funnelling. Fetal fibronectin is not routinely used at her unit at this gestation.

Her previous birth was a spontaneous preterm vaginal birth at 32 weeks with no recognised infection, no antepartum bleeding and no overt cervical instrumentation. She has no other significant medical or obstetric history, takes no medications other than folate and iodine. Her unit follows current RANZCOG guidance recommending vaginal progesterone in women with a singleton pregnancy and short cervix on TVS prior to viability.

data_table.Examination: No contractions, no PV bleed or fluid
data_table.Investigations: TVS cervix 18 mm, no funnelling, FH and AF normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly continued until 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth and perinatal morbidity in women with TVS cervix under 25 mm before 24 weeks, particularly with a prior preterm birth, per RANZCOG.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.text: Intramuscular 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate weekly until 34 weeks gestation
options.rationale: IM 17OHPC is wrong because the PROLONG trial confirmed lack of efficacy and the FDA withdrew approval; vaginal progesterone has the supporting evidence (PREGNANT, OPPTIMUM, individual patient meta-analyses). Would never be correct in current Australian practice (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.text: Rescue cervical cerclage placement now via vaginal approach
options.rationale: Rescue cerclage is wrong because rescue cerclage is for advanced cervical dilation with exposed membranes; this woman has a closed short cervix. Would be correct only with dilated cervix and bulging membranes (RANZCOG).

options.text: Strict bedrest at home until 34 completed weeks gestation
options.rationale: Bedrest is wrong because trials have shown bedrest does not reduce preterm birth and increases VTE and muscle deconditioning; the anti-pattern is offering bedrest as a 'do something' intervention. Would never be correct (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.text: Fetal fibronectin testing now to guide subsequent management
options.rationale: qfFN testing is wrong because fFN has its strongest predictive role in symptomatic women; in an asymptomatic woman with short cervix the management trigger (progesterone) is already in place regardless of fFN. Would be correct only in symptomatic threatened preterm labour (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: TVS cervix under 25 mm before 24 weeks identifies women at high risk of preterm birth. Vaginal progesterone (200 mg nightly) reduces preterm birth and improves neonatal outcomes; cerclage is reserved for those with prior preterm birth whose cervix shortens despite progesterone or who present with dilation.
key_points: TVS cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks: vaginal progesterone (RANZCOG)
Continue progesterone until 36 weeks
Consider US-indicated cerclage if cervix <25 mm and prior PTB
explanation.pearls: TVS is the standard cervical length method; transabdominal underestimates true length.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

subtopic_detail: Preterm birth prediction - TVS cervix

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 at 29+2 attends pregnancy assessment with intermittent abdominal tightening over 8 hours and pelvic pressure. She has no bleeding, no rupture of membranes, and a reassuring CTG. Examination shows no fluid pooling on speculum and the cervix appears long and closed; TVS measures the cervix at 22 mm. Quantitative fetal fibronectin (qfFN) returns at 12 ng/mL. She has no obstetric history of preterm birth and no infections.

She has no past history of preterm birth, no late miscarriageted uterine anomaly. There is no antepartum bleeding, no offensive vaginal discharge and a urine dipstick is unremarkable. The maternity unit uses quantitative fetal fibronectin combined with TVS cervical length as the basis for triage of suspected preterm labour, with a published unit cut-off of 50 ng/mL above which admission and steroids are considered.

data_table.Examination: No pooling, cervix long/closed on speculum
data_table.Investigations: TVS cervix 22 mm, qfFN 12 ng/mL, CTG reactive, MSU pending

lead_in: Which management approach best reflects current evidence?

options.text: Reassure, discharge home with clear safety-netting advice and outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: qfFN below 50 ng/mL combined with a TVS cervix in the lower range still has a very high negative predictive value for birth within 7 days; admission, tocolysis, and steroids are unnecessary.
source_refs: NICE NG25: Preterm labour and birth

options.text: Admit, give a course of antenatal corticosteroids and commence tocolysis
options.rationale: Admit, steroids and tocolysis is wrong because qfFN <50 ng/mL with a closed cervix has very high NPV for birth within 7 days; admission and steroid courses are unwarranted. Would be correct only with positive qfFN or cervical change (RANZCOG).

options.text: Admit and commence prophylactic magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is wrong because neuroprotective MgSO4 requires birth anticipated within 24 hours, which the negative fFN explicitly refutes; the anti-pattern is using MgSO4 'just in case'. Would be correct only with imminent birth at <30 weeks (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.text: Repeat quantitative fetal fibronectin in 24 hours and admit until then
options.rationale: Repeat fFN in 24h is wrong because management does not change for a low qfFN value with no cervical change; the anti-pattern is using repeat testing as a substitute for clinical decision-making. Would be correct only if the clinical picture changed (RANZCOG).

options.text: Insertion of emergency rescue cervical cerclage now in theatre
options.rationale: Emergency rescue cerclage is wrong because cerclage requires advanced cervical dilation with bulging membranes, not a closed cervix with negative fFN. Would be correct only with cervical dilation and exposed membranes (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Threatened preterm labour in pregnancies under 34 weeks is one of the highest-volume obstetric presentations, and most women presenting do not deliver preterm. Risk stratification combines clinical assessment, transvaginal sonographic cervical length, and quantitative fetal fibronectin (qfFN) measured on a cervico-vaginal swab. qfFN must be sampled before any digital exam, before intercourse in the preceding 24 hours, and without lubricant on the speculum, otherwise the result is invalid. A qfFN under 10 ng/mL has the highest negative predictive value for birth within 7 days; a level under 50 ng/mL with a reassuring cervix length (over 25 mm on TVS) allows safe discharge home with clear safety-net advice. Levels over 200 ng/mL or shortening cervix warrant admission, corticosteroids, consideration of tocolysis to facilitate 48 hours of betamethasone, and magnesium sulfate if under 30 weeks and birth anticipated within 24 hours.
key_points: qfFN NPV for PTB within 7 days >95% when <50 ng/mL
Combine with TVS cervical length for best discrimination
Positive qfFN raises risk; manage clinically with steroids, MgSO4, tocolysis as indicated
explanation.pearls: Quantitative fetal fibronectin under 50 ng/mL combined with a TVS cervix over 25 mm has a negative predictive value over 99% for spontaneous birth within 7 days - safely discharges women presenting with threatened preterm labour (RANZCOG; QUIDS).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
NICE NG25: Preterm labour and birth

subtopic_detail: Fetal fibronectin in threatened preterm labour

stem: A 31-year-old G1P0 at 37+1 with well-controlled gestational diabetes on diet alone is reviewed at her routine antenatal clinic. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile, amniotic fluid is normal, CTG is reactive, and self-monitored capillary glucose has stayed within target. She has no hypertension, no IUGR, and no other complication. She has booked into a private hospital and asks whether elective induction at 37 to 38 weeks would be safer than waiting.

data_table.Examination: Cephalic, FH reassuring
data_table.Investigations: EFW 50th centile, AFI normal, BSL diary within target

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with planned delivery around 40+0 to 40+6 weeks
options.rationale: ADIPS and RANZCOG support birth by around 40+6 for diet-controlled GDM with no complications; routine early term induction does not improve outcomes and increases neonatal respiratory morbidity.

options.text: Elective induction of labour at 37+0 weeks gestation now
options.rationale: Elective IOL at 37+0 is wrong because routine 37+0 induction in well-controlled diet-only GDM increases iatrogenic late preterm respiratory morbidity without improving stillbirth or shoulder dystocia outcomes; ADIPS recommends ~40+6. Would be correct only with insulin-treated GDM or comorbidities (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

options.text: Elective lower segment caesarean section at 38+0 weeks of gestation
options.rationale: Elective caesarean at 38+0 is wrong because diet-controlled GDM does not in itself indicate caesarean; macrosomia thresholds and obstetric indications drive mode of birth. Would be correct only with EFW >4500 g, prior caesarean or other indication (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

options.text: Planned induction at 39+0 with cervical ripening regardless of Bishop
options.rationale: Induction at 39+0 regardless of Bishop is wrong because diet-controlled uncomplicated GDM can be managed expectantly to around 40+6 per ADIPS; routine early induction is reserved for insulin-treated or complicated disease. Would be correct only for insulin-treated GDM or other complications (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

options.text: Defer delivery until 41+5 weeks with daily CTG from 39 weeks
options.rationale: Deferring to 41+5 is wrong because even diet-controlled GDM raises stillbirth risk beyond 41 weeks; the upper boundary in ADIPS is around 40+6. Would never be correct in GDM regardless of control (ADIPS).

explanation.summary: ADIPS guidance supports delivery by around 40+6 in uncomplicated diet-controlled GDM. Earlier elective birth is reserved for insulin treatment, macrosomia, poor control, or other complications. Late preterm and early term iatrogenic births carry meaningful neonatal respiratory morbidity.
key_points: Diet-controlled uncomplicated GDM: birth by ~40+6 (ADIPS)
Insulin-treated GDM: consider birth 38+0 to 39+0
Complicated GDM (poor control, IUGR, hypertension): individualise earlier
explanation.pearls: Avoid elective non-medical birth before 39+0 due to neonatal respiratory morbidity.

subtopic_detail: Late preterm / early term decisions

stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 39+3 presents 2 hours after a gush of clear fluid followed by ongoing leakage. Not contracting; speculum confirms a pool of clear amniotic fluid and a closed soft cervix. CTG reactive. GBS swab at 36 weeks was POSITIVE. She has no penicillin allergy. Booking BMI 24, otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about waiting at home for spontaneous labour; she has no childcare for her older child and would prefer to wait if it is safe.

data_table.Examination: Pool of clear AF on speculum, soft closed cervix, no contractions
data_table.Investigations: CTG reactive, GBS POSITIVE at 36 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan in this Australian setting?

options.text: Admit for immediate induction of labour and commence intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin GBS prophylaxis now
options.rationale: Term PROM with GBS-positive status: RANZCOG recommends immediate induction and commencement of intrapartum GBS prophylaxis (rather than expectant management) to reduce risk of early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis. Penicillin is first-line in non-allergic women (RANZCOG term PROM; RANZCOG GBS).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Admit for expectant management up to 24 hours with no antibiotics unless fever develops
options.rationale: Expectancy with no antibiotics unless febrile is wrong because GBS-positive PROM warrants IAP from the time of presentation; waiting for fever signals fully established chorioamnionitis. Would be correct only in GBS-negative term PROM with stable observations (RANZCOG GBS).

options.text: Wait at home for spontaneous labour for up to 5 days with daily review
options.rationale: Home expectancy 5 days is wrong because outpatient management beyond 24h in term PROM raises chorioamnionitis risk and is incompatible with timely IV penicillin in a GBS-positive woman. Would never be correct in GBS-positive PROM (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Mandatory immediate lower-segment caesarean to prevent ascending infection
options.rationale: Mandatory caesarean is wrong because vaginal birth with IAP is the standard approach in GBS-positive PROM; caesarean does not eliminate vertical transmission and adds maternal morbidity. Would be correct only for standard obstetric indications (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Commence oral erythromycin to prolong latency to delivery at term
options.rationale: Erythromycin for latency is wrong because erythromycin latency therapy is for preterm PROM; at term, the goal is induction, not prolongation. Would be correct only at <34 weeks PPROM (RANZCOG; ORACLE I).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Term prelabour rupture of membranes occurs in around 8% of pregnancies and most women labour spontaneously within 24 hours. Shared decision-making at term PROM weighs early induction (lower chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis rates) against limited expectant management (higher rate of spontaneous vaginal birth). The TermPROM and subsequent Cochrane data show no perinatal mortality difference but a clear reduction in maternal and neonatal infection with immediate induction. Australian practice typically caps expectant management at 18-24 hours from rupture. GBS-positive women, women with prior GBS-affected infants, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, intrapartum fever, or unknown-GBS preterm rupture all receive intrapartum benzylpenicillin from the moment induction commences. Minimise digital vaginal examinations until active labour to limit ascending infection.
key_points: Either induction or expectant management for ~24 h is reasonable
GBS positivity tips management toward earlier induction with intrapartum penicillin
Document time of rupture
explanation.pearls: From 37+0 with PROM, RANZCOG accepts up to 24 hours of expectant management as a shared decision; beyond 24 hours infection risk rises sharply, and induction with concurrent intrapartum benzylpenicillin is the default for GBS-positive women.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Term PROM management

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 29+0 is on day 9 of expectant PPROM management. She completed corticosteroids 7 days ago and erythromycin is ongoing. She has been afebrile with normal observations until this evening, when she reports increased uterine tenderness and chills. Observations: T 38.4, HR 118, BP 108/64, RR 18, SpO2 98 on RA. Her uterus is tender on palpation.

CTG shows a baseline fetal heart rate of 175 bpm with reduced variability and no decelerations. WCC has risen to 18.6 x10^9/L, neutrophils 16.2 x10^9/L, CRP 92 mg/L (from 18 mg/L two days ago). She has no offensive vaginal discharge but the speculum view shows turbid amniotic fluid pooling. Maternal lactate is 2.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Uterine tenderness, turbid AF on speculum, no other localising findings
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6, neutrophils 16.2, CRP 92 (up from 18), lactate 2.1, MSU pending, CTG: baseline 175, reduced variability

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and expedite delivery now
options.rationale: Clinical chorioamnionitis in PPROM at 29 weeks is an indication for prompt delivery alongside IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, irrespective of gestation, per RANZCOG.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Continue expectant management with IV antibiotics, aim to reach 32 weeks
options.rationale: Continued expectancy to 32 weeks is wrong because once clinical chorioamnionitis is established, prolonging pregnancy drives maternal sepsis and fetal injury (white matter injury, neonatal sepsis); delivery is the definitive treatment. Would never be correct in active chorioamnionitis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Repeat antenatal steroids and reassess clinical status in 12 hours
options.rationale: Repeat steroids and wait 12h is wrong because steroid benefit takes hours and does not change outcome once intra-amniotic infection is overt; the anti-pattern is delaying delivery to complete steroid courses. Would be correct only in subclinical situations (which is not this case) (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Add tocolysis to allow safe transfer to a tertiary unit
options.rationale: Tocolysis is wrong because tocolysis is contraindicated in chorioamnionitis: it delays definitive treatment and may mask deterioration. Would never be correct in chorioamnionitis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Amniocentesis for Gram stain and glucose before any decision
options.rationale: Amniocentesis first is wrong because the clinical diagnosis (fever, tachycardia, tender uterus, rising CRP, turbid AF) is already established; invasive testing only delays delivery. Would be correct only when subclinical infection needs confirmation and delivery is not yet planned (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is a clinical diagnosis based on maternal fever (38 or above) plus one or more of: maternal tachycardia (above 100), fetal tachycardia (above 160), uterine tenderness, foul or turbid amniotic fluid, or maternal leukocytosis. It complicates 1-4% of all pregnancies and up to 30% of preterm prelabour rupture of membranes managed expectantly. The diagnosis ends expectant management at any gestation because of the rising risks of maternal sepsis, neonatal sepsis, and stillbirth. Management is immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (typically ampicillin or amoxicillin plus gentamicin, with metronidazole or clindamycin added if anaerobic cover needed or post-caesarean) and expedited delivery - vaginal birth where feasible. Fetal tachycardia is often the earliest objective sign and warrants vigilant observation in any woman managed expectantly with PPROM. Post-delivery, antibiotics continue until afebrile for 24-48 hours; neonatal sepsis workup is mandatory.
key_points: Triad-plus signs of chorioamnionitis = deliver (RANZCOG, eTG)
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics started immediately on suspicion
Mode of birth depends on obstetric factors; chorioamnionitis itself is not a caesarean indication
Continue antibiotics intrapartum and postpartum until afebrile
explanation.pearls: Fetal tachycardia (FHR sustained above 160) is often the earliest objective sign of intra-amniotic infection in PPROM, preceding maternal fever by hours; clinical chorioamnionitis ends expectant management at any gestation - broad-spectrum IV antibiotics plus delivery (RANZCOG; ACOG).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Chorioamnionitis in PPROM - delivery trigger

stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 with an MCDA twin pregnancy at 27+4 presents with reduced fetal movements over 24 hours. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated; serial scans have shown concordant growth and no TTTS. Today's ultrasound confirms intrauterine demise of twin A with absent cardiac activity and small pericardial effusion. Twin B has a fetal heart rate of 148 bpm with reactive CTG, normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical artery Doppler, and a peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery of 1.8 multiples of the median. Maternal observations and coagulation profile are normal. She has no contractions and the cervix is 35 mm closed on TVS.

data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, no contractions, no PV bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Twin A demised. Twin B: HR 148, reactive CTG, UA Doppler normal, MCA-PSV 1.8 MoM. Maternal coags normal. Cervix 35 mm.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Urgent transfer to fetal medicine for assessment for fetal anaemia
options.rationale: MCA-PSV above 1.5 MoM in the surviving twin after MC co-twin demise suggests acute fetal anaemia from feto-fetal transfusion across shared anastomoses; intrauterine transfusion may reduce neurological injury (RANZCOG, ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Immediate lower segment caesarean section of the surviving twin at this gestation
options.rationale: Immediate caesarean is wrong because iatrogenic birth at 27+4 inflicts severe prematurity morbidity (RDS, IVH, NEC, ROP) and does not reverse hypoxic-ischaemic injury already sustained from the co-twin demise; intrauterine transfusion offers the chance to rescue the survivor and prolong gestation. Would be correct only after IUT fails or with further fetal deterioration (RANZCOG; ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management with weekly outpatient Doppler surveillance of the surviving twin
options.rationale: Weekly outpatient Dopplers is wrong because MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM is a time-critical red flag for fetal anaemia and requires same-day tertiary intervention, not weekly follow-up. Would never be correct with elevated MCA-PSV (RANZCOG; ISUOG).

options.text: Commence maternal intravenous heparin to prevent disseminated intravascular coagulation in mother
options.rationale: Maternal IV heparin is wrong because clinically significant maternal coagulopathy after single twin demise is rare in the short term, especially with normal baseline coagulation; the anti-pattern is treating maternal DIC reflexively. Would be correct only with documented developing coagulopathy (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.text: Selective fetal reduction of the surviving twin by ultrasound-guided cord occlusion
options.rationale: Cord occlusion of the survivor is wrong because the goal after MC co-twin demise is to rescue the surviving healthy twin; terminating it would be unethical and inverts the management logic. Would never be correct in this scenario (RANZCOG; ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

explanation.summary: After single twin demise in a monochorionic pregnancy, acute feto-fetal transfusion via placental anastomoses can cause severe anaemia in the survivor. MCA-PSV above 1.5 MoM signals fetal anaemia and warrants urgent fetal medicine assessment for in-utero transfusion. Iatrogenic preterm birth at 27 weeks rarely improves outcome and adds severe prematurity morbidity.
key_points: Surviving MC twin: ~15% risk of death, ~25% risk of neurological injury
MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM = significant risk of fetal anaemia (ISUOG)
Urgent neuroimaging (MRI) 4 to 6 weeks later if survival
Birth timing individualised; not routinely immediate
explanation.pearls: MCA-PSV is the same screening tool used in red cell alloimmunisation; same threshold.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Co-twin demise in monochorionic pregnancy

stem: A 29-year-old G2P2 attends her 6-week postnatal review. She delivered vaginally and is exclusively breastfeeding on demand, day and night, no formula or solids. She has had no return of menstruation since delivery, and a urine beta-hCG is negative today. She and her partner do not wish to conceive again for at least 2 years. She has heard friends say 'breastfeeding stops periods so I don't need contraception' and asks whether that is true. She has no UKMEC category 3-4 contraindications.

data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 24, BP 118/74 mmHg. Uterus involuted. Breasts soft, no engorgement, infant feeding well.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. No further investigations performed today.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice and recommendation?

options.text: Counsel that LAM provides about 98% efficacy only up to 6 months post partum and only while she is amenorrhoeic and exclusively/near-exclusively breastfeeding; offer a parallel reliable method (LARC or POP) to avoid the gap when LAM expires
options.rationale: LAM is reliable only while ALL three criteria are met (exclusive/near-exclusive breastfeeding, infant under 6 months, amenorrhoea). At 6 weeks she meets criteria, but planning for the transition is part of good counselling: parallel LARC or progestogen-only methods bridge the gap (FSRH; Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Reassure that breastfeeding alone provides reliable contraception for up to 12 months post partum
options.rationale: LAM reliable only up to 6 months, not 12; failure rate rises sharply once any criterion lapses. 12 months reliance is essentially never correct (FSRH).

options.text: Reassure that any breastfeeding plus amenorrhoea provides reliable contraception regardless of feeding pattern or solids
options.rationale: Partial or mixed feeding (with formula or solids) breaks LAM criteria; reliability drops markedly. Reassurance with mixed feeding is essentially never correct (Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Counsel that LAM is reliable until 6 months only if one normal menstrual period has occurred to confirm cycles have restarted
options.rationale: Return of menstruation INVALIDATES LAM; criterion is amenorrhoea since delivery, not presence of menses. LAM-with-menses is essentially never correct (Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Recommend commencing the combined oral contraceptive pill today as the most reliable bridging method
options.rationale: CHC is UKMEC 4 in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding (UKMEC 2 from 6 weeks to 6 months) due to VTE and supply concerns. COCP is correct >6 months postpartum or not breastfeeding (FSRH UKMEC).

explanation.summary: LAM provides about 98% contraceptive efficacy when all three criteria are met: exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding day and night, infant under 6 months, and amenorrhoea since delivery. Loss of any single criterion mandates an additional method.
key_points: Three LAM criteria: exclusive BF, <6 months, amenorrhoea
Progestogen-only pill can start from day 21 postpartum (any time if BF)
Combined hormonal contraception avoided until 6 weeks postpartum if BF (and 3 weeks if not BF, longer if VTE risk)
Postnatal IUD/IUS: usually inserted 4 to 6 weeks postpartum (immediate post-placental insertion also an option)
Etonogestrel implant: any time postpartum including day 0
explanation.pearls: If a woman wants LAM, document the three criteria explicitly and plan the bridging method for when any one fails first (usually the 6-month limit or weaning).

sources.label: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - lactational amenorrhoea criteria

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman has just had an emergency caesarean section at 38+5 weeks for fetal distress. Her pre-pregnancy BMI was 36 and her booking weight was 102 kg; she now weighs 108 kg on day 1 postpartum. She has a past history of one provoked deep vein thrombosis 8 years ago after a long-haul flight, was treated with warfarin for 6 months at that time, and has been off anticoagulation since.

Her current pregnancy was uncomplicated apart from gestational diabetes managed with diet. She is a non-smoker, has no thrombophilia testing on record, no family history of unprovoked VTE, and her observations are stable. The estimated blood loss at caesarean was 600 mL with no further bleeding postoperatively. Her platelet count is 198 and her creatinine is 62 micromol/L. She is mobilising with help and is keen to breastfeed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Wound clean and dry. Calves soft, non-tender, symmetrical. Mobilising slowly with assistance.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L, plt 198, creatinine 62 micromol/L, EBL at CS 600 mL. No active bleeding.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate postpartum thromboprophylaxis regimen?

options.text: Mechanical prophylaxis (TEDS plus early mobilisation) alone with no pharmacological prophylaxis
options.rationale: CS + BMI >30 + prior provoked VTE together exceed threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis on RANZCOG scoring; mechanical alone insufficient. Mechanical alone is correct in lower-risk patients (RANZCOG VTE).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

options.text: Enoxaparin 20 mg subcutaneously daily for 10 days as postpartum thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: 20 mg daily is standard for <50 kg or low-risk; this woman is 108 kg and high risk, requires weight-based dosing. 20 mg daily is correct in low-weight or low-risk women (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

options.text: Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for 10 days only as postpartum prophylaxis
options.rationale: Weight-based dose (80 mg for 91-130 kg) appropriate, but duration of only 10 days inadequate given prior VTE history. 10-day duration is correct in low-risk women without prior VTE (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

options.text: Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for 6 weeks as postpartum thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: She has prior provoked VTE plus emergency caesarean plus BMI greater than 30 (a high-risk profile on RANZCOG/RCOG scoring). The recommended regimen is weight-banded LMWH (80 mg daily for 91 to 130 kg) for 6 weeks postpartum (RANZCOG; KEMH; RCOG GTG 37a).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum
RCOG GTG 37a Reducing the risk of VTE

options.text: Warfarin 5 mg daily for 6 weeks targeting INR 2.0 to 3.0 with bridging LMWH
options.rationale: Warfarin compatible with breastfeeding but LMWH preferred postpartum because no INR monitoring and avoids early postpartum warfarin instability. Warfarin is correct in long-term anticoagulation with stable INR (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk is stratified by RANZCOG/RCOG point scoring. Women with prior VTE almost always receive 6 weeks of LMWH at a weight-banded prophylactic dose; women with 4 or more transient risk factors receive 10 days; emergency caesarean alone with no other risk factors usually does not require pharmacological prophylaxis.
key_points: Weight-banded enoxaparin (typical bands): <50 kg 20 mg, 50-90 kg 40 mg, 91-130 kg 60-80 mg, 131-170 kg 80 mg twice daily considered
Duration: 10 days for transient risk; 6 weeks for prior VTE, persistent risk factors, high thrombophilia, or sustained admission
LMWH preferred over warfarin and DOACs postpartum (DOACs not used in breastfeeding women)
OHSS adds an independent high VTE risk that may warrant 6 weeks even without delivery risk factors
Hold LMWH if active bleeding or platelets <75 x10^9/L
explanation.pearls: On finals: any prior VTE = 6 weeks postpartum LMWH almost always. The decision is duration first, then dose by weight band.

sources.label: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum
RCOG GTG 37a Reducing the risk of VTE

subtopic_detail: Postpartum VTE thromboprophylaxis - RANZCOG risk-stratified dosing

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P2 woman attends a postnatal review at 5 weeks following an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal birth at 39+4 weeks gestation. She is partially breastfeeding (approximately 60% breast milk, 40% formula because she returns to her finance role in 4 weeks and the workplace lacks lactation facilities) and has had no return of menses since delivery. Her booking BMI was 31, she is a lifelong non-smoker, her blood pressure today is 132/82 mmHg, and her booking and 36-week antenatal BP readings were both normotensive.

She has no personal or family history of VTE or thrombophilia, no migraine with or without aura, no current or prior breast cancer, and no autoimmune disease. She and her partner want effective contraception starting as soon as possible today and. She is comfortable returning at any time for a procedure if that is the most appropriate option after counselling.

data_table.Examination: Well, BMI 30, BP 132/82 mmHg. Uterus involuted. Breasts: lactating, no inflammation.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate contraceptive option to initiate today?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyloestradiol 30 microg/levonorgestrel 150 microg, starting today
options.rationale: CHC avoided in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding (WHO MEC 3-4) due to theoretical effects on supply. COCP is correct >6 weeks postpartum if not breastfeeding (WHO MEC).
source_refs: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

options.text: Defer all contraception until 6 weeks postpartum and rely on LAM in the interim
options.rationale: Does not meet LAM criteria because only partially breastfeeding; deferral risks ovulation. LAM is correct only with exclusive breastfeeding + amenorrhoea + <6 months postpartum (FSRH).

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device at 5 weeks postpartum after speculum examination
options.rationale: Cu-IUD insertion within 48 hours of delivery or after 4 weeks postpartum, so feasible at 5 weeks; however requires procedure scheduling. Cu-IUD is correct option when willing to wait for insertion appointment (WHO MEC).

options.text: Insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system today at 5 weeks postpartum
options.rationale: LNG-IUS insertion follows similar timing; requires procedure scheduling and speculum work. LNG-IUS is correct option when willing to wait for insertion (WHO MEC).

options.text: Etonogestrel 68 mg subdermal implant inserted today during the consultation
options.rationale: The etonogestrel implant is WHO MEC category 1 at any time postpartum in breastfeeding women, can be inserted during the postnatal consultation, has the highest typical-use efficacy of any reversible method, and avoids the VTE and lactation concerns of combined hormonal contraception in the early postpartum window (WHO MEC; FSRH; Family Planning Australia).
source_refs: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception timing: progestogen-only methods (POP, implant) can be started any time postpartum including day 0. Cu-IUD and LNG-IUS are inserted within 48 hours of delivery or after 4 weeks. Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided until 6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding (and until 3 weeks if not breastfeeding, longer if VTE risk factors).
key_points: Implant: any time, WHO MEC 1 in BF women
POP: from day 21 (any time in BF women)
Cu-IUD / LNG-IUS: <48 h or >=4 weeks postpartum
COCP: avoid <3 weeks postpartum (VTE), <6 weeks if BF
LAM only reliable with exclusive BF + <6 months + amenorrhoea
explanation.pearls: Best practice is to discuss postnatal contraception antenatally and offer the implant at hospital discharge or within the first 5 days to capture women before contact is lost.

sources.label: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

subtopic_detail: Postnatal contraception - timing of method initiation in a partially breastfeeding woman

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P1 woman has just delivered a 4.1 kg infant by spontaneous vaginal birth with a 30-minute active second stage. The delivery was attended by a midwife with an obstetric registrar called for shoulder dystocia which was resolved with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure within 90 seconds. There was a head-to-body interval of 80 seconds. After delivery of the placenta, careful inspection of the perineum demonstrates a tear extending through the perineal skin, perineal muscles, and partial-thickness laceration of the external anal sphincter involving approximately 40% of its thickness; the internal anal sphincter and rectal mucosa appear intact on careful per rectum examination.

The registrar grades the injury as 3a. Maternal observations are stable, the infant is in good condition with Apgars 9 and 9, and the estimated blood loss is 350 mL with no ongoing bleeding. The hospital has a theatre available now and a senior obstetrician on site.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Grade 3a tear: <50% external anal sphincter thickness, IAS and rectal mucosa intact. EBL 350 mL.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L. Group and screen on file.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management approach for repair and after-care?

options.text: Repair on the labour ward bed under local anaesthesia using 2-0 polyglactin (Vicryl) for all layers, no postoperative antibiotics, encourage normal diet, no physiotherapy referral
options.rationale: On-ward local-anaesthetic repair with no antibiotics or follow-up is wrong because OASI requires theatre repair under regional/GA with adequate lighting and exposure; broad-spectrum antibiotics, laxatives and structured follow-up (physiotherapy, perineal clinic) are mandatory. Would never be correct (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair on the ward without anaesthesia, give one course of oral metronidazole, no laxative and no perineal clinic follow-up
options.rationale: Ward repair without anaesthesia is wrong because OASI repair requires theatre-level anaesthesia for adequate visualisation and sphincter alignment; on-ward repair without anaesthesia compromises outcome. Would never be correct (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics intraoperatively then oral course, lactulose for 10 days, pelvic floor physiotherapy referral, perineal clinic follow-up
