options.rationale: OASI requires repair in theatre with adequate anaesthesia, regional or GA, broad-spectrum antibiotic cover, stool softeners (typically lactulose) for at least 10 days, structured pelvic floor physiotherapy referral, and follow-up in a specialist perineal clinic at 6 to 12 weeks with assessment for symptoms of incontinence (RCOG GTG 29; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.text: Repair in theatre, oral cephalexin only, no stool softener (constipation will protect the repair), no physiotherapy referral, GP review at 6 weeks
options.rationale: Theatre repair but no laxative is wrong because constipation increases dehiscence and pain; lactulose for at least 10 days is standard. Narrow staphylococcal cover alone is also inadequate - broad-spectrum cover is needed. Physiotherapy and perineal clinic are part of structured follow-up. Would never be correct (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.text: Defer repair for 24 hours to allow tissue oedema to settle, then repair in theatre, no antibiotics, lactulose for 3 days, physiotherapy referral
options.rationale: Defer repair 24h is wrong because OASI should be repaired as soon as feasible by a trained operator; delay increases infection risk. Antibiotic prophylaxis is required and laxative for at least 10 days. Would never be correct (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: OASI (grade 3a, 3b, 3c, 4) repair: theatre with regional or general anaesthesia, end-to-end or overlap repair of the external anal sphincter with 2-0 or 3-0 PDS or polyglactin, separate IAS repair if torn, broad-spectrum IV then oral antibiotics, stool softeners for at least 10 days, and structured pelvic floor physiotherapy plus perineal clinic follow-up at 6 to 12 weeks. Counsel about mode of next delivery once symptomatic status is known.
key_points: Grades: 3a <50% EAS, 3b >50% EAS, 3c IAS torn, 4 anal mucosa torn
Repair in theatre with adequate lighting and assistance
Suture: 2-0 or 3-0 PDS for sphincters, 2-0 polyglactin for vaginal mucosa/perineal muscles
Antibiotics: cefuroxime + metronidazole IV then oral course (Therapeutic Guidelines analogous regimen)
Lactulose 10 days; physiotherapy referral; perineal clinic 6-12 weeks
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for OASI: primiparity, instrumental delivery (forceps > vacuum), prolonged second stage, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, persistent OP. Mediolateral episiotomy reduces OASI risk in instrumental delivery.

sources.label: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

subtopic_detail: Obstetric anal sphincter injury repair - principles of management

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 woman attends her general practitioner 5 months after the delivery of her second child. The pregnancy itself was uncomplicated until delivery, when she had a massive postpartum haemorrhage estimated at 3500 mL secondary to uterine atony plus a small lower segment extension during an emergency caesarean section for fetal distress; she required 6 units of packed red cells, 2 units of fresh frozen plasma, 1 unit of cryoprecipitate, intraoperative tranexamic acid, intramyometrial carboprost, a Bakri balloon, and spent 36 hours in the high-dependency unit before stabilising.

Since then she has been unable to establish breastfeeding despite repeated attempts in the first week with a lactation consultant, has had no return of menses at all over the last 5 months, has lost approximately 4 kg of muscle mass with reduced exercise tolerance, sleeps 11 hours daily and is still fatigued during the day, feels persistently cold even in warm rooms, has noticed loss of axillary and pubic hair, has had two episodes of presyncope on standing in the last month, and has reduced libido. On examination today she is thin, pale, has dry skin, fine sparse hair, and a postural blood pressure drop from 108/68 mmHg supine to 86/52 mmHg standing. Her thyroid gland is non-tender and non-enlarged on palpation, and there is no goitre.

data_table.Vital signs: BP supine 108/68 mmHg, standing 86/52 mmHg. HR 58 bpm, T 36.2 degC.
data_table.Examination: Thin, pale, dry skin, fine sparse axillary and pubic hair. Thyroid non-palpable. No goitre.
data_table.Investigations: Pending - GP is determining the most appropriate first-line endocrine workup.

lead_in: Which combination of investigations is most appropriate as the first-line workup to establish her most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Morning 0800 cortisol, TSH plus free T4, LH, FSH, oestradiol, prolactin, IGF-1, and MRI pituitary
options.rationale: Sheehan syndrome causes panhypopituitarism after pituitary ischaemic necrosis following major PPH. The investigation strategy is to assess each pituitary axis: cortisol (ACTH axis), free T4 with TSH (TSH axis - TSH may be inappropriately normal or low), LH/FSH and oestradiol (gonadotrophin axis), prolactin (lactotroph axis - typically low or undetectable), IGF-1 (GH axis), with MRI demonstrating an empty or partially empty sella (BMJ Best Practice; Endocrine Society).

options.text: TSH and free T4 only, treating empirically with levothyroxine if either is low
options.rationale: TSH/T4 only with empirical thyroxine is wrong because TSH/T4 alone miss the potentially fatal cortisol deficiency; giving thyroxine before replacing glucocorticoid can precipitate adrenal crisis. Would be correct only after cortisol replacement is confirmed adequate (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Random cortisol and random TSH on the day of consultation only as initial work-up
options.rationale: Random cortisol and TSH is wrong because random cortisol is unreliable due to diurnal variation; 0800 morning cortisol plus the full pituitary axis screen plus imaging is required. Would never be correct as a complete workup (Endocrine Society).

options.text: 24-hour urinary free cortisol and an overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the first step
options.rationale: 24h urinary cortisol and dexamethasone suppression is wrong because these tests screen for Cushing syndrome (excess cortisol), not deficiency; the workup is in the wrong direction entirely. Would be correct only when suspecting Cushing (Endocrine Society).

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound and anti-Mullerian hormone level to assess her ovarian reserve as first step
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound and AMH is wrong because amenorrhoea in Sheehan is central (low LH/FSH and oestradiol), not primary ovarian failure; AMH would not establish the pituitary diagnosis. Would be correct only for ovarian reserve assessment, not pituitary workup (BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum haemorrhage. Failure to lactate (loss of prolactin) is often the earliest feature; secondary amenorrhoea, cold intolerance, fatigue, hyponatraemia and postural hypotension follow. Workup screens each pituitary axis and includes MRI. Treat with glucocorticoid replacement first (hydrocortisone), then thyroxine, then sex steroid replacement; GH replacement is considered in symptomatic adults.
key_points: Failure to lactate is the most specific early clue
Treat cortisol before thyroxine to avoid adrenal crisis
Hyponatraemia is common (cortisol deficiency, hypothyroidism)
MRI may show empty or partially empty sella
Prolactin is typically low or undetectable (versus high in pituitary adenoma)
explanation.pearls: Any postpartum woman with prior major PPH who fails to lactate, fails to menstruate, and presents with non-specific fatigue, hypotension or cold intolerance should have a pituitary workup until proven otherwise. Hydrocortisone before levothyroxine - always.

subtopic_detail: Sheehan syndrome - investigation strategy after severe postpartum haemorrhage

stem: A 28-year-old G2P2 on day 2 post-vaginal-birth (PPH 1100 mL controlled with uterotonics and tranexamic acid; no transfusion) feels tired but not breathless, ambulates without symptoms, breastfeeds well. Booking Hb 124 g/L. Today: Hb 78 g/L, MCV 76, ferritin 12 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 9%, platelets 240, normal renal function. No active bleeding, no chest pain. She wishes to be discharged tomorrow to care for her toddler. Local protocol follows the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Module 5 (Obstetrics).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/72 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae. Lungs clear. Cardiac exam unremarkable. Mobilising independently. No active bleeding.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 12 micrograms/L, transferrin sat 9%, plts 240. EBL 1100 mL at delivery.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management of her postpartum iron deficiency anaemia?

options.text: Single dose IV ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg before discharge with review at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Hb 70-80 g/L in a stable postpartum woman with no ongoing bleeding does not mandate transfusion (PBM Module 5: transfusion thresholds Hb <70 g/L in stable patients). IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) corrects iron stores rapidly, supports breastfeeding and avoids transfusion risks (NBA PBM5; AMH).
source_refs: National Blood Authority PBM Module 5 - Obstetrics and Maternity

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells before discharge
options.rationale: Transfuse 2 units is wrong because she is asymptomatic at rest with stable haemodynamics and no ongoing bleeding; the NBA PBM5 restrictive threshold is Hb <70 g/L in stable patients. Would be correct only with symptomatic anaemia, ongoing bleeding or Hb <70 (NBA PBM5).
source_refs: National Blood Authority PBM Module 5 - Obstetrics and Maternity

options.text: Oral ferrous sulphate 325 mg three times daily for 3 months
options.rationale: Oral ferrous sulphate TDS for 3 months is wrong because at this Hb level oral iron corrects slowly (months) and is poorly tolerated (GI side effects); IV iron is preferred for postpartum severe deficiency. Would be correct only for mild postpartum anaemia with good tolerance (NBA PBM5).
source_refs: National Blood Authority PBM Module 5 - Obstetrics and Maternity

options.text: Oral ferrous fumarate 200 mg three times daily with no scheduled follow-up
options.rationale: Oral ferrous fumarate TDS no follow-up is wrong because oral iron alone for severe deficiency is suboptimal and follow-up is required to confirm correction. Would never be correct (NBA PBM5).
source_refs: National Blood Authority PBM Module 5 - Obstetrics and Maternity

options.text: Erythropoietin-stimulating agent subcutaneously now plus oral iron for 3 months
options.rationale: ESA plus oral iron is wrong because ESAs are not routinely indicated in postpartum iron deficiency without renal disease; IV iron alone suffices. Would be correct only with renal-disease-associated anaemia not responding to iron (NBA PBM5; AMH).
source_refs: National Blood Authority PBM Module 5 - Obstetrics and Maternity

explanation.summary: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines recommend: transfuse if Hb less than 70 g/L or symptomatic; IV iron if Hb 70 to 90 g/L with iron deficiency or oral iron intolerance or need for rapid response; oral iron for Hb at or above 90 g/L without urgency. Ferritin less than 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency in the postpartum population.
key_points: Transfusion threshold postpartum: Hb <70 g/L or symptomatic compromise
IV iron indications: Hb 70-90 g/L with ID; oral intolerance; need for rapid response; ongoing absorption issues
Ferritin <30 micrograms/L = iron deficiency (consider <100 if inflammation)
Ferric carboxymaltose: 1000 mg single dose, infused over 15 minutes
Oral iron: alternate-day dosing improves absorption; review Hb at 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: In the postpartum setting, IV iron is increasingly the workhorse for moderate anaemia because it is faster, more reliable and avoids the constipation that compounds perineal pain and post-caesarean recovery.

sources.label: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

subtopic_detail: Postpartum iron deficiency anaemia - transfusion vs IV iron vs oral iron thresholds

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P1 woman is reviewed 7 hours after a forceps-assisted vaginal birth at 40+1 with a mediolateral episiotomy. She had an epidural sited in labour and her last top-up was 5 hours ago; sensation in her legs has now fully returned. The estimated blood loss was 450 mL and her perineal tear is a grade 2 episiotomy repair with no extension into the sphincter complex.

She last passed urine spontaneously 9 hours before the start of pushing, which was 11 hours ago in total. She has been encouraged to attempt voiding three times over the last 4 hours but each attempt has produced less than 50 mL despite a sensation of fullness. Bladder ultrasound at the bedside shows 720 mL of urine in the bladder. She has had no haematuria, no flank painin, and her observations are stable. She is keen to mobilise to the shower and start skin-to-skin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/74 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic fullness, non-tender. Episiotomy repair intact. Sensation in legs fully returned. Pad: minimal lochia.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside bladder USS: 720 mL. Urinalysis pending.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Encourage further oral fluids now and then re-scan her bladder again in 4 hours
options.rationale: Encourage more fluids and re-scan in 4 hours is wrong because 720 mL after 11 hours of failed voiding meets retention criteria requiring drainage; continued conservative measures risk detrusor overdistension and long-term voiding dysfunction. Would be correct only with smaller residual volume and short time since last void (KEMH; RCOG).

options.text: Insert in-out catheter, drain bladder once, then discharge to postnatal ward without further plan
options.rationale: Single in-out catheter then discharge is wrong because single drainage without a structured plan risks recurrent retention; indwelling catheter for 24-48h plus structured TWOC is needed when residual >500-700 mL. Would be correct only with residual <500 mL and good spontaneous voiding (KEMH).

options.text: Refer her urgently to urology for cystoscopy under general anaesthesia today in theatre setting
options.rationale: Urgent urology cystoscopy is wrong because postpartum urinary retention is typically transient and managed by obstetric teams with catheterisation and TWOC; urology referral is not first-line. Would be correct only with persistent retention after multiple failed TWOCs or suspected structural pathology (RCOG).

options.text: Administer IV furosemide 20 mg and then re-scan her bladder again in 1 hour
options.rationale: IV furosemide is wrong because furosemide treats fluid overload not retention; it would worsen the problem by increasing bladder volume further. Would never be correct in retention (KEMH).

options.text: Insert indwelling urinary catheter on free drainage for 24-48 hours, then trial of void with bladder scans
options.rationale: Bladder volume greater than 500 to 700 mL with failed voiding after vaginal birth defines covert/overt postpartum urinary retention. Management is indwelling catheterisation for 24 to 48 hours to allow detrusor recovery, followed by a structured trial of void with pre- and post-void scans; persistent residual volumes greater than 150 mL prompt repeat catheterisation and further investigation (KEMH; RCOG; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Postpartum urinary retention is defined as failure to void within 6 hours of vaginal birth or post-void residual greater than 150 mL after attempted void. Risk factors include epidural, prolonged second stage, instrumental delivery, OASI, episiotomy, and large infant. Management is indwelling catheter for 24 to 48 hours then trial of void with bladder scans.
key_points: Catheterise within 6 hours of vaginal birth if no spontaneous void
Bladder volume >500-700 mL: indwelling catheter 24-48 h preferred over single in-out
TWOC after 24-48 h with pre- and post-void scans
PVR >150 mL: re-catheterise and reassess
Risk factors: epidural, instrumental, prolonged labour, OASI, big baby
explanation.pearls: Detrusor overdistension can cause permanent voiding dysfunction. Document time and volume of every void in the first 24 hours postpartum, and act on the first failed attempt rather than waiting.

subtopic_detail: Postpartum urinary retention - identification and management

stem:
A 31-year-old G1P1 woman was diagnosed with preeclampsia at 36 weeks gestation and delivered at 37+0 by induction of labour with a spontaneous vaginal birth, complicated only by a small first-degree perineal tear that was sutured at the time. Antenatally she received labetalol 200 mg three times daily plus methyldopa 250 mg three times daily for blood pressure control, achieving target BP below 140/90 mmHg from 34 weeks.

She is now day 6 postpartum and is breastfeeding her infant exclusively with good supply. Her blood pressure today on home monitoring has been 158/102 mmHg, 154/96 mmHg and 156/100 mmHg recorded over the last 24 hours despite continuing both of her antenatal antihypertensives at full antenatal dose. She has no headache, no visual disturbance, and no peripheral oedema beyond mild ankle swelling.

Her bloods this morning show a normal full blood count without thrombocytopaenia, normal renal function with creatinine 70 micromol/L, AST and ALT within normal limits, and a urine protein-creatinine ratio elevated at 60 mg/mmol (down from a peak of 180 mg/mmol antenatally).

data_table.Vital signs: BP today average 156/99 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: No focal neurology. No epigastric tenderness. Mild ankle oedema. Breasts soft.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, plts 220, creatinine 70 micromol/L, ALT 22 U/L, urine PCR 60 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate adjustment to her antihypertensive regimen?

options.text: Increase methyldopa to 500 mg three times daily and continue current labetalol dose
options.rationale: Increase methyldopa is wrong because methyldopa is associated with postpartum depression and sedation and is typically weaned in the puerperium rather than uptitrated; SOMANZ prefers other agents postpartum. Would never be correct as escalation strategy (SOMANZ).

options.text: Wean and stop methyldopa, increase labetalol, add nifedipine controlled-release 30 mg daily if BP elevated
options.rationale: SOMANZ recommends weaning methyldopa postpartum (depression risk, no clear postpartum benefit), continuing or uptitrating labetalol and adding a calcium channel blocker such as nifedipine controlled-release as a second agent; all three are compatible with breastfeeding (SOMANZ; AMH).

options.text: Switch labetalol to atenolol 50 mg daily and continue current methyldopa dose
options.rationale: Atenolol is wrong because atenolol concentrates in breast milk and can cause neonatal bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycaemia; it is avoided in breastfeeding. Would be correct only outside breastfeeding (AMH).

options.text: Commence oral enalapril 5 mg daily and stop labetalol now in this patient
options.rationale: Enalapril replacing labetalol immediately is wrong because while enalapril is breastfeeding-compatible, SOMANZ prefers stepwise change with labetalol or nifedipine as first-line postpartum and methyldopa weaning pending. Would be correct only after stepwise titration of preferred agents (SOMANZ).

options.text: Stop all antihypertensives now because she is more than 5 days postpartum currently
options.rationale: Stop all antihypertensives at >5 days postpartum is wrong because BP characteristically peaks at days 3-6 postpartum and pre-eclampsia can present or worsen up to 6 weeks postpartum; treatment continues while BP remains >=150/100. Would be correct only with sustained BP normalisation (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: Postpartum hypertension management after preeclampsia: continue and adjust antihypertensives, monitor BP for at least 6 weeks postpartum, wean methyldopa (depression risk), and use labetalol, nifedipine, enalapril or captopril as preferred agents in breastfeeding. Preeclampsia can present de novo up to 6 weeks postpartum.
key_points: Wean methyldopa postpartum (depression risk)
Labetalol, nifedipine CR, enalapril, captopril all compatible with BF
Avoid atenolol in BF (neonatal beta-blockade)
Treat BP >=150/100 mmHg sustained; aim BP <140/90 mmHg postpartum
Monitor BP and proteinuria up to 6 weeks; postpartum review at 6 weeks plus 6 to 12 months for CVD risk
explanation.pearls: Postnatal new-onset headache plus elevated BP within 6 weeks of delivery is preeclampsia or eclampsia until proven otherwise. Always screen mood in postpartum hypertensive women - methyldopa is a hidden contributor.

subtopic_detail: Postpartum hypertension - antihypertensive choice in a breastfeeding woman with prior preeclampsia

stem:
A 36-year-old G1P1 woman attends her general practitioner at 10 days postpartum because, despite frequent on-demand feeding and continuous skin-to-skin contact since birth, she has produced very little breast milk and her infant has lost 11% of birth weight on weighed feeds today. The delivery was at 38+5 by elective lower segment caesarean section for breech presentation; the third stage was complicated by a placenta with a retained cotyledon noted on inspection that was manually removed in theatre under spinal anaesthesia, with no postpartum haemorrhage (estimated blood loss 380 mL total).

She had no antenatal complications, normal booking and 36-week bloods including a normal FBC and ferritin, and was discharged on day 4 in stable condition. She noticed no antenatal breast enlargement during pregnancy, which was unusual compared with her friends. On examination her breasts are small, tubular, widely spaced and noticeably asymmetric (left larger than right), with minimal glandular fullness on palpation and no breast engorgement; there are no signs of inflammation, infection, fluctuance, or mastitis.

Her uterus is involuted appropriately to size, her perineum is healed, and her observations are all stable. She is not on any medications, has no past breast surgery, no nipple piercings, and has been seen by an IBCLC lactation consultant twice with optimal latch, optimal positioning, and a normal infant suck assessment confirmed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Breasts small, asymmetric, widely spaced, minimal glandular tissue, no inflammation. Uterus involuted. Infant: well, tone good, suck normal on assessment.
data_table.Investigations: Pending - GP planning investigations.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to clarify the cause of failure to establish lactation?

options.text: Infant tongue-tie clinical assessment by paediatric ENT for surgical release if confirmed
options.rationale: Infant tongue-tie assessment is wrong because optimal latch and positioning and a normal infant suck have already been confirmed by lactation consultant assessment; a primary infant-side cause is unlikely. Would be correct only with suspected suck problems (ABA).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.text: Maternal full blood count and ferritin level only as initial work-up
options.rationale: Maternal FBC and ferritin only is wrong because anaemia may contribute to fatigue but rarely causes complete failure of lactogenesis II; targeted prolactin and pituitary axis testing is needed. Would be correct only as adjunct to the targeted workup (ABA).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound only as the initial single investigation for her presentation today
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound only is wrong because while pelvic USS helps exclude retained products, it is most useful in combination with prolactin and wider pituitary workup; alone it misses pituitary, glandular and endocrine causes. Would be correct only as part of comprehensive workup (ABA).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.text: Serum prolactin and pituitary axis screen (cortisol, TSH and free T4, LH and FSH)
options.rationale: Failure to establish lactation despite optimal latch and positioning prompts investigation for hypoprolactinaemia (Sheehan), retained products causing persistent progesterone elevation, primary insufficient glandular tissue (suggested here by tubular, widely spaced, asymmetric breasts) and significant stress. Serum prolactin is the targeted first investigation, with concurrent screening of the pituitary axis to exclude Sheehan especially in any woman with peripartum bleeding or retained tissue (ABA; LactMed; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.text: Empirical trial of oral domperidone 10 mg three times daily without further investigation today
options.rationale: Empirical domperidone without investigation is wrong because galactagogues should follow characterisation of the underlying cause; empirical treatment risks missing Sheehan and retained products which need specific management. Would be correct only after underlying cause is established and primary low supply is confirmed (ABA; AMH).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

explanation.summary: Failure to establish lactation has several distinct causes: delayed lactogenesis II (most common, transient), retained placental fragments (progesterone continues to inhibit prolactin), Sheehan syndrome (low prolactin after major PPH), insufficient glandular tissue (tubular, asymmetric, widely spaced breasts), prior breast surgery, severe stress, and PCOS. Investigation is targeted: prolactin and pituitary axis first, plus pelvic USS for retained products if any third-stage concern.
key_points: Lactogenesis II is the copious milk production phase that normally begins at day 2 to 5 postpartum
Retained placental tissue continues progesterone production and inhibits lactogenesis II
IGT clinical features: tubular, widely spaced, asymmetric breasts; minimal antenatal growth
Sheehan presents with failure to lactate as an early sign
Galactagogues (domperidone, metoclopramide) only after diagnostic workup
explanation.pearls: If you cannot tick off latch, positioning, frequency, and infant transfer as adequate, fix those first. If they are adequate and supply remains poor, investigate the mother.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

subtopic_detail: Failure to lactate - differential and investigation

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P2 woman presents to her general practitioner 4 months postpartum with a 6-week history of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety and a 3 kg weight loss despite an increased appetite. She is breastfeeding her infant exclusively. She has no neck pain, no recent viral illnessse, and no past psychiatric history. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated, the delivery was a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39+4, and she had no obstetric or postpartum complications.

Her bloods today show TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L, free T4 32 pmol/L, free T3 9.2 pmol/L, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive at 480 IU/mL, and thyroid receptor (TRAb) antibodies negative. A radioiodine uptake scan would be contraindicated because of breastfeeding but a thyroid ultrasound shows a diffusely heterogeneous gland with reduced vascularity on Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/76 mmHg, HR 108 bpm regular, T 36.9 degC.
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, no goitre, no eye signs. Breastfeeding well.
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, fT4 32 pmol/L, fT3 9.2 pmol/L, anti-TPO 480 IU/mL (strongly +), TRAb negative. USS thyroid: diffusely heterogeneous, reduced vascularity.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management of her current thyrotoxic phase?

options.text: Carbimazole 30 mg orally daily, titrated to repeat thyroid function tests every 4 weeks
options.rationale: Carbimazole is wrong because postpartum thyroiditis causes thyrotoxicosis by destructive release of preformed hormone, not new synthesis; antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, PTU) are ineffective. Would be correct only in Graves or other synthesis-mediated thyrotoxicosis (BMJ Best Practice; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.text: Radioiodine ablation as soon as breastfeeding can be temporarily ceased entirely
options.rationale: Radioiodine ablation is wrong because radioiodine is for Graves disease or toxic nodular disease, not transient destructive thyroiditis; postpartum thyroiditis typically resolves spontaneously. Would never be correct here (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.text: Propranolol 10-40 mg three times daily for symptom control, monitoring thyroid function every 6-8 weeks
options.rationale: The thyrotoxic phase of postpartum thyroiditis is destructive (reduced vascularity, anti-TPO positive, TRAb negative) and treated symptomatically with a beta-blocker such as propranolol while monitoring TFTs every 6 to 8 weeks. Spontaneous resolution into euthyroidism or progression to a hypothyroid phase typically follows; permanent hypothyroidism occurs in approximately 20% at 1 year (BMJ Best Practice; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.text: Levothyroxine 50 microg orally daily and review her thyroid function tests in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Levothyroxine is wrong because she is currently thyrotoxic (TSH <0.01, fT4 32); levothyroxine would worsen her state. Would be correct only in the subsequent hypothyroid phase or permanent hypothyroidism (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.text: Lugol iodine and oral dexamethasone for treatment of thyroid storm now
options.rationale: Lugol iodine plus dexamethasone for thyroid storm is wrong because thyroid storm requires severe features (high fever, marked tachycardia, altered consciousness, organ dysfunction) which are absent; her thyrotoxicosis is mild-to-moderate. Would be correct only with established thyroid storm (BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis is a destructive lymphocytic thyroiditis presenting 1 to 12 months postpartum, classically biphasic: thyrotoxic phase (1 to 4 months postpartum, lasting weeks to months) followed by a hypothyroid phase (4 to 8 months postpartum, also transient). Most resolve to euthyroidism; approximately 20% develop permanent hypothyroidism. Anti-TPO antibodies are usually positive. Treat the thyrotoxic phase with a beta-blocker only, and the hypothyroid phase with levothyroxine if symptomatic.
key_points: Biphasic course: thyrotoxic (months 1 to 4) then hypothyroid (months 4 to 8)
Anti-TPO positive in approximately 70 to 80%
Distinguish from Graves: TRAb negative, reduced uptake on RAIU (low Doppler flow on USS as proxy in breastfeeding)
Treat thyrotoxic phase with beta-blocker; treat hypothyroid phase with thyroxine if symptomatic
20% develop permanent hypothyroidism; annual TFT screening thereafter
explanation.pearls: If TRAb is positive, think Graves disease (which can also present postpartum). If TRAb is negative and anti-TPO is high in a postpartum woman, think postpartum thyroiditis. Doppler ultrasound is a useful surrogate for radioiodine uptake in lactating women.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

subtopic_detail: Postpartum thyroiditis - biphasic course and management

stem:
A 29-year-old nulligravid woman presents with 7 months of secondary amenorrhoea, intermittent bilateral galactorrhoea and reduced libido. She has had no recent pregnancy or breastfeeding, no headaches and no visual symptoms. She started risperidone 4 mg daily 9 months ago for chronic schizoaffective disorder, prescribed by her psychiatrist, and is responding well with no recent admissions. She takes no other regular medications and uses no recreational drugs.

BMI 24, BP 116/70. Visual fields are full to confrontation. Bloods: beta-hCG negative, repeat mid-morning serum prolactin 1900 mIU/L (reference <500) on two occasions one week apart, TSH and free T4 normal, U+Es normal. She is keen to conceive in the next 12 months.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/70 mmHg, BMI 24
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible galactorrhoea, no breast mass, visual fields normal to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative, prolactin 1850 mIU/L (reference <500), TSH 1.4 mIU/L, free T4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request urgent MRI pituitary with gadolinium before any further investigation
options.rationale: Urgent MRI first is wrong because when a known dopamine antagonist (risperidone) is the strongly suspected cause, identifying and managing the drug effect should precede imaging; pituitary MRI is reserved for sustained unexplained hyperprolactinaemia off the offending drug. Would be correct only after switching to a prolactin-sparing agent confirms persistence of hyperprolactinaemia (Endocrine Society 2011).

options.text: Liaise with the treating psychiatrist about switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, then re-check prolactin
options.rationale: Risperidone is a strong dopamine D2 antagonist and a common cause of pharmacological hyperprolactinaemia. The first step is collaborative medication review with the prescribing psychiatrist; switching to a prolactin-sparing agent (aripiprazole) and re-measuring before imaging avoids unnecessary MRI and identifies the cause (Endocrine Society 2011; eTG Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly empirically and reassess prolactin in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Empirical cabergoline is wrong because dopamine agonists can precipitate or worsen psychosis in patients with schizophrenia and are not first-line when a drug cause is likely; the anti-pattern is treating the lab abnormality without addressing the cause. Would be correct only for prolactinoma confirmed on imaging in stable patients (Endocrine Society 2011).

options.text: Macroprolactin screen with polyethylene glycol precipitation as the next test
options.rationale: Macroprolactin screen is wrong because macroprolactin testing is for asymptomatic hyperprolactinaemia; this woman is clinically symptomatic (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, low libido), confirming biologically active prolactin. Would be correct only in asymptomatic elevation (Endocrine Society 2011).

options.text: Stop risperidone abruptly without psychiatric consultation to allow prolactin to normalise
options.rationale: Abrupt risperidone cessation is wrong because stopping antipsychotic without psychiatric input risks relapse and self-harm; switches require shared decision-making with the prescribing team. Would never be correct unilaterally (Endocrine Society 2011).

explanation.summary: Hyperprolactinaemia in a patient on a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic should be presumed iatrogenic until proven otherwise, since drug effect is far more common than pituitary adenoma in this group. Confirm with a fasting morning prolactin and exclude pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism, renal failure and chest wall stimulation. Antipsychotic-induced prolactin typically sits between 500 and 2000 mIU/L; levels above 5000 mIU/L raise concern for a macroadenoma and warrant pituitary MRI even on therapy. Management is shared with psychiatry - switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine where clinically appropriate, then recheck after 4-6 weeks. Dopamine agonists like cabergoline are second-line because they can destabilise psychosis. Persistent hypogonadism risks bone loss, so DXA and consideration of HRT are part of long-term care.
key_points: Common secondary causes: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, dopamine antagonists, oestrogens, opioids, renal failure, chest wall stimulation
Prolactin >5000 mIU/L strongly suggests prolactinoma
Macroprolactin screen if asymptomatic and isolated lab finding
MRI pituitary if confirmed persistent elevation with secondary causes excluded
explanation.pearls: Risperidone and amisulpride drive the largest prolactin elevations among second-generation antipsychotics; aripiprazole is partial-agonist at D2 and is usually prolactin-neutral or prolactin-lowering, making it the preferred substitute (eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

subtopic_detail: Hyperprolactinaemia - first-line investigation

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is reviewed 8 days after IVF oocyte retrieval (21 oocytes). She reports 48 hours of worsening abdominal distension, nausea and reduced oral intake. BP 108/64, HR 108, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air. Abdomen distended, tense ascites palpable to the costal margin, mild generalised tenderness without peritonism. Pelvic ultrasound: ovaries 11 cm right and 10 cm left with multiple cysts; large-volume ascites extending above the umbilicus; small right pleural effusion.

Bloods: haematocrit 0.48 (baseline 0.38), WCC 13.2, sodium 132, potassium 4.6, creatinine 96 micromol/L (baseline 62), albumin 27 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, urine output 25 mL/h for the past 4 hours.

data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, shifting dullness, mild tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Hct 0.45 (baseline 0.38), WCC 12.5, Na 137, K 4.2, Cr 72 micromol/L, Alb 32 g/L; USS: ovaries 10 cm R / 9 cm L, moderate ascites pelvic + lower abdo, not above umbilicus

lead_in: Which classification and management plan best fit her ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?

options.text: Moderate OHSS: discharge home with daily phone review and oral fluids
options.rationale: Moderate OHSS labelling is wrong because the haematocrit >=0.45, rising creatinine, oliguria, hypoalbuminaemia and ascites above the umbilicus push her into the severe category; outpatient management would miss thromboembolic and renal complications. Would be correct only with mild ascites and no biochemical derangement (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

options.text: Severe OHSS: admit for IV crystalloid, VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, strict fluid balance and consider paracentesis
options.rationale: Haematocrit 0.48, oliguria, creatinine rise, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites above the umbilicus and pleural effusion meet severe OHSS criteria. Management is admission for IV fluids, prophylactic LMWH (high VTE risk), strict input/output and paracentesis for symptomatic tense ascites (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

options.text: Critical OHSS: transfer to ICU now for invasive ventilation and renal replacement
options.rationale: Critical OHSS labelling is wrong because critical OHSS requires anuria, ARDS, thromboembolism or multiorgan failure; she has oliguria not anuria and normal oxygenation. Would be correct only at the critical end of the spectrum, not now (RANZCOG OHSS).

options.text: Severe OHSS: admit but give large-volume normal saline boluses until haematocrit normalises
options.rationale: Large-volume saline boluses is wrong because aggressive crystalloid worsens third-spacing and ascites in OHSS; the anti-pattern is treating it as straightforward hypovolaemia. Would be correct in haemorrhagic shock, not OHSS (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

options.text: Severe OHSS: admit but withhold thromboprophylaxis until haemoconcentration resolves
options.rationale: Withholding thromboprophylaxis is wrong because OHSS is markedly hypercoagulable (raised oestrogen, haemoconcentration, immobility) and early LMWH is recommended; the anti-pattern is treating bleeding risk and clotting risk symmetrically. Would never be correct in severe OHSS (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

explanation.summary: OHSS severity is classified mild/moderate/severe/critical. Moderate OHSS adds sonographic ascites to mild features. Severe OHSS requires clinical ascites with haematocrit >0.45, WCC >15, hypoalbuminaemia and oliguria. Critical adds tense ascites, ARDS, VTE or renal failure (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).
key_points: Risk factors: young age, low BMI, PCOS, high antral follicle count, high AMH, >20 oocytes retrieved
Prevention: GnRH antagonist protocol + GnRH agonist trigger + freeze-all embryos
Severe/critical OHSS = admission, VTE prophylaxis, fluid balance, paracentesis if tense
Most cases resolve by next menses; symptoms can be prolonged if pregnancy occurs
explanation.pearls: OHSS adds an independent high VTE risk; thromboprophylaxis is mandatory in admitted moderate-to-severe disease.

subtopic_detail: OHSS - severity recognition

stem:
A 38-year-old woman and her 40-year-old male partner have been trying to conceive for 18 months. The woman has regular ovulatory cycles, mid-luteal progesterone confirms ovulation, AMH 6 pmol/L (low for age), antral follicle count 6, TSH and prolactin normal, BMI 24, HyCoSy confirmed bilateral tubal patency. The partner has had two normal semen analyses by WHO 2021 criteria 4 weeks apart.

Neither has had pelvic surgery, endometriosis or STI. They are non-smokers and drink within recommended limits. They have not had any prior pregnancies. They ask which ART pathway gives the highest live-birth chance given her age and ovarian reserve.

data_table.Examination: Both partners healthy; female BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: Female: regular ovulatory cycles, normal mid-luteal progesterone, AMH 18 pmol/L, AFC 14, normal TSH/prolactin, bilateral tubal patency. Male: normal semen analysis x2 by WHO 2021

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue timed intercourse for a further 12 months before referral to a fertility specialist
options.rationale: Another 12 months of timed intercourse is wrong because women >=35 with infertility >=6-12 months warrant referral now; spending another year erodes cumulative live-birth probability, especially with low AMH. Would be correct only in women under 35 still inside the 12-month diagnostic window (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).

options.text: Proceed to in vitro fertilisation given her age and low ovarian reserve
options.rationale: At 38 with AMH 6 pmol/L and AFC 6 (low ovarian reserve), IVF gives the highest cycle live-birth chance and allows aneuploidy management; IUI is less effective in this context (NICE CG156; RANZCOG).

options.text: Three cycles of intrauterine insemination with clomiphene before considering IVF
options.rationale: Three IUI cycles is wrong because IUI offers minimal incremental benefit over expectant management in unexplained infertility with low ovarian reserve at 38, and cycles spent on IUI reduce her usable IVF window. Would be correct only for mild male factor or cervical factor infertility with adequate reserve and younger age (NICE CG156).

options.text: Commence clomiphene citrate alone with timed intercourse for six cycles
options.rationale: Clomiphene alone is wrong because she is already ovulating; clomiphene targets anovulation and does not address her age-related and reserve-related decline. Would be correct only in WHO-II anovulation (e.g. PCOS) (NICE CG156).

options.text: Recommend donor oocyte IVF as her age and reserve preclude autologous IVF success
options.rationale: Donor oocyte IVF as first line is wrong because at 38 with AMH 6, autologous IVF still has reasonable cumulative live-birth probability; donor oocytes are reserved for very low reserve plus repeated autologous failure or POI. Would be correct only after failed autologous IVF or POI (RANZCOG; NICE).

explanation.summary: For unexplained infertility in a woman under 36 with normal investigations and short duration, expectant management with timed intercourse is appropriate. Stimulated IUI is considered if pregnancy has not occurred after a further 6 months, and IVF is offered for prolonged unexplained infertility, age >=36, or after failed IUI cycles (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).
key_points: Investigate at 12 months if female <35; at 6 months if female >=35; earlier if known cause
IUI is first ART step for mild male factor or ovulatory disorder responsive to mild stimulation; offers little benefit in unexplained infertility with normal semen
IVF first-line if: bilateral tubal disease, severe male factor, failed IUI, age >=40, advanced endometriosis
Single embryo transfer minimises multiple pregnancy risk
explanation.pearls: The female partner's age is the single strongest predictor of ART outcome; don't delay referral past 35.

subtopic_detail: IUI vs IVF - eligibility selection

stem:
A 36-year-old woman and her 38-year-old male partner attend the GP after 8 months of regular unprotected intercourse without conception. She has had regular 28 to 30 day cycles since menarche, no dysmenorrhoea, no abnormal bleeding and no pelvic pain. She has had no pregnancies and her partner has no children from previous relationships. Her past history includes appendicectomy at age 16 without complications.

She has had no pelvic infections, no chlamydia exposure, and her cervical screening is up to date. Her partner has no chronic disease, takes no regular medications, is a non-smoker and works as a teacher. They have intercourse 2 to 3 times per week. BMI 23 (female) and 25 (male). She is on folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Pelvic examination is unremarkable.

They are aware of her age and ask what investigations should be commenced now rather than waiting to the conventional 12-month threshold for younger couples.

data_table.Examination: Female pelvic exam unremarkable; both partners systemically well
data_table.Investigations: None done yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the couple and review in 4 months if there is no conception
options.rationale: Reassure and review in 4 months is wrong because infertility is defined as 12 months in women <35 or 6 months in women >=35; this 36-year-old has crossed that threshold and ovarian reserve declines steeply through this age band. Would be correct only in a woman <35 within the 12-month window (RANZCOG; NICE CG156; ASRM).

options.text: Commence parallel investigation: semen analysis, mid-luteal progesterone, ovarian reserve and tubal patency
options.rationale: At >=35 years, investigation is recommended after 6 months of unprotected intercourse; investigation is parallel in both partners and includes semen analysis (WHO 2021), ovulation assessment, ovarian reserve (AMH + AFC), thyroid, prolactin and tubal patency assessment by HyCoSy or HSG (RANZCOG; NICE CG156; ASRM).

options.text: Order AMH and pelvic ultrasound only and defer semen analysis until a second visit
options.rationale: AMH and ultrasound only, deferring semen analysis, is wrong because male factor accounts for 30-40% of infertility and semen analysis is the single most informative test; deferring delays diagnosis. Would never be correct in initial workup (RANZCOG; ASRM).

options.text: Refer immediately for IVF without baseline investigations given her age
options.rationale: Immediate IVF without baseline tests is wrong because baseline tests identify treatable causes (anovulation, tubal blockage, male factor) and guide stimulation protocol choice; IVF without a semen analysis can miss severe male factor needing ICSI. Would be correct only when baseline workup has been completed and IVF chosen (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy first to exclude endometriosis as a contributing factor
options.rationale: Diagnostic laparoscopy first is wrong because laparoscopy is not first-line workup; non-invasive tests (semen analysis, hormones, HyCoSy/HSG) come first. Would be correct only with strong suspicion of endometriosis or adhesive disease after non-invasive workup (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months in women <35 (or 6 months in women >=35) of regular unprotected intercourse. Workup is parallel in both partners: semen analysis (WHO 2021 criteria), ovulation assessment (mid-luteal progesterone), ovarian reserve (AMH + AFC), TSH and prolactin, and tubal patency assessment by HyCoSy or HSG (RANZCOG; NICE CG156; ASRM).
key_points: Earlier workup if known anovulation, prior pelvic surgery, chemo, endometriosis, varicocele, cryptorchidism
Semen analysis: 2 samples, 4 weeks apart, after 2 to 7 days abstinence
AMH and AFC predict response to ovarian stimulation, NOT spontaneous conception
Day-2 to day-5 FSH and oestradiol are an alternative ovarian reserve marker
explanation.pearls: 30 to 40% of infertility has a male factor component; never defer semen analysis.

subtopic_detail: Infertility - couple workup timing and content

stem:
A 34-year-old nulligravid woman is being assessed prior to commencement of IVF for tubal factor infertility (bilateral tubal occlusion confirmed on HyCoSy and laparoscopy). She has regular 28-day cycles with confirmed ovulation, BMI 22, normal TSH and prolactin, and her partner has a normal semen analysis. Her AMH is 4 pmol/L (low for age) and her antral follicle count is 5 (total both ovaries).

Day-3 FSH is 11 IU/L with oestradiol 180 pmol/L. She has had no chemotherapy, no pelvic surgery beyond diagnostic laparoscopy, no autoimmune disease and no family history of premature ovarian insufficiency. She is anxious about the implications of these results and asks what they mean for her IVF cycle planning and her chance of natural conception. She has no menopausal symptoms and her BP today is normal. She is anxious about the implications for her treatment and asks specifically what these numbers mean for her IVF stimulation response.

data_table.Vital signs: BMI 22
data_table.Investigations: AMH 4 pmol/L (low for age), AFC 5 (total), Day-3 FSH 11 IU/L, oestradiol 180 pmol/L; normal TSH and prolactin; bilateral tubal occlusion

lead_in: Which statement most accurately interprets her ovarian reserve markers in the context of planning IVF?

options.text: Low AMH and AFC predict poor ovarian response and low oocyte yield, not per-cycle spontaneous conception
options.rationale: AMH and AFC are the best validated markers of ovarian response to controlled ovarian stimulation in IVF (low values predict poor response and high values predict OHSS risk); they do NOT reliably predict natural conception probability, time to menopause, or live-birth rate per oocyte (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

options.text: AMH below 5 pmol/L confirms premature ovarian insufficiency, so IVF with her own oocytes is inappropriate
options.rationale: Saying AMH <5 confirms POI is wrong because POI requires amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea PLUS FSH >25 IU/L on two readings 4 weeks apart in a woman <40; AMH alone does not diagnose POI. Would be correct only after biochemical and clinical POI criteria are met (ESHRE POI Guideline; AMS).

options.text: Her elevated day-3 FSH means she will achieve a high oocyte yield on standard stimulation protocols
options.rationale: High FSH predicting high yield is wrong because elevated day-3 FSH reflects reduced reserve and predicts poor response to stimulation; the relationship is inverse. Would never be correct (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

options.text: AMH and AFC accurately predict the absolute number of years remaining until menopause for an individual
options.rationale: AMH predicting years to menopause is wrong because AMH correlates with biological ovarian age at a population level but cannot reliably predict an individual's menopause timing; clinical predictors must be integrated. Would be correct only as population-level prediction, not individual counselling (ESHRE POI Guideline; SREI).

options.text: An antral follicle count above 4 excludes POSEIDON poor-responder classification regardless of the AMH
options.rationale: AFC >4 excluding POSEIDON poor-responder is wrong because POSEIDON integrates age, AMH, AFC and previous stimulation response; AFC of 5 with AMH 4 can still fall into poor-prognosis categories. Would never single-handedly exclude POSEIDON classification (ESHRE POSEIDON).

explanation.summary: Ovarian reserve testing in subfertility uses anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count (AFC) as the primary measures, with day-3 FSH and oestradiol as adjuncts. Low values (AMH under 7 pmol/L, AFC under 5-7 follicles) predict poor response to controlled ovarian stimulation in IVF, lower oocyte yields per cycle, and may warrant higher gonadotrophin doses, dual stimulation (DuoStim), oocyte accumulation strategies across multiple cycles, or earlier consideration of donor oocytes. High values (AMH over 35 pmol/L, AFC over 24) predict ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome risk and lower the gonadotrophin starting dose. POSEIDON poor-responder classification stratifies women into four groups based on age (under or over 35) and ovarian reserve, guiding personalised stimulation protocols. Critically, AMH and AFC do not predict per-oocyte live birth rate, spontaneous conception likelihood, or absolute time to menopause - many women with low AMH conceive naturally, and the markers should not be used to discourage attempts at natural conception.
key_points: Day-3 FSH >10 IU/L with oestradiol <200 pmol/L = diminished reserve; high E2 can mask FSH
AMH <7 pmol/L = low reserve; >35 pmol/L = high (PCOS-like) with OHSS risk
AFC <7 (total both ovaries) = poor responder
POSEIDON criteria integrate age + reserve markers + prior cycle response
explanation.pearls: AMH and antral follicle count are the best validated predictors of ovarian response to controlled ovarian stimulation, but neither reliably predicts spontaneous conception, time to menopause, or live birth rate per oocyte. Low AMH counsels for IVF strategy, not against trying naturally (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: Ovarian reserve - AMH and AFC interpretation

stem:
A 37-year-old woman presents to her GP after 8 months of unprotected intercourse without conception. Her partner has had a normal semen analysis. Her cycles are 26 to 28 days and she has confirmed ovulation on mid-luteal progesterone. The GP arranges day-3 cycle bloods which return as follows: FSH 9 IU/L, LH 5 IU/L, oestradiol 350 pmol/L (high), AMH 6 pmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, prolactin within reference range.

AFC is 7 total. She has no abnormal bleeding and no significant dysmenorrhoea. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus, no fibroids, normal-appearing ovaries with the AFC noted, and no endometrioma. She has had no chemotherapy and no pelvic surgery. She asks how to interpret the day-3 FSH given that it appears reassuring. Her BMI is 23 and she is otherwise well, with no symptoms suggesting menopause.

data_table.Investigations: Day-3 FSH 9 IU/L, LH 5 IU/L, oestradiol 350 pmol/L (high), AMH 6 pmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, prolactin normal, AFC 7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these ovarian reserve markers?

options.text: Day-3 FSH within reference range reliably excludes diminished ovarian reserve in this patient
options.rationale: Saying normal day-3 FSH excludes diminished reserve is wrong because high day-3 oestradiol (>250-290 pmol/L) suppresses FSH by negative feedback and falsely normalises the level; FSH cannot be interpreted in isolation. Would be correct only with confirmed low/normal day-3 oestradiol (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

options.text: Elevated day-3 oestradiol may falsely suppress FSH; reserve is better assessed by AMH and AFC here
options.rationale: Day-3 oestradiol >250 pmol/L suppresses FSH and renders the FSH uninterpretable; the AMH (6 pmol/L, low) and AFC (7, low) both indicate diminished ovarian reserve and should drive counselling and ART planning (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

options.text: Her LH-to-FSH ratio of less than 1 confirms PCOS as the dominant cause of her subfertility
options.rationale: LH:FSH ratio confirming PCOS is wrong because LH:FSH ratios were dropped from PCOS diagnostic criteria; PCOS is diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound or raised AMH). Would never confirm PCOS alone (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

options.text: An AMH of 6 pmol/L with AFC of 7 confirms premature ovarian insufficiency, excluding IVF with own oocytes
options.rationale: Confirming POI is wrong because POI requires FSH >25 IU/L on two readings 4 weeks apart plus menstrual disturbance in a woman <40; low AMH/AFC alone is diminished reserve, not POI. Would be correct only with biochemical and menstrual POI criteria met (ESHRE POI Guideline; AMS).

options.text: Repeating day-3 bloods next cycle without changing strategy will give a definitive answer
options.rationale: Repeat day-3 bloods without changing strategy is wrong because the high oestradiol is the interpretive problem; AMH (cycle-independent) and AFC are the appropriate markers regardless of cycle day. Would be correct only after timing or technique is corrected (ESHRE POSEIDON).

explanation.summary: On day-3 cycle bloods, a high oestradiol (>250 to 290 pmol/L) suppresses FSH via negative feedback and can mask diminished ovarian reserve. AMH (not cycle-dependent) and AFC are more reliable in this setting; both low here, indicating diminished reserve and warranting prompt referral (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).
key_points: Day-3 FSH must be interpreted alongside oestradiol
High oestradiol with apparently normal FSH = uninterpretable; reserve still may be low
AMH is the most reliable single ovarian reserve marker; not cycle-dependent
AFC adds prognostic information and should be measured early follicular
explanation.pearls: A 'normal' day-3 FSH with high oestradiol can be falsely reassuring.

subtopic_detail: Day-3 FSH and oestradiol interpretation

stem:
A 25-year-old nulligravid woman has just been diagnosed with PCOS by her GP (Rotterdam criteria: oligomenorrhoea, biochemical hyperandrogenism with elevated free androgen index, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound with 24 follicles per ovary). Her exclusion bloods (TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP, beta-hCG) were all normal. She has acne, mild hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey 9) and recent 5 kg weight gain over 12 months. BMI 29.

Family history: mother with type 2 diabetes diagnosed at 52, paternal uncle with myocardial infarction at age 60. She is not planning pregnancy in the next 2 years. Her GP plans the recommended metabolic screen at diagnosis per the 2023 international PCOS guideline. Blood pressure today is 124/78 mmHg. She has no symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea, no chest pain and no peripheral oedema, and her cardiovascular examination today is unremarkable. The GP is using the 2023 international evidence-based PCOS guideline as the framework for baseline assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, BMI 29
data_table.Examination: Acne, mild hirsutism (FG 9), no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP normal; beta-hCG negative; free androgen index elevated; TVUS 24 follicles/ovary

lead_in: Which combination of investigations represents the most appropriate metabolic screen at the time of PCOS diagnosis in this woman?

options.text: Fasting lipid panel and a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test plus blood pressure measurement
options.rationale: The 2023 international PCOS guideline recommends a 75 g OGTT (preferred over fasting glucose or HbA1c due to higher sensitivity in PCOS), a fasting lipid panel and blood pressure measurement at diagnosis, with repeat OGTT every 1 to 3 years based on risk factors (2023 International PCOS Guideline; Jean Hailes).

options.text: Fasting glucose and HbA1c alone are sufficient screening in women under 35 with PCOS
options.rationale: Fasting glucose plus HbA1c alone is wrong because both have lower sensitivity than the 75 g OGTT for detecting impaired glucose tolerance in PCOS, where post-load hyperglycaemia is the dominant abnormality; the 2023 PCOS guideline explicitly prefers OGTT. Would be correct only when OGTT is impractical and an initial low-yield screen is accepted (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

options.text: Annual fasting insulin level to monitor for insulin resistance and guide treatment
options.rationale: Annual fasting insulin is wrong because the international guideline does not recommend fasting insulin or HOMA-IR for clinical use due to assay variability and lack of management impact; OGTT and lipid screening are the recommended tools. Would be correct only in research settings (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

options.text: Cardiac MRI with stress testing given her family history of cardiovascular disease at this age
options.rationale: Cardiac MRI plus stress testing is wrong because PCOS diagnosis does not warrant imaging-based cardiac assessment; risk stratification uses traditional calculators with intensified screening intervals. Would be correct only with symptoms or risk-calculator-driven indication for ischaemia testing (2023 International PCOS Guideline; NHMRC CV risk).

options.text: Liver biopsy because PCOS is associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
options.rationale: Liver biopsy is wrong because metabolic screening at PCOS diagnosis uses non-invasive markers (LFTs, FIB-4, ultrasound) for NAFLD when suspected; biopsy is reserved for staging significant fibrosis. Would never be correct at initial diagnosis (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

explanation.summary: At PCOS diagnosis, the 2023 international guideline recommends a baseline 75 g OGTT, fasting lipid panel and BP measurement, with repeat OGTT every 1 to 3 years based on risk factors. Fasting insulin and HOMA-IR are not recommended for clinical use (2023 International PCOS Guideline; Jean Hailes).
key_points: OGTT preferred over HbA1c or fasting glucose for IGT detection in PCOS
Lipid screening recommended at diagnosis
BP, weight and waist circumference monitored yearly
Increased background risk of T2DM, GDM, dyslipidaemia, OSA, NAFLD, endometrial cancer
explanation.pearls: PCOS confers a 4-fold lifetime risk of T2DM independent of BMI; OGTT is the preferred screen.

subtopic_detail: PCOS - metabolic screening at diagnosis

stem:
A 28-year-old nulligravid woman has been on continuous combined oral contraceptive pill (30 mcg ethinyloestradiol + levonorgestrel) plus naproxen as needed for 8 months for clinically suspected endometriosis. Her cyclical pelvic pain has not improved (still requires time off work 2 days each month with pain rated 7/10), her deep dyspareunia persists, and a repeat transvaginal ultrasound now demonstrates a 3 cm right ovarian endometrioma not previously seen.

She has had no abnormal bleeding and no new bowel or bladder symptoms in the last 2 years. She uses condoms with her long-term male partner. Beta-hCG is negative. She has no family history of breast cancer or VTE, no smoking and BMI 23. She is willing to continue medical therapy but wants more effective symptom relief; she remains reluctant to undergo surgery in the short term.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, BMI 23
data_table.Examination: Tenderness right adnexa, no peritonism, normal speculum
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: new 3 cm right ovarian endometrioma; beta-hCG negative; CA-125 not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to LNG-IUS or trial a 3-6 month GnRH analogue with add-back HRT
options.rationale: If first-line continuous COCP plus NSAID fails, second-line options include progestogen-only therapy (LNG-IUS, dienogest, DMPA) or a short course of GnRH analogue with add-back HRT to control symptoms and reduce vasomotor and bone-density side effects; this is preferable to surgery in a woman who declines it (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

options.text: Stop hormonal suppression and proceed to abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy
options.rationale: Hysterectomy with BSO is wrong because definitive surgery in a 28-year-old with endometriosis requires completed childbearing and severe refractory symptoms after thorough medical and conservative surgical management; she has not yet had second-line therapy. Would be correct only after exhausting medical and conservative surgical options in a woman who has completed her family (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

options.text: Add tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses to current therapy
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is wrong because it targets heavy menstrual bleeding rather than endometriosis-associated pain, and continuous COCP suppresses cyclical bleeding anyway. Would be correct only for HMB, not endometriosis pain (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

options.text: Empirical IVF using fresh embryo transfer for presumed endometriosis-related infertility
options.rationale: Empirical IVF is wrong because IVF is for endometriosis-associated infertility (or advanced disease with planned pregnancy), not for pain management in a woman not currently planning conception. Would be correct only when fertility is the goal (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

options.text: Continue current therapy and add long-acting oxycodone for breakthrough cyclical pain
options.rationale: Long-acting opioids are wrong because chronic opioid use in endometriosis pain causes dependence, hyperalgesia and no disease-modifying effect; the anti-pattern is opioid escalation rather than mechanism-targeted hormonal escalation or laparoscopic excision. Would be correct only as short-term peri-operative analgesia, never chronic (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022).

explanation.summary: After first-line COCP plus NSAID failure in suspected endometriosis, second-line medical options include progestogen-only therapy (LNG-IUS, dienogest, DMPA, etonogestrel implant) or a 3 to 6 month course of GnRH analogue with add-back HRT. Laparoscopic excision is offered when medical therapy fails, when fertility is impaired, or when deep infiltrating disease is suspected (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).
key_points: Endometriomas: laparoscopic cystectomy improves pain but may reduce ovarian reserve; weigh against fertility plans
GnRH analogues require add-back HRT if used >6 months to protect bone density
MRI for surgical planning of deep infiltrating endometriosis
Opioids are not recommended for chronic pelvic pain
explanation.pearls: Laparoscopic excision is preferred over ablation for deep infiltrating endometriosis.

subtopic_detail: Endometriosis - escalation after failed first-line

stem:
A 34-year-old G0 woman is referred with 14 months of secondary subfertility and a 9-month history of progressively heavy menstrual bleeding requiring iron supplementation (Hb 108 g/L on presentation, now 118 g/L). Her cycles are regular and ovulatory. Her partner has a normal semen analysis and her tubes are patent on HyCoSy. Transvaginal ultrasound and MRI both demonstrate a single 5 cm submucosal fibroid that is FIGO type 2 (>=50% intramural component, projecting into the endometrial cavity and distorting it) and two further small subserosal fibroids that do not distort the cavity.

Her endometrial biopsy is benign. She has no other gynaecological pathology, no chronic disease, and is actively trying to conceive. She has discussed expectant management and medical options with her clinician and would prefer a definitive intervention that addresses both her heavy bleeding and improves her chance of conception.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (treated iron deficiency anaemia); TVUS + MRI: 5 cm FIGO type 2 submucosal fibroid distorting cavity, two small subserosal fibroids; endometrial biopsy benign; HyCoSy bilateral patency; normal semen analysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Hysteroscopic myomectomy as a fertility-sparing intervention addressing both HMB and subfertility
options.rationale: FIGO 0-2 submucosal fibroids distorting the cavity reduce fertility and cause HMB; hysteroscopic myomectomy is the fertility-sparing intervention of choice per RANZCOG: Fibroids and AAGL Fibroids guidance.

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system insertion as definitive treatment for both subfertility and HMB
options.rationale: LNG-IUS is wrong because cavity-distorting submucosal fibroids contraindicate Mirena placement (high expulsion, reduced efficacy) and the LNG-IUS is contraceptive rather than fertility-enhancing in a woman trying to conceive. Would be correct only for HMB without cavity distortion and without conception plans (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation to reduce fibroid volume and HMB while preserving the uterus
options.rationale: UAE is wrong because uterine artery embolisation is not recommended for women who wish to conceive due to reduced ovarian reserve from non-target embolisation, raised placental complication risk and uncertain fertility outcome. Would be correct only for women with completed family or those declining surgery (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive management for both fibroid bulk and HMB
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive for HMB and fibroid bulk but ends fertility; would be correct if the patient had completed childbearing, but this patient is actively trying to conceive per RANZCOG: Fibroids and NICE NG88.

options.text: GnRH analogue with add-back HRT as long-term medical therapy for HMB and subfertility
options.rationale: Long-term GnRH analogue is wrong because GnRH analogues induce hypogonadism and suppress ovulation; they are short-term (3-6 month) pre-operative or bridging agents and are not a fertility-preserving long-term solution. Would be correct only as pre-operative shrinkage before myomectomy (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

explanation.summary: The FIGO leiomyoma classification categorises fibroids by location: type 0 (pedunculated intracavitary), type 1 (less than 50% intramural extension), type 2 (50% or more intramural), type 3 (intramural abutting endometrium), type 4 (intramural), type 5 (subserosal more than 50% intramural), type 6 (subserosal less than 50% intramural), type 7 (subserosal pedunculated), type 8 (parasitic, broad ligament, cervical). Submucosal fibroids (types 0-2) distort the endometrial cavity, reduce implantation and pregnancy rates, and cause heavy menstrual bleeding. Hysteroscopic myomectomy is the fertility-sparing intervention of choice and combines treatment of HMB and improvement of fertility. Type 0 and small type 1 fibroids resect in a single procedure; type 2 fibroids often need a staged second-look hysteroscopy at 6-8 weeks. LNG-IUS requires an undistorted cavity and is therefore inappropriate when significant submucosal disease is present. Uterine artery embolisation and hysterectomy are reserved for women who do not desire fertility. Pregnancy is usually delayed 3-6 months post-resection.
key_points: FIGO 0 to 1 fibroids almost always removable hysteroscopically
FIGO 2 fibroids >=50% intramural may need staged resection
Laparoscopic or open myomectomy for intramural or subserosal causing symptoms in fertility-seeking women
Risk of caesarean delivery after deep myometrial myomectomy due to scar integrity
explanation.pearls: FIGO type 0-2 (submucosal) fibroids distort the endometrial cavity and reduce implantation rates; hysteroscopic myomectomy improves both fertility and heavy menstrual bleeding, with a 30-50% pregnancy rate within 12 months. Type 2 fibroids may need a second-look hysteroscopy at 6-8 weeks (RANZCOG; AAGL).

subtopic_detail: Fibroids - fertility-sparing surgical choice

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has been formally diagnosed with premature ovarian insufficiency: 6 months of secondary amenorrhoea, FSH 56 IU/L and 62 IU/L on samples 5 weeks apart with low oestradiol, negative beta-hCG, normal TSH and normal prolactin. She has hot flushes, vaginal dryness with deep dyspareunia and disturbed sleep. Family history: her mother had menopause at 41 and a paternal aunt is on bisphosphonate therapy for osteoporosis.

She has had no chemotherapy, no pelvic radiotherapy and no autoimmune disease known to date. Karyotype is pending and fragile X premutation screen, adrenal antibodies and thyroid antibodies have been ordered. She has no contraindications to oestrogen (no breast cancer, no current VTE, no migraine with aura). BMI 23. BP 118/74. She is in a long-term partnership, not currently planning pregnancy, but is open to consideration of IVF with donor oocytes in the future. A baseline DXA is planned.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, BMI 23
data_table.Investigations: FSH 56 + 62 IU/L (4 weeks apart), low oestradiol, beta-hCG negative, normal TSH/prolactin; karyotype, FMR1, adrenal/thyroid antibodies pending; DXA planned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hormone management strategy for bone and cardiovascular protection?

options.text: Standard-dose physiological oestradiol with cyclical progestogen or LNG-IUS until the average age of menopause
options.rationale: POI confers significantly increased risk of osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline; physiological-dose HRT (oestradiol with progestogen if uterus present) until at least age 51 reduces these risks and treats vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI; Endocrine Society).

options.text: Bisphosphonate therapy as first-line bone protection without any concurrent hormone therapy
options.rationale: Bisphosphonate first-line is wrong because POI is fundamentally an oestrogen-deficiency state; physiological HRT addresses bone, cardiovascular, vasomotor and genitourinary needs simultaneously, while bisphosphonates only target bone. Would be correct only when HRT is contraindicated or established osteoporosis fails to respond (AMS POI; ESHRE POI Guideline 2024).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill is equivalent to HRT and may be continued lifelong
options.rationale: Calling COCP equivalent to HRT lifelong is wrong because while COCP is an acceptable alternative (especially when contraception is needed - spontaneous ovulation can occur in POI), physiological HRT generally provides better bone protection; both should continue at least to age 51 rather than truly lifelong. Would be correct only with the COCP-HRT equivalence overstated and the lifelong claim modified (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI).

options.text: Defer all hormone therapy and review symptoms again in 6 months
options.rationale: Defer HRT 6 months is wrong because delay in oestrogen replacement accelerates bone loss, cardiovascular risk and vasomotor/urogenital symptoms; the anti-pattern is treating POI like natural menopause where 'watchful waiting' might be acceptable. Would never be correct (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI).

options.text: Topical vaginal oestrogen alone as the primary hormone management strategy for this woman
options.rationale: Topical vaginal oestrogen alone is wrong because vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms only with negligible systemic absorption; it provides no bone or cardiovascular protection. Would be correct only as adjunct to systemic HRT for persistent vulvovaginal symptoms (AMS POI).

explanation.summary: POI confers significantly increased risk of osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline. Physiological-dose HRT (oestradiol with progestogen if uterus present) until at least the average age of natural menopause (around 51) is the cornerstone of management. HRT is NOT contraceptive; spontaneous pregnancy occurs in ~5 to 10% (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI; Endocrine Society).
key_points: Diagnosis: amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea >=4 months + FSH >25 IU/L on 2 readings 4+ weeks apart in woman <40
Workup: karyotype, FMR1 premutation, adrenal (21-OH) and thyroid antibodies, baseline DXA
HRT options: oral or transdermal oestradiol + cyclical progestogen or LNG-IUS
Counselling: HRT is not contraceptive; spontaneous pregnancy ~5 to 10%; donor oocyte IVF main fertility pathway
explanation.pearls: Discuss contraception separately - HRT is not contraceptive.

subtopic_detail: POI - bone and cardiovascular protection plan

stem:
A 37-year-old G2P2 woman attends her GP for contraceptive review. She has been on a combined oral contraceptive pill (30 mcg ethinyloestradiol with levonorgestrel) for the past 4 years. At today's review her blood pressure is 162/96 mmHg, confirmed on a repeat reading 15 minutes later at 158/94 mmHg. Home BP readings over the past 2 weeks have averaged 156/94 mmHg.

She has no headaches, no visual disturbancedema. Urinalysis is negative for protein and blood. She has no history of stroke, transient ischaemic attack, ischaemic heart disease, VTE or migraine with aura. She is a non-smoker, BMI 31, has otherwise normal bloods (renal function, electrolytes, lipids), and no diabetes (HbA1c 5.4%). She has completed her family and would like ongoing reliable contraception. She is reluctant to use barrier methods alone. She has no postnatal depression or mood disorder and her family history is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/96, repeat 158/94, home avg 156/94; BMI 31; HR 76
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds dual, no oedema, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: no protein/blood; HbA1c 5.4%, normal lipids, renal function, electrolytes

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Continue the current combined oral contraceptive pill and re-check blood pressure in 3 months
options.rationale: Continuing COCP is wrong because systolic >=160 or diastolic >=100 is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) for combined hormonal contraception; waiting 3 months exposes her to stroke/MI risk. Would never be correct at UKMEC 4 levels (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Switch to a progestogen-only method such as the LNG-IUS, POP, etonogestrel implant or DMPA
options.rationale: Hypertension >=160/100 is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception, contraindicating COCP. Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, LNG-IUS) are UKMEC 1 to 2 in hypertension; DMPA is UKMEC 2 in BP 140-159/90-99 and UKMEC 3 in BP >=160/100 due to its slight adverse lipid and vascular effects (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Switch to a transdermal combined hormonal patch as this avoids the first-pass hepatic metabolism
options.rationale: Switching to patch or ring is wrong because UKMEC categorises all combined hormonal methods (pill, patch, ring) the same in hypertension; the route does not modify oestrogen-driven vascular risk at this BP. Would never be correct (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Add an antihypertensive and continue the combined oral contraceptive at a lower oestrogen dose
options.rationale: Adding antihypertensive and lower-dose COCP is wrong because FSRH guidance is to avoid combined methods if BP is uncontrolled or vascular disease is present; treated hypertension is still UKMEC 3 with adequate control and UKMEC 4 if uncontrolled. Would be correct only when BP is well-controlled in low-risk younger women (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Recommend tubal ligation as the only acceptable contraceptive option for hypertensive women over 35
options.rationale: Tubal ligation as the only option is wrong because progestogen-only LARC methods (implant, LNG-IUS) are highly effective, reversible and UKMEC 1-2 in hypertension; offering sterilisation only is reductive. Would be correct only when she explicitly declines reversible methods (FSRH UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG: Contraception).

explanation.summary: Hypertension >=160/100 (uncontrolled or with vascular disease) is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception.
