Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, LNG-IUS) are UKMEC 1 to 2 and are appropriate alternatives. DMPA carries a UKMEC 3 rating at this BP level due to vascular and lipid effects (FSRH UKMEC 2016).
key_points: BP 140-159/90-99: COCP is UKMEC 3; progestogen-only methods UKMEC 1-2
BP >=160/100: COCP is UKMEC 4; progestogen-only methods UKMEC 1-2; DMPA UKMEC 3
Hypertension with established vascular disease: COCP UKMEC 4
Hypertension is the single most common cardiovascular risk encountered in contraception
explanation.pearls: UKMEC 4 means 'unacceptable health risk' - the method must not be used.

subtopic_detail: Contraception - hypertension UKMEC application

stem:
A 29-year-old G0 woman with PCOS diagnosed 18 months ago (Rotterdam criteria: oligomenorrhoea, biochemical hyperandrogenism with elevated free androgen index, polycystic ovarian morphology with 26 follicles per ovary) has been trying to conceive for 12 months with intercourse 2 to 3 times per week. Her partner has a normal semen analysis on two occasions. She has bilateral patent tubes on HyCoSy.

AMH 38 pmol/L, AFC 28, normal TSH and prolactin. She has lost 6 kg over 6 months with structured lifestyle intervention (current BMI 28, down from 31), and her cycles remain oligomenorrhoeic (45 to 70 days). HbA1c 5.3% and OGTT normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, BMI 28 (down from 31)
data_table.Examination: Mild hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans, no virilisation
data_table.Investigations: AMH 38 pmol/L, AFC 28, TSH 1.6, prolactin normal, HbA1c 5.3%, OGTT normal; HyCoSy bilateral patency; partner normal semen analysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological agent for ovulation induction in this patient?

options.text: Letrozole 2.5 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 2 to 6, titrated upward if anovulatory
options.rationale: The 2023 international PCOS guideline and ASRM both recommend letrozole as first-line ovulation induction in PCOS for anovulatory infertility; letrozole achieves higher ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates than clomiphene with lower multiple pregnancy risk (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM; RANZCOG).

options.text: Clomiphene citrate 50 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 2 to 6 with serial follicular tracking
options.rationale: Clomiphene is wrong because PPCOS II and subsequent meta-analyses showed letrozole achieves higher ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates with lower multiple pregnancy risk; clomiphene is now second-line where letrozole is unavailable or fails. Would be correct only if letrozole is contraindicated or inaccessible (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM).

options.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1 g twice daily as sole agent for ovulation induction
options.rationale: Metformin monotherapy is wrong because it gives lower ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates than letrozole; it is an adjunct (particularly in BMI >25 or IGT) rather than primary ovulation induction. Would be correct only as adjunct to letrozole or clomiphene (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM).

options.text: Recombinant FSH gonadotrophin injection from cycle day 2 with daily follicular ultrasound monitoring
options.rationale: Injectable gonadotrophins are wrong because they are second-line after oral failure due to higher cost, OHSS risk, multiple-pregnancy risk and need for daily follicular monitoring. Would be correct only after letrozole/clomiphene resistance (2023 International PCOS Guideline; RANZCOG).

options.text: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling under general anaesthesia as a first-line surgical option for her
options.rationale: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is wrong because it is reserved for women with clomiphene/letrozole resistance, particularly when laparoscopy is already indicated for another reason; first-line surgical treatment in treatment-naive PCOS would skip the evidence-based oral therapy. Would be correct only as second-line after oral failure (2023 International PCOS Guideline; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS, achieving higher live birth rates and lower multiple pregnancy rates than clomiphene (PPCOS II trial). Metformin is an adjunct (particularly with BMI >25 or impaired glucose tolerance). Gonadotrophin injection and laparoscopic ovarian drilling are second-line (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM; RANZCOG).
key_points: Letrozole: 2.5 mg daily day 2-6; titrate to 5 mg then 7.5 mg if anovulatory
Monitor first cycle with ovulation tracking (LH urine or follicular USS)
Lifestyle intervention foundational - aim for 5 to 10% weight reduction in BMI >25
Refer to fertility specialist if anovulatory after 3 to 6 ovulatory cycles or age >=35
explanation.pearls: Letrozole is teratogenic if taken during early pregnancy; use only in early follicular phase and confirm non-pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: PCOS - ovulation induction in fertility-seeking woman

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is referred to endocrinology with 14 months of secondary amenorrhoea, bilateral galactorrhoea, reduced libido and a 4-month history of headaches behind her eyes worse on waking. Two months ago she noticed difficulty seeing the side of her vision when driving. On examination today she has bitemporal hemianopia confirmed on confrontation and Humphrey perimetry. Prolactin is 9800 mIU/L (confirmed on a repeat fasting morning sample), TSH and free T4 are normal, beta-hCG negative, renal function normal and she takes no dopamine-blocking medications, antipsychotics, antidepressants or opioids.

MRI pituitary demonstrates a 14 mm pituitary mass with suprasellar extension contacting the optic chiasm with no cavernous sinus invasion. Other anterior pituitary hormones (ACTH/cortisol axis, IGF-1, TSH/T4, LH/FSH) are otherwise within reference range. She is keen to preserve future fertility. She has no symptoms of pituitary apoplexy (no thunderclap headache, no collapse) and her visual loss has been gradual over months rather than days.

data_table.Examination: Bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation and Humphrey; no other focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 9800 mIU/L (repeat fasting morning sample), TSH/T4 normal, beta-hCG negative, renal function normal; pituitary MRI: 14 mm mass with suprasellar extension contacting optic chiasm; other anterior pituitary axes intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly initially with close ophthalmology and endocrine follow-up
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability) are first-line for macroprolactinomas including those with visual field deficits; tumour shrinkage and visual recovery occur in the majority within weeks to months. Surgery is reserved for failure of medical therapy or apoplexy (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011; eTG: Endocrinology).

options.text: Urgent transsphenoidal surgical resection of the pituitary mass within 48 hours
options.rationale: Urgent transsphenoidal surgery is wrong because prolactinomas, unlike other pituitary adenomas, are exquisitely sensitive to medical therapy; dopamine agonists shrink the tumour and restore vision in most cases within weeks. Would be correct only with failed/intolerant dopamine agonist therapy, pituitary apoplexy or rapidly progressive visual loss not responding to medical therapy (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

options.text: External beam radiotherapy to the pituitary fossa as primary management
options.rationale: External beam radiotherapy is wrong because radiotherapy is third-line after failed surgery or for residual aggressive disease; slow onset and risk of hypopituitarism make it unsuitable for treatment-naive prolactinoma. Would be correct only in refractory or aggressive prolactinoma after surgery (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

options.text: Observation with serial MRI and visual fields, deferring treatment until prolactin >20,000 mIU/L
options.rationale: Observation is wrong because a macroadenoma with visual field defect requires active treatment; chiasmal compression untreated causes permanent visual loss, and dopamine agonists are highly effective. Would be correct only for asymptomatic microprolactinomas with no compressive features (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

options.text: Cyclical combined oral contraceptive pill alone to restore menses and protect bone density
options.rationale: COCP alone is wrong because it treats symptomatic amenorrhoea without addressing the tumour or visual compromise, and can mask prolactin monitoring; the anti-pattern is treating the downstream symptom rather than the macroadenoma. Would be correct only for microprolactinomas with stable imaging where contraception/menstrual regulation is the priority (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

explanation.summary: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred) are first-line for prolactinomas, including macroprolactinomas with chiasmal compression; the majority show tumour shrinkage and visual recovery within weeks to months. Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for medical failure, intolerance, apoplexy or progressive visual loss despite treatment (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011; eTG: Endocrinology).
key_points: Cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly, titrate to prolactin response; monitor for impulse control disorder and (high cumulative dose) cardiac valve effects
Repeat MRI at 3 to 6 months to assess shrinkage; visual fields at similar interval
Pre-pregnancy planning: bromocriptine has more safety data than cabergoline in early pregnancy
Pituitary apoplexy = emergency: glucocorticoid replacement + neurosurgical referral
explanation.pearls: Don't add an SSRI or antipsychotic to a patient with new amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea without first checking prolactin and considering prolactinoma.

subtopic_detail: Hyperprolactinaemia - macroprolactinoma management

stem:
A 28-year-old G0 woman with PCOS (AMH 48 pmol/L pre-stimulation) presents to the emergency department 9 days after oocyte retrieval (28 oocytes collected, fresh embryo transferred). She reports 3 days of progressive abdominal distension, breathlessness on minimal exertion and reduced urine output. On examination she is tachycardic (HR 112), BP 102/64, RR 24, SpO2 94% on room air, T 36.9.

Abdomen is markedly distended with tense ascites and reduced bowel sounds; she has bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation. Bloods: haematocrit 0.51, WCC 22 x10^9/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L (baseline 60), urea 9.5 mmol/L, albumin 26 g/L, ALT 75 U/L, AST 68 U/L. CXR shows small bilateral pleural effusions. Pelvic ultrasound shows ovaries 12 cm bilaterally with large volume ascites extending above the umbilicus. Urine output has been 18 mL/hour over the last 4 hours.

data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, bilateral basal crackles, distended abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Hct 0.51, WCC 22, Na 131, K 5.0, Cr 124 (baseline 60), urea 9.5, Alb 26, ALT 75; CXR bilateral small effusions; USS ovaries 12 cm bilaterally, ascites above umbilicus; urine output 18 mL/hour; D-dimer elevated

lead_in: Which combination of interventions is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Admit; commence IV crystalloid with albumin, prophylactic enoxaparin, fluid balance and urgent paracentesis
options.rationale: Severe/critical OHSS with haemoconcentration (Hct >0.50), WCC >20, oliguria, tense ascites and respiratory compromise requires admission, IV crystalloid (with albumin in severe hypoalbuminaemia), VTE prophylaxis (high independent VTE risk in OHSS), strict fluid balance and paracentesis to relieve tense ascites/respiratory compromise/renal dysfunction (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).

options.text: Discharge home with oral fluids, simple analgesia and outpatient review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharge home is wrong because haemoconcentration, oliguria, tense ascites and respiratory compromise meet severe OHSS criteria that mandate inpatient IV management and close monitoring; outpatient management risks VTE, renal failure and rapid deterioration. Would be correct only for mild OHSS with adequate oral intake (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).

options.text: Admit and commence intravenous frusemide infusion to address oliguria and reduce the ovarian volume
options.rationale: Frusemide infusion is wrong because diuretics in an intravascularly depleted, third-spaced state worsen haemoconcentration and renal dysfunction; volume replacement must precede any diuretic consideration. Would be correct only after intravascular volume is restored and pulmonary oedema persists, not first-line in OHSS (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).

options.text: Urgent laparotomy with bilateral oophorectomy to remove the hyperstimulated ovaries definitively
options.rationale: Laparotomy with oophorectomy is wrong because hyperstimulated ovaries are friable and bleed readily; surgery is reserved for torsion, rupture with significant haemorrhage or ectopic pregnancy. Would be correct only for surgical complications, not for severe OHSS itself (RANZCOG OHSS).

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and antiviral therapy pending blood culture results
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals are wrong because the elevated WCC in OHSS reflects the inflammatory state rather than infection; empirical antibiotics are not indicated without clinical evidence of infection. Would be correct only when superimposed infection is clinically suspected (RANZCOG OHSS).

explanation.summary: Severe/critical OHSS with haemoconcentration, oliguria, tense ascites and respiratory compromise requires admission, judicious IV crystalloid (albumin if albumin <30 g/L), VTE prophylaxis (OHSS confers independent high VTE risk), strict fluid balance and paracentesis for tense ascites or respiratory/renal compromise. Diuretics are contraindicated until intravascular volume is restored (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).
key_points: Critical OHSS thresholds: Hct >0.55, WCC >25, tense ascites, ARDS, VTE, hepatorenal dysfunction, anuria
Severe OHSS thresholds: Hct >0.45, WCC >15, clinical ascites, oliguria, hypoalbuminaemia <35 g/L
VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin throughout admission and at least until clinical resolution; longer if pregnancy ensues
Continued worsening if pregnancy occurs (HCG-driven) - persistent symptoms warrant beta-hCG check
explanation.pearls: OHSS is one of the few conditions where IV albumin is routinely used; diuretics are explicitly contraindicated until intravascular volume is restored.

subtopic_detail: Severe OHSS - inpatient management priorities

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P2 woman attends her GP for contraceptive review. She was diagnosed 14 months ago with stage II oestrogen-receptor-positive, progesterone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. She had wide local excision plus axillary node sampling (1 of 3 nodes positive), adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and commenced tamoxifen 20 mg daily 6 months ago which she plans to continue for at least 5 to 10 years.

She has been amenorrhoeic since chemotherapy but recent bloods show a partial return of menses and an FSH of 18 IU/L with oestradiol 280 pmol/L, suggesting recovery of ovarian function. She uses condoms intermittently with her long-term male partner. She has completed her family. She is anxious to avoid pregnancy because she does not wish to interrupt her endocrine therapy and is aware of the teratogenicity of tamoxifen. She has no other major comorbidity. BMI 24, BP 118/74.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 18 IU/L, E2 280 pmol/L (recovering ovarian function); on tamoxifen 20 mg daily

lead_in: Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for this woman?

options.text: Copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) inserted at the next available family planning visit
options.rationale: Current and past breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for ALL hormonal contraception (combined and progestogen-only). The copper IUD is UKMEC 1 and is the recommended highly effective reversible option in a woman with breast cancer who has completed her family; female sterilisation is also acceptable (FSRH UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG: Contraception).

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena) inserted at the next available appointment
options.rationale: LNG-IUS is wrong because current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for the LNG-IUS; despite local progestogen action, systemic exposure means it is contraindicated in current/recent breast cancer (UKMEC 3 only when remission is >5 years). Would be correct only after >5 years' disease-free remission and only as UKMEC 3 (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill at the lowest effective oestrogen dose available
options.rationale: COCP is wrong because current/recent breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception due to oestrogen-driven recurrence risk; absolute contraindication. Would never be correct in current/recent breast cancer (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal contraceptive implant (Implanon NXT) for 3 years
options.rationale: Etonogestrel implant is wrong because UKMEC 4 applies to all progestogen-only methods (implant, POP, DMPA, LNG-IUS) in current breast cancer; the systemic progestogen exposure is unacceptable. Would never be correct in current breast cancer (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks
options.rationale: DMPA is wrong because depot progestogen is UKMEC 4 in current breast cancer; all hormonal methods are contraindicated. Would never be correct in current breast cancer (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

explanation.summary: Contraception choice in women with current or past breast cancer is governed by the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC), adopted by Australian practice. Current breast cancer (within 5 years of diagnosis) is UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication) for all hormonal contraception, including combined oral contraceptive pill, progestogen-only pill, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, etonogestrel implant, and levonorgestrel intrauterine system - despite the LNG-IUS often being framed as 'local action'. Past breast cancer with 5 years free of disease is UKMEC 3 for hormonal methods (theoretical risk outweighs benefit). The copper intrauterine device is UKMEC 1 in all phases and is the preferred long-acting reversible option. Female sterilisation by tubal ligation or salpingectomy is the highest-efficacy permanent option. Male partner vasectomy is equally effective and lower-morbidity. Barrier methods are UKMEC 1 but have higher typical-use failure rates and are reserved for women who decline the above.
key_points: Current breast cancer (any subtype, any time on treatment): UKMEC 4 for all hormonal methods
Past breast cancer (>5 years remission): UKMEC 3 for hormonal methods
Copper IUD: UKMEC 1 in current and past breast cancer
Tamoxifen is teratogenic - contraception is mandatory throughout treatment and for 2 months after
explanation.pearls: Current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for ALL hormonal contraception including LNG-IUS - the 'local action' framing of the levonorgestrel IUD does not change the categorisation. Copper IUD (UKMEC 1) or female sterilisation are the appropriate highly-effective options (UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG).

subtopic_detail: Contraception - current breast cancer (UKMEC 4)

stem:
A 31-year-old G1P1 woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (diagnosed 6 years ago) attends for contraceptive review. Her disease has been clinically and serologically stable for 18 months on hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisolone (5 mg daily). She has previously had two episodes of cutaneous lupus and one episode of mild lupus nephritis treated with mycophenolate, now in remission. Her most recent immunology shows positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart, anticardiolipin IgG strongly positive, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I positive (triple positive antiphospholipid profile).

She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism, stroke or ischaemic heart disease and no obstetric morbidity but is high risk for VTE. BP 120/76, BMI 25, non-smoker. She has completed her family, uses condoms inconsistently and would like a more reliable method. She is concerned about both medication interactions with hydroxychloroquine and the impact of contraception on her lupus and VTE risk.

data_table.Examination: No active rash, no active arthritis
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive x2 (12 weeks apart), anticardiolipin IgG strongly positive, anti-beta-2-GPI positive; complement and dsDNA stable; renal function normal

lead_in: Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for this woman?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with the lowest available oestrogen dose to minimise VTE risk
options.rationale: COCP is wrong because SLE with positive (or unknown) antiphospholipid antibodies is UKMEC 4 for all combined hormonal contraception due to substantially elevated VTE and arterial thrombosis risk; lowering the oestrogen dose does not change the category. Would never be correct with APL positive (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) inserted at the next available appointment
options.rationale: In SLE with positive antiphospholipid antibodies, the LNG-IUS is UKMEC 1 to 2: highly effective, no systemic oestrogen, minimal interaction with hydroxychloroquine, low VTE risk, and acceptable in a woman who has completed her family. The Cu-IUD (UKMEC 1) is also acceptable but the LNG-IUS additionally reduces menstrual blood loss (relevant if anticoagulation is initiated later) (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

options.text: Combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring as it avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism
options.rationale: Combined ring is wrong because UKMEC 4 applies to all combined methods regardless of route in APL-positive SLE; route does not modify thrombotic risk. Would never be correct in this group (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks for ongoing contraception
options.rationale: DMPA is wrong because it is UKMEC 3 in APL-positive SLE (adverse lipid profile and small but increased VTE association), so an IUD is preferred. Would be correct only when LARC IUDs are not feasible and benefits are judged to outweigh risks (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

options.text: Continue barrier contraception alone (condoms) given the complexity of medication interactions
options.rationale: Condoms alone is wrong because typical-use failure ~13%/year is inadequate when she has completed her family and seeks reliable contraception; effective LARC is available and appropriate. Would be correct only when she explicitly preferred barrier methods after counselling (FSRH UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG: Contraception).

explanation.summary: Contraception choice in systemic lupus erythematosus integrates disease activity, organ involvement, and antiphospholipid antibody status (anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-GP1, lupus anticoagulant). Active disease or positive aPL antibodies makes combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication) because oestrogen significantly increases the thrombotic risk that aPL antibodies already confer. Progestogen-only methods are generally safer: the LNG-IUS (UKMEC 1-2 depending on aPL status) is the preferred LARC, with the copper IUD (UKMEC 1) the alternative if hormone-free is desired. DMPA is UKMEC 3 due to small VTE association and effect on lipids and bone density. Progestogen-only pill and etonogestrel implant are UKMEC 3 in active disease. Pregnancy planning should occur with rheumatology in stable disease, with hydroxychloroquine continued, and aspirin and low molecular weight heparin added for aPL-positive women through pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum. Folate supplementation, vaccination review, and counselling about flare risk in early pregnancy are part of pre-conception care.
key_points: Triple-positive antiphospholipid profile carries highest thrombosis risk
Stable SLE without antiphospholipid antibodies: COCP UKMEC 2
Pregnancy planning in antiphospholipid syndrome requires multidisciplinary management with aspirin +/- LMWH
Hydroxychloroquine is safe in pregnancy and reduces lupus flares and obstetric APS complications
explanation.pearls: In SLE, positive (or unknown) antiphospholipid antibodies make combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication) because of synergistic VTE and arterial thrombosis risk. LNG-IUS (UKMEC 1-2) and copper IUD (UKMEC 1) are first-line LARC (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

subtopic_detail: Contraception - SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P2 woman attends for contraceptive review 7 months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. She has lost 28 kg (BMI now 32, down from 42 pre-operatively). She has not yet resumed menses since surgery and reports breast tenderness, fatigue and intermittent nausea, which she attributes to her vitamin and mineral supplementation. A urine beta-hCG today is negative. Her past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily (BP today 128/78) and previous gestational diabetes (no current diabetes; HbA1c 5.5%).

She uses condoms inconsistently with her long-term male partner. Pre-operatively she was on the combined oral contraceptive pill which was stopped 6 weeks before surgery as part of the VTE risk minimisation protocol. She is fully aware that bariatric surgery is associated with rapid return of fertility and that pregnancy is recommended to be deferred for 12 to 24 months post-operatively. She wishes to use a highly effective method until she is ready for a third pregnancy in 18 months.

data_table.Examination: Surgical scars healed; otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative; HbA1c 5.5%; no anaemia

lead_in: Which contraceptive method is most appropriate for this woman?

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena), copper IUD or etonogestrel subdermal implant
options.rationale: After malabsorptive bariatric procedures (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion), oral hormonal contraceptive absorption is unreliable; LARCs that bypass the gut (LNG-IUS, Cu-IUD, etonogestrel implant) are preferred. The COCP also carries elevated VTE risk in the post-operative period and may be UKMEC 3 to 4 with persistent obesity and other risk factors; pregnancy should be delayed 12 to 24 months post-bariatric surgery (FSRH UKMEC 2016; ASMBS/ACOG; RANZCOG).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill at standard dose with continued condom backup
options.rationale: COCP after RYGB is wrong because the malabsorptive bypass impairs absorption of oral hormonal contraception, making efficacy unreliable regardless of condom backup; FSRH advises against oral methods after malabsorptive bariatric surgery. Would be correct only after restrictive procedures (sleeve gastrectomy, band) where absorption is preserved (FSRH UKMEC 2016; ASMBS/ACOG Bariatric Pregnancy).

options.text: Progestogen-only pill taken daily with a 3-hour mistiming window
options.rationale: POP is wrong because, like the COCP, POP absorption is impaired after Roux-en-Y; the narrow timing window worsens the reliability problem. Would be correct only after restrictive procedures (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

options.text: Fertility awareness method timed to predicted ovulation each cycle
options.rationale: Fertility awareness is wrong because typical-use failure ~24%/year is incompatible with the need for reliable contraception, and post-bariatric menstrual irregularity makes cycle tracking unreliable. Would be correct only as personal preference after counselling about high failure rates (Therapeutic Guidelines: Contraception).

options.text: Recommend immediate pregnancy attempts given strong weight loss and improving metabolic profile
options.rationale: Immediate pregnancy attempts is wrong because ASMBS/ACOG and RANZCOG recommend deferring pregnancy 12-24 months post-bariatric surgery to allow weight stabilisation, micronutrient optimisation (B12, iron, folate, vitamin D) and reduce SGA, prematurity and nutritional deficiency in the fetus. Would be correct only after the 12-24 month interval and nutritional optimisation (ASMBS/ACOG Bariatric Pregnancy; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: After malabsorptive bariatric procedures (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion), oral hormonal contraception has reduced and unreliable absorption. LARCs that bypass the gut (LNG-IUS, Cu-IUD, etonogestrel implant, DMPA injection) are preferred. Restrictive procedures (sleeve gastrectomy, gastric band) do not impair absorption to the same degree. Pregnancy should be delayed 12 to 24 months post-bariatric surgery (FSRH UKMEC 2016; ASMBS/ACOG Bariatric Pregnancy; RANZCOG).
key_points: Malabsorptive procedures (RYGB, BPD): avoid oral hormonal contraception
Restrictive procedures (sleeve, band): oral methods acceptable if absorbed
Rapid return of fertility post-weight loss; high unintended pregnancy risk
Multidisciplinary pre-conception planning: micronutrient repletion, optimised glycaemia, mental health
explanation.pearls: After Roux-en-Y, treat oral hormonal contraception as you would an enzyme-inducing medication - assume unreliable absorption.

subtopic_detail: Contraception after bariatric surgery

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of thin grey-white vaginal discharge with a fishy odour, worse after intercourse. She has no vulval itch, no dysuria, no abnormal bleeding and no fever. She is in a monogamous relationship of 18 months using a copper IUD, last cervical screening 14 months ago was normal. Speculum: thin homogeneous off-white discharge coating the vaginal walls without inflammation.

Vaginal pH at the lateral wall 5.2; KOH whiff test positive; wet mount shows clue cells, scant lactobacilli, no motile trichomonads, no pseudohyphae. She is not currently pregnant. She had a similar episode 5 months ago which was treated with a 7-day course of oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily; she completed the course, and symptoms resolved for 4 months before recurring.

data_table.Examination: Speculum: thin homogeneous grey-white discharge coating vaginal walls, no inflammation, no strawberry cervix.
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.2. KOH whiff test positive. Wet mount: clue cells present, few lactobacilli, no motile trichomonads, no pseudohyphae.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the same 7-day oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily course
options.rationale: Repeating the same 7-day metronidazole alone is wrong because recurrent BV (>=3 episodes/year) needs re-induction PLUS suppressive maintenance therapy; standard courses alone have high recurrence rates due to residual biofilm. Would be correct only for a first or non-recurrent BV episode (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Treat with oral metronidazole 400 mg bd for 7 days, then commence intravaginal metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4-6 months as suppressive therapy
options.rationale: Recurrent BV in Australia is managed with re-induction (oral or intravaginal metronidazole) followed by intravaginal metronidazole or clindamycin twice weekly as suppression for several months to reduce recurrence (Australasian STI Guidelines; eTG).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Reassure that this is normal discharge and no treatment is needed
options.rationale: Reassurance is wrong because all four Amsel criteria are met (homogeneous discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, clue cells); symptomatic BV warrants treatment. Would be correct only with normal discharge and no Amsel criteria met (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Empirically treat both her and her male partner with metronidazole
options.rationale: Empirical partner treatment is wrong because routine treatment of male partners is not currently standard in Australian guidelines (though emerging evidence is evolving the picture); suppressive therapy for the index woman is the established next step. Would be correct only within research protocols or jurisdictions adopting recent partner-treatment data (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Remove the copper IUD as it is the underlying cause of recurrent BV
options.rationale: IUD removal is wrong because the copper IUD has not been clearly established as a cause of recurrent BV and removal sacrifices effective contraception; suppressive vaginal therapy should be tried first. Would be correct only after suppressive therapy fails with strong temporal IUD association (Family Planning Australia).

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed clinically by Amsel criteria (3 of 4: thin grey-white discharge, pH > 4.5, positive whiff with KOH, clue cells) or by Nugent score >= 7 on Gram stain. First-line treatment is oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5-7 days.
key_points: Amsel: 3 of 4 (discharge, pH > 4.5, whiff, clue cells)
Nugent score >= 7 confirms BV on Gram stain
Candida: itch, curdy, pH < 4.5, pseudohyphae
Trichomonas: frothy yellow-green, strawberry cervix, motile
Lactobacillus loss is the unifying pathophysiology of BV
explanation.pearls: A positive whiff test plus clue cells is virtually pathognomonic. BV is not classified as an STI but is associated with sexual activity and increases HIV/STI acquisition risk.

sources.label: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

subtopic_detail: Vaginal discharge - microscopy and Amsel recall

stem: A 21-year-old woman at 18 weeks of pregnancy presents with multiple soft non-keratinised fleshy lesions on the vulva and perianal area, first noticed 6 weeks ago and increasing in number. She is otherwise well with an uncomplicated pregnancy on midwifery shared care. She did not receive the HPV vaccine in school. On examination there are approximately 10 papillomatous lesions 2-5 mm distributed over the labia majora and perianal area; no internal vaginal, cervical or intra-anal lesions; cervical screening normal 4 months ago. She is keen to treat them before delivery and prefers home application.

data_table.Examination: Approximately 10 soft non-keratinised papillomatous lesions 2-5 mm on labia majora and perianal area. No cervical, vaginal, urethral or intra-anal lesions.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. Cervical screening test 6 months ago: normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her anogenital warts?

options.text: Self-applied podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution twice daily for 3 days, then 4 days off, repeated up to 4 cycles
options.rationale: Podophyllotoxin is wrong because it is contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity (antimitotic activity); self-application is doubly inappropriate when she is pregnant. Would be correct only outside pregnancy (Australasian STI Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.text: Self-applied imiquimod 5% cream three nights per week for up to 16 weeks
options.rationale: Imiquimod is wrong because imiquimod has limited pregnancy safety data and is not recommended in pregnancy; the immunomodulatory mechanism creates additional uncertainty. Would be correct only outside pregnancy (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.text: Clinician-applied cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen weekly
options.rationale: Cryotherapy is safe in pregnancy and is the preferred first-line treatment for anogenital warts in pregnant women in Australian guidelines; trichloroacetic acid is an alternative. Self-applied options are contraindicated (Australasian STI Guidelines; eTG).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.text: Watch and wait until after delivery as warts always regress postpartum
options.rationale: Watch and wait is wrong because anogenital warts may proliferate dramatically during pregnancy and obstruct the birth canal at term; antenatal treatment reduces burden at delivery rather than waiting for postpartum regression. Would be correct only for very small isolated lesions in late pregnancy (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section solely to prevent vertical HPV transmission
options.rationale: Elective caesarean for HPV is wrong because caesarean is not indicated solely for HPV transmission risk; vaginal delivery is acceptable unless warts physically obstruct the birth canal. Would be correct only with mechanical obstruction at term (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

explanation.summary: Patient-applied first-line options for external anogenital warts are imiquimod 5% cream three nights per week up to 16 weeks, or podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution. Clinician-applied options include cryotherapy, TCA and surgical removal. Counsel about HPV vaccination (Gardasil 9 covers HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) regardless of past exposure.
key_points: Imiquimod 5%: 3 nights/week, wash off after 6-10 h, up to 16 weeks
Podophyllotoxin 0.5%: BD x 3 days then 4 days off, up to 4 cycles; avoid in pregnancy
Cryotherapy / TCA / excision are clinician-applied
HPV vaccine still recommended after warts diagnosis
Recurrence common; warts are not cancer-causing types (6/11)
explanation.pearls: HPV 6 and 11 cause 90% of anogenital warts and are not oncogenic. Cervical screening continues per national programme; warts diagnosis does not change screening intervals.

sources.label: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines - Anogenital warts

subtopic_detail: Anogenital warts - patient-applied therapy choice

stem:
A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder that has worsened over the past 36 hours, with a pleuritic component that is worse on deep inspiration and on lying flat. She also reports four days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and intermenstrual bleeding. She has had two new male partners over the past three months and uses condoms inconsistently.

She is not pregnant (serum beta-hCG < 5 IU/L today). On examination her temperature is 38.1 degrees C, pulse 104 regular, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air. There is right upper quadrant tenderness without Murphy's sign, mild generalised lower abdominal tenderness without peritonism, and bilateral adnexal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination. Speculum shows mucopurulent cervical discharge with contact bleeding.

Liver function tests show mild transaminitis (ALT 78 U/L, AST 62 U/L) with normal bilirubin and ALP. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows normal gallbladder and biliary tree with no stones, no wall thickening and no pericholecystic fluid. Pelvic ultrasound shows no tubo-ovarian abscess but trace pelvic free fluid. Endocervical NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 104 bpm, T 38.1 degC.
data_table.Examination: RUQ tender, Murphy's negative. Lower abdominal tenderness without peritonism. CMT, bilateral adnexal tenderness. Mucopurulent cervical discharge.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG < 5 IU/L. ALT 78, AST 62, bilirubin 14, ALP 92. RUQ US: normal GB, no stones. Pelvic US: no TOA, trace free fluid. NAAT: C. trachomatis positive.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis explaining the right upper quadrant pain?

options.text: Acute viral hepatitis A infection
options.rationale: Viral hepatitis A is wrong because acute HAV would produce more dramatic transaminitis (often >1000 U/L) and prodromal/systemic features but would not explain CMT, mucopurulent cervicitis, positive chlamydia NAAT or pleuritic RUQ pain; the constellation of PID plus RUQ pain points to perihepatitis. Would be correct only with isolated severe transaminitis and HAV serology positive (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Acute calculous cholecystitis with ascending cholangitis
options.rationale: Acute cholecystitis is wrong because ultrasound shows no stones, wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and Murphy's sign is negative; the combination essentially excludes cholecystitis. Would be correct with characteristic ultrasound findings and positive Murphy's sign (BMJ Best Practice).

options.text: Tubo-ovarian abscess with subdiaphragmatic spread
options.rationale: Tubo-ovarian abscess is wrong because pelvic ultrasound shows no TOA (trace free fluid is non-specific) and TOAs typically cause severe pelvic, not primarily RUQ, pain. Would be correct only with an imaged abscess and corresponding clinical picture (Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemoperitoneum
options.rationale: Ruptured ectopic is wrong because serum beta-hCG <5 IU/L excludes pregnancy and therefore ectopic; this is a definitive exclusion. Would never be correct with a negative beta-hCG (RANZCOG).

options.text: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis (gonococcal or chlamydial)
options.rationale: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis is perihepatitis from haematogenous or transperitoneal spread of chlamydia (or gonorrhoea) complicating PID. RUQ pain with mild transaminitis, normal biliary imaging and concurrent PID with positive chlamydia NAAT fits the classical picture (ASHM; BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis complicating PID, classically due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, producing RUQ pain with characteristic 'violin-string' adhesions between liver capsule and abdominal wall at laparoscopy. Mild transaminitis is common; biliary imaging is normal. Treatment is the same as for PID (ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole for 14 days).
key_points: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis = chlamydial/gonococcal perihepatitis
RUQ pain + PID + normal biliary tree
Violin-string adhesions on laparoscopy (classical)
Treat as PID (no different regimen)
Other PID complications: TOA, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, 6-10x ectopic risk
explanation.pearls: Suspect Fitz-Hugh-Curtis in any sexually active young woman with RUQ pain and pelvic findings, even when LFTs are only mildly deranged. It is a clinical and supportive imaging diagnosis - laparoscopy is rarely performed.

subtopic_detail: PID complication - right upper quadrant pain

stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with chronic HIV-1 infection is reviewed at 36+2 weeks gestation in the antenatal HIV clinic to plan delivery. She has been on tenofovir/emtricitabine/dolutegravir throughout this pregnancy, commenced at 9 weeks gestation, and her adherence has been excellent on pharmacy refill audit. Her booking CD4 count was 540 cells/microL with a baseline HIV viral load of 8400 copies/mL prior to recommencing therapy.

Her most recent HIV viral load taken at 36+0 weeks is < 50 copies/mL (suppressed) and her last three viral loads in the third trimester (at 28, 32 and 36 weeks) have all been < 50 copies/mL. She had a normal vaginal birth with her previous pregnancy four years ago when she was already on suppressive cART. She has no obstetric contraindication to vaginal birth, the fetus is cephalic with appropriate interval growth on the 50th centile, there is no placenta praevia on the 32-week scan, and she has not had any complications this pregnancy.

She is asking about the recommended mode of delivery, whether she requires intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, whether her baby will require post-exposure prophylaxis, and whether she can breastfeed.

data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 36 cm. Cephalic presentation. No oedema.
data_table.Investigations: HIV viral load at 36+0: < 50 copies/mL (suppressed). CD4 540 cells/microL. HBV/HCV negative. GBS swab pending. Growth scan 34 weeks: 50th centile, normal Dopplers.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for mode of delivery and neonatal prophylaxis?

options.text: Planned vaginal birth, no intrapartum zidovudine required, neonatal zidovudine monotherapy for 2-4 weeks postnatally
options.rationale: Vaginal birth plus 2-4 weeks zidovudine is wrong because Australian practice specifies 4 weeks of neonatal zidovudine for low-risk infants of suppressed mothers; the 2-4 week phrasing introduces imprecision and the question demands the precise duration. Would be correct only if the duration were stated as 4 weeks (ASHM; RANZCOG).

options.text: Planned caesarean section at 39+0 weeks, intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, neonatal zidovudine for 6 weeks, no breastfeeding
options.rationale: Planned caesarean at 39+0 with IV zidovudine is wrong because viral load <50 copies/mL near term obviates the need for caesarean and intrapartum IV zidovudine; vaginal birth is preferred with suppression. Would be correct only with viral load >=50 copies/mL near term (ASHM; RANZCOG).

options.text: Planned caesarean section at 38+0 weeks, intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, neonatal triple-drug PEP for 4 weeks, breastfeeding permitted if exclusive
options.rationale: Planned caesarean plus triple-drug PEP plus breastfeeding is wrong on multiple counts: caesarean is reserved for unsuppressed viral load, triple-drug PEP is for higher-risk infants, and breastfeeding is not recommended in Australia regardless of suppression. Would never be correct in this scenario (ASHM).

options.text: Planned vaginal birth at term, no intrapartum intravenous zidovudine, neonatal zidovudine monotherapy for 4 weeks, no breastfeeding
options.rationale: When maternal HIV viral load is < 50 copies/mL near term, planned vaginal birth is recommended; intravenous intrapartum zidovudine is NOT required for suppressed viral load; the neonate receives oral zidovudine monotherapy for 4 weeks; breastfeeding is not recommended in high-income settings where safe formula is available (ASHM; RANZCOG).

options.text: Planned vaginal birth with intrapartum intravenous zidovudine infusion regardless of viral load, neonatal nevirapine single dose only
options.rationale: Routine intrapartum IV zidovudine plus single-dose nevirapine is wrong because IV intrapartum zidovudine is reserved for unsuppressed/unknown viral load, and single-dose neonatal nevirapine is inadequate cover under Australian standards (oral zidovudine x 4 weeks is the regimen). Would be correct only with unsuppressed viral load and even then the neonatal regimen would differ (ASHM).

explanation.summary: Women on cART with viral load < 50 copies/mL near term can safely have a planned vaginal birth; intrapartum IV zidovudine is not required. Neonate receives 4 weeks of oral zidovudine monotherapy (low-risk). Formula feeding is recommended in Australia. Planned caesarean at 38-39 weeks is reserved for viral load >= 50-1000 (or unknown) near term, with IV zidovudine intrapartum and consideration of neonatal triple therapy.
key_points: VL < 50 at 36 weeks: vaginal birth, no IV zidovudine, neonatal AZT x 4 weeks
VL 50-1000: individualised; consider CS at 38-39 weeks
VL > 1000 or unknown: pre-labour CS at 38-39 weeks + IV zidovudine + neonatal triple PEP
Avoid invasive monitoring (FSE, FBS) if possible during labour
Formula feeding recommended in Australia (no breastfeeding)
explanation.pearls: Vertical transmission risk falls to < 1% (and approaches 0.1%) when maternal viral load is suppressed throughout pregnancy. The biggest modifiable factor is maternal adherence, not mode of delivery.

subtopic_detail: HIV in pregnancy - mode of delivery decision

stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends the emergency department 28 hours after condomless receptive vaginal intercourse with a male partner she has just learned is living with HIV-1. He told her his combination antiretroviral treatment was 'on and off' over the past six months because he had run out of his prescription, and she does not know his current viral load. She has no symptoms, no genital ulcerationosure, the partner does not inject drugs, and there was no concurrent intercourse with other partners.

She is not pregnant (urine beta-hCG negative today), has no significant past medical history, is on no regular medications other than the etonogestrel implant, has no drug allergies, has normal renal function on baseline pathology (creatinine 64 micromol/L, eGFR > 90), is hepatitis B surface antibody positive (vaccinated as a teenager), HIV antibody/antigen negative on today's baseline 4th-generation test, hepatitis C antibody negative, and syphilis EIA negative. She is not breastfeeding and has no plans for pregnancy in the next month.

data_table.Examination: Well. No mucosal lesions.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. Baseline HIV Ag/Ab negative. HBsAb positive (vaccinated). HCV Ab negative. Syphilis EIA negative. Gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT sent. Creatinine 64 micromol/L, eGFR > 90.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis regimen and follow-up plan?

options.text: Single-dose tenofovir 300 mg given today, then simply repeat HIV testing again at the 6-week timepoint after exposure
options.rationale: Single-dose tenofovir is wrong because PEP requires a 28-day course of combination antiretrovirals; single-dose or monotherapy approaches do not prevent HIV acquisition. Would never be correct as PEP (ASHM PEP guidelines).

options.text: Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg daily for 28 days, with no third agent required
options.rationale: Dual NRTI PEP is wrong because Australian guidance now recommends three-drug PEP (TDF/FTC plus dolutegravir or raltegravir) for high-risk exposures; dual NRTI-only PEP is outdated. Would be correct only under older guidelines, not current practice (ASHM).

options.text: Tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg plus rilpivirine 25 mg daily for 7 days only
options.rationale: TAF/FTC/rilpivirine 7 days is wrong because PEP duration is 28 days (not 7) and rilpivirine is not a standard third agent due to drug interactions and resistance considerations. Would never be a recommended PEP regimen (ASHM).

options.text: Tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine plus dolutegravir 50 mg daily for 28 days, with HIV testing at baseline, 6 weeks and 3 months
options.rationale: Australian PEP for a high-risk exposure (condomless receptive vaginal intercourse with a source person with HIV not on effective treatment, within 72 hours) is TDF/FTC plus dolutegravir for 28 days, with HIV testing at baseline, 6 weeks, and 3 months post-exposure (ASHM Australian PEP guidelines).

options.text: Defer PEP until the source partner's plasma viral load is known, then retest her at 4 weeks only
options.rationale: Defer PEP until source viral load is known is wrong because PEP efficacy falls rapidly with time and must start within 72 hours (ideally <24); waiting for source results risks missing the treatment window. Would be correct only if exposure were truly low risk and pending data could rapidly redirect care (ASHM).

explanation.summary: Non-occupational HIV PEP for a high-risk exposure (condomless receptive anal/vaginal sex with a source with HIV who is not virally suppressed, within 72 hours) is TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg daily for 28 days. Baseline tests: HIV Ag/Ab, syphilis, HBV, HCV, beta-hCG, renal function. Follow-up HIV tests at 6 weeks and 3 months (4th gen). Counsel on adherence, side effects, and condom use during follow-up.
key_points: Window: < 72 hours, ideally < 24 hours
Regimen: TDF/FTC + dolutegravir (or raltegravir) x 28 days
Baseline: HIV, syphilis, HBV, HCV, beta-hCG, U&E
Follow-up: HIV Ag/Ab at 6 weeks and 3 months
If source has confirmed undetectable VL, PEP may not be needed (U=U)
explanation.pearls: U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable): a source with confirmed sustained viral load < 200 copies/mL transmits HIV through sex effectively at zero risk - in those cases, PEP is not required.

subtopic_detail: Non-occupational HIV post-exposure prophylaxis

stem:
A 29-year-old cisgender woman attends a sexual health service requesting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. Her current male partner of three months has HIV-1 with a viral load that he reports has been detectable on most recent testing because of treatment interruption while changing jobs. They have condomless vaginal sex 2-3 times per week. She has no symptoms of acute HIV illness in the past 6 weeks (no fever, rash, lymphadenopathy or sore throat), is not pregnant (urine beta-hCG negative), is on the etonogestrel implant for contraception, has no history of renal disease, and is hepatitis B surface antibody positive (vaccinated).

She has not injected drugs. Her last STI screen 8 months ago was negative. She has no allergies and no regular medications other than the implant. She is asking whether she is eligible for PrEP, what baseline tests are required, and what monitoring she will need on therapy.

data_table.Examination: Well. No mucosal lesions, no rash, no lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. HBsAg, anti-HBc and HBsAb pending today. HIV Ag/Ab pending today.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan for PrEP initiation and monitoring?

options.text: Prescribe daily tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg only after a 4-week negative HIV window-period repeat test
options.rationale: Deferring PrEP 4 weeks is wrong because a single recent negative HIV test plus absence of acute HIV symptoms is sufficient to start PrEP; deferring prolongs an unnecessary exposure window. Would be correct only if there are symptoms suggestive of acute seroconversion (ASHM PrEP guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe on-demand (2+1+1) tenofovir disoproxil plus emtricitabine, suitable for all genders in this clinical scenario today
options.rationale: On-demand (2+1+1) PrEP is wrong because on-demand dosing is only recommended for cisgender MSM with infrequent exposures; cisgender women require daily PrEP due to slower tissue drug levels in cervicovaginal tissue. Would be correct only for selected MSM, not for cisgender women (ASHM).

options.text: Prescribe daily tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg plus emtricitabine 200 mg with baseline HIV/HBV/renal screen, then HIV/STI screening every 3 months
options.rationale: Daily oral TDF/FTC is the recommended PrEP regimen for cisgender women at substantial risk. Baseline workup includes HIV Ag/Ab, HBV serology, HCV antibody, syphilis serology, gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT, renal function and beta-hCG. Quarterly monitoring includes HIV testing and STI screen; renal function 6-monthly (ASHM PrEP guidelines).

options.text: Defer PrEP and recommend condom use only, as PrEP is contraindicated when the partner has detectable viral load
options.rationale: Defer PrEP because partner is detectable is wrong because a partner with detectable viral load is exactly the indication for PrEP; PrEP is strongly indicated, not contraindicated. Would never be correct (ASHM).

options.text: Prescribe daily oral dolutegravir 50 mg as PrEP monotherapy in this scenario at first visit
options.rationale: Dolutegravir monotherapy is wrong because dolutegravir is not a PrEP agent; PrEP uses TDF/FTC (daily or, for selected MSM, on-demand). Would never be correct (ASHM).

explanation.summary: Cisgender women eligible for PrEP receive daily oral TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg. Baseline workup: HIV Ag/Ab, HBV serology, HCV antibody, syphilis EIA, gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT (multi-site), renal function, beta-hCG. Quarterly: HIV test, STI screen, adherence and side-effect review. Renal function 6-monthly. On-demand (2+1+1) dosing only for cisgender MSM with predictable infrequent exposures. PrEP can be continued in pregnancy if substantial risk persists.
key_points: Daily TDF/FTC for cisgender women (no on-demand)
MSM may use daily or on-demand (2+1+1)
Baseline: HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, GC/CT, renal, beta-hCG
Monitoring: HIV + STI every 3 months; renal every 6 months
HBV must be screened pre-PrEP (rebound on cessation)
explanation.pearls: Exclude acute HIV before initiation: ask about fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, sore throat in the past 6 weeks. Acute HIV may have a still-negative Ag/Ab and starting PrEP could select for resistance.

subtopic_detail: HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis - eligibility and monitoring

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department at 0300 hours, brought by police, reporting that she was sexually assaulted approximately 14 hours ago at a private residence by an unknown male. The reported assault involved vaginal penetration without a condom, and she believes ejaculation occurred. She has showered once since the assault but has not changed her underwear, brushed her teeth, eaten or passed urine since the event.

She has no significant medical history, is on no regular medications, has no drug allergies, has had a normal menstrual period that finished 8 days ago, and is sexually active with a regular partner from whom she uses no contraception. She is alert, oriented, distressed but cooperative, has minor bruising on her right upper arm and a small abrasion on her left knee, and has not previously had a forensic examination.

There is no immediate life-threatening injury, no head injury, no loss of consciousnesspromise, and she has not consumed alcohol or other substances in the past 24 hours. A specially trained forensic medical examiner is available on call at the local sexual assault service, with chain-of-custody documentation procedures in place, and a social worker can be paged. She is asking what will happen next, what medications she can be offered tonight to reduce pregnancy and infection risk, and whether the examination is mandatory. She has not yet decided whether to formally report to police and is uncertain about disclosing to her family.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Alert, distressed, cooperative. Bruise 3 cm on right upper arm. No external genital injury visible without colposcopic examination.
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG negative. Baseline HIV Ag/Ab, HBsAg/Ab, HCV Ab, syphilis EIA, gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT and trichomonas NAAT sent. Pregnancy and STI follow-up planned per local sexual assault service protocol.

lead_in: Which set of medical and forensic actions is the most appropriate tonight?

options.text: Defer forensic examination until daylight to reduce patient distress, commence empirical STI prophylaxis and offer emergency contraception
options.rationale: Defer forensic examination until daylight is wrong because forensic evidence degrades within the <72-hour window; delaying loses DNA, secretions and trace evidence regardless of patient distress (a trained sexual assault examiner is best placed to balance comfort with timeliness). Would never be correct (RANZCOG; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance).

options.text: Proceed only with forensic examination tonight; defer STI prophylaxis and emergency contraception until after kit processed
options.rationale: Forensic-only first is wrong because medical priorities (EC within 120 hours, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP within 72 hours, HBV cover, safety planning) cannot be deferred to await kit processing; they run in parallel with forensic care. Would never be correct (RANZCOG).

options.text: Forensic examination can only proceed if the patient agrees to formally report the assault to police today
options.rationale: Linking forensic exam to police reporting is wrong because forensic examination should be offered regardless of reporting intent, with anonymous kit storage available to preserve future options; mandating reporting acts as a barrier to disclosure. Would never be correct under Australian best practice (RANZCOG; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance).

options.text: Forensic examination is contraindicated because the patient has showered; reassure and discharge with general practice follow-up in 1 week
options.rationale: Showered as contraindication is wrong because showering reduces but does not eliminate forensic yield; trace DNA and other evidence can still be recovered, and discharging without addressing EC, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP, HBV cover and safety is unsafe. Would never be correct (RANZCOG).

options.text: Offer immediate forensic examination with chain-of-custody, emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP if eligible, hepatitis B vaccination and safety planning
options.rationale: Acute sexual assault management within 72 hours requires concurrent attention to medical priorities (EC within 120 hours, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP assessment within 72 hours, HBV protection, mental health support and safety planning) and forensic priorities (kit collection with chain of custody by a trained examiner), regardless of whether the patient has decided to report (RANZCOG; ASHM; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance). Full care includes: forensic examination by trained examiner with documented chain of custody; LNG or UPA or copper IUD for emergency contraception; ceftriaxone IM plus azithromycin or doxycycline plus metronidazole for empirical STI prophylaxis; HIV PEP if eligible; hepatitis B vaccination (and HBIG if indicated); safety planning, counselling and follow-up.
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Sexual assault

explanation.summary: Acute presentation within 72 hours of sexual assault requires concurrent medical and forensic priorities: forensic examination with chain of custody by a trained examiner regardless of reporting intent; emergency contraception (levonorgestrel up to 96 hours, ulipristal up to 120 hours, or copper IUD up to 5 days); STI baseline tests and prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 500 mg IM, azithromycin 1 g or doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days, metronidazole 2 g single dose); HIV PEP eligibility assessment for source with HIV or unknown source with high-risk features; hepatitis B vaccination and HBIG where indicated; safety planning; mental health support and follow-up at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 3 months.
key_points: Forensic kit window: 72 hours (some up to 7 days for specific samples)
EC: levonorgestrel < 96 h, ulipristal < 120 h, Cu-IUD < 5 days
STI prophylaxis: ceftriaxone + azithromycin/doxycycline + metronidazole
HIV PEP: assess within 72 h; high-risk sources warrant PEP
HBV: vaccinate if unvaccinated; HBIG if source HBsAg-positive
Forensic exam offered regardless of reporting intent
explanation.pearls: Documentation matters - use trained examiners (FAMU/SARC), follow chain-of-custody, photograph injuries, store kit per jurisdiction protocol. Mental-health and safety planning are not afterthoughts; ongoing risk of further violence is high in the first weeks.

subtopic_detail: Acute sexual assault - forensic and medical priorities

stem: A 32-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her 4-month-old infant (exclusive breastfeeding, no formula) presents with 3 weeks of frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge, vulval irritation and dyspareunia. Strawberry cervix on speculum, vaginal pH 5.6, KOH whiff positive, saline wet mount shows motile flagellated protozoa. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia NAAT have been sent. She has had two new male partners in the past 4 months. She has no allergies and no liver disease. She wishes to continue breastfeeding without interruption if possible.

data_table.Examination: Strawberry cervix with punctate haemorrhages. Copious frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge. No cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass.
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.6. Saline wet mount: motile flagellated protozoa. Trichomonas NAAT pending. Gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT sent. Urine beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Single 2 g oral metronidazole dose to her and her recent partners; pause breastfeeding for 12-24 hours and discard expressed milk
options.rationale: Single-dose metronidazole 2 g is first-line for trichomoniasis in adults, including breastfeeding women, with brief interruption of breastfeeding (12-24 hours) and discarding milk during peak levels to minimise infant exposure. Partner treatment is essential to prevent reinfection (Australasian STI Guidelines; eTG).

options.text: Intravaginal metronidazole 0.75% gel nightly for 5 nights; no partner treatment
options.rationale: Intravaginal metronidazole gel is wrong because topical metronidazole achieves <50% cure for trichomoniasis (parasites in urethra, glands, etc. not reached); systemic therapy is required and partners must be treated to prevent ping-pong reinfection. Would never be correct for trichomonas (Australasian STI Guidelines).

options.text: Tinidazole 2 g orally as a single dose with continued breastfeeding throughout
options.rationale: Tinidazole with continued breastfeeding is wrong because tinidazole has a longer half-life requiring an approximately 3-day breastfeeding pause; metronidazole 2 g single dose with a 12-24h pause is preferred in breastfeeding. Would be correct only outside breastfeeding (Australasian STI Guidelines).

options.text: Permanently cease breastfeeding so that metronidazole can be given safely
options.rationale: Permanently cease breastfeeding is wrong because a brief 12-24h pause is sufficient to clear peak metronidazole levels; permanent cessation is unnecessary and harmful. Would never be correct (Australasian STI Guidelines).

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg bd for 7 days to her only
options.rationale: Doxycycline to her only is wrong because doxycycline has no activity against Trichomonas vaginalis and is contraindicated in breastfeeding due to enamel staining; treating her alone also leaves partners to reinfect. Would never be correct for trichomoniasis (eTG; ASHM).

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis in non-pregnant adults is treated with oral metronidazole 2 g single dose, or 400 mg BD for 7 days (alternative for those at higher risk of treatment failure such as HIV). In pregnancy, treatment is still recommended (oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5-7 days). Always treat sexual partners empirically. Test of cure not routine but re-test for reinfection at 3 months.
key_points: First-line: metronidazole 2 g PO stat OR 400 mg BD x 7 d
Strawberry cervix (colpitis macularis) in 2-5% but pathognomonic when present
Motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount confirms; NAAT most sensitive
Partner notification and empirical treatment essential
Pregnancy: treat with oral metronidazole; avoid topical preparations
explanation.pearls: Avoid alcohol during and for 24 hours after metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction). HIV co-infection increases treatment failure risk; consider 7-day BD regimen in that group.
